publishes two journals ("Cuadernos de Ufología" and "@nomalía"), as well

Regarding:

>From: TPrinty@aol.com
>Date: Tue, 31 Dec 2002 13:55:13 EST
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham

Tim wrote:

>For those of us on this side of the pond who watch FOX-
>News, we were entertained last night with a brief
>discussion of Rendlesham on "The Factor". After all the
>tease throughout the show, I sort of expected to see Ian
>Ridpath, James Easton, Jenny Randles, David Clarke, or
>Andy Roberts discussing the matter. However, the one
>individual who was presented talking about the "newly
>released" documents was Peter Robbins. Needless to say,
>I couldn't believe it. Chris Gibson really demonstrated
>no preperation for the brief interview...

Tim,

Thankfully, that's not always the situation.

I know from contacts, especially via 'rendlesham.com',
that many media sources are more informed about the true
facts.

It's not accidental that any online search for
information on the "bentwaters ufo", or "woodbridge ufo",
or "rendlesham forest ufo" normally returns
'rendlesham.com' as the most prominent source of
information.

In December, for example, the local BBC radio station for
the Eastern Counties [covering the south-east England
area where the case has its origins] broadcast a feature
on the newly released documents and I was asked to
participate. As Dave Clark and Andy Roberts had direct
involvement with the documents release, I suggested they
would be ideal guests and was able to quickly arrange
this with Dave.

I'm also aware of several mainstream media sources who
intended to significantly highlight certain 'UFO cover-
up' claims published during the last couple of years.
After I had been asked for a formal comment to be
included and was able to factually set the 'cover-up'
nonsense in perspective [even before the MoD's file was
available], not one of those proposed 'sensationalist'
articles or programs went ahead.... that was their call.


>...Robbins was able to say anything (stating there were
>three nights vice two to include Larry Warren...

>...If I recall correctly, Col. Halt stated that Warren
>was never involved with the incidents in question.

Halt's argument is that he believes Warren hadn't
completed his training and could not therefore have been
on duty.

It isn't proven and Halt may be mistaken. As recently
noted, there are elements of Warren's story which appear
to include specific references to parts of the radio
communication we can hear on Halt's microcassette
recording. It seems Warren first described these before a
copy of Halt's recording was generally available,
although Warren could simply have heard the radio traffic
without being involved.

Warren is probably correct in claiming there were 'three
nights' - it was one of the first points which John
Burroughs mentioned to myself.

It doesn't exactly strengthen the 'alien spaceship
[repeatedly] landing' scenario when 'strange lights' are
observed in the same vicinity three nights in a row and
we now appreciate the base personnel were unfamiliar with
coastal lights that could deceptively be seen from within
Rendlesham forest, which was off-base.

As it happens, I was speaking with Ian Ridpath earlier
tonight and on his new web site Ian has uploaded a night-
time photograph of the general 'landing site' area which
he took in 1983, see:

http://users.macunlimited.net/ianrid/ufos/rendlesham

The larger version available is more revealing.


>It was too that somebody with a firmer grasp on the case
>conducted the interview or had been included in on the
>debate.
All going well, there might just be more than one
prominent, factually insightful, media development later
this year.


James.

From: "Erick Maillot" <erick.maillot@wanadoo.fr>

I wrote :
>> When L.Zamora is in the south of the town, on the N.85, he said saw the
object at S.E (at left of the road 85), and describe a flame. L.Z see the
flame at the moment (in town ?) he stopped to chase a car at high speed
(strange attitude for a police officer). Is the object masked, totally or
partially, by hills at this moment ?

Only Quintanilla said the object is to South-East (an error?). The other
versions indicate _all_ south-west. L.Z stops the car chase when he thinks
that the flame is close to the shack... and the dynamite (detail which
confirms the S-W direction and why L.Z stopped his chase).

James wrote :
> To recap: in his official report, Zamora explained: « Did not notice any
object at top, did not note if top of flame was level. Sun was to west and
did not help vision... Could not see bottom of flame because it was behind
the hill ».

The hill masked the bottom. But what masked the top is also a problem...
The roof of L.Z car is a possible explanation as said by Larry Hatch.

> If it was a hot-air balloon, those 'legs' would be the struts supporting a
platform/basket.

The struts are very thin, as your link showed it. Very very thin for the
platform without basket. Is it possible to note it at 200 meters?

> Strictly, Zamora did not claim to have seen « two legs », only « what
appeared to be two legs of some type from the object to the ground ».

If there is a basket (vertical position), the "legs" don't touch the ground.
The "legs" converge and don't diverge (from his point of view) as described
by L.Z. If there is no basket the "legs" are too thin so that L. Z. sees
them (and he must see the two entities on the platform when the object is on
the same level as its car).

> There wasn't necessarily a basket, possibly only a basic platform. For
example, see the contemporary, early, 1963 platform on display at the 'Musee
des Balloons', Château de Balleroy [.]

The balloon can be only in the south-west of the platform or the basket. Two
reasons:
1) to be in conformity with the drawing of L.Z: the "legs" are in front of
the oval shape which then is well seen towards south-west.
2) blowing wind of the North-East and which thus carries out the balloon
towards south-west (to be logical with this hypothesis!).

Zamora did not see either the gas bottles (sphere or cylinder) of this
platform.

As regards the large bush, are there photographs of the site? To see whether
there exists or not, and where it would be.

> Zamora also confirmed that when he first viewed the landed object from
distance, it was only for a couple of seconds and again, he didn't, « pay
much attention » [...]

It does not pay any attention at too many moments. L.Z said he stopped his
car a couple of seconds to pay no much attention and report that one entity
turns to him, jumps in something. Note : jump on a platform is a strange
attitude (more coherent with a basket).

> « When I first saw the object (when I thought it might be a car) I saw
what appeared to be two legs of some type from the object to the ground.

There is an error in your text. He started to chase the speeder.
He then became aware of the roar, and stopped chasing the speeder
because he thought a dynamite shack in the area might have blown up.

Is the object
@ masked, totally or
@ partially, by hills at this moment ?

@ b/ At this* moment, if there is a balloon, the low sun (approx W =
@ Az°280/h°10) must reflect brightly (L.Z said the sun embarass
@ his view and
@ he had sun glasses) on his envelopp ("in mylar", very reflective !?).
@ Strangely , Zamora dont't see the big envelope, nor the
@ basket but _only_
@ the flame who is under the envelope. How the list can explain this ?

He was in the drivers seat (on the left) and looking out the right side
window. The roof of the car could have hidden the envelope. Or it might
have nearly matched the sky (Zamora was wearing sunglasses).

There were no baskets on hot-air balloons in 1964. Instead, they used
flat platforms. (Some had just harnesses, like parachute harnesses, for
the balloonists.) See attached image of a 1964 balloon.

Mylar was not in general use for anything except recording tape in 1964.
The aerostat (envelope) was probably made of nylon sail material.

@ c1/ When L.Z enter with his car on the gravel road, he saw an
@ vertical egg
@ or "car on the radiator" with two legs . Where or what are
@ this legs on a
@ balloon, that L.Z can see _at high_ distance when he saw the
@ two whitecloses
@ entities?

Probably the A-Frame that holds up the burner over the platform.
Possibly he saw the tipped over platform edge-on, plus the A-frame
tubing. Or he might have seen the ripdown cords hanging down. These
are used to suddenly open the top of the balloon to collapse it
after a landing - never in flight. They prevent the balloonists from
being dragged by the wind.

@ c2/ L.Zamora saw 2 entities but don't saw the basket. It's
@ only possible if
@ the envelope is N.E side and the basket S.W (masked at his view by
@ the envelope). Is it logic if the wind and the balloon go to S.W ?

He would have had to wait a year to see a basket. The first basket on a
modern hot-air balloon was used in 1965. Gas balloons used them earlier,
but not hot-air balloons (too much weight). Flat platforms were used in
1964.

The wind was from the northeast, at Zamora's left back. (You aren't the
first UFOlogist to get wind directions backward. The reported direction
for wind is always the direction the wind comes FROM, not the direction
it blows to. Why do you think weather vanes point into the wind?)

In fact, Coral Lorenzen ALWAYS got it backwards, as she did in this case.

The platform and men were actually hidden behind a low ridge between
Zamora and the landing site. Remember that the platform is very small
compared to the aerostat (see photo).

@ d/ Are the soil traces conform with a basket which bump into ground ?
@ Precisly, has somebody a proof that a basket with rectangles
@ (how many ?) on
@ his floor exist in 1964 and can make this 4 imprints
@ concordant with the
@ mesurement of the trace?

It probably went bump-bumpity-bump when it hit, bouncing to make the
traces. Hot air balloon landings are rarely a single touchdown.
Sometimes the platform rotates as it hits, striking successive corners.

@ Was it a triangle basket or a
@ rectangle basket ?

I have photos of platforms of both kinds.

@ e/ If the basket was lied down, to make burning some bush,
@ how would you
@ explain the relative central position of the burned trace*
@ with the four
@ imprints?

Two possibilities:

1. The impact jerked open the burner valves before the platform
came to a final rest.

2. They probably had to move the platform to line it up with the
envelope (now on the ground, but still full of air), and to
stretch open the mouth.

During the re-inflation stage, the burner fires sideways. In early
designs, they laid the platform on its side.

HEY! I just thought of something. They needed something to hold up
the mouth ring of the balloon. Maybe they used that bush.

@ The flame can't be "in" the basket imprints but only outside
@ in the
@ direction of the fall/movement. If the basket only touch and
@ go (always in
@ vertical position), any burnd trace is coherent.

Like I said, the platform was light, and they probably moved it
to line up the burner with the mouth of the envelope.

@ f/ Others witness are referenced in this story (tourist of
@ Colorado, man in

The reports are not complete at all. The tourist never came

Here is the part which makes me think it was a balloon. The
appearances and the sounds match the proper times for the use of
the burner in flying the balloon, but not for any rocket or engine
powered device:

1. Zamora reported the long axis of the ellipse is horizontal when
he arrived at the place where he parked his car. The aerostat
(envelope) is now lying on the ground (not enough lift), and the
balloonists are out of sight behind a low ridge, as is the bottom
edge of the aerostat. The burner is off, and there is no sound.

2. The balloonists turn on the burner. Zamora hears a roar, and
sees flames at the bottom of the object. He run, and loses his
glasses. At this point, he is thinking of a gas tank truck about
to explode.
3. One account (I can't find it now) says that Zamora reported a
brief glance which showed the long axis of the ellipse was at a 45
degree angle to the horizontal.

4. When Zamora looks back while running away toward a gully on
the other side of the road, he sees that the object has risen up
off the ground, and the long axis is vertical. The roar is
persisting. At this point, the aerostat has become airborne, but
does not have enough lift to raise the platform and balloonists,
which are still behind the low ridge.

5. Zamora reaches the gully, slides down into it, and hides. The
roar stops. He looks over the ridge, and sees the object, long axis
vertical, flying away from him. The aerostat has achieved enough
lift to raise the platform and men, so the balloonists shut off
the burner. The wind then carries them away.

The flames, and especially the sounds heard, match a balloon takeoff
perfectly. Had the object been a rocket or plane, it should have
fallen or landed the moment the roar ceased. I have witnessed many
hot air balloons (we have three balloon teams in the area), and can
tell you that they are LOUD when heard up close.

Some things that have not been mentioned much in this case:

1. As in the Washington National case of 1952, and the Kincheloe AFB
case
in 1967, MTI (moving target indicator) systems had just been installed
shortly before the 1956 L-B sighting. RADAR operators unfamiliar with
the
"new" operation easily got the set out of calibration by continuing to
use it the old way. When so misadjusted, stationary targets, instead of
disappearing, were brighter than moving ones.

2. The same operator was on duty in both the Lakenheath and Kincheloe
cases.

3. Sending planes after spurious targets wan nothing unusual in 1956.
They
were still trying to find out what caused spurious targets, and needed
to
know what could be found at the target location.

4. They were thinking of Soviet "alien invasions", not extraterrestrial
ones, at the time.

Which reminds of a story told to me by a retired Air Traffic Controller.
When he was working at Coventry Airport in the UK during the 1960's a new
radar system was installed. To their shock a number of low-level
unidentified targets were detected which had never been seen before. After
a period of some hours someone had the bright idea to ask the local RAF
base if they were operating in the area. They said "Of course we are,
why? Haven't you ever seen us on your radar before!" It turned out that
the RAF were using that part of the sky to practice low level flying and
that the new radar was able to see through the ground clutter.

Cheers

John

sound is MUCH LOUDER. It seems to be concentrated by the

dog was barking straight up. So I ran out, and saw the
balloon about 200 - 400 feet up, flying over the house. I
could hear faintly the voices of the balloonists. As the
balloon moved away, the burner fired again, and the sound
like a distant airliner - not loud at all.

So, with the balloon on its side, Zamora was in a position
to hear the maximum sound, but the neighbor was not.

again, but Zamora was no longer in a position to hear the
loud roar.

it was, but it contained several detailed line drawings.

I took out ten books about UFOs on the same day in 1969. By
the time I started to look for this again (in 1994), the
public library had discarded most of its UFO books (and
most of the engineering books as well) to make room for a
larger art section. I remember taking out books by Hynek,
Sanderson, Klass, Lorenzen, Menzel, David*, Condon*, Binder*,
and Ruppelt* (* = I have acquired the book since then, and
it does not contain the interview.)

Zamora may have rationalized the flames as going down in
most of his accounts, because flames going up made no sense
to him.

@ Is there any other aerial vehicle comparative to what
@ Zamora describes here and which can also, silently,
@ remain airborne after the propulsion unit has evidently
@ been switched-off after only a few seconds initial
@ thrust.
@
@
@ >A witness said he was not far of an airfield at Socorro.

@ >in this airfield. It can close the debate on the wind

@ >tour?
@
@ We don't know that they didn't...

It was very low.

At the time, sport ballooning was new, and sport balloonists
had two very real worries:

1. Staying out of the way of airplanes (it wasn't yet fully
recognized by the FAA). That meant staying away from airports
and airways.

2. Being arrested (or shot) for trespass when they landed.

@ Incredibly, it seems nobody ever contacted Socorro
@ Municipal Airport to ask if they knew of anything flying
@ at the time of Zamora's sighting and which might explain
@ the object he reported.

Actually, I think Coral Lorenzen did. That's where she got
the backwards wind direction she quoted (she though the wind
direction was the way the wind blew towards).

Here is the BIG MISTAKE many amateur UFOlogists make. They
call ONE airport, air base, or air traffic control center,
and assume that they know about everything up in the sky.
THEY DON'T! Private airports have no info on commercial or
military flights. Commercial airports have no info in
private or military flights. Military airports (you guessed
it) don't know about private or commercial flights. And air
traffic control centers have info on commercial, and some
military, flights, but almost no info on private planes.

@ >The balloon's hypothesis is overall tempting, very
@ >convincing on certain details but on others it poses
@ >problems which are not taken into account by many
@ >sceptical ufologist (ie : the high tension line at 1
@ >miles west).

The balloonist has no way to steer away from these lines,
except to go over them. And since power lines go cross
country, he has to cross them somewhere. They really are
not a factor.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 11 Jan 2003 12:07:57 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Lakenheath-Bentwaters incident 1956

Larry Robinson wrote:

> 3. Sending planes after spurious targets wan nothing unusual in 1956.
> They were still trying to find out what caused spurious targets, and
needed
> to know what could be found at the target location.

There is a considerable amount of evidence, both documentary and oral,
to support your comment Larry.

I have just returned from the Public Record Office in London where I have
been reviewing the 2003 releases of British MoD UFO files under the
30 year rule.

The latest releases contained some new testimony from one of the pilots
involved in the famous 1956 Lakenheath-Bentwaters incident that seems to
deliver the coup de grace against the 'UFO' status of this case.

In an MoD briefing file dated 1972 the Commanding Officer of the RAF
No 23 Squadron scrambled to investigate the 'UFO' detected by USAF
and RAF radars on 13/14 August 1956 answers questions about the
incident. In the file, Air Commodore Anthony Davis reveals that he was i
nvolved in the incident and makes the following comments:

"Our detailed UFO reports going back before 1962 have been destroyed
but if there had been any evidence to indicate the existence of an
unidentified but real flying object (and not just an anomalous radar echo)
it [the file on the case] would of course have been retained and
investigated in great depth.

"I was airborne myself at the time of the incident, in a Venom Night Fighter
from [RAF] Coltishall, and was vectored on to a suspected UFO but made
no radar contact and found myself chasing a star."

Davis' comments can be added to those made by the two aircrew from
his squadron who were traced and interviewed for 'Out of the Shadows'.
They were scrambled later that night and asked to investigate a radar
blip detected by the ATC radars at USAF Lakenheath. They did make
radar contact with a 'target' but were unable to intercept it because
it appeared to be stationary at around 4-5,000 feet and, in the words
of one of the navigators:

"...the first run we had at it I saw nothing...the next time we turned onto
a reciprocal heading and I then obtained a contact which I held 10-15
degrees off dead ahead and noticed that it raced down the tube at
high speed. We were flying at around 300-350 knots, I remember
saying to David [the pilot], "CONTACT...there, it's out 45 starboard
now at one mile' and he kept saying to me 'Where is it? Where is it?
I can't see it!' as we rushed past on each pass. And it would go down
the right-hand side or the left-hand side depending upon which way
we went at it and it would be a little paint [on the AI radar]. Two
further runs were made with the same result and it was fairly obvious
that whatever it was, it was stationary. There was no movement. Dave
looked out on each run but could see nothing. My radar contact was
firm but messy but there *was* something there. We continued to fly
around looking until returning to base."

The second RAF Venom scrambled to investigate fared no better,
and the conclusion reached is preserved in 23 Squadron's logbook
under the relevant date:

"...two aircraft were scrambled after a strange object had been
picked up by Lakenheath GCA. The GCA became a GCI and
several attempts were made to intercept the 'object' but as
it was standing [still] it was most difficult and nothing was
seen by either of the crews...it was decided that the object must
have been a balloon."

So much for the standing of that great UFOlogical classic, the
much-vaunted 'Lakenheath-Bentwaters incident' - R.I.P.

>
> 2. The same operator was on duty in both the Lakenheath and Kincheloe
> cases.
>

That is most interesting -- do you mean Forrest Perkins was the
ATC operator in two separate radar UFO incidents?

Best,

Dave Clarke

From: Jim Giglio <jgiglio2@polaris.umuc.edu>
Date: Fri, 17 Jan 2003 10:09:10 -0500 (EST)
Subject: [UFORL] 15 minutes of fame in Frisco


The San Francisco Chronicle's on-line edition quotes me:

http://sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?file=/c/a/2003/01/12/CM200763.DTL

--------------------

The reporter on this story, Rick Delvecchio, contacted NCAS some
months ago and wound up talking to me, since I was the
coordinator of the project to put the Condon report on-line. Only
a small fraction of the conversation found its way into the
story. That's no surprise, since this is a standard "bunch of
talking heads" piece used to fill up some space. My part of the
story is this:

> Jim Giglio says the phenomenon is best understood by looking at
> its reflection in the culture.

> "I don't think there's anything to it," said Giglio, a former
> science teacher who belongs to a skeptics' group in the
> Washington, D.C., area. "And this is from a guy who's seen a
> UFO."

> He was visiting his grandpa's turkey ranch in the South when
> the gobblers for some strange reason looked skyward. Giglio
> looked up, too, and saw strange lights that moved overhead for
> several minutes. He noticed that the turkeys tracked the lights
> by turning their heads in unison. This was odd, but it never
> occurred to Giglio that they and he had seen a flying saucer.

> Because the term hadn't been invented yet.

THE REST OF THE STORY:
=====================

The location was my grandfather's back yard in Birmingham Alabama
(not a ranch). He kept a flock of turkeys (about 25 or so) to
sell around Thanksgiving. I was 13, visiting for a week or two in
the summer. The "lights" were white spots (perhaps reflective,
perhaps producing their own light) moving at a moderate angular
speed across the sky. There were three spots in an apparently
triangular formation, making no sound. The time was just after
sunset, with full daylight and a cloudless sky. Nothing else was
in the sky, not even birds. That business about the turkeys
tracking the lights is uncertain; I have no way to know for sure
what the animals were looking at, only that they tilted their
heads to look upward and my grandfather and I followed suit.

After the spots got to the horizon and disappeared, we went back
inside, commented that what we had seen was strange, but said
nothing more about it (I don't recall that we even mentioned it
to my grandmother). The next summer I visited again. Sitting in
the living room with my grandfather, each of us reading a section
of the daily newspaper, he passed his part of the paper to me,
pointing out the headline story. It was coverage of the 1952 flap
involving "flying saucers" over the US capitol, the scrambling of
fighters, and associated excitement. For the first time, it
occurred to us that what we had seen may have been these "flying
saucers" that seemed to be causing such a stir.

Obviously the term had been invented by 1951, but for some reason
neither my grandfather nor I had been aware of it until the
summer of 1952, about a year after our sighting in the back yard.

What's always seemed interesting to me about this sighting is
that with no preconceived notions about "flying saucers," neither
of us formed any opinion about what we had seen until a year
later, other than the fact that we had no idea what the three
objects were. We did not, for instance, attempt to estimate speed
or altitude; we knew that the cloudless sky made that impossible.
We drew no imaginary "fuselages" around the triangular formation,
inserted no portholes, and saw no mysterious beams or rays. So
taken as seen, our "sighting" contains precious little
information, and nothing that might support the idea of ET
visitors tooling around over Birmingham in interstellar
spacecraft on a late summer afternoon in 1951.

For some time I've thought that the most likely explanation would
be a set of three weather balloons tethered together, riding
along with the wind at a not-too-high altitude, reflecting the
light of the sun that had just gone below our horizon but not
theirs; they appeared larger than simple points of light, and if
at some great altitude would have been moving at a much smaller
angular speed, assuming they were being carried by the wind. But
we saw no sign of a suspended instrument package, which should
have been visible at a low altitude. So that possibility is not
strongly supported by the evidence, and fifty years later there's
no possibility of collecting any more.

So to sum up, what we have is a witness report containing very
little data, adding up to not much other than a mildly
entertaining story when the subject of UFOs comes up in casual
conversation.

Therein, Halt allegedly stated:

"My recollections fit very closely with all of the
people, the four or five people that were with me that
night, and I've had an opportunity through the years to
talk with them. In fact, Bobby Ball, you remember him?

...I talked with him when we did the NBC thing, I talked
with Verrano [spelling?] at great length, and everything
all fits together. There were no discrepancies other than
somebody remembers this detail a little better or that

little-known 1987 commentary, Halt reportedly claimed:

"Captain Mike Verrano was involved in the first incident
during the day, he went to the landing site and made some
observations, pictures on the ground, he was a player
early on".

Although this confirms Verano, as we know, was "a player
early on", there's no indication of his later
involvement.

Zickler, as you know, was Chief of Security Police.

That would surely explain why the unidentified person we

I can't confirm Zickler's participation for absolute

From: "bobdog1973 <bobdog1973@yahoo.ca>" <bobdog1973@yahoo.ca>
Date: Tue, 28 Jan 2003 18:34:00 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] IRRIDESCENT SPHERES

Driving home from work, approx 11.25pm, along a dark, quiet roadway,I
noticed an intensely bright blue ball (of light?)hovering in a field
to the right of my car, approx 50 feet from me.It was keeping pace
with me, paralelling my route.It kept up with me for about a half
mile, I was of course fascinated, I had never seen anything like it
in my life!It was making no noise except for a sort of hissing noise,
almost like a kettle boiling.It was a typical warm summer night,the
sky was clear(no thunder or lightning), I had the car windows open,
relaxing after my workshift had ended. All of a sudden, my car radio
went off, as did the car lights, the engine however continued to run,
the shining sphere which was approximately 15" in diameter, took a 90
degree turn and headed straight for my drivers side window! It seemed
to come into my car, and I can only describe it as if I was sitting
inside a light bulb, the light was so bright. I can remember that I
was not in any way scared, in fact I was laughing quite loudly at the
experience! As quickly as it happened, it was over, the shining
sphere had gone, the radio came back on as did the car lights, which
is when I discovered I was driving on the wrong side of the road.This
happened to me twelve years ago, I never talked about it much, I
guess I didnt want people to think that I had lost my marbles. If
anyone has experiencd this, or has any suggestions as to what it
could possibly be, please let me know.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 30 Jan 2003 10:33:38 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] IRRIDESCENT SPHERES

Kugelblitz?

This sounds like a form of kugelblitz, or ball lightning. The
description
is similar to typical descriptions of kugelblitz. See "Strange Fires and
Lights" by Vincent Gaddis for more on kugelblitz. Note that the physics
behind kugelblitz are not yet well understood.

I have seen two phenomena myself which might be kugelblitz, and one of
them was under totally clear sky conditions. Both were associated with
power line faults, not thunderstorms.

The first one was in 1969. I saw a brilliant red-violet ball come out
of a 4 KV power line just as the power failed. It floated around for
about 15 seconds The power failure was caused by a shorted turn in a
substation transformer two miles away. Such a failure can cause voltage
spikes. The weather was clear with very little wind.

The second one was in 1988, and was started when a high wind whipped
a 120 volt pair of service drop lines with bad insulation together
during a rainstorm. Suddenly a dazzling cyan ellipsoid of light at
least the size of a car erupted from the lines. (This time I had an
absolute distance reference - the power lines themselves - so there
could be no mistaking the distance or size.) The ball lifted up from
the lines and became spherical, lasting for 4 or 5 seconds. It
disappeared by shrinking to nothing. The display was repeated two more
times as the lines touched again in the wind.

The interesting part of the second one was that the ball was NOT
dragged away by the high wind, but stayed over the faulty lines. It
was also so bright that it saturated the cones in my eyes. It looked
like some computer video captures look when the image is brighter
than the brightest the capture board can take, with a center region
of constant brightness that looks silvery.

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 30 Jan 2003 17:51:40 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] RAF Tornado / UFO encounter

John Burtenshaw wrote:

> Does anyone have any information on an alleged encounter by a squadron of
> RAF Tornado aircraft and an UFO which overtook them at high speed. This
> event was alleged to have taken place over the North Sea on 5th November
> 1995. Every crew member reported the sighting which was, if the report is
> true, filed by the MoD as "unknown object, case closed".
>

The correct date of this report was 5 November 1990, and the pilot's report
was released by the MoD late last year.

The UFO which 'overtook them at high speed' whilst above the North Sea
was also reported by the crews of a number of civil airliners, one above
the Alps and another above the Pyrenees.

The 'object' was in fact part of the Russian Gorizont-Proton rocket body
which decayed over northwest Europe at the precise time of the Tornado
report - 6pm. This was confirmed by RAF Fylingdales space tracking
station in Yorkshire.

Therefore the 'unknown object, case closed' is incorrect. 'Known object,
case closed' would be more appropriate.

The full details and explanation were published in a recent issue of UFO
Magazine (UK).

Best,

Dave Clarke

May, 2003 Predicted Upheavals

There follow four predictions about next May, 2003's upheavals,
as told by Dr. Leo Sprinkle, Native teacher Nestor NightOwl, John
Kimmey, and psychic Marian MacNeils Star Visitor guide, Neuman.

Very recently I received a communication from venerable UFO
researcher, Dr. Leo Sprinkle, Ph.D., emeritus Professor at the
University of Wyoming. Dr. Sprinkle and I are old friends, and I
count him a mentor, he having been in UFO research since several
decades before the modern era of interest in UFOs/Star Visitors.

Dr. Sprinkle passed on to me a personal message from his "Higher
Guides". Among the contents of the message was a warning that
there will be a momentous global event during May, 2003,seven
months away. I do not choose to divulge most of the personal
message, but feel that one element of it must be shared widely
with those who are inclined to attend to it. This 05/03 Event
will be of either geophysical or societal-political
devastatingness. The message was not detailed, but Alternative
One seems to indicate a geophysical disaster affecting the Earth
and a sizeable percentage of humanity, which would not survive
the disaster.

Alternative Two seems to be that if the geophysical disaster is
averted, the surrounding circumstances will be such that the Old
Order will crumble, and the government will have to acknowledge
Star Visitor reality. That is tantalizingly all the details that
were relayed. Apparently, humans have some potential, mostly
metaphysical and spiritual I suppose, to avert the crippling
planetary geophysical disaster. In so doing, a "better" upheaval
will occur in the societal-political order, as the
Establishment's efforts to control global information,
technology, wealth and political control are radically diminished
by the inability to any longer maintain denial of Star Visitor
presence. Disclosure will destabilize the building New World
Order/Cabal.

Like you I am tempted to fill in the dots with a plausible
scenario which fits the available 05/03 data. One such scenario
_could_ involve a near-pass by a planetoid object, which sets off
massive geophysical calamities. And if collective human (and
apparently enlisted Star Visitor assistance) focus succeeded in
averting the object from too close a pass-by, then the resulting
fact of helpful Star Visitor intervention surely would make clear
globally that "they are here". (And not as invaders, as the Cabal
have been trying to propagandize.) Thus, the UFO Cover-Up would
be broken irretrievably. And the beneficent nature of the
Visitors made apparent to all. <br>

That is likely not the only scenario that could fit the
advisement that the Higher Guides provided through Dr. Sprinkle.
But it is a plausible one. At any rate, I feel that Dr. Sprinkle
is sufficiently unimpeachable, that I tend to take soberly what
he relates. And thus I pass this advisement on.

Please do not ask me to press Dr. Sprinkle for more details. He
values his privacy, and I do not pester him. The information is
shared, because those who are forewarned can more prudently
prepare.

offered a curious taxonomy in his book

"When the Saucers pick up someone from the
Earth they are only picking up their own!" (p. 274)

Besides that, the very first UFO Occupant study was
presented by none other than Jacques Vallee:
"A descriptive study of the entities associated with
the Type-I sighting", FSR (Jan & May 1964)

these articles in Spain. Can anybody send me a
scanned file, xerox, or at least his conclusion (and
the volume of cases considered)?

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Wed, 12 Feb 2003 18:18:47 +0000 (GMT)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] First UFO Occupants study



Hi Luis, list members,

Thanks for the photocopies, by the way, Luis.

I don't have the material you're looking for but I was
interested to see the 1954 reference to abductions
that you have come across. It may not be the earliest
(we'd have to go back some way for that, to the 19th
century, and then come back and delve into Charles
Fort), but I will certainly take note.

You never know what might turn up about early
references to abductions. For example, I recall a
supposedly true UFO report received by the Spanish
magazine "La Actualidad Española" in 1968. The
article, written by someone identifying himself as F.
Sinod, was presented in two chapters with the title
“Yo he hablado con un ser extraterrestre” [I have
spoken to an extraterrestrial being]. It described
Sinod’s close encounter with an alien called Francisco
Atienza on the Valencia-Madrid road. Atienza, who
claimed to be a “descendent of earth-men but born on a
different planet,” told Sinod how his Spanish
ancestors had been abducted in the seventeenth century
and taken to the utopian planet Urln.

After a short period of ufological fame, during which
fragments of Atienza’s technical and philosophical
ravings were published in several popular magazines,
the case fell into obscurity and was forgotten. In
hindsight we can see the whole affair was no more than
a hoax from beginning to end, but the reference to
alien abductions in the seventeenth century is
curious, especially for a story concocted in 1968.

I think Atienza would today be classified as a
possible ‘hybrid offspring’ between earthlings and the
aliens of Urln!

Un abrazo,

Chris

(in the versions I have personally experienced) to actually lift
themselves off of the ground. But the devices could be applied to
lighter than air craft using fuel cells or even solar power, creating
thrust using no moving parts and producing little or no pollution.

From: "Chris Gibson" <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>
Date: Sat, 15 Feb 2003 09:21:50 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Prestwick

Up until recently, Prestwick also housed HMS Gannet, a Royal Navy
anti-submarine Sea King helicopter base. It also houses the Oceanic Control
centre handling trans-Atlantic air traffic. It's fog-free location means it
also acts as a diversion field for just about every other airport in the UK.

Prestwick also provided the air link for US Navy operations at the Holy
Loch, ie had a Military Airlift Command office (on the concourse, next to
the check-in desks) and was visited regularly (every week) by USAF C-141 and
C-5 aircraft hauling personnel and material for the Holy Loch. I suspect the
US Navy would have a liaison officer at Prestwick to work with MAC.

Can't see why that officer would be sent to Bentwaters to debrief some
squaddies.

Chris

PS it's only 40 miles from Macrahanish if that makes things more interesting
/ conspiratorial. :-)

Interesting point James.&nbsp; When I was stationed aboard USS Lafayette (SSBN
616) we flew into Scotland from the states at Prestwick airport and then took a
wonderful bus ride up to the Holy Loch area.&nbsp; Ballistic missle subs ran a "two-
crew" rotation where half the time you were on the sub and half the time you were in
the states conducting training.&nbsp; Upon arrival in Holy Loch, you spent several
days with the other crew relieving them, and then assumed "ownership" of the
sub.&nbsp; As a result, Prestwick received flights every couple of weeks that brought
these crews in and, about a week later, flew the relieved crew out.&nbsp; It is possible
this individual may have flown in on one of the routine flights that brought in sub
crews thus creating the apparent confusion.<BR>
<BR>
Tim Printy<BR>

From: "Robert Mclean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>
Date: Tue, 18 Feb 2003 00:08:33 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] RAF Bentwaters

Bill

The former airbase is owned and operated by Bentwaters Parks Ltd. Their main
office is in the Bentwaters control tower. Many of the buildings and hangers
are being rented out to small businesses - mainly light industrial. The base
is huge compared with your average industrial park, with many widely
dispersed buildings, so security is an issue. The gate at the control tower,
which gets you onto the airfield and the interesting part of the base, is
normally locked out of working hours. The people that work there have a key,
and can come and go as they please, but visitors are all supposed to sign in
at the control tower. This involves signing an indemnity, by which you also
promise not to enter any of the disused buildings, which are potentially
dangerous. Imagine if you somehow got locked in one!

At weekends, the office is unmanned and the gate is often open. I wouldn't
recommend entering the base at such times, if only because you might find
the gate has been locked when you try to leave!

When signing in, you need to give a reason to be there. Being interested in
the military history of the base, should be good enough. You could explain
that you would like to walk around the Weapons Storage Area (WSA). They will
ask you to give them at some point copies of any photos you take.

The WSA is very interesting. Some of the bunkers are open, and it's
interesting to see how much care was taken to ground every bit of metal, and
also provide fire extinguishing.

There is nothing to stop you going up the guard tower in the WSA, which is
at one end of the "hot row". In 1980 there was a second, shorter guard
tower, which is visible in http://www.homestead.com/81sps/files/bwwsa_1_.JPG

For the same view today, see

http://www.homestead.com/81sps/files/View_of_the_Hot_Row_from_the_Whiskey_
Tw
o_Tower.jpg

The old photo gives the impression that one could not have seen over the
height of the trees in 1980 when in the guard tower - but the tower from
which the photo was taken is tall enough to see over the trees when looking
south towards RAF Woodbridge.

If you really wanted to get into a building, you'd have to ask the owners of
the site. But they have a business to run, and they probably wouldn't
bother, unless you had a really good reason.
If you want to visit the site, I'd suggest you either write: Bentwaters
Parks Ltd., Control Tower, Rendlesham, Woodbridge, Suffolk, IP12 2TW, or
give them a phone call first 01394 460655 (fax 460355) to introduce yourself
and to make sure they will let you onto the site when you arrive.

I might be able to join up with any visitors, too, so let me know.

Former SP Don Laisure lives locally, and might be able to give a tour.
Incidentally, Don was the guy who signed out two starlight scopes to Bruce
England and Bobby Ball the night of Col. Halt's expedition.

Best regards

Robert McLean

"Let's remember that a number of professional US air force (sic)
personnel, including the base commander, witnessed and recorded,

performing strange movements over and around their base, that

Chris,

Although it was alleged that some of the nearby trees had been
felled due to 'radiation', there seems to be zero evidence for
this and the area was already being used for logging.

Consequently, I believe we can safely conclude not one Corsican
pine tree was secreted away to the US - first time I've heard
that claim!

to be authentic."

A-2 was the area security patrol & A-1 was the entry

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Wed, 19 Feb 2003 23:18:03 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] F-111 Crash at RAF Woodbridge

Regarding:

>From: John Burtenshaw <jburtens@bournemouth.ac.uk>
>Date: Tue, 17 Dec 2002 09:00:20 +0000
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham

John wrote:

>I did hear that one possibility was that a F-111E had a tactical
>nuke come adrift and as the US was trying to get cruise missiles
>in to the UK at about the same time a cover up was ordered so
>that public opinion would not turn against US bases in the UK.
>
>Probably a load of BS but worth a mention.

John,

I commented on this and noted how it evidently didn't equate with
those 'UFO' perceptions, however, can you say where you heard the
story?

I've now come across reference to an actual F-111 crash which
allegedly occurred just after Christmas 1980, as the aircraft was
approaching RAF Woodbridge's runway!


The data comes from a military aviation enthusiast in the U.S.,
who was unaware that any such incident assuredly related to our
'UFO' story.

Both the F-111 type and its serial number are given.

I'm advised this information originated from the U.K. and I now
have relevant contact details which are being followed up.


As it seems untenable an aircraft could have crashed, or crash-
landed, without this being evident, it wasn't a surprise that I
could locate the present whereabouts of an F-111 bearing the same
serial number.

If it ever crashed, the damage was presumably repairable.

Maybe that's the origin of stories about the aliens being offered
"parts from the electronics division" to fix their spaceship!
Alternatively, as the serial number comes with a caveat that it's
only suggested as identifying the F-111 which crashed on approach
to RAF Woodbridge, it's conceivably another F-111 which was
involved.

Although I remain dubious about the claim, it would be
interesting to confirm where this originated and whether it's the
same source as your own.


Certainly, the approach to RAF Woodbridge's runway would be in
the exact vicinity of those 'unfamiliar lights' within Rendlesham
forest.

However, we know for sure that Orfordness lighthouse was
responsible for much of the confusion.

That acknowledged, there's possibly one facet which has perhaps
never been appreciated until recently.

The now defunct UK 'Sightings' magazine featured a December 1994
interview with Col. Halt [volume 2, issue 3], which reports:

"It seemed peculiar, but an unscheduled American CS Galaxy
transport aeroplane landed at RAF Woodbridge a few days after the
first incident, bringing with it its own security personnel and
Halt wasn't even allowed to know what their mission was.

With that, why did a Lt. Colonel and Deputy Base Commander, with
a security clearance too high to mention, not have the authority
to know what a visiting plane is doing on his base?

He also said that following the planes arrival un-marked
helicopters, that were not from Woodbridge, were seen above the
landing site during the following days".


I hadn't seen this detailed interview until a few weeks ago -
David Clarke pointed out there's a copy online, at:

http://www.ufology.org.uk/modules/sections/index.php?op=viewartic
le&artid=123

[This URL will 'wrap around']

Note that those helicopters were supposedly operating over the
landing site for "days".

I can't recall Halt ever mentioning this in any other interview.
However, it seems comparable with a story I became aware of
before reading the above.

A member of the 81st Security Police Squadron (I won't name him
for now) told me about events which occurred between 29-31
December, 1980.

For three days, he was posted to the now infamous east gate and
witnessed both personnel and helicopters [unfortunately, he
wasn't aware where either came from] operating in the 'landing
site' area.

Advised by his Shift Commander that 'the base' knew what was
going on, he was given no further information, except for being
warned not to report over the radio anything observed.

He could only conclude it looked like they were all searching for
something.


I would be cautious about directly relating this to the overall
case evidence - it still requires verification.

Also, as I commented in reply to your original posting, on the
night of that second 'UFO' excitement:

"...the Base Commander, Ted Conrad, had stayed behind at the
belated officer's Christmas party, the Wing Commander, Gordon
Williams, was at another function and the RAF Liaison Officer,
Don Moreland, had not been recalled from his Christmas holiday
leave".

There might be circumstances where Halt had no need to be advised
about operations outwith the Security Police, however, surely
Williams and Moreland would have to be briefed, especially as the
forest was strictly outwith USAF jurisdiction.


All good fun though and I'll see if I can help resolve the origin
of this F-111 crash rumour [even if it already doesn't make much
sense!].

Incidentally, where would F-111s have been based in the UK at
that time - RAF Lakenheath?


James.

From: "THE WATCHDOG" <ufowatchdog@earthlink.net>
Date: Sun, 23 Feb 2003 13:32:36 -0800
Subject: [UFORL] Release

PRESS RELEASE


LAWSUIT AIMS TO SILENCE VOICE OF CRITIC IN UFO DEBATE
Supposed Psychic and Self Proclaimed UFO Authority Alleges Libel In
Unfounded Lawsuit
21-February-2003

Sean David Morton, who has promoted himself as "one of America's greatest
psychics" and as the "world's foremost UFO researcher", has filed a
one-million dollar defamation lawsuit against UFOWATCHDOG.COM.

Morton was the subject of a series of UFOWATCHDOG.COM articles, most notably
'The Shameless Psychic and His Prophecy of Lies' in which many of Morton's
claims were called into serious question. Morton was invited to directly
comment on the story, which was later published in February 2001. Morton
failed to respond to several invitations for comment, including a posted
open invitation on the UFOWATCHDOG.COM website.

In his lawsuit, Morton alleges all information pertaining to him published
by UFOWATCHDOG.COM is "false", including an autobiography and a list of
production/writing credits both authored by Morton himself. This leaves the
question of why Morton would actually claim something written by him is
false.

UFOWATCHDOG.COM editor Royce J. Myers III calls the lawsuit "completely
meritless and an absolute abuse of the judicial system." Myers further
added, " Mr.Morton is simply trying to use the courts by trampling on the
First Amendment in an attempt to silence one of his numerous critics."

When asked about Morton's claim of being libeled, Myers said, "Mr.Morton's
allegations are pure fantasy, as are the vast majority of his UFO and
psychic claims. Mr.Morton was invited to comment and has, by choice,
continually failed to respond or comment. Mr.Morton has been aware of
UFOWATCHDOG.COM since it debuted in February 2001. You can't hold someone
else accountable for your own failure to speak up."

"Mr.Morton apparently will go to any length in trying to silence someone
with something to say about him, as he has named UFOWATCHDOG.COM's
webhost
as a defendant, which is ludicrous. Thanks to Mr.Morton's baseless lawsuit,
the webhost has shut down the UFOWATCHDOG.COM website. The webhost has
nothing to do with the content of the website. The lawsuit is clearly
retaliatory and intended to stifle any debate about Mr.Morton's public
claims about UFOs, the paranormal, and his alleged credentials. Essentially,
he's trying to scare anyone from engaging him in the eye of the public and
apparently is under the assumption that issues pertaining to UFOs and the
paranormal are one-sided debates solely for him to participate in." Myers
stated.

Prominent Los Angeles civil rights attorney Carol A. Sobel, representing
UFOWATCHDOG.COM, responded to the complaint. On February 20, 2003, Sobel
filed a motion to have the lawsuit dismissed on the grounds that Morton is
"...prevent[ing] Defendants from engaging in protected expressive
activities -- namely calling into question [Morton's] self-proclaimed
national expertise on extraterrestrial life, UFOs, and the paranormal."

Filed under a special California state law enacted in 1992 to combat what
the California Legislature called "...a disturbing increase in lawsuits
brought primarily to chill the valid exercise of the constitutional rights
of freedom of speech", the state law protects people from defamation and
other SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) lawsuits. The
motion allows for the lawsuit to be quickly dismissed when such complaint
arises from the exercise of First Amendment petition and free speech rights
on an issue of public interest.

Sobel noted in the motion to dismiss the lawsuit, "The existence of
extraterrestrial life is unquestionably a matter of great public interest.
People all over the world are engaged in research to answer the question of
whether such life exists. Needless to say, this matter is quite
controversial, bringing with it vehemently contrasting positions based on
scientific and religious grounds."

A hearing on the motion is scheduled for March 14, 2003 at 8:30AM in L.A.
Superior Court in department E at 825 Maple Ave., Torrance, California.

Since early 2001, UFOWATCHDOG.COM has been a news source for both UFOs
and
the paranormal. Most notably, UFOWATCHDOG.COM has challenged a number of
the
claims made by well known UFO personalities, has provided commentary on the
UFO and paranormal fields, as well as having exposed UFO hoaxes all in an
effort to further more rational and scientific debate regarding issues such
as UFOs and the paranormal.


Contact: ufowatchdog@earthlink.net

From: "Chris Gibson" <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>
Date: Mon, 24 Feb 2003 13:15:14 -0000
Subject: RE: [UFORL] F-111's

Good Morning.


1) Naval F-111B was for air defence and cancelled early on in the F-111
development programme in 1968.

2) SAC used FB-111As for strategic nuclear strike, based in the USA.

3) The F-111E and F models based at Upper Heyford and Lakenheath
respectively were for deep penetration of Warpac rear areas. I quote Rick
Stephens in the "World Air Power Journal"

"F-111s were designed as Cold Warriors of the first degree, and carriage of
nuclear weapons was a vital part of that mission." He later states that only
the F-111C didn't carry nuclear weapons and these were based at Cannon AFB.
NM

I can't see a F-111 cavorting about East Anglia with a B61 nuke on the wing.
Stranger things have happened though.

Chris

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Feb 2003 03:45:28 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] F-111 Crash at RAF Woodbridge

I had queried the crash claims on a dedicated F-111A mailing list
and Denis Lefebvre observes:

"I think f-111.net has it mistaken... I took a good look at the
image that they claim is tail number 67-0069. First, you cannot
make out the tail number. Second, it has a 'MO' designation with
'366th TFW' on the tail. Unless those markings are counterfeit,
as an alumni of the 366th, I can say with confidence that
aircraft is not an 'A' model... it is an 'F' model and its tail

lives".

investigate further.

At 15:26 21/02/2003 +0100, you wrote:
>The movie 'Defence of the Realm' features an F-111 crashing with a nuke on

The "lost Nuke" theory has always been my favourite explanation of the
events ( I heard it many years ago from a retired RAF officer) and keeping
in mind that the US wanted to base cruise missiles here in he UK during
1980's I don;t think the public would be too keen on the fact that the USAF
were carrying nukes over their heads so to speak.

Also RAF Vulcans carried "Yellow Sun" H-bombs during "training" flights
over the UK just in case the Soviets launched a surprise attack. I had not
realised this until I spoke to a friend of mine who was a Vulcan pilot. He
told me that it was never spoken about publicly as the RAF / MoD did not
want the public to start worrying in case one crashed!!

<BR>
<A
HREF="http://www.guardian.co.uk/international/story/0,3604,897579,00.html">http:/
/www.guardian.co.uk/international/story/0,3604,897579,00.html</A><BR>
<BR>
Tim Radford, science editor<BR>
Tuesday February 18, 2003<BR>
The Guardian <BR>
<BR>
Abduction by imaginary aliens can be almost as traumatic as being <BR>
caught up in real horror, according to US psychologists. The only <BR>
difference is that when asked "would you go through it again?", <BR>
most of ET's abductees replied: "Yes." <BR>
In one of the more out-of-this-world research projects, <BR>
Richard McNally [1] of Harvard University told the American Association <BR>
for the Advancement of Science meeting in Denver, Colorado [2], <BR>
that he had interviewed 10 of the thousands of Americans who <BR>
claimed to remember being carried off by extraterrestrials. <BR>
<BR>
The Harvard scientists measured heartbeat, facial tension and <BR>
sweating on the palms as they played back audiotapes of the <BR>
subjects recounting their experience. "Our question is: do <BR>
people who have apparent false memories of trauma show the <BR>
same psycho-physiological reactivity? The answer appears to <BR>
be yes," Prof McNally said <BR>
<BR>
Prof McNally IMAGE:<BR>
<A HREF="http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/02.20/photos/08-mcnally-
450.jpg">http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2003/02.20/photos/08-mcnally-
450.jpg</A><BR>
<BR>
[Prof McNally IMAGE:<BR>
<A
HREF="http://www.hup.harvard.edu/images/MCNREM_au.jpg">http://www.hup.har
vard.edu/images/MCNREM_au.jpg</A><BR>
<BR>
"In fact, the heart rate responses and skin conductance responses <BR>
were at least as great in the alien abductees, when they heard <BR>
their memories of being abducted and molested by space aliens, <BR>
and subjected to these experiments on spaceships, as for people <BR>
with genuine traumatic events. <BR>
<BR>
"The moral of the story appears to be that it underscores the <BR>
power of emotional belief." <BR>
<BR>
In his research, Prof McNally also identified the recipe for <BR>
an alien abductee. Most of the subjects were interested in <BR>
astral projection, tarot cards, telling the future, bioenergetic <BR>
therapies and, of course, aliens. "So they had a whole set of <BR>
new age beliefs to begin with," he said. <BR>
<BR>
They were also prone to fantasies, and vivid images. Third, and <BR>
crucially, they had had episodes of sleep paralysis and <BR>
hallucinations upon awakening. Sleep paralysis is not imaginary: <BR>
it occurs on awakening from the dream state marked by rapid eye <BR>
movement, and is experienced by 30% of the population. Some victims <BR>
of sleep paralysis also report hypnopompic ("upon wakening") <BR>
hallucinations. <BR>
<BR>
"It is part of the basis of believing in ghosts," Prof McNally said. <BR>
"In the European middle ages it was the incubus and the succubus <BR>
who were the agents of the devil. In Cambridge, Massachusetts, <BR>
it is space aliens. During REM sleep, the body is fully paralysed <BR>
except for the eyes ... Often elements of dream will intrude <BR>
into wakefulness." <BR>
<BR>
Such experiences were often terrifying. So, typically, his <BR>
abductees would consult mental health professionals, who would <BR>
suggest they had repressed memories. <BR>
<BR>
"So when we piece together the new age beliefs, the hypnopompic <BR>
hallucinations, the absorption, and sometimes a little help from <BR>
the memory recovery folks, you have got yourselves an alien abductee." <BR>

I wrote:

[BEGIN]
I had queried the crash claims on a dedicated F-111A mailing list
and Denis Lefebvre observes:

"I think f-111.net has it mistaken... I took a good look at the
image that they claim is tail number 67-0069. First, you cannot
make out the tail number. Second, it has a 'MO' designation with
'366th TFW' on the tail. Unless those markings are counterfeit,
as an alumni of the 366th, I can say with confidence that
aircraft is not an 'A' model... it is an 'F' model and its tail
number is most likely prefaced with 72 - xxxx".

David de Botton, who operates 'f-111.net', is also a subscriber
to the same mailing list and has responded, commenting he will
investigate further.
[END]


David now replies to Denis Lefebvre's comments:

"Regards this A model at The Southern Museum of Flight.

I appreciate & welcome your questions with verification of the
true identity of this particular aircraft.

I can't begin to convey the 100's of email that went into
updating the museums page over a 12 month period!!

This involved emailing everyone in our email address book. It
gave me leads to follow that meant I also had to chase up plenty
of promises for images. Many aircraft on display at various
museums do not in fact have the paint schemes they should/or last
had. Some even have the incorrect tail numbers?

Can assure you Dennis that this aircraft has a intake splitter
plate making it an 'A'& not 'F' model".

From: "David Clarke" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 8 Mar 2003 13:36:50 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] MOD TV programme records released

BBC Online, 6 February 2003
www.bbc.co.uk

UFO PROGRAMME 'PANIC' GRIPPED MINISTRY

By Dominic Casciani
BBC News Online at the Public Record Office


The truth may be out there but in 1972 the Ministry of Defence was agonising
about a televised debate on UFOs, fearing it would encourage the British
public to believe in little men from outer space.

Many of the public are convinced about UFO's
Documents released at the Public Record Office reveal official anxiety as to
what would happen if the Royal Air Force took part in a BBC programme about
unidentified flying objects.

On one hand they feared they would fuel UFO hysteria - but on the other hand
they feared conspiracy theorists would have a field day if they refused to
take part in the show.

When an official did give an interview to the BBC, it just sparked more
controversy - with one letter writer requesting to meet the government's
expert in languages from outer space.

During the 1960s and early 1970s, there was a huge growth in sightings of
apparently unidentifiable flying objects, many of them near to RAF bases.

In 1971, the BBC's current affairs programme Man Alive decided to
investigate sightings over Banbury, Oxfordshire, and asked the Ministry of
Defence for assistance.

Mr Davis could well be the target for cranks and fanatics and others who
profess to believe in 'little men from outer space'

Air Commodore Brothers, Ministry of Defenc

This was not such a straightforward request as it would seem.

Air Commodore Anthony Davis found himself nominated as the ministry's
official UFOs spokesman - though his colleagues had deep concerns as to the
whether he should take part in the programme at all.

"We do not know who will be in the audience," wrote Air Commodore Brothers.
"Mr Davis could well be the target for cranks and fanatics and others who
profess to believe in 'little men from outer space'."

"Unless you have any other thoughts on the matter we propose to tell the BBC
that we are only prepared for Mr Davis to take part in a filmed interview."

David Filkin, the programme's producer, urged the ministry to think again
and he won round the top brass.

"On balance, it would be better to do this and face up to the possible
difficulties of dealing with a hostile audience of cranks and fanatics
rather than the alternative risk of leaving the field to the fanatics and
giving the impression that we are afraid to stand up to questions,"
concluded officials.

Full sympathy

Having decided to take part, the ministry was so determined to quash UFO
rumours, officials arranged for RAF Lightnings and one US Air Force Phantom
to be filmed flying in formations that they said were the basis for the
rumours.

"Good colour film taken [by the BBC] at dusk should show the fire-cones of
their jet effluxes in re-heat, apparently hovering and then moving sharply
away, as often described in UFO sightings," Air Commodore Davis told the
ministry.

"On UFOs, I found both the producer and interviewer apparently fully in
sympathy with the MOD point of view; they have probably had their fill of
the cranky ufologists whom they have already interviewed at length."

The man from the ministry came away satisfied that the MOD has quashed the
rumours for good - not least after his successful performance during the
subsequent studio discussion.

Unfortunately, that did not turn out to be the case and the letters kept
coming in to the ministry - including one from a Mr Creighton of
Rickmansworth, Hertfordshire.

Like many UFO enthusiasts, Mr Creighton thought the programme was a seminal
moment in the battle to prove the existence of extraterrestrials.

"It was not only epoch-making for its treatment of the subject but that the
star performer of the evening was a gentlemen who, if my memory is not at
fault, holds a government certificate of proficiency in the more exotic
branches of xenoglossy and speaks fluent Uranian or Plutonian," he wrote.

Mr Creighton said he and other enthusiasts desperately wanted this official
to appear as a guest-speaker at UFO clubs around the country.
"I have made several unsuccessful attempts to locate him - could you be so
good as to put me in touch with him or indicate how he may be contacted?"

Unfortunately for Mr Creighton, the men from the ministry denied they had a
chap conversant in alien languages.

"This department has no knowledge of the person you mention," came the terse
reply.

"I can only suggest that the staff of the BBC programme may be able to
assist you."

Specifically, said Duncan, can you fill us in on what's happened
since ITV's 'Strange But True?' feature some years back.

I suggested:

On 9 December, 1994, 'Strange But True?' asserted, "the Americans
were well aware of the lighthouse and said that wasn't what they
saw".

The critical development was that it has now long been proven
otherwise and uncovering those original witness statements was
devastating to the 'aliens landed in Suffolk' mythology.

Far from examining a 'landed craft' at his leisure for some
twenty minutes and actually touching its 'strange symbols', SSgt
Jim Penniston had in truth never been closer than 50 metres to
what were merely some unfamiliar lights somewhere within
Rendlesham forest.

Worse yet, Penniston, Burroughs and Cabansag trekked for two
miles through the pitch black countryside before realising they
were pursuing a coastal lighthouse.

These were the true facts, documented at the time and never
disclosed by Burroughs or Penniston in their TV appearances.


Although Lt. Col. Halt was oblivious to the abortive lighthouse
pursuit when he had his own coastal 'UFO encounter', in exactly
the same location, he took those statements at the beginning of
January 1981 and would then have become aware how deceptive those
coastal lights were, when viewed through the forest trees.

Halt never disclosed this either.

it's been five years since the 'ET visitation' story had

Hi James,

Thanks very much for your reply.

I've read the article with interest - I had not actually heard before of
scintillating stars.

I'm certain, though, that this isn't the explanation here, for amongst
others, the following reasons:

1) Our initial observation was of two distinct formations of 8-10 lights
each - arranged in circles - the circumferences separated by a distance
roughly equal to their (equal) radii. My mother (the other observer)
describes them as each looking like the European flag.

2) The motion of the bulk of the lights (which moved off) after split-up was
fast - certainly seemingly at least as fast as an aircraft. Most of these
travelled out of view completely towards the horizon/cloud bank - in two or
three different directions. It was fortunate that the sky was almost clear
at the time. To our view at least two or three made the return trip and back
to the original position, where some paused very close together.

3) The relatively short distance was short compared only with the motion of
those that disappeared from view altogether. It was certainly not the motion
of a star or planet.

4) The objects which flashed were similar to the description of the
scintillating stars, but these had an overall rapid motion over large
distances.

We observed the lights with naked eye and binoculars mainly. The main one
which stayed put in one place for the longest periods of time I even had
enough time to focus my telescope on to, but this didn't really add much.

It's obviously a bit difficult to describe briefly the motions/relative
motions and brightnesses of what amounted to about 20 lights, so I wondered
who might be interested in a more full report on this. I would have thought
that other people must have seen it too.

I would be glad of any more suggestions.

Ben Walker

> >brightened and dimmed 2 or 3 times, such that they were easily
> >the brightest object that either of us have ever seen in the
> >night sky (except the moon).
>
>Just a suggestion; one common possibility for comparative
>observations are scintillating stars. There's an excellent
>explanation in the following article:
>
>http://members.aol.com/TPrinty/UFOstars.html
>
>If your experience lasted for two hours, during which some of the
>lights, "remained roughly in the same vicinity and moved only a
>relatively short distance", could scintillating stars be the
>overall explanation?
>
>If some of the lights seemed to be in motion, how far did they
>move away from their original positions?
>
>Were they also still visible some two hours later?
>
> >The motion of several of them seemed very jerky and had lights
> >which flashed at a constant rate.
>
>As you will see from the article, this could be entirely
>consistent.
>
>It would be interesting to know what you think of the
>possibility.

>I'm certain, though, that this isn't the explanation here, for amongst
>others, the following reasons:
>
>1) Our initial observation was of two distinct formations of 8-10 lights
>each - arranged in circles - the circumferences separated by a distance
>roughly equal to their (equal) radii. My mother (the other observer)
>describes them as each looking like the European flag.
>
>2) The motion of the bulk of the lights (which moved off) after split-up was
>fast - certainly seemingly at least as fast as an aircraft. Most of these
>travelled out of view completely towards the horizon/cloud bank - in two or
>three different directions. It was fortunate that the sky was almost clear
>at the time. To our view at least two or three made the return trip and back
>to the original position, where some paused very close together.
>
>3) The relatively short distance was short compared only with the motion of
>those that disappeared from view altogether. It was certainly not the motion
>of a star or planet.
>
>4) The objects which flashed were similar to the description of the
>scintillating stars, but these had an overall rapid motion over large
>distances.
>
>We observed the lights with naked eye and binoculars mainly. The main one
>which stayed put in one place for the longest periods of time I even had
>enough time to focus my telescope on to, but this didn't really add much.
>
>It's obviously a bit difficult to describe briefly the motions/relative
>motions and brightnesses of what amounted to about 20 lights, so I wondered
>who might be interested in a more full report on this. I would have thought
>that other people must have seen it too.
>
>I would be glad of any more suggestions.
>
>Ben Walker

Hello List,

I´m not surprised of this "phenomenon" because I can see it self all night long
since more as two years here in Mannheim/Germany. It is furthermore a very
common matter for Germany and more as 20 % of all UFO reports here in Germany
reporting the same.

The "UFO-light-effect-producer" sitting on the grounf in mid of a open
air-festival or disco or a thing like this - a relativly small "machine" called
SKYTRACKER which is used for attraction to a commercial happening. In few cases
is the SKYTRACKER-engine also mounted on a pick-up-truck and works on the spott
only for the night of happening. On the next night is nothing more to seen
because the pick-up is at home by a leasing-company hundred miles away.
Leasing-rate for a night here in Germany: around 200 Euros. Power-output of the
"laser"-light ist until 8000 Watts. You can seen the lights until 20 or 25 km`s
away. A computer-regulated light-display in the sky makes up few different
motion-pictures of the projection possible. A programm projected a perfect
"saucer" in the sky. Under a special clear air in the sky your can seen NOT the
"lightfingers" from the ground to the air and only reflections on small clouds
hight enough above for not seening them himself. A sightings-duration of many
hours is normal. Many times in the last ten years I have hunted such "lights" in
Germany and ever I came out after a fantastisc hunt quer across the country by a
theater, disco, mall etc with the SKYTRACKER-machine on the parking lot or on
the top of the building. :-(

Best wishes,

Werner Walter

From: YoungBob2@aol.com

is treated by this local Pittsburg newspaper. As long as there are
promoters of a "mystery", and people who want to get into the
