Hi James,

Thanks for your reply to my message about the Dropa
stones.

I hope my previous note has provided enough
bibliographical details for you to see that the usual
"story behind the story" has, as I said in my first
message, been tangled up in incorrect data.

There has been some very sloppy research done on this
issue to date. I smiled when I read your note that
Hesemann had written

"Regarding the alleged Baian Kara Ula crash, the story
started here in Germany in the late 1950ies (1956 or
7) and was originally a science fiction story
published in 'Das vegetarische Universum'."

I wonder how the story could have started in the 1950s
but not be published until the 1960s in 'Das
vegetarische Universum'? I wonder how he was able to
date it at all without any bibliographical reference
to go by?

One of the main problems I had with the Dropa trail
was the publication date of the Sputnik journal. A
Google search will tell you it was published anywhere
between 1960 and 1968, whereas my Russian colleagues
gave me a firm date of 1967 (which makes sense for
historical reasons, too). In fact, this is the
magazine sometimes referred to as the Russian Digest,
and not that 1960 publication as others would have it.
The University of Kansas Libraries Slavic Department
has the following description:

******************************************************
SPUTNIK: digest of the Soviet press (Moscow: Novosti,
1967-) Monthly. Periodicals/Stacks 050 Sp97n

In a format similar to the Readers' Digest. Features
mainly abridged articles from the Soviet press.
Original source given with each article.
******************************************************
If the story had been published in Russian in 1963 and
not four years later the origin of the story would
still be the German magazine, of course. I understand
that he was living in Japan at the time, so maybe the
story was not German after all.

Best wishes,

Chris

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Tue, 29 Apr 2003 08:54:22 +0100 (BST)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Seeking original source



Hello list,

This is the information I have gathered so far. I
think I now only need to acquire the original
published version(s) to finish off my investigation.
It will be interesting to see where the accretions
were added.

Bibliographical history:

July 1962 "Das vegetarische Universum." (German)

July 1964 "UFO-Nachrichten" (German)

March-April 1965 "BUFOI" Newsletter (French, Belgium)

1966 "Neman" (Russian)

The "Russian Digest" did not exist as such. The
publication some writers have become confused about
was "Literaturnaja Gazeta," in which V. Ritsch and M.
Tschernenko published "Were Alien Visitors on Earth?"
in 1960. However they do not mention the Dropa disks.

Dr. Vyatcheslav Zaitzev wrote about the disks for
"Sputnik" in its first edition, published in 1967,
based on "Das vegetarische Universum."

David Agamon (a pseudonym of ‘Gamon’) edited a book
about the Dropa called Sungods in Exile in 1979,
claiming it was the posthumous work of a British
scientist named Karyl Robin-Evans. Robin-Evans (who
did not exist) supposedly led an expedition to the
Baian-Kara-Ula area in 1947 in order to find out more
about a disc that had been bought in India or Nepal by
his colleague at Oxford, Polish Professor Sergei
Lolladoff (who did not exist, either). Agamon writes
that the expedition came across a tribe of dwarfs in a
remote valley in Baian-Kara-Ula. These dwarfs, the
Dropa, told him that their ancestors had come from a
planet in the Sirius system and had crash-landed on
earth in 1014 AD. (There is no evidence that the Dropa
have ever existed.)
Agamon, using his real name Gamon, wrote to the
British magazine Fortean Times (issue 75) stating that
“Sungods in Exile” was his “favourite hoax,” and
adding that “The author of this leg-pull received
correspondence from as far away as Kiev. Don't ask me
how I know.” When Bob Rickard telephoned Gamon while
preparing a note on the case for issue 109 of the same
publication, Gamon confessed to the deceit. To add to
the confusion Gamon had produced photographs of
another, fake disc that many still believe to be
genuine.

Does anyone have access to the original German
articles? I'd love to see them, scanned or otherwise.

Regards,

Chris

Hi to all,

article of possible interest.

Best regards,
Roberto Labanti

***
Italian Committee for Project Hessdalen
Comitato Italiano per il Progetto Hessdalen
http://www.itacomm.net/PH

Matteo Leone
"A rebuttal of the EMBLA 2002 report on the optical survey in Hessdalen"

On August 2002, a scientific expedition to the Hessdalen valley (Norway) -
code-named EMBLA - aimed at investigating on an unidentified atmospheric
light-phenomenon, was carried out by the physics section of an Italian team
of scientists. According to the EMBLA 2002 physics report, the evidence
collected point at an unknown atmospheric light phenomenon "able to produce
a luminous power of up to 100 kW". The photometrical and spectroscopical
data collected by the team of scientists on August 2002 are analysed and
reasons for rejecting the suggested conclusions are presented in this
paper. Furthermore, it is proposed an explanation that satisfactorily
explains the evidence in terms of a known phenomenon. In spite of this
negative findings, the anecdotal evidence collected by this author at
Hessdalen suggests that clearly-defined, specific studies into the field of
anomalous aerial phenomena should be supported.

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Mon, 28 Apr 2003 13:51:40 +0100 (BST)
Subject: [UFORL] Seeking original source

Dear list,

I am searching for the original source of the "Dzopa
discs" story and have come to a dead end. Could anyone
on this list help me untangle the threads?

The source of the confusion is as follows:


Hartwig Hausdorf, the latest champion of the case,
notes in the sources for The Chinese Roswell that the
first mention of the discs in a non-specialist
publication was in an article by V. Ritsch and M.
Tschernenko in Russian Digest. Hausdorf says this
article, titled Were Alien Visitors on Earth?, was
included in a 1960 issue. However, this conflicts
firstly with the claim that Tsum Um Nui translated the
hieroglyphics in 1962 and secondly with Hausdorf’s
statement that “…Dr. Vyatcheslav Saitzev…first told
the story of the alien discs of Bara Kara Ula for the
Soviet Magazine Sputnik…” This becomes even less clear
when we read in the same book that the German magazine
Das vegetarische Universum also published an article
about the discs based on the Sputnik report, yet the
edition of the German magazine cited is dated July
1962 and the Sputnik article was apparently published
in its first issue in 1963!

Bruno Mancusi, who has also looked into the problem of
when the story was first published, has written that
the report was first published in UFO-Nachrichten #95,
July 1964, p.3. The author was one Reinhardt Wegemann,
Tokyo correspondent of a DINA news agency. (UFO
UpDates July 26th 1998)

On the other hand, Gordon Creighton wrote (in Flying
Saucer Review Vol.19, No.1 January 1973, p24-27) that
he had learnt that Zaitsev “had done no original
investigation of his own and had simply taken the
story as it had appeared in the German publication Das
Vegetarische Universum (no date given) and in the
German publication UFO-Nachrichten, No. 95 (of 1964).”

So, where was the story first published, who wrote it
and in which language?
I've been working on this problem on and off for over
a year and I'd sincerely appreciate a hand in reaching
some sort of a conclusion and obtaining a copy of the
original source.

Subject: Re: [UFORL] Amazing Discovery

Categorised by British Pathe as 'Unissued/Unused material',
undated and attributed to be, "British soldiers examine a balloon
bomb", the following footage [annoyingly no soundtrack] is in
fact evidently of an unexploded FuGo or Fu-Go, 'balloon bomb'
which has landed in the U.S. and is duly being dealt with by the
military:

http://www.rendlesham.com/ftp/2080_28.wmv

As there was an agreed U.S. press embargo not to report any
'balloon bomb' landings and thus reveal to the Japanese their
success rate, presumably that's why this film was never
broadcast?

Interestingly, we can see that the 'balloon bomb' material is
eventually added to an already large collection of same.

At the end of this short film, it's demonstrated [not too clear]
on a map where the balloon originated.

As the film is mistakenly attributed, you could be amongst the
first to see exceptionally rare and quite significant historical
footage, which was never released at the time and has perhaps
since been buried in the British Pathe archives.

From: "david CLARKE" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 1 May 2003 21:31:11 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Lakenheath case investigation on-line

CLASSIC CASE NOW ON-LINE



The RAF Lakenheath-Bentwaters 'radar visual' incident of 1956 has long been
regarded as one of the classic cases in the annals of UFOlogy.



This is one of the few incidents classified as 'unexplained' by the 1969
Colorado University UFO study commissioned by the US Air Force, which
conceded that "the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved
appears to be fairly high."



But the true extent and complex nature of the events in East Anglia have
never been fully revealed, and divining the truth from a mass of
contradictory evidence has confounded even the most dedicated of UFO
researchers.



Now for the first time in UFOlogical history, a website dedicated to an
in-depth re-investigation of a classic case is available on-line at:



http://www.parcellular.fsnet.co.uk/Lakenheath.htm



The website is the product of three years work by the Lakenheath
Collaboration - a team of British researchers that includes Martin Shough,
David Clarke, Paul Fuller, Andy Roberts and Jenny Randles. Please remember
the site remains under construction, with further documents (including
several that are the subject of FOIA requests) to be added in the near
future.



Building upon new testimony unearthed by Jenny, since 2000 extensive
fieldwork by Clarke and Roberts has uncovered a host of new testimony and
documentary evidence. Shough, the author of a detailed analysis of the case
published in 1987, has compiled the existing and new material presented on
the website.
Our front page opens with a surprise - a photograph dated 1955/56 showing
the control console in the tower at RAF Bentwaters complete with UFO
graffiti.



Follow the links into the body of the Lakenheath/Bentwaters/Neatishead
incident of 13/14 August 1956. The Collaboration have gathered together all
the available evidence, including new material relating to the RAF's
response to the incident that has slowly emerged since 1996.



The re-investigation did not set out to debunk the case, but rather to look
closer at what might have happened, with surprising results for both
'believers' and 'skeptics.' We present the evidence and take care to
separate facts from speculation. We provide no resolution as it emerges
that Lakenheath-Bentwaters is a far more complex and multi-layered mystery
than was ever suspected in 1969.



All five contributors, despite having differing approaches and opinions,
agree this is an instructive case and its re-investigation has brought to
light information that not only overturns all previous accounts, but
provides the sort of data that scientists claim has been previously lacking
in the field of UFOlogy.



The site contains:



 a.. More than 270 text and image files, including in addition to the
original USAF intelligence reports and other Blue Book documents:
 b..
 22 new official British Royal Air Force and Ministry of Defence documents;
 c..
 36 new interview transcripts and statements from pilots, ground personnel
 and operations staff;
 d..
 23 web-pages of in-depth commentary and analysis, fully interlinked;
 e..
 14 pages of meteorological data, with detailed tables, charts and
analysis;
 f..
 14 pages of detailed radar and avionics specifications;
 g..
 30 archived letters between investigators and principal witnesses between
 1975 and 2001;

Plus much more, with numerous links and bibliographical references to
research material.



The Lakenheath Collaboration would be pleased to receive your comments,
criticisms and contributions to what we hope will be a on-going peer review
process of our evolving case file.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>

Subject: Re: [UFORL] Amazing Discovery

Regarding:

>From: Ktperehwon@aol.com
>Date: Wed, 30 Apr 2003 15:21:50 EDT
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Amazing Discovery

Karl wrote,

>...why are you concerned about 26 April 64. The Zamora incident
>occurred on 24 April.

Karl,

Indeed, like Arnold, the 24th was a big day.

For general list interest, a further significant discovery is now
available online.

I once mentioned:

"Some three months prior to events at Socorro, on 19 January
1964, the recently formed California Balloon Club hosted a
balloon race to highlight the new sport of modern hot-air
ballooning. It was 'fastest time wins', from Catalina Island to
the California mainland".

It proved to be a tragic event.

Remarkably, I was also able to locate, from the same source, some
footage of this competition and it can be downloaded, with no
copyright issues, via:

http://www.rendlesham.com/ftp/3155_17.wmv


Note that at beginning [far left] and end, Ed Yost's balloon is
featured.

Once again, it's the 3-man, model S-50 'Channel Champ', which can
now be seen in scale and looks comparatively smaller than in film
of the channel crossing.

Don Piccard, highlighted in the Catalina footage [although his
balloon isn't], was flying a specific Raven model S-45 which was
the S-50's back-up.
It was both of these which were used in those 'classified'
1963/64 New Mexico flights.

It's not suggested either were involved with Zamora's incident.

However, Coral Lorenzen described comparative 'UFO' sightings in
that period:

"Other tales of objects similar in appearance, which 'buzzed'
cars and homes in the general area from Las Cruces north to
Albuquerque along the Rio Grande river, seem to support the
evidence that strange objects were flying and landing there".

Those classified, hot-air balloon test flights were launched from
a site on the banks of the Rio Grande, north of Albuquerque.

There's a bigger picture and of course, earlier on the 24 April,
1964, a reported 'shiny, oval or egg-shaped UFO' near
Albuquerque.

Other, related, material I can't presently make available and
meantime, this historical footage, as with additional 'UFO'
archive film found at 'British Pathe', I thought would be of
interest and it should be regarded as no more than that.


James.
E-mail: voyager@jeaston.com

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Tue, 29 Apr 2003 14:52:17 +0100 (BST)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Seeking original source


Hi James,

Thanks for your reply to my message about the Dropa
stones.

I hope my previous note has provided enough
bibliographical details for you to see that the usual
"story behind the story" has, as I said in my first
message, been tangled up in incorrect data.

There has been some very sloppy research done on this
issue to date. I smiled when I read your note that
Hesemann had written

"Regarding the alleged Baian Kara Ula crash, the story
started here in Germany in the late 1950ies (1956 or
7) and was originally a science fiction story
published in 'Das vegetarische Universum'."

I wonder how the story could have started in the 1950s
but not be published until the 1960s in 'Das
vegetarische Universum'? I wonder how he was able to
date it at all without any bibliographical reference
to go by?

One of the main problems I had with the Dropa trail
was the publication date of the Sputnik journal. A
Google search will tell you it was published anywhere
between 1960 and 1968, whereas my Russian colleagues
gave me a firm date of 1967 (which makes sense for
historical reasons, too). In fact, this is the
magazine sometimes referred to as the Russian Digest,
and not that 1960 publication as others would have it.
The University of Kansas Libraries Slavic Department
has the following description:

******************************************************
SPUTNIK: digest of the Soviet press (Moscow: Novosti,
1967-) Monthly. Periodicals/Stacks 050 Sp97n

In a format similar to the Readers' Digest. Features
mainly abridged articles from the Soviet press.
Original source given with each article.
******************************************************
If the story had been published in Russian in 1963 and
not four years later the origin of the story would
still be the German magazine, of course. I understand
that he was living in Japan at the time, so maybe the
story was not German after all.

Best wishes,

Chris

From: "Phenomena Research Australia" <praufo@aol.com>
Date: Sat, 03 May 2003 13:08:41 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] PRA - "Lore Of The Rings".


"LORE OF THE RINGS"

April 30, 2003

The Australian Bulletin Magazine 2003
Australia

~ Crop circles - an alien landing evidence, a message from the ~
~ outer cosmos or an elaborate hoax? Anthony Hoy embarks on a ~
~ journey to the twilight zone.                    ~


When Don White discovered a seemingly inexplicable pattern of
30 circles in a wheat crop on his Victorian farm in October 2001,
he put it down to "some sort of weather phenomenon". "I certainly
didn't give any thought to extraterrestrials or flying saucers,"
he says. And there the matter would have finished had he not
mentioned it to his sister, Ruth Ellis, who farms nearby.

Ellis, who once worked for the Victorian Department of Natural
Resources, mentioned the circles to her former colleagues and
"it sort of - snowballed from that point", White says.

Television crews and press photo-graphers suddenly began climbing
all over White's 400ha Corrymeela property, 50km north of Bendigo.
If aliens had arrived - as many of Australia's pseudo-scientists
and UFOlogists preferred to believe - they could have picked a
better time. At one stage, White's lamb- eeding and cropping routine
was being disrupted by as many as 50 phone calls and visits a day.

While all that distraction eventually died down, it is threatening
to blow up again after the inclusion of the Corry-meela case in a
recent ABC radio broadcast about the crop circle phenomenon.
"I would rather the whole thing went away. I'm sick of talking
about it," White says.

Australian crop circles first achieved major media coverage with
the appearance of "saucer nests" in a wheat field near Wokurna,
a community south-east of Adelaide, in December 1973. Soon after,
seven circles up to 4.26m in diameter appeared in a field of oats
at nearby Bordertown.


In December 1989, as many as 90 intricate circles - ranging from
a few centimetres to a few metres in diameter - appeared on land
owned by the Jolly family in the Mallee wheat belt, north-west
of Melbourne. Unusual nocturnal lights were also reported in the
sky, as were strange high-pitched warbling, swirling or screaming
noises.

Some sharper UFOlogists have been quick to capitalise on interest
in the phenomenon - mainly at the expense of amateur enthusiasts.
To the chagrin of Australia's legitimate space science fraternity,
one entrepreneurial UFOlogist registered the company name The
National Space Centre, established a 1900 telephone hotline and
charges about $5 a minute to field "inquiries and reports" from
true believers and the curious.

Staff at the only legitimate NASA facility in Australia - the Deep
Space Communications Complex at Tidbinbilla, near Canberra - have
since fielded calls from irate, unsuspecting UFOlogists slugged
as much as $250 by calling The National Space Centre.

More money may change hands if the recent radio broadcast rekindles
interest. The program featured an interview with Nancy Talbott,
a music producer with "a research background" at the University
of Maryland and Harvard and a member of the so-called BLT Crop
Circle Research Team. The name comes from the first initials of
the surnames of Talbott and her two associates, New York businessman
John Burke and Michigan biophysicist William C. Levengood.
The organisation, Talbott claims, is funded by New York
philanthropist Laurance S. Rockefeller.

Crop circle plants examined by BLT associates were covered in a
pure iron glaze associated with magnetic meteorite dust, according
to Talbott. The Corry-meela crop circles, she says, could have
been the direct result of the annual Perseids meteor shower.

"There are pervasive, re-occurring abnormalities in crop circle
plants and soils which are consistent with exposure of these plants
and soils to an intense and complex energy system which emits heat
(possibly microwaves) along with highly unusual electrical pulses
and strong magnetic fields," Talbott told listeners of A Country
Breakfast.

She and her colleagues claim to have jointly sampled 300-plus
crop circles between 1990 and 2000. "More than 90% showed the
characteristic anomalous changes in plant tissues, and magnetic
material was consistently documented in those formations where
soil sampling had also been conducted."

The media, Talbott said, was making progress "more difficult" by
labelling the phenomenon as "fringe". "But hard data is difficult
to ignore. And following such data wherever it leads will most
likely lead us - eventually - to an understanding of this most
enigmatic, peculiar phenomenon."

Darren Osborne is editor of the CSIRO's science magazine, The
Helix. Before taking up his post, Osborne served for five years
as public relations officer at NASA's Tidbinbilla complex - one
of three global tracking points for inter-planetary space orbiters
probing Jupiter, Saturn and Mars.

"Tidbinbilla's expertise is often called upon for anything that
is space-related," says the man who in five years possibly fielded
more UFO calls than almost any other Earthling. "It was amusing,
really. We weren't looking out for these things. But I became
an expert of sorts, and certainly came to know which UFOlogists
were serious, and which were downright shonky."

His first crop circle call while at Tidbinbilla turned out to
be a publicity stunt perpetrated by Canberra radio station FM104.7.
Other stunts were staged by self-admitted crop circle hoaxers
Doug Bower and David Chorley. They operated in northern Queensland
before exporting their crop circle expertise to England, where
they conjured up about 250 intricate circles.

Matthew Williams, 30, of Wiltshire, was fined £100 ($256) by a
British -magistrate in November 2000 after admitting on the
internet to damaging a farmer's crops near Marlborough, England.
He subsequently made a film revealing the secrets and techniques
of crop circle creators, who use posts, -ladders, tapes, planks,
ropes, rollers and even computer-generated designs.

The hoaxers' handiwork was undoubtedly a factor in the popularity
of the Glastonbury Symposium, now in its 12th year and said to be
the largest international gathering of "cereologists", people who
study crop circles (after Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture
and fertility).

"Just because it doesn't sit in a gallery doesn't mean it's not
art," Williams says. "It's a living sculpture. But for some -
people it forms a temporary religious site. Some people get very
angry when you tell them, because they really want to believe.
It tells you a lot about religion and belief ... how these cults
are created."

Says Osborne: "In my view, the crop circle thing is a furphy.
Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. And a couple
of trampled bits of wheat don't add up to much. The most simple
explanation is the most likely one. And scientists have yet to be
convinced that little green men and/or big-eyed -monsters are
leaving impressions in our wheat fields."

Movie-makers routinely use delusion and superstition to suggest
the supernatural - ignoring any reasoned expla-nation. Such was
the scenario in Signs, the recent movie in which Mel Gibson
played a farmer and former pastor whose faith was tested when
his Pennsylvania cornfield was transformed overnight into what
looked like an alien landing pad.

"At the end of the day, government-related organisations have
not got the resources to investigate pseudo--scientific claims,"
says Osborne. "And people are let down that they don't get the
answers they are seeking. So they turn to the pseudo-scientists
and UFOlogists, some of whom profit from the exercise. It's a
problem that no one really knows how to address."

But Barry Williams, full-time officer of the NSW Skeptics
Association, is prepared to have a crack at addressing the issue.
He dismisses crop circles as acts of art or hoaxes. "It is one
of the strangest beliefs people have ever come up with. If
some inter-galactic entity is really out there trying to send
us messages using ancient Sumerian symbols or representations
of alien DNA, why not write it in English so we can understand
it? Crop circles tend to happen in places where a lot of people
have got a lot of time on their hands - near universities,
for instance."

Don White doesn't subscribe to improbable UFO theories. All
the same, he is still nervously posting a lookout around
Corrymeela's wheat and canola paddocks.

~end~

here has. If it were seen from the side, and not in silhouette, the
advertizing printed on it would be visible. It is a balloon shaped like
a blimp with fins.

Hi,

Diego Cuoghi has a very clarifying page on supposed UFOs on medieval art. He
deals with "Baptism of Christ" by Aert De gelder and offers this conclusion:
http://www.sprezzatura.it/Arte/Arte_UFO_3.htm
"In the "Baptism of Christ" by Aert De Gelder there is no UFO. The light
disc in the sky is similar to other discs seen in many other "Baptism of
Christ" paitings. At Jesus' baptism, the Dove (often inside the light
circle) represented the presence of the Holy Spirit, and so is most
frequently used to symbolize the third person of the Trinity. In the
Fitzwilliam Museum catalogue the painting is described in this way: "In the
foreground of a hilly landscape, Christ is baptised by St. John, amid a
circle of onlookers. The two figures are brilliantly lit by rays from the
Dove high above, against general darkness..."
Indeed, we can see a very small dove on the supposed UFO.

Regards,

MK

I had an interesting phone call last Friday from an American FOIA
officer who was dealing with my request, which read:

[BEGIN]
I request that a copy of the following documents are provided:

1) Any records pertaining to the crash/crash-landing of an F-111
aircraft in the United Kingdom during December 1980, specifically
in the vicinity of RAF Woodbridge.

2) Any records pertaining to the loss of a bomb/missile from an
F-111 aircraft in the United Kingdom during December 1980,
specifically in the vicinity of RAF Woodbridge.
[END]


Apologising and explaining the reasons for a delay in replying,
the officer confirmed which airbase in the U.S. was now handling
that query.

The officer seemed to be inexperienced in dealing with FOIA
matters, perhaps an infrequent departure from their normal
duties.

I speculatively asked if they could say whether any related file
existed and expecting a response that either they didn't know or
couldn't discuss this informally, I was somewhat surprised to
hear the reply, "I believe so".

The officer recalled reading about the crash in a U.S. newspaper.

I pointed out there was no report of it in the British press and
the officer reiterated that "even though it was 23 years ago",
they remembered that both crew members had been killed.
I asked if it was known whether anyone else had ever submitted a
similar FOIA request and was informed that at least one was
received last year.

The officer then noted that most FOIA queries processed
concerning RAF Bentwaters or RAF Woodbridge were about 'UFOs'.

I said nothing.


Having had time to consider this bewildering conversation, I
would be confident the officer is in fact recalling another
incident.

On 29 April 1980, an Upper Hayford based F-111E crashed on
Mapperton Farm Estate, near Almer, Dorset and indeed, both crew
members were killed.

This was prominently reported.

Eventually, a formal USAF response will doubtless clarify.


James.

Hi Rebecca,

Cash-Landrum will of course be of particular interest to you!

I can now reveal some more from ongoing developments.

As mentioned, this contact has a distinguished military career
and although Cash-Landrum is of inherent intrigue to ourselves,
given its nature, it's such an awkward incident to highlight and
ask questions about.

I had hoped, at worst, he would be willing to discuss even the
general background to 'Task Force 158', especially overall
activities in Texas during late 1980.

As, in truth, that proverbial bigger picture is personally of
more importance and interest, this was the approach taken, with
only a cursory reference to Cash-Landrum observations.


The outcome has been a privileged insight into formation of 'Task
Force 158' and all activities from its inception during May 1980,
through to December 1980. That encompasses particulars of all
bases used by the special task force and code names of all
operations.

It's information not to be found on any web site and seemingly
unpublished, period.


This was a point expressed to myself; that early history of 'Task
Force 158' has never fully been documented and what subsists is
only "bits and pieces" with never, "a complete or accurate
account of what took place out there in the western mountains and
deserts between May 1980 to Dec 1980".

I expect it's because of my stated intention to redress same, I
have now been entrusted with an appreciably insightful first-hand
account.

Great result; great deal of work now required.


In, 'The Age of the UFO', a recommended book with an
"introduction by Dr J. Allen Hynek" and "edited by Peter
Brookesmith", there's a lengthy article on Cash-Landrum.
Reporting comparative 'UFO' sightings the day previously, it's
noted that "residents of Ohio County, Kentucky" had witnessed
"strange moving lights" and how when a helicopter arrived on
scene, the "UFOS left".

lights", aka "UFOS', were not contemporarily being seen in

Any targeted FOIA request is always capable of producing
unexpected results and ongoing is one I had submitted re the
Cash-Landrum case:

[BEGIN]
I am requesting any information or records pertaining to
operations involving 'Task Force 158', a forerunner to the
legendary Night Stalkers. This is the genesis as told by the
Night Stalkers themselves:

"After the failure of Operation RICE BOWL, the attempted U.S.
hostage rescue in Iran in April 1980, the United States Army
began testing and evaluation to develop special operations
aviation capabilities. Volunteers were selected from the 101st
Aviation Group's C/158 and D/158 (UH-60), A/159th (CH-47), and
B/229th (OH-6) to form and develop tactics, techniques and
procedures for aviation in special operations mission profiles.

The 101st Airborne Division (AASLT) provided the UH-60s and CH-
47s while the National Guard initially provided the OH-6s. The
101st was selected because it had recently fielded the UH-60
Black Hawk helicopter, which was already proven to be extremely
reliable and safe while conducting demanding mission.
Additionally, the 101st possessed a large number of CH-47 medium
lift helicopters that could complement the smaller Black Hawks
and agile OH-6.

Beginning in June 1980, intensive training was conducted focusing
on long range, low level, flying at night with primitive full-
faced AN/PVS-5 night vision goggles. As proficiency increased,
mission profiles became more demanding and complex - challenging
the Task Force to develop additional capabilities of blacked-out
and close formation flight. The testing and evaluation resulted
in the development of the light helicopter company, the extended
range and lift UH-60, and the extended range FARP capable CH-47".

Bringing the Night Stalkers story up to date:

"Upon resolution of the hostage crisis early 1981, the Army
recognized that it took a great deal of time, training, and
resources to develop the unique capabilities to accomplish
special operations mission and there may not be sufficient time
to prepare and respond to future crisis. The decision was made to
form a standing Army Special Operations Aviation Task Force known
as Task Force 160 consisting of volunteers from Task Force 158.
The 160th quickly established a reputation in the Special
Operations community as a unit that could deliver: always at the
right place at the right time with the right assets. On 1 April
1982, Task Force 160 was designated as the 160th Aviation
Battalion. However, the 160th continued to be referred to as Task
Force 160 until the present".

Specifically, I request any information or records pertaining to
operations involving 'Task Force 158' during December 1980, in
Texas.

This should encompass all training exercises and any incidents
arising from them which involved members of the public.
[END]


In 'Voyager Newsletter - Issue No. 9', I first suggested a
connection:

[BEGIN]
I believe a military 'special ops' training exercise was at least
in part responsible for another classic UFO encounter, a drama
which was soon to unfold on the other side of the Atlantic.

During the evening of 29th December, 1980, Betty Cash, Vickie
Landrum and Colby Landrum were travelling along Highway FM1485 in
eastern Texas. It was a quiet road in a sparsely populated area.

They noticed a bright light above the trees and as it descended
towards them, it hovered at tree-top level.

Diamond-shaped and much larger than their car, the object
intermittently expelled a 'cone of fire', apparently downwards.
This caused it to rise slightly, similar to a hot-air balloon
using a burner to keep aloft.

The object also reportedly glowed brightly and something emitted
an occasional beeping noise.

With the object now above the road, the witnesses got out of
their car, reportedly experiencing an intense heat and light from
the object.

Suddenly, a large number of helicopters appeared overhead,
seemingly arriving from all directions. The unidentified object
was then lost from sight behind some trees and the helicopters
left.

Driving further on, the object and helicopters were again seen in
close proximity. The witnesses counted 23 helicopters and these
were identified as mainly CH-47 Chinooks, plus faster single-
rotor helicopters, similar to a Bell-Huey.

The witnesses apparently all suffered from illness afterwards,
with Betty Cash, who was closest to the object, being the most
poorly. It's generally assumed this was directly related to the
incident.


Despite extensive enquiries, no trace of the helicopters' origins
was ever found, with Houston Airport unable to assist and
military bases in Texas and Louisiana denying any possible
involvement.

It remained a mystery.

One statement came from the US Army's Fort Hood press officer,
Major Tony Geishauser, who confirmed no aircraft from that base
were in the Houston area at the time. He commented, "I don't know
any other place around here that would have that number of
helicopters. I don't know what it could be... unless there's a
super secret thing going on and I wouldn't necessarily know about
it".

It's a point which I can maybe help substantiate in this case.
Although there could now be a rational explanation for the
brightly glowing, diamond-shaped object, that's still the subject
of investigation and is left aside for now.

However, of arguably more importance, I can identify the special
operations unit who would appear to be most likely responsible
for the helicopters witnessed.

It seems this was probably 'Task Force 158', a forerunner to the
legendary Night Stalkers.
[END]


I can now reveal there is documentary evidence which confirms
that during late 1980, a named USAF base in Texas was being used
by a large number of 'Task Force 158' CH-47 Chinooks.

It wasn't Fort Hood and Major Tony Geishauser correctly surmised,
"...unless there's a super secret thing going on and I wouldn't
necessarily know about it".

The related operations couldn't in fact have been any more "super
secret".


In a new and recent breakthrough, I have also located and
contacted someone who served with 'Task Force 158' during that
formative period.

Those top-secret 1980 operations are the real story and I asked a
simple question of him, "Can that story now be told?"

The answer, so far, is affirmative.

He has a distinguished military career and is documented as being
involved with a landmark combat incident.

It's seemingly the most promising lead ever in this case and like
ongoing FOIA processing, we shall see what's revealed.

Given the nature of 'Cash-Landrum' and that possibility of
civilians being seriously injured as a consequence of reported
events, I have proceeded with due caution.

Potentially, this is proverbially treading on dangerous ground,
for a number of reasons I'm now acutely aware of.

[BEGIN]
I request that a copy of the following documents are provided:

in the vicinity of RAF Woodbridge.

2) Any records pertaining to the loss of a bomb/missile from an

hear the reply, "I believe so".

the officer reiterated that "even though it was 23 years ago",
they remembered that both crew members had been killed.

similar FOIA request and was informed that at least one was
received last year.

The officer then noted that most FOIA queries processed
concerning RAF Bentwaters or RAF Woodbridge were about 'UFOs'.

I said nothing.

would be confident the officer is in fact recalling another
incident.

On 29 April 1980, an Upper Hayford based F-111E crashed on
Mapperton Farm Estate, near Almer, Dorset and indeed, both crew
members were killed.

This was prominently reported.

curious case from the 17th century in which a genuine
anomalous phenomenon _may_ have been observed and
given a religious interpretation. The following is
from my notes and the translation is my own:

*****************************************************
A fascinating case was included in a small volume
written by Silva-Caldas in 1879. The sighting took
place on January 29th 1640 and was recorded for
posterity because it coincided with an important
moment in Portuguese history: the discussions that
would eventually lead to Portugal’s political
independence. We do not know what it was that they saw
in the sky (or ‘on the moon,’ though this cannot be
taken literally) over Braga but it was probably round
and flat because they thought it was thought to be a
consecrated wafer. Two humanoid entities were seen to
accompany it. The following is the complete text
referring to the ‘miracle,’ the original of which is
in Portuguese:

***

Apparition of a Wafer in the sky in Braga in 1640.

Favouring the fortune of Portuguese glory
Correia de Melo – Joanneida
Cant. X Oit. 133

Two prodigious cases are described in our history,
which amazed Portugal during the restoration of 1640,
and heightened the belief amongst our ancestors that
the sky had to be protected from the Spanish.
The first sign was the stretching out of the Arm of
the Image of Christ in Lisbon, as a sign of approval
of the liberation of our autonomy, oppressed for 60
years by the tyranny of the Kings [King Philip - CJA].

The second apparition was that of a wafer in the
firmament over Braga, also seen from other distant
points, understood by all as amazing proof of the
divine assistance given to our daring patriots.

Here is the document pertaining to the prodigy of
Braga, transcribed from the Favores do Ceo [Celestial
Favours], from the bookseller Francisco Lopes, of
Lisbon, reprinted in Braga in April 1878 with
preliminary considerations from Dr. Pereira Caldas,
high school professor in that city:

“Year of the birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1641, May
9th, in this city of Braga, in the lodgings of
Reverend Doctor Jao d’Abreda Rocha, ecclesiastic judge
and general vicar of this court, the archbishop of
Braga: there the Reverend Judge was alerted by D.
Gastao Coutinho, general of the province of Entre
Douro e Minho, of the fact that many people going
towards the area of Porto acting upon a warning given
in this city that the enemies were approaching in
that area, saw some signs on the moon, in which there
appeared a Wafer and two human figures that looked
like Angels; and that the said judge know the truth of
it: about which the Reverend Doctor ordered this writ
to be made, that I sign; and he asked the following
witnesses. Father Simao Alvares, apostolic notary,
wrote it.”

***
******************************************************

Regards,

Chris

Hi list,

One thing that bothers me about these attempts to find
UFOs in ancient art is that the more Adamski-like the
object appears to be, the happier the UFO-seekers
become. This makes very little sense and is far more
telling of the "art critic" than of the art itself.

Another problem in finding UFO-like objects in old
religious paintings is that it is difficult to imagine
the chain of events that would have converted a casual
sighting by someone in the community into a correct
depiction of the object by the artist. Would the
witness have spoken to the artist in order to get the
full details, or were painters time and again
fortunate enough to see UFOs themselves?

There is also the question of why a religious painting
should depict a UFO at all. There were many
unexplained aerial phenomena at the time, ranging from
meteorites to ball lightning and other electromagnetic
effects. Why would anyone have singled out a UFO of
the kind we study for their painting of Christ?

Chris

Brian,

I wouldn't go so far as suggesting a hot-air balloon is
responsible for the Cash-Landrum sighting [the Socorro scenario
has been around for a few years now and they're unrelated],
merely noting that the object did not always require its 'flame
propulsion system' to remain aloft.

As highlighted, "how to explain its reportedly, quite phenomenal,
well over a hundred feet away, heat output".

I don't have the answer to that question, although if it exists
and _is_ related to 'task force 158' [from now on, simply called
TF158], I know precisely where to look for it.

That's ongoing and meantime I can say that my contact who served
with TF158 wasn't involved with those late 1980 operations.

He has offered one intriguing suggestion for the 'UFO', however,
it doesn't equate with the evidence.

I should perhaps add, at least not as we know it.

This whole issue of such intense heat and what was seemingly
radiation poisoning not making sense, inherently questions
whether the witnesses recollections are accurate.

Although no reason whatsoever to doubt Betty Cash and Vicki
Landrum's integrity, their story wasn't told until several days
later.

If someone didn't want that story told, or decided to influence
it in some way, I'm sure they would have had ample opportunity.

Mere speculation, however, we should perhaps keep in mind that
TF158's training exercises were part of a much bigger picture
which was to be kept absolutely secret, at seemingly almost any
cost.

Aside from the USAF, there was also a keen CIA interest in doing
so.

I'll post some more on that background shortly.

Meanwhile, I would recommend taking a look at the following
articles on operation, 'Credible Sport':

http://www.projectblack.net/credible.html

http://www.spectrumwd.com/c130/articles/Credible_Sport.htm


The latter especially is a fascinating insight. Note how highly
classified the operation was and that "every pertinent Air Force
regulation was violated".

During this period, some of the covert operations were a law unto
themselves.

James,

I'm really, really looking forward to learning more about this.
You have me on the edge of my chair.

> 3. I note one claim that the road surface underneath was
> damaged

I'm not sure if this will help, but I recall seeing photo of
the damaged road. I can't say for sure where I saw it, but it
could have been one of two places. I think it's very likely
that I saw the photo in the early '90s at one of John
Schuessler's VISIT meetings in Clear Lake City. It is also
possible that I saw the photo on a television program about the
incident. I remember the photo showing a stretch of two lane
blacktop that was severly damaged with narrow ripples/bumps
that ran across the roadway (from shoulder to shoulder),
somewhat resembling a washboard. The center yellow line was
extremely wavy. If I remember this from a TV program rather
than an actual photo, it could have been a re-creation.

But now I'm having second thoughts on this. This could all be a
false memory. I'm thinking now that when I heard Schuessler
speak of the incident, he might have described the road, not
having seen it himself, but describing it from someone else's
reporting of the damage. I do remember him saying that the road
was repaired very quickly. That remark leads me to believe that
he didn't get photos of it.

[snip]

> When Betty Cash reportedly says, "fire would shoot out of it
> and
> then it would let up, when it would let up", could that
> possibly
> be 'light up', not 'let up'?
>
> No-where else in the transcript does she use a terminology,
> "let
> up" to describe said object intermittently rising.

Could be either way. I would not be surprised to hear someone
from that area of Texas to use the words 'let up' to describe a
sound or brightnes of light. Alternatively, 'lit' could have
been used incorrectly as a past tense of the word light. These
people were from East Texas, where the language is, uhm, really
interesting, to say the least. <G> Misusage and different
pronunciations are certainly not an anomaly in that part of the
state.

For the past four years I worked very near the area of the
sighting and came in contact with many people from East Texas.
Having heard these people speak on a daily basis, nothing would
surprise me.


Rebecca

From: James Easton <voyager@jeaston.com>

Regarding:

>From: "Chris Gibson" <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>
>Date: Fri, 16 May 2003 08:12:46 +0100
>Subject: RE: [UFORL] Cash-Landrum + Chinooks

Chris wrote:

>These twelve CH-47 Chinooks. Could they have actually been
>Vertol CH-46 Sea Knights belonging to the US Marine Corps? Any-
>one checked that out? The USAF don't use Chinooks, whereas the
>US Army use loads.

Chris,

I can now reveal that the connection with TF158 and Texas during
late 1980 was Reese AFB, in Lubbock.

I noted it wasn't a big secret and that's because it's confirmed
on the 'official Night Stalkers' web site.

The background to those Army Chinooks and a whole lot more is
explained therein, see:

http://www.nightstalkers.com/history/1.html


I'm pleased to say I have persuaded my contact within TF158 that
his first-hand insight can be published and he's also agreed to
be identified as the source.

This will make any progress much easier, especially being able to
identify him when contacting others who served during that
formative May to December period.

I won't name said source for now.

That online history is apparently not entirely accurate and this
is a point he seems keen to correct.

In summary, he explained:

"The second attempt, 'Honey Badger', was never executed as
fortunately the hostages were released. Its planning and training
were top secret at the time.
Since then I have never read a complete or accurate account of
what took place out there in the western mountains and deserts
between May 1980 to Dec 1980. We only find bits and pieces here
and there. Even the Night Stalker website description of
operation 'Honey Badger' is flawed. It's probably due to the fact
that the operation, or operations, had a sort of planning creep
due to a changing hostage situation and/or location. Different
people participating in that later stages from the former.

'Honey Badger', the training that I participated in, started in
late May 1980 and was completed by Aug 1980. We fully expected to
deploy at that time. However, we were released and sworn to
secrecy back to our home base at Fort Campbell Ky.

That training, 'Honey Badger' involved the original cast
operating out of Norton AFB California, Dugway Proving Grounds
Utah and White Sands, New Mexico. There were no OH-6 involved
then. Only Army Uh-60s, Ch-47ds, Air Force H-53 pavelow
helicopters and C-130 aircraft. I am sure the 'Honey Badger'
execution was to be very similar to the first rescue attempt.


The one main weakness of the first attempt was the helicopter
element. That is, we had Marine pilots flying Navy helos
conducting an Army aviation mission. Long range night vision
goggle flights through mountains and over desert.

The problem with Army aviation in April 1980 was we were not
trained to that capability as we had just received the Uh-60, so
in May 1980 a decision was made to obtain that mission capability
using the Uh-60 and conduct the second attempt to free the
hostages using Army aviation flying Delta Force and Army Rangers
in Army Uh-60s supported by Army Ch-47d, Air Force H-53 pavelow
and C-130 transports.

That was 'operation Honey Badger'.


After returning to Ft Campbell add on operations which took place
from Aug 1980 until Dec 1980, of which I have only second hand
information; I did not participate.

That's when the Oh-6 'Little Bird' was added to the original task
force with an entirely new plan in mind.

That's the training witnessed in Texas.


Although the second rescue attempt was not required due to their
release in Jan 1981, the lessons learned from 'Honey Badger' and
the long term benefits to our military aviation training, in
particular to special operations, had become quite obvious to
those of us who were involved".


Presently designated the 160th Special Operations Aviation
Regiment (Airborne), the 'Night Stalkers' remain based at Fort
Campbell, Kentucky.

I recently highlighted:

[BEGIN]
In, 'The Age of the UFO', a recommended book with an
"introduction by Dr J. Allen Hynek" and "edited by Peter
Brookesmith", there's a lengthy article on Cash-Landrum.
Reporting comparative 'UFO' sightings the day previously, it's
noted that "residents of Ohio County, Kentucky" had witnessed
"strange moving lights" and how when a helicopter arrived on
scene, the "UFOS left".

It's now evident that the surprise would be if "strange moving
lights", aka 'UFOs', were not contemporarily being seen in
Kentucky, with one or more accompanying helicopters.
[END]

And we can now understand why.


As previously mentioned, between August to December 1980 there
were at least three more operations which superseded 'Honey
Badger' and I was informed of their names. This information is
not in the public domain and currently subject to numerous FOIA
requests.


Tim and Bob's helpful comments re the 1980 election duly noted,
there seems to be a conflict of evidence about whether a second
hostage rescue attempt was a realistic prospect and if TF158 were
to be involved.

Operation 'Credible Sport', apparently aborted in October 1980,
was reportedly to entail commandos aboard the modified C-130,
with helicopters already having been proven unreliable for such a
mission.

Yet, one source within TF158 claims they were only ordered to
"stand down" after Reagan won the election, see:

http://www.nightstalkers.com/articles/
If 'Credible Sport' had been aborted in October, how does the
following relate:

"Barely six months after a botched April 1980 US attempt to
rescue American hostages from Iran, Major General James Vaught,
of the Pentagon's Joint Staff, asked permission for several
'Blackbird' reconnaissance flights in the Gulf region, 'to assist
in selection of low level air penetration routes.' In his letter,
Vaught mentioned a possible 'US military contingency action' in
the region, a reference interpreted by experts from the archive
as an indication that the United States was planning a second
hostage-rescue mission".

See:

http://www.jang.com.pk/thenews/oct2002-daily/18-10-
2002/world/w6.htm

Another source confirms Vaught's letter dates from October.

There's an inherent story which it seems has never fully been
told.


One reason for ongoing TF158 training is reportedly that before
the end of 1980 they had upgraded from 2nd generation 'night-
vision goggles' [NVGs] to 3rd generation NVGs.


In general, what seems to be an objective online summary of the
hostage crisis and why it ended without the need for further U.S.
military action, is:

http://xenohistorian.faithweb.com/neareast/ne17e.html


A TF158 connection to Cash-Landrum seems evident, although only
in respect of the helicopters reported and, currently, nothing
else.

Chris, List:

The specific quote provided, from The UFO Encyclopedia, 2nd
Edition, by Jerome Clark. 1998, Omnigraphics Inc.
(ISBN 0-7808-0097-4), Volume 1: A-K p. 177,

"...the policeman and his wife [who had reported seeing 12
Chinook helicopters in the Huffman area on the night of the
incident] "

seems to indicate that the words "who had reported seeing 12
Chinook helicopters" was an insertion by the editor (ie. Jerry
Clark), not necessarily the actual words of the witnesses.

Do we know what these witnesses said in their own words?

Are we sure that we're not embarking on the usual Ufological
wild goose chase?

Bob Young

strength.&nbsp; This is why lead is often used to shield those operating the equipment

the skin as well as Beta. Both are more dangerous if inhaled/eaten or enter through a
wound (via contamination).&nbsp; Gamma and neutron radiation is highly
damaging.<BR>

<BR>

(if it melted, it would probably include the fingertips)?"<BR>
<BR>
I am not sure but the date was December 1980.&nbsp; Temperatures do get cool in
Texas at that time of year.&nbsp; Perhaps they were linking the event with the fact
their car heater may have been up on high causing the dashboard to be warm.&nbsp;
Just a guess but you never know.&nbsp; <BR>
<BR>
"It seems to me that if the symptoms claimed by Betty actually<BR>
happened, and were caused by radiation, she would be dead. Almost<BR>
immediate sickness, etc? "<BR>
<BR>
Betty would have been exposed to several REM to get this exposure.&nbsp; It seems
that Vicki and Colby were not as exposed but they did not have much shielding
except for the shell of the car, which for a high radiation field is not much. To reduce
the levels by 1/10th, requires about 4 inches of steel.&nbsp; A car may have a thin
layer of perhaps a half-inch or less.&nbsp; They should have had similar
effects.&nbsp; Take a look at:<BR>
<BR>
<A
HREF="http://www.science.uwaterloo.ca/~cchieh/cact/nuctek/safetyexposure.html">
http://www.science.uwaterloo.ca/~cchieh/cact/nuctek/safetyexposure.html</A><BR>
<BR>
There you will discover that Betty's symptoms indicate and exposure of at least100
REM!&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Consider this and then let's talk about our helicopter
pilots who don't have very much shielding in their choppers.&nbsp; Radiation from a
point source falls off by the square of the distance from the source.&nbsp; Betty was
probably at a distance of 3 times that of the pilots.&nbsp; This means they would
have been exposed to 9 times (This is a minimum value since the source would not
become a point source, the closer you got to it) what Betty was making them receive a
generous 900 REM (The pilots also appeared to be exposed for much longer than
Betty making their dose even greater).&nbsp; This is FATAL!&nbsp; Even if we fool
with the distances and add some generous shielding, the pilots still end up
DEAD!&nbsp; I know of no reports that indicate any mass loss of a helicopter pilots
during the time period.&nbsp; The sickness Betty reports could easily have been
something else.&nbsp; Maybe food poisoning or something akin to that which she
immediately related to the "encounter".<BR>
<BR>
"Is there any physical evidence collected by anybody to support this<BR>
tale?"<BR>
<BR>
I am not so sure that the "physical evidence" supposedly obtained by the researchers
involved. It definitely makes a good story but, as in most UFO cases, when closely
examined a lot of the "good evidence" fades/melts away.&nbsp; <BR>
<BR>
Tim Printy<BR>

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Mon, 12 May 2003 14:50:57 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Major 1959 sighting in N.M.?

1959 was sort of one of those blah years in UFO history. Not much went
on.

The only case in my files in that area in 1959 was the Elko NV case.
The flashbulb failed, and the object in the photo was a ceiling light
in the next room.

The only other significant cases in 1959 which are in my files are:

- The Redmond Oregon Radar-Visual case
- The crash of "something" on the Norwegian island of Spitzbergen
- The Reverend Gill case (Boianai, Papua New Guinea)
- The Sumner WA military plane crash (dubious UFO link)
- The Killian case (Phillipsburg PA)
- The Piata Beach, Itapoan Brazil photos (now known to be photos of a
Collaro record changer drive wheel thrown in the air)
- The Diamond Head, Waikiki HI photo of a lamp reflected in a window.

I have seen too many UFO cases where independent events combined in the
observers' mind to create a strange occurrence. You might even recognize
some of these cases:

- A seagull, a car much farther away, and the sounds of construction
machinery behind a hill, combined into a report of a "bird shaped jet
powered UFO chasing a car".

- A farmer burning his fields off, and a prank played by kids, combined
into a CE-III case.

- Mars low on the horizon, some fire balloons, new streetlights seen
scintillating on the horizon, and a garbage dump fire, combined into a
week-long flap of UFO sightings.

- Three balloons, two RADAR operator errors, a weather RADAR return, and
some military officers settling a wager, combined into a major UFO case
at a military base.

- Two RADAR sets interfering with each other, anomalous propagation, ice
crystals, and blowing seeds, combined into another military sighting.
- Two airplanes without flight plans, another plane off course, a long
distance telephone line failure, a RADAR second-trip echo, and a dozing
radio operator, combined to almost send us to nuclear war.

- A fire balloon, the planet Venus, and a kid riding his motorcycle in
circles while waiting for his date, created a CE-II crop circle case.

- Many airplanes coming to and from a major airport were reported as
one object flying back and forth.

@ Larry wrote:

@ "X-ray, ultraviolet, and infrared are easily stopped by metal. Paper

@ I don't think that X-rays can be stopped by metal although it can be
@ reduced in strength.

It depends on the strength of the X-rays. We used aluminum shields in
an X-ray crystallography lab, and they reduced the beam to a safe level.

@ Alpha can be stopped by the skin as well as Beta.

@ Both are more dangerous if inhaled/eaten or enter through a wound (via
@ contamination).

No, it's the alpha or beta emitting ATOMS which are dangerous if they
get
inside the body, not the rays themselves. If the atom is incorporated
into
structural or genetic material, it is like a little time bomb waiting to
go off.

Then, when it emits its ray, it CHANGES INTO AN ATOM OF ANOTHER
ELEMENT.
This new element forms a different chemical compound in place of the old
one. If the change takes place in a crucial part, it can mutate or kill
the cell.

Suppose a beta-emitting atom of sulfur emits its beta ray. It changes
into
a chlorine atom, changing the compound it is in into something else.

@ Gamma and neutron radiation is highly damaging.

@ In any case, it seems that Betty's illness does not seem to be
radiation
@ related.

@ Tim Printy

Actually, it reminds me of a case of insecticide poisoning.

Several thoughts:

1. There are several types of radiation to consider besides nuclear:

- x-ray
- ultraviolet
- infrared

2. Among nuclear radiations, there are several types with different
properties:

- alpha
- beta
- antibeta
- gamma
- neutron
- proton
- antiproton

3. There is no evidence concerning the distance to the UFO except the
statements of the witnesses. And unless the object went in front of or
behind something, cast shadows, approached within 30 feet (two
car-lengths), or in some other way revealed its true distance, there
is no way the witnesses could have determined the distance. Their
statements are nothing but guesses.

4. Remember that the human visual system is not equipped to measure
distance beyond 30 feet without additional information.

5. Given that, the UFO could have been much closer to the witnesses
than it was to the helicopters.

6. X-ray, ultraviolet, and infrared are easily stopped by metal. Paper
can stop alpha rays.

Questions and comments on Cash-Landrum:

1. Is there actual evidence of the fingerprints "melted" into the dash?

2. Nail-polish remover could do the same thing to the dash. Acetone was
a common ingredient in nail-polish remover during that period. It melts
plastic.

3. Is it possible that the UFO story was concocted to explain injuries
caused by some other source (such as playing with a high voltage spark
coil and a Crookes tube for long periods)?

4. There were some quack cures being sold during that time. They were
cloth-covered plastic bags filled with uranium mine tailings.

5. Were the injuries more consistent with nuclear, X-ray, ultraviolet,
or infrared exposure.

6. There are several military air bases in the area.

- LBJ Space Center, Houston
- Corpus Christi NAS
- Chase Field NAS, Beeville
- Lackland AFB, San Antonio
- Kelly AFB, San Antonio
- Martindale Army Airfield, San Antonio
- Randolph AFB, San Antonio
- Bergstrom AFB, Austin
- Fort Hood, Killeen
- Matagorda Is. AFB
- Carswell AFB, Ft Worth
- Dallas NAS
- Barksdale AFB, Shreveport LA
- Fort Polk, LA

There are also many Naval Weapons Reservations in the area, but
I do not know if they have air capabilities.

7. I have seen several night hot air balloon flights, so I do
know that they happen.

8. In the case of a metal cable dangling from a hot air balloon,
that WOULD have been an emergency. It might be that a cable
intended for securing the balloon once it lands accidentally fell
overboard, with one end still secured to the balloon. The other
end then fouled in power lines. If the balloon had landed at that
point, the crew could have been electrocuted.

9. It is always possible that several events totally unrelated to
each other combined to produce the effects reported in the sighting.
This is something that must always be considered in any UFO case.

Tim,

I've come across a couple of insightful online articles.

Both feature an interview with the same person who served with
TF158 in late 1980. He claims it became evident that TF158's
involvement in a second hostage rescue mission was dependent of
the presidential election. If Carter had been re-elected, the
mission would have been undertaken. If Reagan won, it was likely
the hostages would be released.

Within hours of Reagan being declared 'victorious', TF158 were
told to 'stand down'.

So far as I'm aware, the election was held in early November,
1980.

Although I'm not sure when Reagan was formally pronounced to be
America's new President, he was inaugurated on 20 January, 1981.

The hostages were of course released that same day.


When it's alleged that, 'within hours of Reagan being declared
victorious', TF158 were told to back off, that could directly
relate to Reagan being sworn in ['victorious'] and news of the
hostages release on 20 January.

It would make sense.

If that's the factual scenario, then as at 29 December, 1980,
TF158 could still have been training for a second rescue attempt.
The point being, as you note, we can't rule out any such modified
USAF vehicle potentially being part of that latter mission
strategy.


I have located said interviewee, still serving with the 'Night
Stalkers' and if he's prepared to discuss those contemporary
Cash-Landrum exercises, then we're possibly into the heart of
this case.


Outwith Cash-Landrum, is there perhaps a more 'involved' story.

Que, 'The October Surprise' and "allegations that members of the
Reagan/Bush campaign cut a secret deal with the revolutionary
government in Iran before the 1980 election".

See, for example and quoted therein:

http://www.sumeria.net/politics/oct-sur.html


See also, aforementioned:

http://www.spectrumwd.com/c130/articles/Credible_Sport.htm

Which states:

"A test was scheduled for three days before the planned mission
date in October. If the tests were successful, the mission would
be a GO".

"In the end, they said, 'Don't come'. The Iranian leaders wanted
to end the hostage situation but wanted to save face. The
hostages were released shortly after President Reagan was sworn
in".

Some might question why operation 'Credible Sport' was aborted in
October 1980 and the catalyst for reportedly, 'the Iranian
leaders wanted to end the hostage situation', at that time.

Perhaps also why the hostages were not released until the day
Reagan was formally established as President.

Rebecca,

At present, all three are separate elements, with no proof they
are connected.

That acknowledged, I'm not comfortable with the idea that three
strange happenings occurred at almost the same time.

I would conclude; if the object truly did emit such intense heat,
then that's so exceptional it relates to the subsequent injuries.

I would have to then conclude both in tandem are even more
exceptional and are likely to relate to whatever those
helicopters were involved with.

The heat and injuries remain for now a mystery. The helicopters
do not.

Before going any further, it should be noted that both Tim Printy
and yourself have kindly agreed to take on board some further
background information outwith the list. This exclusively
concerns TF158 - I know no more about the enigmatic object than
revealed on the list and that's only what was gleaned from
information already published!


One important issue was identifying to both Tim and yourself the
person involved in the early days of TF158 I had contacted. If I
refer to my 'contact', at least subscribers can be reassured
someone else knows who he is and also how he was located.

That also acknowledged, I can reveal this person has further
explained the role of TF158 in Texas between August 1980 and
December 1980, inclusive.

TF158 had been formed with one mission in mind - rescuing the
hostages in Iran.

After the catastrophic failure of the first rescue attempt, it
was realised that a suitable task force for such missions simply
did not exist.

TF158 trained for a second rescue mission and during August 1980,
the OH-6 'Little Bird' helicopter was added to their inventory.

It was directly as a result of this new capability - a single
rotor helicopter which could carry four people, was small, quiet,
could land in restricted spaces and could also have weapons
mounted giving air support to ground troops - that TF158 moved
their training to Texas and Oklahoma.

The mission strategy and planning changed.

Either Betty Cash and Vicki Landrum mistakenly reported seeing
the key components of a then *absolutely top-secret* special
operations unit - a large number of both Chinooks and
unidentified, smaller, single-rotor helicopters in unison - or it
was TF158.

I'll go with it being TF158.

If one third of our mystery is solved, the other two-thirds
pieces of the puzzle would hopefully then fall into place.

Instead, it seems any rational scenario falls into pieces.

In summary, he explained:

"The second attempt, 'Honey Badger', was never executed as
fortunately the hostages were released. Its planning and training
were top secret at the time.
Since then I have never read a complete or accurate account of
what took place out there in the western mountains and deserts
between May 1980 to Dec 1980. We only find bits and pieces here
and there. Even the Night Stalker website description of
operation 'Honey Badger' is flawed. It's probably due to the fact
that the operation, or operations, had a sort of planning creep
due to a changing hostage situation and/or location. Different
people participating in that later stages from the former.

'Honey Badger', the training that I participated in, started in
late May 1980 and was completed by Aug 1980. We fully expected to
deploy at that time. However, we were released and sworn to
secrecy back to our home base at Fort Campbell Ky.

That training, 'Honey Badger' involved the original cast
operating out of Norton AFB California, Dugway Proving Grounds
Utah and White Sands, New Mexico. There were no OH-6 involved
then. Only Army Uh-60s, Ch-47ds, Air Force H-53 pavelow
helicopters and C-130 aircraft. I am sure the 'Honey Badger'
execution was to be very similar to the first rescue attempt.


The one main weakness of the first attempt was the helicopter
element. That is, we had Marine pilots flying Navy helos
conducting an Army aviation mission. Long range night vision
goggle flights through mountains and over desert.

The problem with Army aviation in April 1980 was we were not
trained to that capability as we had just received the Uh-60, so
in May 1980 a decision was made to obtain that mission capability
using the Uh-60 and conduct the second attempt to free the
hostages using Army aviation flying Delta Force and Army Rangers
in Army Uh-60s supported by Army Ch-47d, Air Force H-53 pavelow
and C-130 transports.

That was 'operation Honey Badger'.


After returning to Ft Campbell add on operations which took place
from Aug 1980 until Dec 1980, of which I have only second hand
information; I did not participate.

That's when the Oh-6 'Little Bird' was added to the original task
force with an entirely new plan in mind.

That's the training witnessed in Texas.


Although the second rescue attempt was not required due to their
release in Jan 1981, the lessons learned from 'Honey Badger' and
the long term benefits to our military aviation training, in
particular to special operations, had become quite obvious to
those of us who were involved".

Regiment (Airborne), the 'Night Stalkers' remain based at Fort
Campbell, Kentucky.

REBECCA ET AL. --

>The same applies to the dashboard.

If one looks at the rather murky photo of the dashboard in John Schuessler's
book, the damage looks just like that caused by exposure to the sun over a
period of years, and there are no finger imprints evident. Practically every car
that spends a lot of time parked outside here in New Mexico has a dash like
that. I suspect the southeast Texas sun can be darn near as brutal.

Qualification of the above: Note that the photo is murky, with poor
contrast, and was shot from outside thru the windshield (highly scientific data
collection, that). So it's possible the important features--finger
impressions--were there but either not picked up on film or, if they were, just got
washed out
in the reproduction process for the book.

Why not ask John for a high-quality print of this pic and of any others he or
others took (IF they did)?... -- Cheers, KARL

Rebecca,

This might be more 'UFO' related then you realise!

Some time ago, I mentioned:

[BEGIN]
Added to this was the potential significance of an article Larry
Robinson recalled seeing:

"1965-Feb 1967: I saw an article or ad showing the results of a
multi-state series of hot-air balloon flights. A map was
included, showing the landing points of the balloon and some
amusing anecdotes of things that happened to the balloonists. One
of these was an encounter with a lawman who they thought was
going to shoot it out with them. The balloon freaked him out. The
article said, 'We later found out that he thought he was seeing a
space ship'."


That 1965-Feb 1967 article about a "multi-state series of hot-air
balloon flights" would most likely have been a feature on the
first transcontinental crossing of the U.S. by balloon. This
endeavour was undertaken by a known balloonist between April to
September 1966, a story which appeared in a number of magazines.

As it seems the article Larry remembers must have been written
after the successful crossing, it narrows the publication date to
September 1966-February 1967. Of course, if it was the tale of a
lawman who was startled by a balloon during the 1966 flights, it
couldn't relate to Zamora's 1964 experience. It would have to be
the account of an earlier incident.

Of more consequence now is having identified the 1966 pilot and
obtaining contact details, he should be able to clear up all of
these points first-hand".
[END]


Since then, I've been in touch with Tracy Barnes and indeed,
presently await his reply to a recent letter.

I have also been in contact with Terry Wright, whose daughter,
Beth Wright-Smith, is a renowned balloonist and co-owner of a
major hot-air balloon company in Albuquerque.

Their comments re Socorro '64 will be published in due course.

Like Cash-Landrum, there's a bigger picture, incorporating those
contemporary 1964 'UFO' sightings near the Rio-Grande, where the
then classified 'Albuquerque flights' - of a hot-air balloon -
were taking place.

I [still] await the CIA's response to related and specific FOIA
requests.

List,

While at the library today I ran across this little article
from UPI via the Houston Post on April 10, 1966:

Cross-Country Balloon Hopes To Continue On

SAN DIEGO, Calif -- UPI -- The pilot of a hot-air ballon said
he brought it down Saturday after 10 miles of a scheduled
transcontinental flight because of lack of wind and impending
darkness.

He hopes to continue Sunday.

Tracy Barnes, 27, the pilot, and Terry Wright, both of Chester,
SC, had started the flight from nearby Coronado Saturday
morning.

They brought the balloon down in a field southeast of San Diego
about three hours later. They were not hurt and the balloon was
not damaged.

Plans are to drift across the country, stopping only every 24
hours to refuel.

Barnes said he was concerned that the balloon might drift over
Mexico and he does not have a night flying permit for that
country.

He said the mountains east of San Diego posed problems that he
would rather meet in daylight.

Barnes operates a company which builds balloons.

Lift for the 70-foot-tall balloon is provided by hot air heated
by liquid petroleum gas.

Tim,

That's most interesting and thanks for highlighting same.

It's the generally accepted, 'Honey Badger' history which does
seem to be erroneous.

If we look again at what my contact within TF158 revealed:

"'Honey Badger', the training that I participated in, started in
late May 1980 and was completed by Aug 1980. We fully expected to
deploy at that time. However, we were released and sworn to
secrecy back to our home base at Fort Campbell Ky.

[...]

I am sure the 'Honey Badger' execution was to be very similar to
the first rescue attempt.

[...]

The problem with Army aviation in April 1980 was we were not
trained to that capability as we had just received the Uh-60, so
in May 1980 a decision was made to obtain that mission capability
using the Uh-60 and conduct the second attempt to free the
hostages using Army aviation flying Delta Force and Army Rangers
in Army Uh-60s supported by Army Ch-47d, Air Force H-53 pavelow
and C-130 transports.
That was 'operation Honey Badger'".
[END]


'Honey Badger' did not extend beyond August 1980.

He continues:

"After returning to Ft Campbell add on operations which took
place from Aug 1980 until Dec 1980, of which I have only second
hand information; I did not participate.

That's when the Oh-6 'Little Bird' was added to the original task
force with an entirely new plan in mind.

That's the training witnessed in Texas".


The operations which took place between August and December 1980
[possibly extending into January 1981] were given different code
names. There were at least three of them that I'm aware of and
zero are seemingly in the public domain.

I can find no reference whatsoever to even one of them.

That has to be, inherently, of foremost significance [FOIA
requests ongoing].


If Cash-Landrum is related to TF158, then one of those latter
operations is the connection [presumably last undertaken?], not
'Honey Badger'.

Bottom line; from exceptional insight given by someone who has a
documented, distinguished, military career, the 'Honey Badger'
training was completed and any planned mission aborted in August
1980 [why...?]. Once TF158 acquired the OH-6 'Little Bird', this
significantly enhanced their capabilities and training
recommenced, "with an entirely new plan in mind".

Cash-Landrum is perhaps a quite extraordinarily 'incidental'
[sic] facet of what is evidently a much bigger story that has
never been told.


>Such a hectic schedule might have specially selected troops
>training during a "stand down" period in order to get ready for
>a final dress rehearsal in January. One can never know until all
>the facts about "Honey Badger" is disclosed.
In ongoing FOIA endeavours to locate any information re those
three [at least] subsequent operations, I have also requested any
material concerning 'Honey Badger' and 'Credible Sport'.


>Another thought crossed my mind about the UFO and the CH-47's.
>Although the UFO seems to have been described as being seen up
>close and near to the ground, is it possible that what really
>was seen was some form of refueling exercise with the CH-47s and
>some other aircraft (like a modified C-130 with a searchlight to
>aid in the refueling process)?

I was also wondering about a vehicle being used for refuelling.
It would conceivably make sense as TF158s training involved long
distance night flights using NVGs, yet... how feasible would this
be?

Interesting though. if considered in the context of why 'Eagle
Claw' had failed and subsequent recommendations, see for example:

http://www.fas.org/man/dod-101/ops/eagle_claw.htm


Bottom line, again; some startling new evidence has
coincidentally appeared in my mailbox.

Although it was revealed publicly back in 1994, I would first of
all like to personally thank the person responsible for
highlighting what I believe to be critical testimony and then
have their approval to disclose it.

Meanwhile, I'm sure a preview from that 1994 'informed source' [a
notable researcher and commentator], would be permissible:


"BTW, the object as depicted in the MUFON journals at the time,
and the subsequent UNSOLVED MYSTERIES show was not what the
ladies reported. The ring of lights which is seen around the
middle of the object was not there at all. In fact... Mrs.
Landrum clearly stated that had it not been for the 'flames'
which intermittently roared from its underside, they might have
not seen it at all!

There was also some indication from their descriptions that at
first when they sighted it from a distance, the flames seemed
horizontal which implied that the object might actually have been
travelling 'sideways', and then later upright when it stopped
them in the road.

At times the flames would seem to subside considerably, and then
would flare up again... and there was the beeping noise they
reported.

The ring of lights came from a little illustration that Colby did
using a child's 'Lite Brite' set. Even Mrs. Cash noted that there
were *no* lights on the object. She was surprised to hear that
the 'principle investigator' had included this in the
illustrations which purported to be accurate....(sigh)".
