Crop circles puzzle farmer
May 16, 2003

THE overnight appearance of dozens of bizarre crop circles in a
field of sorghum has spooked a Sunshine Coast hinterland farmer
and his workers.

The phenomenon, which was accompanied by loud "zapping noises",
a flash of green light, lost power and barking dogs has the Gowen
family of Glass House Mountains flumoxed.

Fifth generation land owner Kel Gowen said he was woken about
midnight on Wednesday by two loud "zaps".

His farm hand, Noel Brady, whose cottage overlooks the 4ha of
sorghum, said he was also woken by the first zapping sound, which
was followed by the loss of power and bright green flashes.

Mr Gowen said it was only during a routine check of his property
early yesterday morning that he noticed the 30 flattened circles
in the sorghum.

Mr Gowen said his family had never taken notice of stories of
crop circles or UFOs.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Fri, 30 May 2003 13:49:54 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] November 1661 Tibet

I have a little trouble with that quote:

'My son, what you witnessed just now was not magic,
because beings from other worlds travel across the
oceans of space, and it was they who breathed the
spirit into the first people who lived on this earth.'

It was definitely NOT written or translated in the 17th century, for the
concept of "space" as being a vast expanse of vacuum between worlds did
not yet exist. The word "space" was not yet used for that purpose. Indeed,
the Copernican solar system was just coming into general acceptance at
that time, and most European people were still thinking in terms of
Ptolmaic crystal spheres moving the stars and planets around a stationary
earth.

It's not in 17th century English, either.

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Fri, 30 May 2003 13:27:19 +0100 (BST)
Subject: [UFORL] November 1661 Tibet



I am trying to trace the original source of an
incident that allegedly occurred in 1661. The story is
as follows:

Albert d’Orville, a Belgium Jesuit missionary, was
among the first Europeans to travel to Tibet. In a
diary entry dated November 1661, d’Orville remarked on
his own UFO sighting. “My attention was drawn to
something moving in the heavens,” he wrote. “At first,
I thought it might be a species of bird, unknown to
me, that lived in these regions. Then the object came
nearer…”

What the priest saw was shaped like “a Chinese
double hat” and seemed to rotate as it flew. “The
object winged its way above the city exactly as if it
wished to be admired. It circled twice, and then was
suddenly enshrouded in fog, and as much as I strained
my eyes I could no longer see it.”

D’Orville asked a nearby lama whether he, too, had
seen the object, or whether it had been an
hallucination. The lama’s reply probably left the
Jesuit as astonished as it left me when I first read
Hartwig Hausdorf’s book, The Chinese Roswell, where
d’Orville’s account is reproduced in full:

‘My son, what you witnessed just now was not magic,
because beings from other worlds travel across the
oceans of space, and it was they who breathed the
spirit into the first people who lived on this earth.
These beings condemn all violence; they counsel
mankind to love one another. Their teachings are like
seeds, but if these seeds are sown on rocky ground,
they cannot germinate. These beings, who are
light-skinned, are always received by us in
friendship, and they often come to earth near our
monasteries. They have continued to instruct us,
revealing truths that were lost in the centuries of
cataclysm which have changed the face of the earth.’

The facts:

i) I know for certain that Albert d’Orville did exist
and wrote about his explorations of Tibet in the 1660s
(accompanied by fellow Jesuit Johann Grueber of
Austria, d’Orville travelled on foot from China
through eastern Tibet to Lhasa, and then to India,
between 1661 and 1664).

ii) The English text reproduced above is from Hartwig
Hausdorf’s “The Chinese Roswell” (1994, p.88-89).

iii) Hausdorf took the reference from Der
Gotter-Schock (Munich, 1992), a book written by Swiss
researcher Erich von Däniken. I have not seen this
book, so I don’t know what von Däniken’s source was.

iv) However, a stroke of luck brought me to an
excellent Spanish case-book, “Fenómeno OVNI” Volume
II, published by Inapp, Madrid 1979. On page 391 an
article entitled “Maestros de Otros Mundos en el
Tibet” provides the same alleged diary entry, in
Spanish. It quotes an Italian publication.

v) The source quoted is the book “Los Extraterrestres
Existen” by Gianni Lucarini. This book is unknown to
me.

vi) According to the Spanish article, Lucarini’s
source was the Italian publication “"l'aeronautica di
altri pianetti."

vii) Eduardo Russo checked the Italian publication for
me and found the reference in there, but without a
source. (Eduardo, I never received a photocopy of that
and cannot locate your original e-mail. Can you send
me the details again?)

Can anyone tell me any more?

Chris Aubeck

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 29 May 2003 12:50:51 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)

But more than one type of RADAR exists. The ATC surveillance radar goes
4 rpm (15 sec sweep), but tactical and approach RADARs operate at 15 or
30 rpm (4 or 2 sec sweeps) because the operators need info much quicker
under those conditions. Also, some RADAR sets do not sweep a full
circle,
but sweep back and forth over a small angle.

Also, during a meteor shower, the next sweep might pick up a different
meteor. I was last year for that big shower, and there were plenty of
them around to be picked up. But the sideways effect you describe might
confine the actual detections to a small portion of the sky - making the
scenario seem even more mysterious.

@ -----Original Message-----
@ From: Martin Shough [mailto:mshough@parcellular.fsnet.co.uk]
@ Sent: Thursday, May 29, 2003 6:38 AM
@ To: UFORL@yahoogroups.com
@ Subject: Re: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)
@
@
@ Larry
@
@ Thanks for an admirable and concise summary of many of the factors
@ in radar interpretation. To focus on the specific point you take up:
@
@ However the real situation is as follows:
@
@ Type 80 surveillance radar in use at Trimmingham was a 10 cm set
@ with an unambiguous range of some 250 miles and a scan rate variable
@ from 4 to 6 rpm. The Type 13 heightfinders were also 10 cms with a
@ nod rate of 6 rpm. The proceedure for getting RHI information was
@ for the operator to place an intertrace marker strobe manually through
@ the target on the PPI. This 'told' the Type 13 to rotate to
@ the correct
@ bearing and the height was then displayed on a separate A scope.
@
@ Now imagine a meteor trail tangent to the maximum first-trip drum at a
@ slant range of 255 miles. The recombination rate of the trail
@ ionisation behind the meteor head is only a second or two, or
@ at most a
@ few tens of meters of trail, which means that it will be
@ scanned in effect
@ as a point target. Echoes returned by this point target will be either
@ undetectable or very weak, since effective cross-section is
@ proportional to the square of the wavelength and reflected power is
@ proportional to the cube of the wavelength. Plank's 1956/1959
@ AFCRL studies (and other sources) agree that even at L-band meteor
@ ionisation offers a target at the margin of possible
@ detection. (Meteor
@ radar works at VHF.) At S-band chances are very slim, and this applies
@ to first-trip echoes. Because returned power from a point target drops
@ as the inverse 4th power of the range a meteor beyond the designed
@ range of the radar is especially unlikely to return a signal above the
@ noise level.
@
@ This means that the meteor *must* be scanned at the most favourable
@ orientation, which requires the trail to be at right-angles
@ to the radar
@ line
@ of sight. As the off-perpendicular angle increases away from
@ the normal,
@ this so-called 'radiant condition', in which the ionisation
@ acts like a
@ metallic skin reflector, is lost and at more acute angles the
@ only energy
@ returned will be a vanishing echo from the wake turbulence (equivalent
@ to the scatter from CAT). So we have the meteor trail passing
@ tangentially
@ to the 1st trip covereage at 255 miles, happening to reach closest
@ approach just as the radar antenna rotates past at normal
@ incidence, and,
@ just conceivably, this results in a rather weak echo at a
@ displayed range
@ of 5 miles.
@
@ What will an operator make of this echo? Not much, unless there is a
@ second or a third. As you say, a whole sequence of 2nd trip
@ echoes would
@ describe a distorted course approaching and receeding from the scope
@ centre. But by the time the antenna rotates back to the
@ sector in which the
@ meteor was last scanned, 10-15 seconds later, it will have
@ vaporised and
@ the trail will have recombined. And since the
@ perpendicularity condition
@ for re-radiant echoes still obtains, even if free-electron densities
@ remained
@ extraordinarily high over the duration of two scans the echo
@ would still be
@ displayed in exactly the same place (save for minimal wind
@ drift) and would
@ not constitute the 'track' of a rapid target.
@
@ So for all these reasons your scenario points either to: a)
@ head-echoes
@ from large fireballs within the 1st-trip design range (big enough to
@ override
@ all considerations of inappropriate wavelength and orientation), which
@ could not explain the course change reported from N to W, and
@ could not
@ travel slow enough to be displayed over a number of successive scans,
@ nor give time for operators to azicate the Type 13s and obtain height
@ reports, not to mention scrambling and vectoring fighters - a
@ proceedure
@ taking many minutes; or b) head echoes from truly enormous
@ fireballs at
@ very extreme range, slowed dramatically on the display from tens of
@ thousands of mph to by 3rd- or nth-trip geometry.
@
@ The latter case is at least geometrically and ballistically
@ possible in
@ principle,
@ but at hundreds of miles closest approach and traversing 90 degrees of
@ azimuth between N and W bearings this implies a period of incandesence
@ within the atmosphere over a ground track of maybe thousands of miles
@ for a duration of at least many tens of seconds, which is
@ astronomically
@ outrageous. Such an event may have occurred (there are
@ historical reports
@ of extreme 'meteor' events that you might want to cite, but
@ we'd have to
@ agree on rules for when eyewitness testimony is a valid
@ import!) but more
@ than one super-fireball would seem to be pushing it.
@
@ The witness here is describing a series of events, an afternoon of
@ excitement, " . . .I was able to hear what all the other
@ stations in the
@ chain was seeing - I could hear their plotters directly - and
@ I was also
@ able, by means of my patch panel, to plug into and
@ legitimately listen to
@ conversations between GCI controllers on the ground, and the fighter
@ aircraft which they were attempting to vector onto their
@ targets." It took
@ a long time to scramble a number of aircraft and "eventually"
@ the targets
@ headed away W over the Atlantic.
@
@ The only way of involving meteors is to assume that the
@ 'tracks' of the
@ targets were imagined by the operators interpolating between
@ stochastically distributed single point echoes, each from one
@ of a large
@ number of quite different successive meteors. In these circumstances
@ the Conchoid of Nicomedes is completely irrelevant.
@
@ An explanation like this is just about physically
@ conceivable, but very
@ highly improbable, and would only succeed by shifting the
@ whole problem
@ into a grey psychological area where supposedly 'anything goes'. Some
@ people find this tactic plausible. I'm personally sceptical,
@ especially if
@ it is
@ introduced as a last resort when previously-'plausible'
@ theories based on
@ *accepting* report details are found to fail. Then it becomes
@ ad hoc and
@ unconvincing. I think we'd need more information about the case to
@ conclude that Roy Dent's testimony is corrupted in the way this theory
@ requires.
@
@ Best
@ Martin Shough

From: "Martin Shough" <mshough@parcellular.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 29 May 2003 12:38:25 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)

Larry

Thanks for an admirable and concise summary of many of the factors
in radar interpretation. To focus on the specific point you take up:

>@ d) There really isn't the remotest likelihood that tracks of the sort
>@ described could be caused by meteors.

>I do not see why not. These are exactly the characteristics of second
>and third trip echoes:
>- The speed displayed is a lot slower than the actual speed.
>- The path appears to curve so the closest approach is closer to the
>RADAR set than a straight-line trajectory. The displayed path is in fact
>the closer curve of the Conchoid of Nicomedes:
>r = a * csc(b) - c
>Where a is the distance of the closest point of the true straight-line
>trajectory, b is the angle of the set to the heading of the meteor, c
>is an integer multiple of the range of the radar set, and a is larger
>than c.
>- If the meteor crosses from a third-trip zone into a second trip zone,
>the target's position will suddenly jump, from very near the RADAR set,
>to a position on the same azimuth, but much farther away. When it leaves
>the second trip zone and re-enters the third trip zone, it will likewise
>jump closer, but on the same azimuth.
>- The target should appear to slow down as it gets closer to the RADAR
>set, and speed up as it moves away.

The geometrical situation is in principle broadly as you describe it. On
a PPI with an effectively continuous sampling rate, a VHF frequency
optimised for ionisation returns, and the high peak sensitivity of a modern
meteor research radar, and given a fireball of abnormally long duration,
this situation might conceivably occur on paper.

However the real situation is as follows:

Type 80 surveillance radar in use at Trimmingham was a 10 cm set
with an unambiguous range of some 250 miles and a scan rate variable
from 4 to 6 rpm. The Type 13 heightfinders were also 10 cms with a
nod rate of 6 rpm. The proceedure for getting RHI information was
for the operator to place an intertrace marker strobe manually through
the target on the PPI. This 'told' the Type 13 to rotate to the correct
bearing and the height was then displayed on a separate A scope.

Now imagine a meteor trail tangent to the maximum first-trip drum at a
slant range of 255 miles. The recombination rate of the trail
ionisation behind the meteor head is only a second or two, or at most a
few tens of meters of trail, which means that it will be scanned in effect
as a point target. Echoes returned by this point target will be either
undetectable or very weak, since effective cross-section is
proportional to the square of the wavelength and reflected power is
proportional to the cube of the wavelength. Plank's 1956/1959
AFCRL studies (and other sources) agree that even at L-band meteor
ionisation offers a target at the margin of possible detection. (Meteor
radar works at VHF.) At S-band chances are very slim, and this applies
to first-trip echoes. Because returned power from a point target drops
as the inverse 4th power of the range a meteor beyond the designed
range of the radar is especially unlikely to return a signal above the
noise level.

This means that the meteor *must* be scanned at the most favourable
orientation, which requires the trail to be at right-angles to the radar
line
of sight. As the off-perpendicular angle increases away from the normal,
this so-called 'radiant condition', in which the ionisation acts like a
metallic skin reflector, is lost and at more acute angles the only energy
returned will be a vanishing echo from the wake turbulence (equivalent
to the scatter from CAT). So we have the meteor trail passing tangentially
to the 1st trip covereage at 255 miles, happening to reach closest
approach just as the radar antenna rotates past at normal incidence, and,
just conceivably, this results in a rather weak echo at a displayed range
of 5 miles.

What will an operator make of this echo? Not much, unless there is a
second or a third. As you say, a whole sequence of 2nd trip echoes would
describe a distorted course approaching and receeding from the scope
centre. But by the time the antenna rotates back to the sector in which the
meteor was last scanned, 10-15 seconds later, it will have vaporised and
the trail will have recombined. And since the perpendicularity condition
for re-radiant echoes still obtains, even if free-electron densities
remained
extraordinarily high over the duration of two scans the echo would still be
displayed in exactly the same place (save for minimal wind drift) and would
not constitute the 'track' of a rapid target.

So for all these reasons your scenario points either to: a) head-echoes
from large fireballs within the 1st-trip design range (big enough to
override
all considerations of inappropriate wavelength and orientation), which
could not explain the course change reported from N to W, and could not
travel slow enough to be displayed over a number of successive scans,
nor give time for operators to azicate the Type 13s and obtain height
reports, not to mention scrambling and vectoring fighters - a proceedure
taking many minutes; or b) head echoes from truly enormous fireballs at
very extreme range, slowed dramatically on the display from tens of
thousands of mph to by 3rd- or nth-trip geometry.
The latter case is at least geometrically and ballistically possible in
principle,
but at hundreds of miles closest approach and traversing 90 degrees of
azimuth between N and W bearings this implies a period of incandesence
within the atmosphere over a ground track of maybe thousands of miles
for a duration of at least many tens of seconds, which is astronomically
outrageous. Such an event may have occurred (there are historical reports
of extreme 'meteor' events that you might want to cite, but we'd have to
agree on rules for when eyewitness testimony is a valid import!) but more
than one super-fireball would seem to be pushing it.

The witness here is describing a series of events, an afternoon of
excitement, " . . .I was able to hear what all the other stations in the
chain was seeing - I could hear their plotters directly - and I was also
able, by means of my patch panel, to plug into and legitimately listen to
conversations between GCI controllers on the ground, and the fighter
aircraft which they were attempting to vector onto their targets." It took
a long time to scramble a number of aircraft and "eventually" the targets
headed away W over the Atlantic.

The only way of involving meteors is to assume that the 'tracks' of the
targets were imagined by the operators interpolating between
stochastically distributed single point echoes, each from one of a large
number of quite different successive meteors. In these circumstances
the Conchoid of Nicomedes is completely irrelevant.

An explanation like this is just about physically conceivable, but very
highly improbable, and would only succeed by shifting the whole problem
into a grey psychological area where supposedly 'anything goes'. Some
people find this tactic plausible. I'm personally sceptical, especially if
it is
introduced as a last resort when previously-'plausible' theories based on
*accepting* report details are found to fail. Then it becomes ad hoc and
unconvincing. I think we'd need more information about the case to
conclude that Roy Dent's testimony is corrupted in the way this theory
requires.

Best
Martin Shough

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 28 May 2003 13:04:29 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)

It should be noted that RADAR was in its infancy at that time. Jenny
Randles, in her book "UFOs, Danger in the Air", quotes an airman as
saying that many intercept missions were flown, not so much to intercept
the "bogies" as to find out what kinds of RADAR distortions were causing
them (by reporting what was found at the scene).

It gradually developed that there were several classes of RADAR "angels"
which had the following causes:

1. Second (or third) Trip Echo: This is caused by a returned RADAR pulse
which is received AFTER the RADAR set has already sent out another
pulse.
Thus, the RADAR set displays the range and speed wrong. The following
targets have been erroneously detected by this process:

- meteors (about 1/3 of the real range and speed displayed)
- aircraft beyond the normal range of the set
- ships and mountains beyond the normal range
- the moon (I wonder how many trips late THAT was)

Note: if the object approaches from second trip to primary range (or
from
third trip to second), it can appear to suddenly jump from one place to
another.

2. Anomalous Propagation: Atmospheric conditions bend the radar beam, so
that it strikes the ground or curves beyond the horizon. This combines
with the second trip echo to make aircraft, ships, and mountains beyond
the horizon appear. As the atmosphere shifts and bends the beam
differing
amounts, the AP target appears to move.

AP errors can make ships, trucks, and topography appear to be objects
flying in the sky. And the speed of an AP object can be as fast as the
speed of a spot of light from a flashlight can move, since the beam, not
the object, is changing.

3. Multiple Reflections: This causes an extra target to appear when the
RADAR beam bounces off of more than one object before returning to the
set.
Usually one of the objects is an efficient corner reflector, which
returns
almost all of the energy that strikes it right back in the direction it
came from. The usual culprits: dump trucks, dumpsters, railroad open
gondola cars, and L-shaped buildings. If the beam bounces off the curved
side of an airplane, strikes a dump truck, and then bounces back, hits
the
plane in the SAME SPOT again, it is reflected directly back to the RADAR
set, it produces a second target on the screen, which is beyond the
plane.

If the beam strikes a stationary flat surface near the RADAR, it can
also
produce a second target, either at the bearing of the flat, or at the
bearing of the plane.

4. RADAR interactions: Anomalous propagation conditions can also allow
two
RADAR sets which are normally out of range of each other to intercept
each
other's signals. This causes a blip that moves at a rate determined by
the
relative pulse and rotation rates of the two sets' antennae.

Other kinds of equipment can also sneak electronic noise into a RADAR
set.

5. Weather: Most weather targets look like weather. But occasionally, a
cloud can reflect the beam selectively, making a target that appears to
be
moving. Adjusting the gain of the set can reveal this one.

6. Noise in the Set: Ringing tubes (remember tubes?), jostled mercury
delay
lines, and other sources of noise can cause spurious blips to appear.
This
one can also be detected by adjusting the gain of the set.

7. Moving Target Indicator (MTI) Errors: The changing parts of weather
returns, and other items that change the strength of RADAR returns, can
make stationary targets appear on this device that is supposed to
eliminate
their displays. AP is especially prone to do this. One recognition point
on
this kind of error is that the erroneous blips are usually brighter than
the blips of real aircraft.

8. Equipment and operator failure: These can cause blips to appear in
the
wrong place, or where no return is present. Often a weak tube caused the
operator to crank up the gain to get a display. Of course, all of the
garbage coming into the antenna is amplified too.

Only a few of these were known causes of false targets in 1956. See my
notes below.

@ b) An incident in April 1957 involved Javelins scrambled to

I do not see why not. These are exactly the characteristics of second
and third trip echoes:

- The speed displayed is a lot slower than the actual speed.

- The path appears to curve so the closest approach is closer to the
RADAR set than a straight-line trajectory. The displayed path is in fact
the closer curve of the Conchoid of Nicomedes:

r = a * csc(b) - c

Where a is the distance of the closest point of the true straight-line
trajectory, b is the angle of the set to the heading of the meteor, c
is an integer multiple of the range of the radar set, and a is larger
than c.

- If the meteor crosses from a third-trip zone into a second trip zone,
the target's position will suddenly jump, from very near the RADAR set,
to a position on the same azimuth, but much farther away. When it leaves
the second trip zone and re-enters the third trip zone, it will likewise
jump closer, but on the same azimuth.

- The target should appear to slow down as it gets closer to the RADAR
set, and speed up as it moves away.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 28 May 2003 13:04:29 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)

It should be noted that RADAR was in its infancy at that time. Jenny
Randles, in her book "UFOs, Danger in the Air", quotes an airman as
saying that many intercept missions were flown, not so much to intercept
the "bogies" as to find out what kinds of RADAR distortions were causing
them (by reporting what was found at the scene).

It gradually developed that there were several classes of RADAR "angels"
which had the following causes:

1. Second (or third) Trip Echo: This is caused by a returned RADAR pulse
which is received AFTER the RADAR set has already sent out another
pulse.
Thus, the RADAR set displays the range and speed wrong. The following
targets have been erroneously detected by this process:

- meteors (about 1/3 of the real range and speed displayed)
- aircraft beyond the normal range of the set
- ships and mountains beyond the normal range
- the moon (I wonder how many trips late THAT was)

Note: if the object approaches from second trip to primary range (or
from
third trip to second), it can appear to suddenly jump from one place to
another.

2. Anomalous Propagation: Atmospheric conditions bend the radar beam, so
that it strikes the ground or curves beyond the horizon. This combines
with the second trip echo to make aircraft, ships, and mountains beyond
the horizon appear. As the atmosphere shifts and bends the beam
differing
amounts, the AP target appears to move.

AP errors can make ships, trucks, and topography appear to be objects
flying in the sky. And the speed of an AP object can be as fast as the
speed of a spot of light from a flashlight can move, since the beam, not
the object, is changing.

3. Multiple Reflections: This causes an extra target to appear when the
RADAR beam bounces off of more than one object before returning to the
set.
Usually one of the objects is an efficient corner reflector, which
returns
almost all of the energy that strikes it right back in the direction it
came from. The usual culprits: dump trucks, dumpsters, railroad open
gondola cars, and L-shaped buildings. If the beam bounces off the curved
side of an airplane, strikes a dump truck, and then bounces back, hits
the
plane in the SAME SPOT again, it is reflected directly back to the RADAR
set, it produces a second target on the screen, which is beyond the
plane.

If the beam strikes a stationary flat surface near the RADAR, it can
also
produce a second target, either at the bearing of the flat, or at the
bearing of the plane.

4. RADAR interactions: Anomalous propagation conditions can also allow
two
RADAR sets which are normally out of range of each other to intercept
each
other's signals. This causes a blip that moves at a rate determined by
the
relative pulse and rotation rates of the two sets' antennae.

Other kinds of equipment can also sneak electronic noise into a RADAR
set.

5. Weather: Most weather targets look like weather. But occasionally, a
cloud can reflect the beam selectively, making a target that appears to
be
moving. Adjusting the gain of the set can reveal this one.

6. Noise in the Set: Ringing tubes (remember tubes?), jostled mercury
delay
lines, and other sources of noise can cause spurious blips to appear.
This
one can also be detected by adjusting the gain of the set.

7. Moving Target Indicator (MTI) Errors: The changing parts of weather
returns, and other items that change the strength of RADAR returns, can
make stationary targets appear on this device that is supposed to
eliminate
their displays. AP is especially prone to do this. One recognition point
on
this kind of error is that the erroneous blips are usually brighter than
the blips of real aircraft.

8. Equipment and operator failure: These can cause blips to appear in
the
wrong place, or where no return is present. Often a weak tube caused the
operator to crank up the gain to get a display. Of course, all of the
garbage coming into the antenna is amplified too.

Only a few of these were known causes of false targets in 1956. See my
notes below.

I do not see why not. These are exactly the characteristics of second
and third trip echoes:

- The speed displayed is a lot slower than the actual speed.

- The path appears to curve so the closest approach is closer to the
RADAR set than a straight-line trajectory. The displayed path is in fact
the closer curve of the Conchoid of Nicomedes:

r = a * csc(b) - c

Where a is the distance of the closest point of the true straight-line
trajectory, b is the angle of the set to the heading of the meteor, c
is an integer multiple of the range of the radar set, and a is larger
than c.

- If the meteor crosses from a third-trip zone into a second trip zone,
the target's position will suddenly jump, from very near the RADAR set,
to a position on the same azimuth, but much farther away. When it leaves
the second trip zone and re-enters the third trip zone, it will likewise
jump closer, but on the same azimuth.

- The target should appear to slow down as it gets closer to the RADAR
set, and speed up as it moves away.

Greetings from a new subscriber.

Browsing the archive I found this interesting message. I'm not
sure if it's been commented on already but there are a couple of
points to note:

a) Javelins were not in general service in the "summer of 1956
pre-Suez". The F(AW) Mk.1 flew that February, but re-equipping
of the Venom QRA squadrons did not begin (with 141 and 23
Squadrons RAF Coltishall) until February/March 1957.

b) An incident in April 1957 involved Javelins scrambled to
intercept fast targets heading SW outbound over the UK and
turning W over the Atlantic (later explained as Hunters). This
incident attracted ministerial attention and could be the 'major flap'
referred to.

c) On the other hand, if the interceptors were not Javelins and the
date is correct then it is interesting to note the Bornholm, Denmark
radar trackings of hypersonic targets heading down from the N
then turning W over the Baltic during late August/early September
1956. It appears these incidents were part of a major NATO flap
and were linked with Lakenhheath at the time.

d) There really isn't the remotest likelihood that tracks of the sort
described could be caused by meteors.

Apologies if this duplicates comments already made. I'd be
interested to know if anyone has more info or opinions on these
matters.
Regards
Martin Shough

I'm pleased to say I've found what seems to be an online
copy of the entire archives, at:

http://anomalies.net/archive/paranet/newsletter/


There are two indexes therein, 'by number' and 'by
subject'.

The latter is by far most useful.

A suggestion; open two browser windows [Alt + Tab will
quickly swap between both] and keep the subject index in
one of them.

The other can be used to easily access specific
newsletters by editing the last three address digits. For
example, following the 'jackie gleason' thread requires
moving from newsletter 307 to 310 and then 315 - simply
change:

http://anomalies.net/archive/paranet/newsletter/307

to

http://anomalies.net/archive/paranet/newsletter/310

and then

http://anomalies.net/archive/paranet/newsletter/315

etc.


Enter 'gleason' in the browser's 'Find/Find Next' menu
option and the relevant text within each newsletter is
readily located.


I'm sure some of this significant archive material will
be of general interest.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Sun, 1 Jun 2003 07:13:07 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Cash-Landrum

There's a reported 1980 'clandestine' operation which
should perhaps be noted in connection to Cash-Landrum.

'Setcon II'.

Anyone previously heard of it?

I hadn't, until coming across the following, detailed and
lengthy account:

'TWO MINUTES'
'The simple line drawn between life and death is luck'.
by Mark S. Daniels.

The Boeing-Vertol CH-47 Chinook helicopter, is considered
to be one of the most complicated aircraft of its kind in
the world today.

Powered by two, Lycoming T-55L-712 turboshaft engines,
the CH-47 is brought to life when shaft horse power is
transmitted into a Combining Transmission via two
connecting drive shafts, one from the nose "bullet" of
each engine.

Those in turn, cause the Combining Transmission to
transmit torque forward and aft to drive the gearing of
the Forward and Aft transmissions via a single row of
"forward" and "aft" reaching drive shafts.

In turn, the Foreward and Aft transmissions convert the
torque vertically, causing the movement of the six
composite rotor blades on their individual, composite
rotor heads.

The two rotor heads are located one on the Forward
Transmission drive spline, the transmission itself
located above and just behind the cockpit in a place
known as the "Forward Crown;" and the other on the Aft
Rotary Wing Driveshaft, which extends upward vertically
from the Aft Transmission, both of which are housed
within the Aft Pylon.

In service for nearly forty years, the six-bladed,
tandem-rotored, Chinook, is viewed as a Godsend to
today's Army, because it can deliver men and material to
a battle area like no other helicopter can.
Today's "Delta" Chinook (CH-47D) can take an M198
Howitzer--an artillery piece that is almost as long as
the Chinook itself--at a breathtaking speed of 120 knots
Nap-Of-The-Earth (NOE), fully stablized via a "triple
hook" external loads system, without any fear of the load
oscillating beneath the aircraft...something that might
cause damage to or loss of the helicopter.

The Chinook is also capable of simultaneously
accomodating the M198's seventeen-man crew, along with a
load of artillery shells slung externally beneath the
M198.

Imagine, if you will, a Company of twelve CH-47Ds, moving
a DIVARTY (Division Artillery) unit in this manner. Rapid
deployment of an Artillery firebase to or beyond the
"Forward Edge of the Battle Area," or FEBA.

Utilizing the CH-47D's upgraded, rather ingenius, "Triple
Hook" external loads system -- which stablizes heavy
loads for high-speed, low level fligh -- the CH-47
provides an Artillery commander with the ability to move
on demand, quickly, efficiently, and lethally, when it
comes to the enemy he must face along the FEBA.

The Chinook is capable of cruising at 143 knots without
external load, and can carry 44 combat-equipped
paratroops, or 33 combat equipped soldiers, or in the
medical role, some 24 litters or stretchers.

To paraphrase the title of an old TV western, "Have Gun,
Will Travel" -- and that's just one sample of a strictly
military use for the CH-47D, "Delta Chinook," which has
since been joined by the MH-47D for Special
Operations/Delta Force missions.

The newest variant of the Chinook is the MH-47E, which is
currently in operation with the famed 160th SOAR (Special
Operations Aviation Regiment), which was formed by
elements of Company A, 159th Aviation Battalion (ASH)
"Press On," a Chinook unit; and the 160th Aviation
Battalion (Author's note, researching unit
information...may have been the 158th Avn Bn...)
"Ghostriders," a Blackhawk unit; both of the 101st
Aviation Group, 101st Airborne Division, Ft. Campbell,
Kentucky.

The MH-47E is capable of individual or unit rapid
deployment, utilizing aircraft operational readiness and
aerial refueling capability, rather than disassembly and
shipment onboard vessels or aircraft. The aircraft is
equipped with two, Textron Lycoming T-55L-714 turbine
engines, each capable of 4,000 shaft horsepower, and
carries a crew of five, including the pilot, co-pilot,
flight engineer, and two side facing gunners, one of
which is likely the crew chief as well. The aircraft can
carry 44 combat equipped troops.

The MH-47E is similar to the AH-47 "Guns A Go Go"
Gunships of Vietnam fame, in that it packs two 7.62 mm
minigun emplacements, and also has provisions for Stinger
missiles in the air combat role. The MH-47E is equipped
with APQ-174A Terrain-following radar at 30 meters, AVR-
2A laser warning receivers, GPS/terrain reference
navigation, AAR-47 MAWS(IR), ALQ-136 pulse radar jammer,
ALQ-162 CW radar jammer M-130 chaff/flare, AAQ-16 FLIR,
NVG APR-39A RWR SATCOM.

However, in the early 1980s, the YCH-47D was undergoing
Operational Testing at Ft. Campbell, Kentucky, and the
MH-47D and MH-47E were just being drawn and detailed at
Boeing Vertol's Engineering facility, in Philadelphia,
Pennsylvania. 1980 saw the continuation of operations by
early model Boeing CH-47B and C model Chinooks, which
were then being allocated for conversion to the new
production "D" model status. One of their missions is
what we'll discuss in the paragraphs that follow:


_Setcon II_

In 1980, Companies "A thru C" of the "Liftmasters"
Battalion, were assigned to an operation known as SETCON
II, a mission involving the "hush-hush" transportation of
obsolete chemical training kits, from a location in
Indiana, to the Rocky Mountain Arsenal, in Colorado.

The chemical sets--which were known to contain trace
amounts of the World War I chemical agent, "Mustard,"
were to subsequently be destroyed by fire at that depot.

At the time, I was working not only as a mechanic, but as
a Battalion Historian and Photographer for the 159th
Aviation Battalion, Assault Support Helicopters (ASH).
Company "A," my primary unit, had the mission -- along
with Company "B" and "C" -- to fly in support of the
101st Airborne Division, Air Assault (AASLT) -- the
legendary "Screaming Eagles," of Ft. Campbell,
Kentucky***.
Ft. Campbell is situated in the Central United States, on
the southern border of Kentucky, between the City of
Hopkinsville, Kentucky, and the City of Clarksville,
Tennessee.

Ft. Campbell itself, is roughly 50 miles north of Capitol
City of Nashville, home of Country Music, The Grand Old
Opry, Belle Meade Mansion, the final resting place of
President James K. Polk.

Rocky Mountain Arsenal is situated about 1000 miles away
to the West, in Colorado.

The mission was called "Setcon II," and was to be kept
low-profile, to avoid agitating environmentalists over
the shipments.

Now, when I say "low profile," let me briefly explain
that there was nothing secretive about these training
sets, which were actually leftover training kits from
World War II.

The safe transportation and destruction of these chemical
sets was of extreme importance to the United States
Government, in that, the sets were no longer needed; the
sets were taking up valuable storage space; and the sets
were taking time away from US Army NBC specialists (MOS
54E), whom -- over the years -- had to constantly monitor
the sets for leakage.

With a growing NBC threat overseas at that time, this
manpower was seriously needed elsewhere.

However, this was a period of time in which environmental
activists were gaining in numbers and strength, as was
Press support for them. Further, it was also a time in
which an important Chemical Non-proliferation Treaty was
under development, in which the outlawing of the use of
these weapons was an extreme possibility, if not a great
opportunity.

The government certainly wanted to accommodate both the
foreign powers and the environmentalists by destroying
these wanton, inhumane pesticides. The trouble was
located in the transport of the kits over state lines,
especially since the government always seemed to catch
hell even for the few noble attempts it makes to dispose
of obsolete and potentially harmful or deadly chemical
caches.
Whether by air, rail, truck or ship...usually, no one
wants these deadly items passing through or stored in
their area.

A small mishap involving the transfer of these chemicals
could have been blown out of proportion -- from molehill
to Mount St. Helens -- thereby thwarting the best
intentions of a special mission that ultimately would
have been in everyone's best interests, worldwide.

In fact, the mission should have been of interest to the
environmentalists, in that, the chemicals were to be
properly destroyed by fire at Rocky Mountain Arsenal, in
Colorado, and rendered non-threatening, beyond just
plain, non-existent

Despite the good intent, and though it was a routine
mission, with the amount of chemicals involved being so
minimal (again, "trace"); someone at Department of the
Army felt that we were begging for trouble if we tried to
cooperate with "Greenpeace," et al, and thus--the mission
went "hush hush...".

...sort of.

Except for Walter Cronkite, the move and destruction of
these elements was ultimately completed rather quietly,
and without much fanfare. However, Walter's presence in
all this comes along a little later in this story, so
read on...


_Special Ops -- Special Procedures_

The government, in response to expected environmental
concerns -- but without notifying the environmentalists
(a Machiavellian oxymoron...), developed special
procedures in which to transport the chemicals.

First: it was decided that each CH-47 Chinook aircraft
would have "Poison Gas" placards installed in the cabin
windows, facing outward, of course, so that all could
see.

Second: two Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical Defense
NCOs, MOS (Military Occupational Specialty) 54Es, had to
be onboard each aircraft -- all for the purpose of
monitoring operational chemical alarms for reports of
leakage, and for monitoring the security of the loads
themselves.

Third: the chemical kits would be maintained in their
four foot long cannisters, with roughly 12 cannisters per
1,000 pound crate, and roughly five crates shipped per
CH-47 helicopter.

Fourth: all personnel on site at the pick-up area at
Crane Army Depot, Indiana, and at the drop off point at
"The Keyhole," on Campbell Army Air Field, Ft. Campbell,
Kentucky; whether they were military or civilian, they
had to receive either training or retraining on the use
of the ABC M17A1 (Ground Personnel) and ABC M-24
protective masks (Aviators), or "Gas Masks," as they are
more commonly known in the civil community.

...and Fifth: this meant filling a tent full of tear gas;
having a soldier or civilian walk into the gas-filled
tent wearing his protective mask; having a 54E
determining if the mask is leaking or not, through the
use of a "banana" scent device; having the soldier or
civilian remove their mask while in the gas-filled tent,
reportedly for "confidence," of all things; and
thereafter, having that soldier or civilian learn to walk
to the exit door -- because if he or she didn't, the exit
door had one final lesson waiting just outside for those
who tried to run...

...a tree parked just outside the exit of the tent!

Sort of a funny little thing that MOS 54Es like to do, to
train soldiers not to panick in a "chemical attack!".


_The Mission_

Subsequent to all this, my unit's mission was to
transport these one thousand pound sets containing
chemical cannisters -- the cannisters themselves holding
the packed, Mustard Training Sets -- that everyone was
supposed to be worried about.

Our Chinooks would remove the sets to this place known as
the "keyhole," a series of keyhole-shaped concrete
revetments on the east side of Campbell AAF, in Ft.
Campbell, Kentucky, where the chemical kits would be
loaded aboard Lockheed C-141B Starlifters for the trip to
Rocky Mountain Arsenal.

Due to my love of aviation, my love of photojournalism,
and the need for a little action...and since I was
serving in the capacity of the Battalion Historian at the
time; I obtained permission to go along on the trip in
order to publicize the 159th's activities in the post
newspaper, The Ft. Campbell Courier.

That permission was granted, and what followed was one of
the most eventful trips of my then young life (24 years
old).

Timing of the mission required four flights of six, CH-47
Chinooks, including the four actually involved in the
transportation of the chemicals; one aircraft carrying
the Military Police of the 101st Airborne, as armed
military security guards; and the back-up "maintenance
bird," which carried spare parts and/or would serve as
necessary, as a spare helicopter.

The maintenance bird, loaded with tool kits, spare parts,
extra mechanics, and its own crew, was the bird I was
scheduled to fly on, though the coverage I was seeking
for the event, was, hopefully, going to involve one of
the mission birds...those with the actual chemical sets
onboard.

That's where "the action" was.

The established "Standard Operating Procedure," called
for the morning arrival of the first flight of six
aircraft at the golf-course staging area for SETCON II, a
satellite facility of Crane Naval Weapons Center, which
in turn, housed Crane Army Depot, in humid, Southern
Indiana.

Humid, but beautiful, the golf course would serve as the
staging and loading area for all aircraft, and would
dispatch the first five aircraft, prior to the second
flight of Chinooks arriving. The maintenance bird would
be on standby at Crane for both flights, then leave with
the last flight for home.

En route, the two flights were organized to literally
greet each other in flight, at the mid-way point between
Crane Army Depot and Campbell AAF.

Is that a flair for precision, or what?

There were to be two flights in the morning, and two more
to follow in the afternoon, completing SETCON II by
nightfall -- or at least -- the Army's involvement was to
be completed. Barring new orders from "Murphy".

The first two flights in the morning were a complete
success, with no incidents reported. I joined the
operation in the afternoon, and was scheduled to be on
the last flight of aircraft out of Crane.


_At Crane Army Depot, Indiana_

Upon arrival at Crane, I found the staging area bustling
with activity. Five-ton forklifts were moving the groups
of crates and cannisters to staging slots behind each
helicopter.

these wanton, inhumane pesticides. The trouble was
located in the transport of the kits over state lines,
especially since the government always seemed to catch
hell even for the few noble attempts it makes to dispose
of obsolete and potentially harmful or deadly chemical
caches.
Whether by air, rail, truck or ship...usually, no one
wants these deadly items passing through or stored in
their area.

A small mishap involving the transfer of these chemicals
could have been blown out of proportion -- from molehill
to Mount St. Helens -- thereby thwarting the best
intentions of a special mission that ultimately would
have been in everyone's best interests, worldwide.

In fact, the mission should have been of interest to the
environmentalists, in that, the chemicals were to be
properly destroyed by fire at Rocky Mountain Arsenal, in
Colorado, and rendered non-threatening, beyond just
plain, non-existent

Despite the good intent, and though it was a routine
mission, with the amount of chemicals involved being so
minimal (again, "trace"); someone at Department of the
Army felt that we were begging for trouble if we tried to
cooperate with "Greenpeace," et al, and thus--the mission
went "hush hush...".

...sort of.

Except for Walter Cronkite, the move and destruction of
these elements was ultimately completed rather quietly,
and without much fanfare. However, Walter's presence in
all this comes along a little later in this story, so
read on...


_Special Ops -- Special Procedures_

The government, in response to expected environmental
concerns -- but without notifying the environmentalists
(a Machiavellian oxymoron...), developed special
procedures in which to transport the chemicals.

First: it was decided that each CH-47 Chinook aircraft
would have "Poison Gas" placards installed in the cabin
windows, facing outward, of course, so that all could
see.

Second: two Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical Defense
NCOs, MOS (Military Occupational Specialty) 54Es, had to
be onboard each aircraft -- all for the purpose of
monitoring operational chemical alarms for reports of
leakage, and for monitoring the security of the loads
themselves.

Third: the chemical kits would be maintained in their
four foot long cannisters, with roughly 12 cannisters per
1,000 pound crate, and roughly five crates shipped per
CH-47 helicopter.

Fourth: all personnel on site at the pick-up area at
Crane Army Depot, Indiana, and at the drop off point at
"The Keyhole," on Campbell Army Air Field, Ft. Campbell,
Kentucky; whether they were military or civilian, they
had to receive either training or retraining on the use
of the ABC M17A1 (Ground Personnel) and ABC M-24
protective masks (Aviators), or "Gas Masks," as they are
more commonly known in the civil community.

...and Fifth: this meant filling a tent full of tear gas;
having a soldier or civilian walk into the gas-filled
tent wearing his protective mask; having a 54E
determining if the mask is leaking or not, through the
use of a "banana" scent device; having the soldier or
civilian remove their mask while in the gas-filled tent,
reportedly for "confidence," of all things; and
thereafter, having that soldier or civilian learn to walk
to the exit door -- because if he or she didn't, the exit
door had one final lesson waiting just outside for those
who tried to run...

...a tree parked just outside the exit of the tent!

Sort of a funny little thing that MOS 54Es like to do, to
train soldiers not to panick in a "chemical attack!".


_The Mission_

Subsequent to all this, my unit's mission was to
transport these one thousand pound sets containing
chemical cannisters -- the cannisters themselves holding
the packed, Mustard Training Sets -- that everyone was
supposed to be worried about.

Our Chinooks would remove the sets to this place known as
the "keyhole," a series of keyhole-shaped concrete
revetments on the east side of Campbell AAF, in Ft.
Campbell, Kentucky, where the chemical kits would be
loaded aboard Lockheed C-141B Starlifters for the trip to
Rocky Mountain Arsenal.

Due to my love of aviation, my love of photojournalism,
and the need for a little action...and since I was
serving in the capacity of the Battalion Historian at the
time; I obtained permission to go along on the trip in
order to publicize the 159th's activities in the post
newspaper, The Ft. Campbell Courier.

That permission was granted, and what followed was one of
the most eventful trips of my then young life (24 years
old).

Timing of the mission required four flights of six, CH-47
Chinooks, including the four actually involved in the
transportation of the chemicals; one aircraft carrying
the Military Police of the 101st Airborne, as armed
military security guards; and the back-up "maintenance
bird," which carried spare parts and/or would serve as
necessary, as a spare helicopter.

The maintenance bird, loaded with tool kits, spare parts,
extra mechanics, and its own crew, was the bird I was
scheduled to fly on, though the coverage I was seeking
for the event, was, hopefully, going to involve one of
the mission birds...those with the actual chemical sets
onboard.

That's where "the action" was.

The established "Standard Operating Procedure," called
for the morning arrival of the first flight of six
aircraft at the golf-course staging area for SETCON II, a
satellite facility of Crane Naval Weapons Center, which
in turn, housed Crane Army Depot, in humid, Southern
Indiana.

Humid, but beautiful, the golf course would serve as the
staging and loading area for all aircraft, and would
dispatch the first five aircraft, prior to the second
flight of Chinooks arriving. The maintenance bird would
be on standby at Crane for both flights, then leave with
the last flight for home.

En route, the two flights were organized to literally
greet each other in flight, at the mid-way point between
Crane Army Depot and Campbell AAF.

Is that a flair for precision, or what?

There were to be two flights in the morning, and two more
to follow in the afternoon, completing SETCON II by
nightfall -- or at least -- the Army's involvement was to
be completed. Barring new orders from "Murphy".

The first two flights in the morning were a complete
success, with no incidents reported. I joined the
operation in the afternoon, and was scheduled to be on
the last flight of aircraft out of Crane.


_At Crane Army Depot, Indiana_

Upon arrival at Crane, I found the staging area bustling
with activity. Five-ton forklifts were moving the groups
of crates and cannisters to staging slots behind each
helicopter.

Hi Larry,

Your message deserves a longer reply, but I don't have
time to write one today.

Couple of comments, though:

1) The text may well have been written in the 17th
century. Remember we are not dealing with people
brought up on a Greek or Roman view of the universe,
but a different people with different ideas
altogether.

2) The date of the translation is irrelevant. It may
have been translated originally from the Latin, the
Italian or the French, or from one of these languages
into another and back again. In fact, I already have
three versions at least: one from the French (into
English), another from the German (into English), and
I also have a Spanish version, translated from the
Italian.

3) A word meaning "space" may or may not have been
used in the original version. There's no point in
analysing the translation.

4) I'd love to argue about Medieval cosmology and why
the d'Orville text does not contain such an
anachronistic notion, but that'll have to wait till
tomorrow!

Regards,

Chris

<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Aristarchus conceived the idea that the earth spins
and orbits in about 300 BC, starting a tradition which led Plutarch to muse
circa 100 AD: "The universe is infinite; and the infinite, which has neither
beginning nor end, has no centre either . . .The universe does not assign any
fixed centre to the earth, which drifts homelessly and unsteadily through the
infinite emptiness without a proper goal. . ." (A 1956 translation admittedly,
but the essence is clear enough.) Much of this was forgotten for centuries in
most of Europe, but not by everybody, and after the rennaissance there were a
number of intellectual coteries familiar with the idea. But they lacked
mathematical grounds. In 1609 Kepler's 'Astronomia Nova' presented a new
astronomy based on quantitative proof in which the planets moved in ellipses
through empty space in response to an attracting force emanating from the sun.
He didn't *quite* invent universal gravity. Galileo knew about empty space and
the mechanics of bodies falling in vacuum and knew that the planets were worlds
in free motion in space. What these world-views lacked was&nbsp;*not* a concept
of space; what they lacked was&nbsp;a concept of MOMENTUM. It was Newton's
understanding of momentum that was the key to the physics of inverse-square
universal gravity already&nbsp;implicit in the work of Kepler. So even a
Graeco-Roman tradition did have room for the idea of infinite empty space in the
17th century.</FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Martin Shough<BR></DIV></FONT>

  translation is irrelevant. It may<BR>have been translated originally from the
  Latin, the<BR>Italian or the French, or from one of these languages<BR>into

From: "Chris Gibson" <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>

Subject: RE: [UFORL] 1956 radar case(s)

Re Javelins in RAF service.

According to Owen Thetford's "Aircraft of the Royal Air Force since 1918"

"...the first of them (Javelin FAW.1) were isssued to No. 46 Squadron at
Odiham in February 1956." Anthony Robinson's "Night Fighter" says March
1956.

87 Sqdn in Germany was issued with FAW.1s in August 1956.

Francis Mason's "The British Fighter" says that "Eastern Sector" didn't
receive its Javelins until early 57. (I don't think RAF Odiham would be in
Eastern Sector)

Chris

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Sun, 1 Jun 2003 12:33:07 -0700 (PDT)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] November 1661 Tibet



Exactly. There's Epicurus' (341-270 BC) "Letter to
Herodotus" in which he says

"There are infinite worlds both like and unlike ours.
For the atoms being infinite in number are borne far
out into space....So there exists nowhere an obstacle
to the infinite number of worlds. We must believe that
in all worlds there are living creatures and plants
and other things we see in this world."

And Lucretius (c. 75 BC), who wrote:

"Granted, then, that empty space extends without limit
in every direction and that seeds innumerable are
rushing on countless courses through an unfathomable
universe. It is in the highest degree unlikely that
this earth and this sky is the only one to have been
created."

This tradition was carried on right up to the time of
d'Orville, and other belief systems (Polynesian,
Indian, etc.) have their own versions of more or less
the same thing.

Chris

http://theshadowlands.net/falconlake.txt

http://www.sacred-texts.com/ufo/canada.htm


In the former, Chris Rutkowski states:

[BEGIN]
A year after his encounter, Michalak returned to the landing
site with an associate. With a geiger counter, they found two
"W-shaped" silver bars, four and a half inches in length, and
several other smaller chunks of the same material. All this was
found two inches under some lichen in a crack in the rock, over
which the UFO was said to hover. Analysis showed that the
silver was of "high purity", and contained low amounts of
copper and cadmium.

[...]

The problem, however, is not the actual radioactive mechanism
on the silver, but why it was missed earlier by other
individuals. The Department of Health and Welfare went to the
site on more than one occasion, and checked the site
thoroughly.

Why was the silver not located?
[END]


Seems an obvious question, to say the least.

Years later and with due hindsight... comments and
determinations now invited re, at the time, a perceived
'verification' of Arnold's utterly misconstrued 'flying
saucer' evidence.

From: James C Giglio <jgiglio2@polaris.umuc.edu>
Date: Fri, 6 Jun 2003 11:27:35 -0400 (EDT)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The Michalak Case

On Fri, 6 Jun 2003, James Easton wrote:

> Cited as foremost evidence of non-earthly contact, what's
> now a conclusion concerning the late Steve Michalak's
> alleged, proverbial, 'close encounter' with seemingly
> inherent 'flying saucers'?

It's Case 22 in the Colorado report (www.ncas.org/condon/). One
detail that marks the account as highly questionable is the
assertion by the primary witness that the UFO set his shirt on
fire and he threw it to the ground. The local forest fire lookout
towers were staffed at the time (the forest was dry). Those
observers commented (1) that any heat source that could set a
man's short on fire at a distance would also have set the local
forest on fire, which would have been spotted, and (2) that even
the smoke from a burning shirt thrown on the ground would have
been spotted as well.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Tue, 3 Jun 2003 09:52:09 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Oct., 1973

I was there. I worked on cases in Bloomington then. Mars was extremely
bright. And I KNOW of many cases where the planet was the cause. In
fact many people admitted that Mars was the cause of their sighting,
when shown the planet the next night. Mars caused about 60 percent of
the total reports in my area in that two-week period when the flap was
at full steam. Fire balloons caused another 30 percent. I have one
account from a friend (who was a teenager at the time) of a series of
fire balloon launches he did in the Bloomington IN area in that
two-week period.

Of course, since all of those cases were solved within a day or
two, they didn't end up in any worldwide databases except mine, where
they were lumped into single mass-sighting cases instead of individual
reports.

I didn't expect Mars to explain the Pascagoula case, or any of the foil
man cases. But I do believe that Mars was the primary cause of the flap
itself. Then, once the flap started (and the press made a big deal about
it), crackpots launched fire balloons and dressed up in foil suits.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Mon, 2 Jun 2003 15:57:04 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Mars-stimulated UFO-cases or flaps???

October 1973

Bloomington IN and surrounding areas. Most of the sightings were either
Mars itself (very bright, and located on the eastern horizon during the
evening hours), or of fire balloons launched by pranksters who were
feeding on the UFO story. Airplanes and debris from a fire in a garbage
dump also contributed to the sightings.

This was part of a two month nationwide UFO flap, which also included:

- The Pascagoula MS abduction case
- Many cases of men or kids in foil suits
- Two cases of men in firefighting suits
- A cab driver (who fell asleep in his cab) reporting a "claw" on the
 roof of his taxi
- Fire balloons over stadiums and chased by helicopters,
- Volunteer firemen staging a prank with a hoop with orange lights
- A report of a UFO killing cows (no bodies, no cows missing)
- An air sculpture launched by an artist.

But the earliest sightings, and the large bulk of the sightings, proved
to be Mars.

chapter covers that formative post April 1980 period,
after the failed Iran hostage rescue attempt.

Emerson notes that operation 'Honey Badger' was one
component of operation 'Snow Bird', a planned second
rescue mission.

The 'Honey Badger' objective was , "focused exclusively
on developing an aviation capability to mount special or
counterterrorist operations in the Middle East and
Persian Gulf areas.

'After all', said a participant in Honey Badger, 'what
good were commandos if you couldn't get them to where
they had to be'."


Emerson refers to 'Task Force 160', perhaps not realising
the unit was at this time designated 'Task Force 158'.

He describes some of their training in Texas and claims
that the largest exercise, which involved, "200 aircraft
and over 2,000 people", took place at Reese AFB, in
Lubbock.

Interestingly, he describes how one early night time
exercise [with the pilots relying on night vision goggles
(NVG)] used an interstate highway as a map reference
point. They would locate the highway and then time
themselves between that point and their destination.

Emerson also notes, "the exercises were not coordinated
with local police authorities and at times ran into
unexpected problems".

He references one exercise held in Southern Texas, where
a night drop of parachutists in full combat gear, armed
and wearing NVGs, was hampered by a sudden thunderstorm
and the operatives couldn't locate the airfield where
they were to be picked up.

Stranded in cotton fields, the operatives decided to
spend the night in a nearby barn. Unfortunately, the
farmer spotted some people entering his barn and called
the police, who subsequently found themselves confronted
by armed and combat ready soldiers.


Significantly, Emerson explains why that second rescue
mission reportedly never materialised. In a crazy
situation, the CIA claimed to have located where the
hostages had been taken after being dispersed following
the first rescue attempt failure. However, as the CIA
refused to reveal their source(s), Major-General Richard
Secord would not accept the information as reliable.

That dispute escalated to the White House, where
ultimately President Carter and his advisors decided they
could not risk a second mission on this basis, especially
as they realistically expected some thirty percent of the
hostages and operatives could be killed or injured.

However, Emerson claims, "throughout November, December
and early January, members of Snow Bird remained on
standby alert to go into Iran".


I'm not surprised to find he makes no mention of the
three code named TF158 operations I'm aware of and which
took place between September 1980 to January 1981. It
does seem there really is no published reference to them,
as yet.

I presume these were all related to that ongoing training
and merely different phases of it. We should hopefully,
in due course, find out for sure.


Outwith Cash-Landrum (as all of this remains, until
proven otherwise), a couple of apparent anomalies.

Operation 'Credible Sport' was, so far as I'm aware,
first revealed by 'Janes Defence Weekly', in a 5 March
1997 article by Nick Cook. See, for example:

http://home.earthlink.net/~quade/crediblesport.html

However, Emerson states of that formative late 1980
period, "Other vital achievements included the extension
of the C-141 transport planes' range as well as the
addition of retrorockets to C-130s that allowed them to
land on a dime".

The latter doubtless refers to 'Credible Sport' and
Emerson's book was published in April 1988.

Yet, 'Credible Sport' seems to be an entirely separate
venture from all that encompassed TF158.

I can't see where this has been reconciled.


Lastly, there seems to be no online material at all
relating to operation "Snow Bird", or even "snowbird".

There is however in UFO mythology a proclaimed 'project
snowbird', where a recovered ET craft, flown by
inexperienced humans, was responsible for the Cash-
Landrum incident...

Somewhat 'Fortean' and quite bizarre.

Any further information about Emerson's apparently
migrated 'Snow Bird'?


James.

'Hawk' Ruth. I believe the first overall commander of the

bird' operational facts after Aug 1980, I can t say for
sure about bases or refueling. I only know that CH-47Ds
from the 159th Aviation Battalion Ft Campbell Ky
performed the refueling for the UH-60 aircraft during my
summer training of 1980".

<HTML>

<FONT FACE=arial,helvetica><FONT SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">Popular Mechanics<BR>
Defence<BR>
June 2003<BR>
<BR>
http://www.popularmechanics.com/science/military/2003/6/roswell_declassified/inde
x1.phtml<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
"Roswell Declassified"<BR>
&nbsp;&nbsp; <BR>
Formerly secret files finally reveal the truth about the world's <BR>
most famous UFO incident.&nbsp; <BR>
&nbsp;&nbsp; <BR>
BY JIM WILSON&nbsp; <BR>
Photos by Louis Jawitz <BR>
<BR>
<BR>
Knowing that old military records often contain startling revelations, <BR>
we were eager to see what surprises awaited us in the latest disclosure <BR>
from the Roswell files. For decades, UFO researchers had clamored for <BR>
the National Archives to come clean about a "flying disc" that <BR>
supposedly crashed during the Fourth of July weekend in 1947. The <BR>
Army started the story when it used the term in a press release about <BR>
a crash that had occurred north of Roswell, N.M. At the time, the <BR>
sleepy town had the distinction of being home to the only atomic <BR>
bomber unit (at Roswell Army Airfield) in the world. By the end of <BR>
that holiday weekend, the Army had retracted its original story, <BR>
claiming it had been a mistake. The debris that ranch manager <BR>
Mac Brazel had found on the J.B. Foster Ranch was simply the <BR>
remains of a weather balloon. The press reported the revised <BR>
version of events, and the story promptly died.<BR>
<BR>
Government paperwork, however, is immortal. Once a Roswell file <BR>
was created it became a collection bin for all sorts of UFO-related <BR>
material. Eventually, the collection moved to a climate-controlled <BR>
archive in College Park, Md., about a half-hour drive east of <BR>
Washington, D.C. And there the files would have remained <BR>
undisturbed were it not for a law that forces the government to <BR>
periodically review a document's security classification.<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
During the 1990s, the time limits on keeping Cold War-era records <BR>
began to expire. Journalists had come to appreciate that these <BR>
automatically declassified files often contained spectacular <BR>
information. Declassified records showed how the Atomic Energy <BR>
Commission intentionally released radiation from its reactors <BR>
in Hanford, Wash., on unsuspecting civilians in that area. <BR>
Other disclosures described how doctors working for the federal <BR>
government were permitted to conduct ghoulish medical experiments <BR>
on women, children and prisoners. Buoyed by these earlier <BR>
disclosures, UFO researchers had good reason to hope the 11 boxes <BR>
of newly opened Roswell files might contain a similar smoking gun.<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
PAPER CHASE<BR>
<BR>
POPULAR MECHANICS was interested too. In 100 years of covering <BR>
military affairs, our editors had come to realize that everything <BR>
the government touches creates a paper trail. If something <BR>
extraordinary had happened at the Roswell Army Airfield in July <BR>
1947, evidence would turn up in the paperwork compiled by sergeants <BR>
and officers. And it was that possibility that lured us to Maryland. <BR>
If aliens had landed, the soldiers who chased them would have left <BR>
a paper trail, too.<BR>
<BR>
As we had hoped, we found the original government records. But <BR>
first we had to do some digging. Most of the boxes were filled <BR>
with newspaper and magazine clippings about flying saucers, old books, <BR>
and government UFO reports that were made public decades ago. <BR>
There were Betamax videotapes about UFOs. We even found the remains <BR>
of the infamous balloon reflector, which UFO buffs claim the <BR>
government planted at the crash site in place of the pieces of <BR>
the flying disc. These pieces, they say, were taken to an <BR>
undisclosed military base.<BR>
<BR>
Then, amid the clutter, in Box 1, we found what we were after. <BR>
It was a seemingly unimportant document titled "Morning Reports, <BR>
July 1947." This was essentially a log of the day-to-day activity <BR>
at the base. In much the same way that a police blotter would provide <BR>
evidence of a bank robbery, the Morning Reports would provide <BR>
unambiguous evidence of unusual military activity.<BR>
<BR>
As we worked through the Morning Reports line by line, we came <BR>
to a simple realization: Absolutely nothing extraordinary had <BR>
happened at Roswell that Fourth of July weekend. There was no <BR>
indication of an emergency, no mention of a deployment of rescue <BR>
and firefighting crews, as was the case with other crashes. <BR>
That was one mystery solved.<BR>
<BR>
For years, UFO researchers had claimed that enlisted men and <BR>
officers involved in the disc recovery operation were transferred <BR>
to other bases to ensure their silence. Sure enough, the transfers <BR>
took place. The paperwork explained why. Several months earlier, <BR>
in a sweeping postwar military reorganization, Army fliers were <BR>
systematically transferred to the newly created U.S. Air Force. <BR>
The men had not been transferred. They had merely changed uniforms. <BR>
Another mystery solved.<BR>
<BR>
We left the National Archives and Records Administration complex <BR>
in College Park more confused than enlightened. Surely there was <BR>
more to the story. As the old saying goes: "Absence of evidence <BR>
is not evidence of absence." So with this thought in mind we <BR>
decided to call Frank Kaufmann, the man at the center of the <BR>
Roswell episode.<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
FORGED RECORDS<BR>
<BR>
Kaufmann was less than the picture of health when we interviewed <BR>
him for our July 1997 cover story about the 50th anniversary of <BR>
Roswell. A respected member of the Roswell business community, <BR>
Kaufmann's name had been tied to the story from the very beginning. <BR>
We were saddened to learn he had died in February 2001.<BR>
<BR>
Kaufmann's credibility arose from his willingness to show journalists <BR>
and book authors a copy of his Separation Qualification Record, <BR>
which supported his claim that he was an intelligence officer <BR>
stationed at Roswell in July 1947. After Kaufmann's death, his widow <BR>
gave UFO researchers access to her husband's papers. One of those <BR>
researchers was Mark Rodeghier, scientific director of the J. Allen <BR>
Hynek Center for UFO Studies. In fall 2002, Rodeghier published his <BR>
findings in the center's journal: "To put it quite plainly, Frank <BR>
Kaufmann created an altered version of an official document to present <BR>
a false version of his military career consistent with his claims <BR>
about his involvement with the events at Roswell. His supposed work <BR>
in intelligence was used to explain how he came to be so knowledgeable <BR>
about what crashed at Roswell and the subsequent military cover-up."<BR>
<BR>
<BR>
DYING CONFESSION<BR>
<BR>
Stanton Friedman, a physicist and author of several books on Roswell, <BR>
tells POPULAR MECHANICS he was not surprised that Kaufmann had <BR>
altered his service record. "He got out of the service in 1945. He <BR>
was a civilian employee doing the same job, as a clerk."<BR>
<BR>
Friedman says his suspicions were raised during a 1999 meeting with <BR>
Kaufmann and several other researchers. He says he asked Kaufmann <BR>
pointed questions about his working relationship with Maj. Jesse Marcel, <BR>
who was an intelligence officer at the Roswell base in '47, and <BR>
Col. William Blanchard, the base commanding officer at that time.<BR>
<BR>
"Kaufmann knew he was dying," Friedman says, explaining why he trusted <BR>
the answers he received. "I asked Kaufmann, 'Did you take Marcel to <BR>
the [crash] site?' He said 'no.' I asked him, 'Did you take Blanchard <BR>
to the site?' He said 'no.'"<BR>
<BR>
Despite the disappointing document disclosure by the National Archives <BR>
and the discovery that Kaufmann had altered his military records, <BR>

>I'm not surprised to find he [Emerson] makes no mention

>

>relating to operation "Snow Bird", or even "snowbird".


Whilst awaiting responses from elsewhere, I asked the
TF158 contact if he could please comment on those points.

He replied:

[BEGIN]
'Snowbird', I think, unlike 'Rice Bowl', was not code for
a specific mission, but more of a code word for a larger
command and control network (headquarters).

Most likely it was command and control at or near
Pentagon level - General Officers and staff.

Remember that, unlike today, there was no Joint Special
Operations Command.

'Snowbird' seems to have been focused at a minimum on two
areas. First, of immediate concern, planning and
executing the second rescue attempt of American citizens
held hostage in Iran - operation 'Honey Badger'.

Secondly, the development of new elite air and ground
units capable of conducting joint unlimited special
operations. 'Task Force 158' was involved in both.

By late July 1980, 'Task Force 158' was informed that
operation 'Honey Badger' was being cancelled. The hostage
location problem you mentioned made any second attempt
too costly.

Thereafter, 'Task Force 158' returned to its base at Ft
Campbell. After returning, 'Task Force 158' was not
disbanded, but started to train under 'snowbird' as part
of the new elite special operations units program.

These would be the '[deleted]', '[deleted]' and
'[deleted]' missions These operations took place
starting Aug 1980 in Southwest U.S. - Texas, Oklahoma,
still under the command of LTC [deleted].

I heard covert units were also formed (seaspray).
[END]


Although I've had to keep some of the ongoing detail back
for now, that is the suggested explanation for Emerson's
cited, operation 'Snow Bird'.

For further information about 'seaspray', see:

http://www.specialoperations.com/Domestic/CIA/Seaspray.ht
m

It's apparently a summary taken directly from material in
Emerson's book.


The generally accepted history of that formative period
seems to be as documented on the 'nightstalkers.com'
['Home of the Night Stalker Association'] web site:

"On 20 January 1981, the hostages were released, and
Operation Honey Badger was cancelled. The men of Task
Force 158 expected to disband and return to their former
units; however, Army leadership determined that the unit
was needed to meet future contingencies".


However, it's since evidently understood that operation
'Honey Badger' had in fact been cancelled circa
July/August 1980 and thereafter, a "new phase" of
training began, instrumental to which was the addition of
OH-6 'Little Bird' helicopters.

This involved at least three, separate, code-named
operations, which, whilst in readiness for a second
hostage rescue attempt, were effectively ongoing
developments of the special operations capabilities
recognised.

Central, was a continual evaluation/experience of task
force helicopters flying in darkness and relying on
night-vision goggles.

In summary, I then queried of our TF158 contact:

"As operation 'Honey Badger' had been aborted, am I
correct in concluding that those three code-named,
September 1980 - January 1981, operations were not
specifically connected to plans for a second rescue
mission, i.e., this was merely ongoing training in
general?"

He explains:

[BEGIN]
James, yes... apparently, as once our intelligence
reports indicated that the hostages where scattered all
over Iran, the conventional concept of operation 'Honey
Badger' was no longer usable.

Those of us in 'Honey Badger, from the 101st aviation
group Ft Campbell Ky, who participated as aircrewmen
onboard those army UH-60 and CH-47 helicopters, along
with Air Force aircrews of C-130s and CH-53 pavelow
helicopters from May 1980 until late July 1980, were
assembled together while still at Dugway proving grounds,
Utah and so informed.

Yes, while 'snowbird' continued on with an ever-changing
scenario of 'how tos and what ifs', with Army and Air
Force aircraft, there was never any final solution until
thankfully Ronald Reagan arrived on the scene and the bad
guys backed down.

I find it hard to believe that anything short of an all-
out military operation by the United States on Iran at
the time, say, similar to how President Reagan did things
later, starting with the invasion in Grenada, would have
accomplished anything without heavy loss of life, to not
only the hostages but the rescue team itself.
Those were desperate times.

The positive that resulted... the current special
operations capabilities of today.

Due to the secrecy and speed with which the original
'Task Force 158' formed for operation 'Honey Badger', no
complete personnel records exist and I have yet to
recognize the name of any person who says he participated
in operation 'Honey Badger'.
[END]


Coincidentally, I have been discussing 'Cash-Landrum'
with John Burroughs, inherent 'Rendlesham' participant
and still USAF reservist, only recently returned from
"forward deployment" elsewhere.

He notes of these contemporary and absolutely founding,
late December 1980, 'UFO' cases:

"The Cash-Landrum angle was looked at by a Curt Brubaker
and after he looked into that, tying in with Bentwaters,
he stopped everything he was doing involving UFOs. Could
never get a answer why!".

Curt Brubaker and 'UFOs'?

So far as I'm aware, the only connection is a 1998,
prominent, U.S. TV broadcast, "UFO Cover-Up? Live!".

Wasn't that the, 'captive Roswell aliens endorsed
strawberry ice-cream and Tibetan chants [whatever]',
debacle?
