A member of the 81st Security Police Squadron (I won't
name him for now) detailed events which occurred between
29-31 December, 1980.

For three days, he was posted to the now infamous east
gate and witnessed both personnel and helicopters
[unfortunately, he wasn't aware where either came from]
operating in the 'landing site' area.

Advised by his Shift Commander how 'the base' knew what
was going on, he was given no further information, except
for being warned not to report over the radio anything
observed.

He could only conclude it looked like they were all
searching for something.

I would be cautious about directly relating this to the
overall case evidence - it still requires verification.
[END]


Although that remains the situation, some further
information from said source does perhaps justify now
being revealed.

As previously mentioned, he is someone publicly known to
have participated in overall events. I do not have
permission to identify him and that's presently
unnecessary.

In various interviews, Halt and Penniston have both
spoken about the swift arrival of an 'unscheduled' cargo
plane and its 'special' personnel.

That article initially referred to in my 19 February
posting was the 1994 'Sightings' [UK] magazine interview
- no longer online. The relevant extract was:

It seemed peculiar, but an unscheduled American CS Galaxy
transport aeroplane landed at RAF Woodbridge a few days
after the first incident, bringing with it its own
security personnel and Halt wasn't even allowed to know
what their mission was. With that, why did a Lt. Colonel
and Deputy Base Commander, with a security clearance too
high to mention, not have the authority to know what a
visiting plane is doing on his base?

He also said that following the planes arrival un-marked
helicopters, that were not from Woodbridge, were seen
above the landing site during the following days.
[END]


If this part of the Rendlesham story has any substance, I
wondered if there might be a connection between the
transport aircraft and alleged helicopters. Simply asked
if he could recall the exact sequence of events, my
source confirms, "it was a C-5 and it came on Sunday. The
Helos were Mon-Wed".

That would date the transporter's arrival as 28 December
and the helicopter operations between 29-31 December, as
initially claimed.

Also asked for details of the helicopters, so far I only
know they were apparently "single blades". I'm trying to
obtain further details of size and any other clues.

Ruled out by my source is that these were HH-53 'Super
Jolly Green Giant' helicopters from the 67th ARRS, based
at RAF Bentwaters. Related and contemporary air-crew I
have been in contact with, during recent years, assure
that no HH-53s were flying during that holiday period.

Discarding the 'lighthouse UFO' sightings and 'beams of
light', leaves a scenario where there might, incredibly,
have been something else going on at the same time.
If the U.S. government/military was transporting
helicopters to RAF Woodbridge, whatever the purpose, it
presumably wasn't a three day training exercise using
Rendlesham forest as a convenient location.

Dependent on the nature of any such theoretical mission,
if it was 'top secret', who you gonna call?

Maybe give the boys from 'Task Force 158' a ring?

We'll see if anything related shows up in material
released from ongoing TF158 FOIA requests.

If this part of the Rendlesham story has any substance, I
wondered if there might be a connection between the
transport aircraft and alleged helicopters. Simply asked
if he could recall the exact sequence of events, my
source confirms, "it was a C-5 and it came on Sunday. The
Helos were Mon-Wed".

That would date the transporter's arrival as 28 December
and the helicopter operations between 29-31 December, as
initially claimed.

Also asked for details of the helicopters, so far I only
know they were apparently "single blades". I'm trying to
obtain further details of size and any other clues.

Ruled out by my source is that these were HH-53 'Super
Jolly Green Giant' helicopters from the 67th ARRS, based
at RAF Bentwaters. Related and contemporary air-crew I
have been in contact with, during recent years, assure
that no HH-53s were flying during that holiday period.

Discarding the 'lighthouse UFO' sightings and 'beams of
light', leaves a scenario where there might, incredibly,
have been something else going on at the same time.
If the U.S. government/military was transporting
helicopters to RAF Woodbridge, whatever the purpose, it
presumably wasn't a three day training exercise using
Rendlesham forest as a convenient location.

Dependent on the nature of any such theoretical mission,
if it was 'top secret', who you gonna call?

Maybe give the boys from 'Task Force 158' a ring?

We'll see if anything related shows up in material
released from ongoing TF158 FOIA requests.


James.

in the narrow jet core are only about 30 mph. These are always roughly westerly
winds. Also bear in mind that although the course of the jet does snake and dip,
the typical altitude of the core is around 35,000 feet, not 25,000. At 25k
average wind speeds drop to around 20 mph, a stiff breeze. (Mean winter jet
speeds are higher, approaching 100 mph, but the core retreats south and west
over the atlantic to the US eastern seaboard and moreover climbs to about

From: "david CLARKE" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Tue, 8 Jul 2003 11:03:13 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Radar UFOs caused by birds?

Greetings list,

Two interesting snippets from the Newsletter of the Royal Air Force
Air Defence Museum (RAF Neatishead), July 2003, on the subject
of unexplained radar echoes known at that time as 'angels':

Barry Huddart writes that:

"During mid 1957 as a Senior Aircraftsman I was posted to the
Research Branch of Headquarters Fighter Command where I
worked in conjunction with Civilian Research Officers for a time
on the 'angel' problem. I well remember my contact with Dr David
Lack FRS, on one occasions I was present at a meeting with hinm
where he explained the habits of migrating birds.

"The RBFC received the 35mm film from each stations'
Photographic Display system and it was one of my tasks to project
and plot the 'angels' onto a map to try and find some correlation
between adjacent radar sites, a long task requiring a lot of
concentration and patience, this having to do be done on a daily
pasis and taking most of the day to correlate each station's film,
which had to take into consideration meteorological conditions
at the time.

"It took several weeks to complete a satisfactory outcome as far
as this project was concerned and I can verify the fact that
senior research officials were loathe to admit that our small
feathered friends could cause such disruption to the radar
screens: larger birds often did and I know of one occasion
when fighters were scrambled to intercept an echo on a radar
screen which turned out to be a Golden Eagle at 25,000 feet
in a Jet-stream, very unusual but none the less true."

In another article, museum manager Doug Robb writes that:

"...[another reader] reminds us that though 'angels' were
eventually attributed to migrating bird flocks, this solution
to the problem of 'spurious echoes' on wartime 10cm coast
watching radars had been rejected in 1945. He recalled such
spurious echoes in 1947, generally out over the Channel, on the
Type 14 radar at GCI Wartling [near Eastbourne].

"Flight Sergeant Dove, the senior radar fitter, strongly
maintained that these echoes were due to flocks of seagulls
from cliffs around Beachy Head, wheeling about over the
sea. Despite the objection, 'how can a few non-reflective
birds provide echoes?' Chiefy's theory was that static
electricity caused by the rubbing together of the flight
feathers created an electro-magnetic field around the birds,
as it was this that provided the 'reflective surface.' We wonder,
in the light of today's knowledge and technology, is F.S.
Dove's theory a runner?"

Dave Clarke

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Sun, 6 Jul 2003 21:04:08 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary

I now have a copy of the program and given the time
constraints involved, it's an exceptional production.

As the producer, Clive Dunn, had indicated to myself,
it's, overall, a damning indictment.

It is however, a fair production and I was pleased to see
the interview with John Burroughs included. It's his
first public interview for many years.

John stated that Halt and Penniston have
'sensationalised' the story and local forestry worker,
Vince Thurkettle [who examined the 'landing site'
directly afterwards], was also scathing about motives for
propagating it - people trying so "save face" and "cheque
book ufology".

I'm aware from my ongoing dialogue with John that's he's
not pleased about some of Halt and Penniston's claims.

I also knew Vince considered this was one related
documentary where he felt able to say exactly what he
wanted.

Kevin Conde (pronounced 'Condy') comes across as the
jovial character he is and makes a strong case for his
hoax being responsible for Halt's beams of light. A
'recreation' was filmed and looks convincing.

Excellent use is made of the Halt tape to illustrate a
tie-in with both the beams and nearby coastal lights,
shown filmed at night. Orfordness lighthouse is still
notably striking.

Vince also helpfully explains that the 'starscope' was
being used when Halt was looking directly at the
lighthouse. This, he comments, would inevitably result in
the lighthouse appearing 'unworldly'.

My own contributions on camera hopefully also set other
aspects in context.

A claim from one former member of the 81st SPS that
"drugs were rampant" was also aired, together with the
fact Halt had left a Christmas party before becoming
involved.
Halt was contacted by the BBC and questioning whether he
had been drinking more than just orange juice beforehand,
they report that Halt told them it was a "family
gathering".

It was in actually a 'covered dish' dinner for officers,
held in the Woody Inn. Elsewhere, Halt has confirmed he
left the party just as speeches were about to be made and
awards presented; that was why the Base Commander, Col.
Ted Conrad, remained behind and ordered Halt to
investigate.

Asked whether his perceived observations could be
mistaken, Halt merely replied he was "insulted by the
question"!


I'll transcribe some of the direct quotes when possible.

The presenter, David Whitely, is particularly affable and
cemented the entire program with a narrative which
revealed he had worked hard to understood the historical
case evidence and developments in recent years.

He concluded that 'Inside Out' had exposed a massive
"black hole" in this local legend.


I hear from Clive that there's a "strong possibility" it
will be broadcast by BBC East again.


James.
E-mail: voyager@jeaston.com

From: "david CLARKE" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Sun, 6 Jul 2003 19:11:59 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] RAF Lakenheath incident 1956

Secret papers tell how RAF hunted aliens

Paul Harris
Sunday July 6, 2003
The Observer

They have been the subject of derision for claiming aliens have visited
Earth from outer space, but believers in the existence of UFOs were this
weekend excitedly poring over newly released military documents that show
how fighter aircraft were scrambled to intercept strange shapes in Britain's
skies.
The secret papers obtained from the US military give an insight into an
astonishing chain of events sparked by UFO sightings over East Anglia in
1956.

After receiving numerous calls reporting bright lights darting across the
sky, fighters from RAF Lakenheath spent more than seven hours trying to
shoot down the objects, which were picked up on army radar screens.

The classified documents were secured under the US Freedom of Information
Act by Dave Clarke, an author researching the subject.

One US Air Force intelligence report described how '12 to 15' objects were
picked up on radar screens on 13 August 1956. They were tracked for more
than 50 miles. One object was logged travelling at 4,000mph. 'Operators
making these radar sightings are of the opinion that malfunctions of
equipment did not cause these radar sightings,' the document said.

The radar logs describe white lights darting across the skies. At times, the
objects travelled in formation and performed sharp turns.

One document describes how an object was tracked by radar for 26 miles,
before it hovered for five minutes then flew away again.

A cable was sent from US Air Force Headquarters in Washington warning of the
'considerable interest and concern' at the sightings and demanding an
immediate inquiry. The cable asked if they were linked to a similar scare
reported by a British radar station on the Danish island of Bornholm in the
Baltic Sea a week later.

Most UFO sightings are explained by phenomena such as clouds, weather
balloons or unusual atmospheric events. At the time of the 'Lakenheath
incident', observers did report an unusual level of meteorite activity.
Meteors, and the trails they leave behind, can register on radars and
critics have said this explains the Lakenheath incident.
Astronomical phenomena are also considered a possible cause. One pilot sent
up to intercept the objects reported 'chasing a star.' Others described
objects they were able to 'lock on' to with their radar systems but that
then manoeuvred around them.

But for UFO believers the new documents confirm their Lakenheath sightings
as the most dramatic of British UFO encounters and provide proof that alien
craft have 'buzzed' Britain for the past 50 years. 'I am absolutely
convinced they were breaches of our airspace by some extraordinary flying
machines,' said Graham Birdsall, editor of UFO magazine.

Clarke admitted this weekend it was difficult to attribute all the visual
sightings and radar activity both from the ground and the on-board radar
systems to meteorites or weather conditions. He believes the incident was
treated so seriously by the military that it sparked a Cold War security
scare. By 1956, the RAF Lakenheath air base, where the fighters were
scrambled from, was on the front line of the geopolitical divide. Lakenheath
played host to the new super-sensitive American U-2 spy planes and also
provided storage facilities for atomic bombs.

Clues to solving the mystery may still lie in secret US archives. After
being told no more documentation existed, Clarke discovered a reference to a
further document on the incident in the US National Archives. He has logged
a request to release it. All British reports were destroyed in a fire five
years after the event, according to RAF records.

Clarke believes the incident had such serious security implications that
documents must still exist. 'I am a UFO sceptic but this is an incident that
has me baffled. It is just possible that some form of Soviet spy craft was
responsible, but difficult to match any of their planes to what was observed
at the time,' he said.

This is categorically untrue:

> I e-mailed Kevin Conde who claims it was his hoax that was

> alleged hoax was not the cause). I felt I was very polite, but

I have never received any email from Georgia. If I did I would
reply. I did what I did, and I have no problem discussing it with
someone that wishes to engage in a rational discussion of it.

I'm going to email her and ask her to provide the dates and texts of
the emails. I will answer her questions, and post the replies here.

Next, I have never claimed I perpetrated a hoax. I played a
practical joke, and common sense indicates to a rational and unbiased
observer that my practical joke might have caused some of the
sightings.

At the same place in time, at the same physical locations as some of
the sightings, I drove in circles in a brand new Plymouth Volare
shining white, red, blue, green and yellow lights into the mist while
making noises over the PA system. The witnesses, as related in the
infamous Halt Memo said they saw white, red, and blue lights.

Now you can interpret these two ways. You can assume that they did
not see my practical joke, which was going on at the same time and in
the same place, or you can assume that they were actually visited by
aliens.

Now, I don't believe my joke is the only thing that happened. Like
many things in life, I think a lot of little things combined in the
same place and at the same time to cause this issue to develop a life
of its own.

You had a gullible and hysterical gate guard. You had me playing a
joke, and you had a Lt Col who was willing to go chase shadows
through the woods.

One of the key points is the Lt Col. The cops would have never made
a 6 mile field trip through the woods on their own. No way! They
only went because of the Lt Col's decision to lead the expedition.

I think it is fair to say that the "Rendlesham Forest Incident" only
came into existence because that particular Lt Col's judgment, or
lack thereof, let him to lead an off base goose chase.

One thing I can state that cannot be challenged is that I was there,
and Georgia was not. Who's the better judge of what happened?


Kevin

From: "kevin_conde" <kevin_conde@yahoo.com>
Date: Mon, 14 Jul 2003 15:34:59 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Re: New Rendlesham Documentary

James:

Some comments:

> It seemed peculiar, but an unscheduled American CS Galaxy
> transport aeroplane landed at RAF Woodbridge a few days
> after the first incident, bringing with it its own
> security personnel and Halt wasn't even allowed to know
> what their mission was. With that, why did a Lt. Colonel
> and Deputy Base Commander, with a security clearance too
> high to mention, not have the authority to know what a
> visiting plane is doing on his base?

Aircraft came and went all the time. Aircraft transiting the base
were known as transient aircraft, and they were never "scheduled."
They could have any number of reasons for coming in.
Familiarization, refueling, etc. There's little reason to suspect
anything odd or to attach too much importance to such an event.

As for its own security - a C5 was a Class B resource - meaning it
had to be guarded. Depending on its mission it would not be unusual
to have its own security personnel. If it did not have on board
security, we would have had to post it. I've guarded C5's all over
the place, including Thule Greenland - it's normal.

As for the Deputy Base Commander not knowing why it was there. That
is absolute no reason to suspect anything. The USAF ALWAYS operated
under the concept of "Need to know." If all that bird was doing was
refueling at an out-of-the-way airbase, and was on a classified
mission, the DBC would have no reason to know what it was doing. The
USAF runs all sorts of classified missions. Must I point out that
just because a bird came in on a classified mission does not mean
that mission involved visits from outer space? By nature what the
USAF does is best done with no fanfare. Unfortunately some people
insist on assuming that the military has nefarious reasons for
wanting to practice routine operational security.

Another point, you need to understand that the DBC was not an
especially important or critical position. Many DBC's were gofers.
(Go for this, go for that) Halt definitely, in my opinion, was in the
gofer category. The DBC is like a fifth wheel, or a spare tire - most
of the time it's kept in the trunk (Boot) and covered with dust.

> He also said that following the planes arrival un-marked
> helicopters, that were not from Woodbridge, were seen
> above the landing site during the following days.
Nonsense! Did not happen!

The ARRS squadron at Woodbridge was an AIR RESCUE SQUADRON.
Commercial fishing boats in the North Atlantic did not normally call
up the local rescue center and ask permission to schedule and
emergency. Can you imagine a phone call to the rescue
center: "Hello, this is a fishing boat in the North Atlantic, if its
not too much trouble can we schedule our selves to sink suddenly next
Tuesday at 0330 GMT? Lovely! Thanks ever so much. Ta!"

The ARRS was always flying unscheduled missions. It's what they
did. Their birds also had the subdued grey USAF camouflage paint
scheme that makes them look unmarked from a distance, or at night or
on a grey day.


Kevin

From: Georgina Bruni <georgina@easynet.co.uk>Date: Sat, 12 Jul 2003 17:15:55
+0100
Subject: Re: Rendlesham UFO 'Hoax'


>From: David Rudiak <DRudiak@earthlink.net>
>To: UFO UpDates - Toronto <ufoupdates@sympatico.ca>
>Date: Fri, 11 Jul 2003 13:51:53 -0700
>Subject: Re: Rendlesham UFO 'Hoax'

>Now we have the latest "flavor-of-the-month" debunking
>explanation - some guy in a beat up car with colored lights on
>it. Yep, that must have been it.

I e-mailed Kevin Conde who claims it was his hoax that was
responsible for the incident. I asked him if he would kindly
answer some questions (those which I put to the list as why his
alleged hoax was not the cause). I felt I was very polite, but
so far I haven't received a reply.

After reviewing the questions he'd have a hard time answering
them if he aims to continue fooling the media that he was
responsible.

I did a search on Conde and I found something really
interesting. Debunker James Easton, who was responsible for
promoting Conde's story, first mentions the hoax in his Voyager
Newsletter No 18.

Conde appears to have had second thoughts about his hoax being
connected to the incident. He wrote:

"This incident [hoax] occurred right after Christmas. For
reasons that are hard to explain it is my impression that I
pulled my stunt during an exercise. We would not have had an
exercise during the Christmas holiday. That is a strong
indication that my stunt is not the source of this specific
incident".

Easton cannot accept the fact that Conde has decided his hoax
was not responsible for the incident and he points out the
following.

"My personal conclusion about Kevin's prank remains unaltered;
if his hoax, or a copycat exercise, wasn't responsible for those
'beams of light', it would be an exceptional coincidence.

Typical!

So ask yourself why Easton still promoted Conde's hoax as being
the sole cause of the Rendlesham incident. And why Conde decided
to change his mind yet again.

It's a well known fact that certain people can get addicted to
being in the media limelight. There is one well-known debunker
of the case who actually apologised to me for continuing the
lighthouse saga. He knows the truth but TV appearances are far
too tempting to ignore. And were he to say that he no longer
believes the lighthouse theory, then he would be of no further
use. Because as we all know the media need a sceptic (or
debunker) to balance their programmes.

Alas, this is what I call egomania. Never mind the poor
witnesses who are still being ridiculed, and never mind the
evidence. What matters to these people is their fifteen minutes
of fame. And what's more they get upset at the idea of answering
certain questions that could make THEM look bad. Questions that
no doubt go against their ridiculous made up theories. And from
what I've heard from producers, you think they were stars!

Sorry, but as you may have gathered, I have absolutely no time
for these people. I just don't tolerate them. My greatest
pleasure has been doing live TV and radio shows when I am up
against one (or several) of them. I have developed a reputation
for making them look foolish, so much so that when I did a
London radio show recently, nobody from a sceptical group could
be found to argue with me.

That said, I have no problem with sceptics who genuinely want to
debate a theory or case. But please don't ever ask me to be
sympathetic with people who go to extremes to try to prove that
a lighthouse or battered car was responsible for the famous
Rendlesham Forest case.

Georgina Bruni

miles. They didn't see much of anything, they did fall in

uncomfortable. Keep in mind this is Suffolk in the
winter. It's about 35, 40 degrees and the wind's blowing
off the coast. And, uh, Penniston ...[unclear]... right
around in the vehicle left his jacket behind. Burroughs
did have his jacket on, but he was starting to get cold".

were lights ...[unclear]... I thought 'There's an
explanation for this. The lighthouse is out there, we
know where the lighthouse is. There's probably some
moisture in the sky. There's a prism effect off the
cloud, or something. There's an explanation for this'."

Halt knew the truth was otherwise and how the lighthouse

the farmhouse at Capel Green, pinpoints it as Orfordness
lighthouse. As I detailed in an article:

Halt was asked about the assertion he had been deceived
by the Orford Ness lighthouse and replied:

"First, the lighthouse was visible the whole time. It was
readily apparent, and it was 30 to 40 degrees off to our
right. If you were standing in the forest where we stood,
at the supposed landing site or whatever you want to call
it, you could see the farmer's house directly in front of
us. The lighthouse was 30 to 35 degrees off to the right,
and the object was close to the farmer's house and moving
from there to the left, through the trees".

the perspective he believed to be accurate. When he
states, "If you were standing in the forest where we
stood, at the supposed landing site or whatever you want
to call it, you could see the farmer's house directly in
front of us", that's correct and the Orford Ness
lighthouse is in a direct line of sight, east, towards
the coast.

degrees off to the right." that seems to be
consequentially incorrect; the Shipwash lightship was
"off to the right", the lighthouse was straight ahead,
where Halt observed the 'unidentified light' to be.

His comment that "the object was close to the farmer's
house", again places the light source in the line of
sight to Orford Ness lighthouse, whereas he believed the
lighthouse to be much further south.

http://www.rendlesham.com/map2.jpg

Of course, admitting the truth was devastating
[especially at a UFO conference!] to his own UFO sighting
of a flashing light, in exactly the same location where
Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston had been deceived by a
coastal 'beacon'.
[END]

Why has Halt never admitted he knew about the lighthouse
chase and instead, proclaimed it would never have fooled
anyone, especially himself?


2. Halt's precise location of the 'UFO', as observed near
the farmhouse at Capel Green, pinpoints it as Orfordness
lighthouse. As I detailed in an article:

Halt was asked about the assertion he had been deceived
by the Orford Ness lighthouse and replied:

"First, the lighthouse was visible the whole time. It was
readily apparent, and it was 30 to 40 degrees off to our
right. If you were standing in the forest where we stood,
at the supposed landing site or whatever you want to call
it, you could see the farmer's house directly in front of
us. The lighthouse was 30 to 35 degrees off to the right,
and the object was close to the farmer's house and moving
from there to the left, through the trees".

Here, as never before, Halt provides specific details of
the perspective he believed to be accurate. When he
states, "If you were standing in the forest where we
stood, at the supposed landing site or whatever you want
to call it, you could see the farmer's house directly in
front of us", that's correct and the Orford Ness
lighthouse is in a direct line of sight, east, towards
the coast.

However, when he claims, "The lighthouse was 30 to 35
degrees off to the right." that seems to be
consequentially incorrect; the Shipwash lightship was
"off to the right", the lighthouse was straight ahead,
where Halt observed the 'unidentified light' to be.

His comment that "the object was close to the farmer's
house", again places the light source in the line of
sight to Orford Ness lighthouse, whereas he believed the
lighthouse to be much further south.
[END OF ARTICLE EXTRACT]

There's a map on my web site which unequivocally proves
this:

http://www.rendlesham.com/map2.jpg
[END]

Where is any evidence otherwise?


3. Those original witness statements are authentic and
all contain Halt's hand-written appraisal of the author.

John Burroughs confirms, in writing:

"As far as the part about Penniston saying he examined it
[the 'craft' - James] at his leisure, I believe that came
out when he went under hypnotic regression".

"As far as the lighthouse goes, the statements that
everybody made such a big deal about were first made
available by Col Holt during the filming of 'Unsolved
Mysteries'."

"One thing I can say from what I have pulled off of the
internet about Halt and Penniston is that their story's
sure changed a lot since Strange but True. Also I feel
some of Penniston story is being influenced by him going
under hypnosis".

"Anyway I have went over many of the articles that you
have written from talking to witness over the years.
First of all everybody makes a big deal about the
lighthouse, including you, how it was being held back.
Well if you read my statement I described seeing several
things before coming to a Farmers House then seeing a
beacon, mind you a beacon, not the lights we saw before.
We followed it for 2 miles and could see it was coming
from a Lighthouse".
[END]

Why does Penniston still maintain those statements were
forgeries and part of a 'cover up'?


How can any proponents cite this pivotal 'British
Roswell' case as anything other than an embarrassing
shambles, which ultimately only reflects on ufology
worldwide.


I have received an amusing e-mail from Tracy Williams,
series director of 'Inside Out'. Bruni's rants had
reached Tracy, who writes, "I told her we had been
planning this for eighteen months. It's actually more
like two years, I now realise".

I updated Tracy about Bruni's further predilection for
such as 'Alternative 3' and 'crop circles' being evidence
of the great British MoD cover-up, etc.

I'm sure Tracy can work out the credibility score.

In a brief, official BBC statement endorsing the program,
he affirms, "The programme presented the evidence as Mr
Conde gave it and had no reason to doubt he was telling
the truth".

The bottom line is now even more firmly established than
as I recently summarised:

"'Inside Out' was a spectacular coup which caught all but
the informed completely unaware.

As for the 'wailing and gnashing of teeth' from
perceivable straw-clutchers, some might conclude that 'a
day late and a dollar short' would be charitable.

The program was a landmark 'fait accompli'...".


'UFO Magazine' might wish to inform their readers that,
"To mark World UFO Day", BBC Online invite, "test your
knowledge of unidentified flying objects", see, as
previously mentioned:

http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/3036596.stm

"On 27 December 1980, a number of US Air Force police in
Rendlesham Forest, near RAF Woodbridge, Suffolk saw what
they thought was a UFO. After the incident, Rendlesham
became known as the 'British Roswell'. But what did the
UFO turn out to be?"

A: A British Army weather balloon
B: A top secret US Air Force Stealth Bomber
C: President Ronald Reagan in his Air Force One jet
D: A 1979 Plymouth Volare Air Force Police patrol car

Well, it can't be 'C', because Reagan wasn't inaugurated
as President until 20 January, 1981...

John,

If it helps, the following summary [source?] is declared
at various web sites:

1922 - County Donegal, Ireland: Irish Republic Army man
Lawrence Bradley, wrote to the editor of 'Watford and Wet-
Hersts Post' magazine (4/30/64) that while he was fighting a
scattered rear-guard, mostly in the mountains of Donegal, he
came upon a cave with vegetation at the entrance that had
been scorched. The only occupants in the cave were the sick
and the wounded that had been unable to walk. The six able-
bodied soldiers that were looking after them said they had
been awakened early pre-dawn by a whirring noise outside of
the cave and had fired their rifles in the direction of the
noise, thinking that it was an armoured car. Suddenly the
object retaliated by firing jets of flame at the cave
entrance. After near suffocation, the soldiers ran out to
see the flame throwing UFO ascending into the sky. Clearly
visible, it was circular in shape and glowing and of a shiny
metal.
[END]

From: "david CLARKE" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Wed, 23 Jul 2003 16:50:49 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary


Rob McClean wrote:

> I think it is quite likely that Col. Halt was looking forward to a
midnight
> excursion in the woods. Brenda Butler wrote one article in which she
pointed
> out that it would have taken at least an hour for Halt to arrive at East
> Gate from the party.

I recently re-located my video-copy of the "Strange But True" special
on the Rendlesham incident, transmitted by UK's ITV network in 1996.
It features interviews with Halt, Penniston & Burroughs, which at the time
was a 'first.' Whilst re-watching this recently with Andy Roberts, he
pointed out a few intriguing details I had overlooked, which in retrospect
do support the impression that Halt & his party were indeed looking forward
to their expedition in the woods, and that - despite his protestations -
Halt
was not quite the skeptic he has always claimed to have been.

I've transcribed lots of little bits and pieces in shorthand, and present
the
most interesting here:

*Firstly, John Burroughs admits that he had played a number of practical
jokes on his immediate superiors before the 'first' sighting in the early
hours
of 26 December 1980 (shades of Kevin Conde) -- and as a result he was
not initially believed when he reported strange lights "like a Christmas
tree"
in the forest beyond the East Gate.

*On arrival at East Gate, (circa 2-3 AM??) Sgt Penniston says he "contacted
control" (? Bentwaters Tower ?) who checked with Air Defence radar (RAF
Watton), who reported back that "about 15 minutes before" they had tracked
a unidentified target "that was also seen by Heathrow in London". The exact
quote is: "...They notified me that they had tracked a bogey about 15
minutes
before and they confirmed it with Eastern Radar and Heathrow in London.
It's approximate location was about five miles off base when they lost it."
This is a clear distortion of memory as the 'sighting' recorded by Heathrow
is fixed by documentary evidence - the tracking they made (also reported
visually by a 737 crew outbound) was the re-entry of the COSMOS satellite
after 2100 hours on 25 December. Here you can see how the myth of the
'radar tracking' arose!
*John Burroughs states that afterwards "I heard a rumour that it [the UFO]
was possibly a British exercise with ships and planes out to sea." Has
anyone followed this up -- there certainly was a suggestion years ago there
had been a British naval exercise off the Suffolk coast, involving if I
recall
HMS Norfolk.

* Crucially important is the revelation that as a result of the first
night's
sightings - presumably on Halt's orders - the 'Light Alls' were moved into
the forest, with the clear expectation that the UFO would return:

*According to the programme it was "the next night" (ie night of 26 Dec)
that Halt's dinner party was interrupted and he led his team into the
forrest. In fact it was not the night of the 26 Dec, but the following night
(27/28 December).

*Halt: "I was sure something had happened. I was not convinced it was
a UFO but I did not know what it was...there was only one way to find
out...I assembled a small team of experts and we set off into the forest
really to debunk it."

"It was time to put this thing to bed. *I know there was something
there* [my emphasis], there had to be something there. But I also
knew there had to be a logical explanation for what was going on."

*However - the impression given that this action was a 'spur of the
moment' decision is contradicted by the admission that the decision
had been taken on the 26th (the day before) to set-up light alls in the
forest in anticipation of the return of the UFO.

*Much is made of the fact it was Christmas, there were no flights in
or out of the base, and the impression is given that the UFOs helped
to relieve the boredom.

*Later in the programme Halt says: "Here I am, a senior official that
routinely denies this sort of things and diligently works to debunk 'em
[UFOs], and I am involved in the middle of something I can't explain."

*"I'm certainly glad we made that tape because without the tape even
I would have trouble believing what happened that night."

*During the expedition into the forest Halt says he called up Eastern
Radar [via Bentwaters RAPcom] on several occasions asking them to
check their scopes for unidentified targets [confirmed by the testimony
of the RAF commander there]...this, he said happened at the time that
beams of light were reported coming down on the base (ie around
3am on 28 December 1980).

Halt ends by saying: "At this stage my skepticism had disappeared...
I was really in awe."

Greetings list,

I thought you might be interested to read what's planned for the August
2003 issue of 'UFO Magazine':

>RENDLESHAM: WERE THE BBC DUPED

>Georgina Bruni and Nick Pope deliver their verdict on recent claims made by
>Kevin Conde, a former USAF Security Patrolman, that while serving at RAF
>Woodbridge, Suffolk, his prank was responsible for the famed Rendlesham
>Forest incident of December 1980.

>COMMENTARY
>By Graham W. Birdsall
>
>* Talking of spurious claims, what are we to make of those issued by former
>USAF security policeman Kevin Conde, who alleged that a prank he played on
>colleagues was the cause of the Rendlesham Forest incident of December
1980?
>Well, not much. Especially since learning that because his prank was
>conducted during an exercise, he now doubts whether it had anything to do
>with the Rendlesham incident at all. But given that those doubts were
>expressed a long time ago, how come they were never raised in the BBC's
>Inside Out programme, or the Daily Mail article which followed two days
>later? A suitable term comes to mind: 'Don't bother me with the evidence,
my

From: "Robert Mclean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>

Subject: Re: [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary

James

I think it is quite likely that Col. Halt was looking forward to a midnight
excursion in the woods. Brenda Butler wrote one article in which she pointed
out that it would have taken at least an hour for Halt to arrive at East
Gate from the party. I think 1 1/2 hours is more like it: leave the party at
Woodbridge base, drop by his office to pick up his dictaphone and tapes, go
home to change into outdoor clothes, pick up Nevels and wait while he
calibrated two AN-PDR 27's and chose to take one; drive back to RAF
Woodbridge. Then it would have taken at least another half an hour from
there to get organised and find the alleged landing site. Absolutely no
sense of urgency, despite Lt Englund's alarming news.

Chris Armold in his email of 11 July 1997 to Crow & Raine states:
-------------
Halt essentially said he planned on coming out to the site in theevening and
one way or another several of us said we'd keep himcompany. The guys I
remember were John Burroughs, Adrian Bustamante,and me. I think another
officer joined Halt, I believe it was LtBruce England, but I'm not
absolutely certain and maybe two otherguys (Possibly one named Pennington,
just can't remember for sure)There was however, no army of USAF guys out in
the woods.. No fleetof vehicles, no towed light rigs, just a half-dozen or
so of usstomping around goofing off. I brought a camera with me and I think
Halt had a tape recorder. Wewere out there for hours and someone noticed
some lights in thedistance. While they often seemed to be very close in
reality as wetried to approach them we discovered they were very far away.
Nowdon't confuse what I just wrote. Little balls of light were not
flyingaround us or getting closer and flying away. We initially thoughtthe
lights were closer than they actually were.---------------So, according to
Chris Armold, the excursion was planned in advance,and he was a member of
Halt's party. However, due to variousinconsistencies in his recollections
with what we know happened,no-one has really paid much attention to this.
Was Armold really with Halt?RegardsRobert----- Original Message -----

From: "kevin_conde" <kevin_conde@yahoo.com>
Date: Tue, 22 Jul 2003 15:15:03 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Re: New Rendlesham Documentary

James:

Georgina was heard from again:

My reply:

Georgina:

As to the alert/exercise - why don't you ask James.

Two man LE patrols. You are categorically wrong. Routine procedure
with LE was one man units. I was an LE flight chief for the majority
of my time in the cops. Even when stationed in a ghetto in SE
Washington DC the LE standard was one man patrols. Only exception
was times when there was a temporary excess of personnel.

LE did not have the manpower or case load to justify two man
patrols. Exception was during alerts, and sometimes not even then.
In this case I am a no shit expert, and any one that tells you
differently is wrong. You are the one who is factually challenged.

Zickler was the Commanding Officer of the 81st SPS, and had
jurisdiction over the 81st SPS, and nothing else. The fire
department was a part of the 81st Civil Engineering Squadron, and
came under the authority of the 81st CES squadron commander. The
Combat Support Group commander had jurisdiction over both.

You are wrong, and probably either asked the question incorrectly or
misunderstood the answer.

During an incident or emergency there was something called the on-
scene commander. Depending on the incident that could be a SSgt or
TSgt flight chief. If the incident was one that was primarily a fire
department issue, the senior fireman or CES officer was technically
in charge.

Until the incident was resolved or higher ranking personnel arrived,
the on-scene commander had control of all forces responding the
incident. If it were primarily a law enforcement or security issue,
the flight chief would be superceded by a higher ranking cop, and the
highest ranking cop would be superceded by the base or deputy base
commander once they arrived, assuming the incident was serious enough
to warrant their response.

Zickler did not have authority over the fire department. Period.
The base or deputy base commander did. If the base commander or his
deputy decided not to respond to an incident, and directed the Chief
of Security Police act in the capacity of on-scene commander, then
and only then would the CSP have authority over all forces involved
in the incident, but only for the duration of the incident.

You wrote:

>Halt and others have confirmed this too. And last night I spoke to
General
>Williams who was in charge of the bases at the time and he confirmed
this
>to be a fact. You will have to do better than that Kevin. I would
have
>thought a TSgt would have known this information.

I actually retired as a SMSgt, not a TSgt, and in your frustration
you are resorting to personal attacks. Something that I kinda
expected.

I'm going to post this reply to James' list, and solicit any readers
with actual experience as members of the USAF to comment as to the
accuracy of my reply.

As I said, you are the one who is factually challenged.


Kevin Conde

leave traces radiating outwards in all directions from a
central point.

It could, however, equate with flames from a single HAB
burner, which had been upturned.


>In this letter, McDonald was impressed with the matter
>and added that fused sand seems to be "conclusive
>evidence of a high temperature source," other than the
>mysterious melted rock (not familiar with that one - KY)
>or the "charred vegetation."

Stanford notes there was a rock which seemed to have
traces of burning on it.


>So in conclusion, I summarize the above to inquire if
>there is any particular reason this issue is not 'on the
>table' with regards to the Socorro Incident?

Quite the contrary.

Some further evidence which is related:

Stanford writes of State Patrolman Jordan:

"Jordan said that what most impressed him at the landing
site was the way the 'flame' had evidently 'sliced' a
large greasewood bush, located almost centrally in the
landing gear quadrangle, without leaving any signs of
strong turbulence, as the exhaust of a powerful rocket
thrust unit or even the whirling of helicopter blades
would have done".

"'The flame from that damn thing just sliced that
greasewood bush in half, just burned it off clean like a
blade of fire had cut right through it'".


Stanford also recalls that when with Hynek at the site,
"I could not help but deduce that the 'fiery finger' from
beneath the craft had extended itself from northeast to
southwest, reaching out for some yards from where the
mysterious object had been elevated above the ravine,
probably during its landing approach and manoeuvre, prior
to orienting the exhaust directly downward for the final
descent".

"Further, after the roaring engine was cut off, the craft
accelerated away in complete silence. Thus, we see that
still a second mode of propulsion, also different from
anything terrestrial technology now produces, was
involved for acceleration and sustained movement.

One may wonder why two different propulsive modes were
evidently utilized by the Socorro craft".

One may indeed.

Given Zamora's stated bewilderment that, on departure,
the object's exhaust wasn't apparently making any impact
on the ground, there's still one simple, terrestrial,
aerial vehicle which fits the overall profile.


Another which certainly meets key criteria is 'the bean'.

Although I haven't been able, as yet, to obtain a copy of
the book recently mentioned, I can now reveal it's
called, 'Flying Saucers - Key to Creation?', by George H.
Eastland.

A summary of the author's claims - he seemingly doesn't
relate them to Zamora's sighting - can be seen at:

http://www.weirdload.com/nm-ufo.html

Compliments to all. Kevin wrote:

>In the event of real tensions, and the belief that the Russians were
>coming, we would also have operated freely off base.
>
>The exercises that have figured into some of this controversy are an
>example. The majority of the hard core "combat" occurred off base.
>
>When in the air base ground defense mode he knew that if we waited until
>we had Russians in the wire we were already too late. It was our mission
>to go off base and engage them as far from the flight line as possible.

I've no reason to doubt this. I'm equally sure that such
off-base exercises as occurred would have been cleared with
everyone concerned in the proper order, including the British
police (it would take no more than a phone call with the Chief
Constable to become legal -- it's up to him who else, including
no one, he chooses to tell about it).

Likewise, in a shooting war, the preliminary stages from
political crisis to outbreak of hostilities generally take a
long time. Someone once calculated there were something like
42 discrete steps in this process. There is nothing in law
(but may be rather a lot in secret annexes to the leases of
US bases from HMG) to prevent the British Army or the police
from requesting assistance from the USAF. Indeed given the
overstretch of British forces this is the obvious thing to
do. However: these diplomatic niceties would have been
observed long before any shooting started. Clearly you don't
wait until that stage to tell those who will actually defend
the base that that is what they are going to do, or to train
them how to do it. One would expect, too, during the run-up
to hostilities that US perimeter defences would be very
heavily reinforced, by whatever country's armed forces.

I suspect that the responsibility of USAF police for finding
downed aircraft was also covered in the leases, and involved
some kind of standing licence to cover such emergencies. Once
again it would clearly be mad to have to go through a diplomatic
rigmarole before getting people to twisted metal and roasting
flesh. But a USAF fire crew (for example) wouldn't need to know
what gave them the right to proceed. Still, if anyone wanted to
go nosing around the PRO again, or use such FOI as we have in
this furtive little country, there is the starter for a bit of
research. Just what were the arrangements/agreements/contracts
by which (even allied) foreign troops could go into action on
British soil?

As Tim Printy points out by implication, on the second night,
when Hall went poaching in the woods, there seems to have been
no triggering misapprehension about downed planes. Ergo he and
his gang had not even a specious excuse to go hunting. But buried
in the literature somewhere is an account in which someone told
Halt "It's back... the UFO's back", which suggests a high degree
of psychological priming, and the inspiration to go on their
little spree. Add a bit of festive cheer and an armchair pilot...
Has anyone ever asked Halt if he's ever been especially concerned
about his bodily fluids? Worried about fluoride? No?

Halt, in any case, should have known the law, the constitution
and the conventions. If he didn't, he should have; if he did,
he was out of order. If Pope, Bruni & Co know about them,
they're certainly being remarkably shy about admitting it.
I cannot imagine why.

Apology: I referred (I now see) to "the Woodbridge/R'sham
complex". I meant, of course, the Bentwaters/R'sham complex.

best wishes
Peter B

Subject:    [UFORL] Socorro "fused sand"
Author:     Kenny Young <ufo@fuse.net>
Date:        Mon, 21 Jul 2003 02:42:18 +0000

Since I haven't seen the following issue raised much, could someone please inform if
the matter involving the 'fused sand' found at the Socorro, N.M. case of April, '64 has
been refuted or otherwise dismissed with a good deal of satisfaction?

The situation I refer to involves Miss Mary G. Rumph (later Miss Mary Nayes who,
in 1968 was a technician with the Radiological Health Laboratory, U.S. Public Health
Service, Las Vegas). At the time of the incident in 1964, Rumph/Nayes was working
at the Lovelace Foundation while also doing graduate work at UNM She and two
other graduate students were contacted by Air Force officers immediately after the
Zamora sighting and came down from Albuquerque, arriving the following morning
at 10:00 a.m. to examine some of the 'burnt brush' at the site.

I have a memo which states that: "the plant sap (phloem and sylem) on the stems of
creosote and mequite had burst out through the bark in many places." The memo goes
on to state that Rumph/Nayes had "immediately noticed a patch of fused sand on the
southeast side of the diamond-shaped area defined by the four depressions in the
wash." The memo, a letter dated Aug. 26, 1968 from James E. McDonald, goes on to
say that Rumph/Nayes thought "some intensely hot jet might have sprayed down on
the sand, melted it, and caused it to puddle and run."

Rumph/Nayes informed that the patch of fused material was 30-inches long, 10-
inches wide, tapering to a narrow end of about 1-inch on the downstream side. It was
generally rather smooth on top, with some ridges on the southeastern edge of the
patch.

The letter states: "She was in some doubt as to whether it might be hazardous to touch
it, but her curiosity led her to touch it and to feel the edge of it, whereby she
established that it appeared to be somewhat like a layer of ice might form on wet sand
or like a layer of ice floating on a pond."

McDonald, in this 4-page memo, is apparently trying to pursue this 'fused material'
issue 4-years after the incident, requesting investigative assistance from another
researcher. The follow up to McDonald only informs that neither Socorro State Police
Captain Sam Chavez nor Socorro City Engineer Raymond L. Senn "appear to have no
memory" of Rumph at the site (as if they would have had the area cordoned off 24/7
to take names and numbers of all interested parties visiting the site with 100%
accuracy upon being questioned 4-years later...? - KY). However, it was reported that
City Engineer Raymond Senn did recall that the mesquite bush bled in a peculiar way,
'bubbling' for quite an extended duration after the Zamora sighting.

In this letter, McDonald was impressed with the matter and added that fused sand
seems to be "conclusive evidence of a high temperature source," other than the
mysterious melted rock (not familiar with that one - KY) or the "charred vegetation."

McDonald states: "It would take some doing to fuse a puddle of sand a couple of
square feet in the area."

One item that sounds curious is how Rumph/Nayes claimed to McDonald that her
samples and results had been 'taken off' by Air Force personnel and she was instructed
not to discuss the matter further. McDonald, who also personally met with
Nayes/Rumph, states "I am certainly impressed by Mrs. Nayes' honesty and
positiveness about the matter, and I do think it merits further search."

So in conclusion, I summarize the above to inquire if there is any particular reason
this issue is not 'on the table' with regards to the Socorro Incident?

Thanks,
KENNY YOUNG

Greetings,

Kevin Conde and the Duke of Mendoza make some good points. Re Halt's
credibility, Kevin writes:
>
> >Knowing the USAF as I do I am still convinced that if the USAF was
> >covering anything up, it was a vice base commander leading a search
> >for UFO's off base accompanied by people responsible for guarding
> >nuclear weapons. The fact that senior leadership did nothing to Halt
> >can be attributed to their desire to keep the situation low key.
> >Relieving Halt would have made a splash, especially if he threw a
> >public fit, coupled with a lack of firm evidence. They may have
> >believed he was a wacko, but could not prove it.
>


This may be what is implied in the responses I obtained from some of the
senior RAF

Operations staff who were consulted about the 'incidents' at Woodbridge in
1981. The

most senior I have traced is RAF Group Captain who was Deputy Director of

Operations (Ground Environment), Neil Colvin. He told me: "I remember the
alleged

sightings by US airmen at Bentwaters [sic]. I recall that we could not
explain them but

were very sceptical of the reports. We were not privy to the actual evidence
of the

sightings by the personnel concerned, nor did we have the opportunity to
interview

the individuals involved."



Group Captain Colvin would not be drawn upon the reasons why the Air Staff
were

"sceptical of the reports" but assured me they were good reasons.
If there is a 'smoking gun' it may well be some suggestion that Halt was a
'wacko',

as Kevin suggests. This is not the sort of thing the US-UK would want to
emerge

at the time, given the context of Cold War/Greenham Common, highlighted by

Mendoza.


>
> But then R'sham and Roswell follow similar tracks: on the one
> hand the myth multiplies; on the other, the truth, or what one
> can discern of it, simplifies. Sorry, Kevin: Bruni is impervious.
>
I was most amused to see the correspondence between Bruni and
Kevin Conde. She clearly expects him to take as red assertions
that the rest of us know are garbage - specifically:

a) That that a "D Notice" was slapped on the British media to prevent
them talking about the case. Nonsense, as any real journalist will
know, all "D-Notices" are published and have no legal status, they are
merely advisory. Editors are free to ignore them, and frequently do. Any
UK editor faced with a D-Notice on a UFO story would be over the
moon - the MOD's attempt to suppress the story would be splashed
over the first page of the next edition.

I know Kevin has more sense, but he should challenge Bruni on this
one -- where's the evidence for the D-Notice? She has none.

b) That there was something wrong with UK's radar system during
the sightings, Kevin's prank cannot explain the radar evidence of UFOs
etc....more garbage.

There was nothing wrong with the UK radar system either on 26 December
or the night of Halt's expedition. Even the USAF men describe calling
up Eastern Radar (RAF Watton) to ask the ATC room to check their
scopes *while the sightings were happening.*

The MoD file makes it clear that no UFOs were either seen by operators
or captured by the radar cameras. The RAF's central air defence station,
RAF Neatishead, in the Norfolk Broads, was fully operational and its
'live' displays of the radar picture were linked directly with Watton at
the relevant time. The MoD file makes it explicit that:

"an examination of the executive logs revealed no entry in respect of
unusual radar returns
or other unusual occurrences."
If that was not sufficient in itself, I traced the Commanding Officer of
Eastern Radar at
the relevant time, Squadron Leader Derek Combe. He told me:

"I recall the incident well as I was on duty at the time it occurred....the
call came from
Bentwaters RAPcom. They requested that we scan the radars for any radar
targets
in their area: there were NONE. They reported flashing lights in the
Rendlesham
Forest area, outside the airfield runway and that the base police were
investigating
the incident."

In retrospect the "flashing lights" and lack of any radar confirmation
described by
Combe are completely consistent with Kevin's recollection of his practical
joke.

I find it utterly amazing that Bruni and Nick Pope continue to use the
so-called
"radar evidence", along with the discredited 'radiation readings' to bolster
their claims
about this case. They are fully aware of the information I have cited above,
but I
guess commercial considerations overtake honesty.

All the best,

Dave Clarke

From: Kenny Young <ufo@fuse.net>
Date: Sun, 20 Jul 2003 22:42:18 -0400
Subject: [UFORL] Socorro "fused sand"

Since I haven't seen the following issue raised much,
could someone please inform if the matter involving the
'fused sand' found at the Socorro, N.M. case of April,
'64 has been refuted or otherwise dismissed with a good
deal of satisfaction?

The situation I refer to involves Miss Mary G. Rumph
(later Miss Mary Nayes who, in 1968 was a technician
with the Radiological Health Laboratory, U.S. Public
Health Service, Las Vegas). At the time of the incident
in 1964, Rumph/Nayes was working at the Lovelace
Foundation while also doing graduate work at UNM She
and two other graduate students were contacted by Air
Force officers immediately after the Zamora sighting and
came down from Albuquerque, arriving the following
morning at 10:00 a.m. to examine some of the 'burnt
brush' at the site.

I have a memo which states that: "the plant sap (phloem
and sylem) on the stems of creosote and mequite had
burst out through the bark in many places." The memo
goes on to state that Rumph/Nayes had "immediately
noticed a patch of fused sand on the southeast side of
the diamond-shaped area defined by the four depressions
in the wash." The memo, a letter dated Aug. 26, 1968
from James E. McDonald, goes on to say that Rumph/Nayes
thought "some intensely hot jet might have sprayed down
on the sand, melted it, and caused it to puddle and
run."

Rumph/Nayes informed that the patch of fused material
was 30-inches long, 10-inches wide, tapering to a narrow
end of about 1-inch on the downstream side. It was
generally rather smooth on top, with some ridges on the
southeastern edge of the patch.

The letter states: "She was in some doubt as to whether
it might be hazardous to touch it, but her curiosity led
her to touch it and to feel the edge of it, whereby she
established that it appeared to be somewhat like a layer
of ice might form on wet sand or like a layer of ice
floating on a pond."

McDonald, in this 4-page memo, is apparently trying to
pursue this 'fused material' issue 4-years after the
incident, requesting investigative assistance from
another researcher. The follow up to McDonald only
informs that neither Socorro State Police Captain Sam
Chavez nor Socorro City Engineer Raymond L. Senn "appear
to have no memory" of Rumph at the site (as if they
would have had the area cordoned off 24/7 to take names
and numbers of all interested parties visiting the site
with 100% accuracy upon being questioned 4-years
later...? - KY). However, it was reported that City
Engineer Raymond Senn did recall that the mesquite bush
bled in a peculiar way, 'bubbling' for quite an extended
duration after the Zamora sighting.

In this letter, McDonald was impressed with the matter
and added that fused sand seems to be "conclusive
evidence of a high temperature source," other than the
mysterious melted rock (not familiar with that one - KY)
or the "charred vegetation."

McDonald states: "It would take some doing to fuse a
puddle of sand a couple of square feet in the area."

One item that sounds curious is how Rumph/Nayes claimed
to McDonald that her samples and results had been 'taken
off' by Air Force personnel and she was instructed not
to discuss the matter further. McDonald, who also
personally met with Nayes/Rumph, states "I am certainly
impressed by Mrs. Nayes' honesty and positiveness about
the matter, and I do think it merits further search."

So in conclusion, I summarize the above to inquire if
there is any particular reason this issue is not 'on the
table' with regards to the Socorro Incident?

Thanks,
KENNY YOUNG

From: Mendoza <Horseman@onetel.net.uk>
Date: Mon, 21 Jul 03 00:23:36 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Re: New Rendlesham Documentary


Compliments of the Duke of Mendoza:

In his correspondence with Georgina, Suntan of Bruni, Kevin Conde
wrote:

>Knowing the USAF as I do I am still convinced that if the USAF was
>covering anything up, it was a vice base commander leading a search
>for UFO's off base accompanied by people responsible for guarding
>nuclear weapons. The fact that senior leadership did nothing to Halt
>can be attributed to their desire to keep the situation low key.
>Relieving Halt would have made a splash, especially if he threw a
>public fit, coupled with a lack of firm evidence. They may have
>believed he was a wacko, but could not prove it.

A few years ago when my brain was still able to maintain order among
the various claims and counter-claims in this case, I spoke at length
with the RAF press officer at the MoD about this question of USAF
personnel wandering around in the woods, tho' I didn't mention the
UFO case -- merely asked where the USAF's territorial responsibility
ended and who would defend the perimeter if it were attacked. What I
gathered I passed on to James, but it might be worth reminding everyone
of what I found out.

1. USAF responsibility starts (and ends) with the fenceline of an
RAF base leased to the USAF.

2. Beyond that, i.e. outside the base, responsibility for security
rests with the local police.

That's right: Mr Plod. If hordes of Soviet Speznas (sp?) troops
were to land in the night as Soviet ICBMs landed on Birmingham (etc),
the protocol would be for the US base commander to complain to the
RAF base commander, who calls Mr Plod, who requests the Army to
give military aid to the civil community (MACC). Note that formula:
the British military would aid the police (and by implication the
British people, NOT the US military. This is important.

In real life, everyone would have had plenty of warning of such a
crisis and no doubt -- or so one hopes -- USAF base perimeters
would already be well invested with British troops ready to deal
with the red peril. [The irony has benefit of hindsight. Soviet
special forces were not like those in the West -- they were trained
for suicide missions, and treated like animals in training. They
were very nasty, but not particularly sophisticated.] Nonetheless
the forms would have been observed.
For constitutional and historical reasons this separation of the
military and police is taken rather seriously by the Brits, and
Lt Col Halt *should* have been well aware of it. He and his gang
really had no business poking around in the forest AT ALL. Sqn Ldr
Moreland certainly would have known that [and wasn't he a bit more
than the "Liaison Officer" Bruni titles him?]. Legally speaking,
Halt & Co were trespassing: even under the law at the time, had
they caused significant damage in the forest, they would have been
committing a crime & could have been prosecuted. Unlikely, for
diplomatic reasons perhaps, but not impossible by any means.
US forces overseas are subject to local law for crimes committed
on the host's territory, i.e. off base. I had that from the USIS.

This seems a rather minor issue, but really it is not. I think
Kevin has pinpointed the nature of such "cover-up" as there was
quite accurately, and the key to it is this question of territory,
who was responsible for what, and the natural & legal obligation
of the guest nation (USA) to respect the laws and constitutional
conventions of the host (UK).

If you then look at the context (the Greenham Common protest,
cruise missiles in general, the nukes at the Woodbridge/R'sham
complex, the *real job of the USAF police*, etc), then there is
a potentially huge embarrassment for the USAF and the US if, at
such a time, a bunch of American airmen stop doing what they're
supposed to do -- guarding the base -- and trespass in the forest.
Wow! What an opportunity those nitwits at Greenham Common missed
for distracting the USAF and pouring in over the fence!

None of this bears on what happened in the forest or caused anyone
to mill around in it with precious little military discipline, no
understanding of night-vision equipment or rad. detectors, or any
of the other incompetences the believers so carefully overlook.
But it does reasonably, Occam-like even, explain why both the UK
MoD and the US DoD were very shifty about what no one disputes
happened -- a bunch of US airmen, one of field rank who should have
known a lot better, went rambling where they should not have been.
Recently some Brit paratroopers and MPs did something not quite
dissimilar in Iraq, and six redcaps died as a result. We may be a
little less touchy in this country, but in principle Halt's action
was as stupid and as crass, and I'm not remotely surprised that
in the interests of good international relations there was a cover-up.

Halt's later promotion, which the buffs bandy about like it was proof
of something, is irrelevant. One bout of foolishness needn't prevent
-- oh, a good penpusher, for instance -- getting in line for a decent
pension, and a good OTR bollocking may work wonders in keeping a
man in line. Cynics may wish to ompare similar a-logical claims over
the promotions of various key players in the Roswell saga.
But then R'sham and Roswell follow similar tracks: on the one
hand the myth multiplies; on the other, the truth, or what one
can discern of it, simplifies. Sorry, Kevin: Bruni is impervious.

best wishes
Peter B
Keeping The Lighthouse Clean For Pelicans

Kevin's reply to Georgina:

Georgina:

"Malcolm Zickler features heavily in my book, having interviewed him
several times. Apparently he was the commander of all four units, the
SPs, LEs, Fire Group and the SPIs."

Major Zickler was the Chief of Security Police. LE and Security were
separate functions within the Security Police Squadron. By Fire I
assume you mean the Fire Dept. They were within the 81st Civil
Engineer Squadron. Zickler was not responsible for them. If by SPIs
you mean the OSI (Office of Special Investigation), they are a
separate operating agency not under the direct command of anyone on
base. They are the USAF equivalent of the FBI. If by SPIs you mean
Security Police Investigations section, they were part of the LE
branch under Zickler.

"Who was working when." Don't know what to tell you. If they were
on weird shifts - I would have been as well.

It is my opinion that it was not a UFO, I think it is much more
likely that at least one of the so called "sightings" was a 1979
Plymouth Volare. I realize that you can martial all sorts of
arguments to the contrary, and you could be right. Regardless, the
1979 Plymouth makes much more sense to me.

If you read some of what James has published I think you'll find he
asked me once if I was the only one that pulled such a prank. I told
him words to the effect that "good" jokes tended to be repeated.
Anyone could have repeated the prank, and probably did.

We keep coming back to the concept of coincidence and common sense.
The witnesses reported bright white, red and blue lights. In the
same physical area and at the same general time in history I used
bright white, red and blue lights to fool a gate guard into thinking
he saw a UFO.

That is a little too much coincidence to dismiss.

Kevin

Major Malcolm Zickler was the 81st SPS commander.

Commander.

Diego Rivera (1886-1957), the most important Mexican
muralist painter of the twentieth century, is said to
have described an interesting UFO sighting that he had
in August 1921. During a sea voyage from Hamburg to
Mexico with his friend David Alfaro, “an incident
occurred that left a deep impression on me. It was a
brilliant red sphere that suddenly came out of the sea
and, after flying silently above us, settled on a
distant bank of greenish white clouds.” Rivera added
no more information about his observation in his
autobiographical notes.

Source:

Miguel Roberto Forero García, "El extraordinario
encuentro de Diego Rivera," Enigmas, núm. 33, p.24-29
(c.1999)

this case, and the author of the article, Miguel
Roberto Forero García, is equally untraceable. The

have told me they do not remember who Forero Garcia
was (and one even hinted that it was probably a
pseudonym).

support the story I'd be very grateful.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 30 Jul 2003 17:48:44 -0500
Subject: [UFORL] "UNSOLVED UFO MYSTERIES"

I just got a book, "Unsolved UFO Mysteries", by Birnes and Burt. I found
so many errors in science there that I have to speak out:

It starts out to appear to be a scientific inquiry. But there is very
little science in this book.

THE PHOENIX LIGHTS:

Page 6: The object "passed over landmarks that allowed the witnesses to
estimate wingspan and length."

Impossible, unless it threw a shadow that was visible! The witnesses
had absolutely NO idea how far away the object was. It may have lined
up with the landmarks from the viewpoint of the observer, but whether
or not it passed directly over them is unknown. It might have been a
lot closer or a lot farther away, and none of the witnesses had the
tools needed to find out.

Page 7: "The aircraft passed above the triangle as if it weren't there."

Again, either the witness or the author has incorrectly assumed that
the UFO and the aircraft were both the same distance from the observer.
If the "triangle" were a lot closer to the witness, or a lot farther
away, the pilot of the aircraft might not notice anything at all.

Page 7: A "metallic structure" which became transparent when the UFO
passed in front of the moon.

This is a commonly reported characteristic of a fire balloon. When the
suit-bag "aerostat" is reflecting light from the ground, it can look
"metallic." But when the moon shines through it, its true nature is
revealed.

Page 9: (Objects reported to go overhead from north to south)

It is interesting that the video tapes do not show the motion reported
by many observers. Which means that the objects in the videos and what
the observers saw may be two different things.

Page 16: "Some witnesses reported that they were almost looking down at
the objects" (from their high vantage points).

Again, this may indicate that more than one kind of object was present.

Page 19: (An argument is raised that the flares used were white, but
most witnesses saw yellow - thus the objects were not flares)
This is a common distance phenomenon of scattering in the atmosphere
which is responsible for the color of mountains, the blue sky, and
yellow and red sunsets. Scattering WOULD turn a white flare yellow to
a distant observer.

Page 23: Citizens Against UFO Secrecy filed suit against the government
to force an end to "unlawful violations of civil, legal, and
constitutional rights by non-human entities."

Oh really????

In Chapter 2, most of the descriptions match fire balloons.

RENDLESHAM:

Page 41: "Objects without transponders -- simply appear as unidentified
blips.

WRONG! They do not appear on most ATC RADAR sets at all. Computerized
ATC uses much lower power RADAR which works entirely from transponders.
Planes with pressurization capable of flying high enough to be in air
lanes are now required to have transponders.

Read the book "Miracle Landing" (or watch the movie) for a look at this.
A jetliner had all 4 engines shut down due to lack of fuel. (Somebody
murphied an Imperial to Metric conversion and underfilled its tanks.)
The plane disappeared from RADAR when the transponder no longer had
power.

Page 53: (The author hints that the shutdown of the YB-49 program had to
do with alien technology used in the flying wing, and that's why all
remaining models were destroyed.)
