July 27, 2003
A Bad Trip Down Memory Lane
By BRUCE GRIERSON


It is not considered good judgment to wade into the issue
of recovered memories without skin as thick as permafrost
and caller ID on the phone. Rare is the academic field in
which colleagues on opposite sides of a debate -- people
with international reputations -- dismiss the very
foundations of one another's work, sometimes not so
privately, with common barnyard epithets; in which two of
the most prominent reference books are almost
Jesuitically contradictory; in which more than a decade
of fairly sound research has done little to settle a
debate that has raged ever since Freud popularized the
term ''repression.''

Yet this is just where Susan Clancy found herself eight
years ago when she joined the psychology department at
Harvard University as a graduate student. At one end of
the field of ''trauma memory'' were people like her new
professors and future co-authors, the clinical
psychologist Richard McNally and the cognitive
psychologist Daniel Schacter, chairman of the Harvard
psychology department and one of the world's leading
experts on memory function. At the other end were
Harvard-affiliated clinicians, including Judith Herman,
Bessel van der Kolk and Daniel Brown, whose scholarly
writing on the psychological effects of trauma remains
highly influential.

What the two sides disagree on is whether painful
memories of traumatic events can actually be repressed --
completely forgotten -- and then ''recovered'' years
later in therapy. Many clinicians say yes: it is how we
instinctively protect ourselves from childhood
recollections that would otherwise be too dire to bear.
Most cognitive psychologists say no: real trauma is
almost never forgotten; full-blown, traumatic memories
dredged up decades later through hypnosis are almost
invariably false.

Clancy, now 33, wasn't fully alive to the schismatic
politics back then. She simply saw a puzzling, inviting
gap in the data. ''You had two groups in opposite camps
that were battling each other out'' over the validity of
recovered memories, Clancy says. ''But nobody was doing
research on the group that was at the center of the
controversy -- the people who were reporting recovered
memories. Memory function in that group had never been
examined in the laboratory.''

So she decided to devote herself to that task, which
would end up occupying her pretty much full time for the
next seven years. Interview subjects, mostly women but
some men, all with recovered memories of child sexual
abuse, would come to her office in William James Hall --
a 15-floor concrete cracker stack among the brick
heritage buildings of Harvard. They would settle in and,
shifting their gaze from Clancy's blue eyes to the John
Hancock Tower in the distance, tell her their stories as
the tape in her recorder unspooled.

The stories were troubling. Often she found herself,
somewhat inappropriately, tearing up. Clancy's upbringing
-- feminist, lapsed Catholic -- had prepared her to
believe what she was hearing. But as her interviews went
on, she came to the conclusion that many of the most
elaborate, most terrifying tales she was hearing had an
air of confabulation about them. ''There was a moment
where I said, 'Oh, my God, I'm not sure this really
happened,''' she recalls.
Though the term ''false memory'' is slippery and
inadequate, there is now little doubt that the phenomenon
exists. A rash of satanic ritual abuse claims in the
1980's and 90's -- claims that were never substantiated
but destroyed families and ruined reputations --
demonstrated fairly conclusively that both adults and
children sometimes report things they think happened that
didn't.

Still, genuine memories of real sexual abuse are often
prosecutors' only tools to combat what remains a
significant social problem. To distinguish, in some
definitive way, then, true memories from false memories
is a trick with enormous personal and political and
public-policy implications.

Clancy guessed that there was a category of people who
are prone to create false memories and who might
demonstrate this tendency when given a standard memory
test. Her strategy was to present a list of semantically
related words, like ''candy,'' ''sour'' and ''sugar,'' to
those who purported to have recovered memories. Then she
would test their recall of those words. On the test, she
would throw in words that weren't on the list but were
like the words on the list -- ''sweet,'' for example. Her
hypothesis was that these people would be especially
inclined to ''remember'' seeing the word ''sweet'' -- in
effect creating a recollection out of a contextual
inference, a fact from a feeling. In the end, the data
strongly supported her thesis. She published her findings
in 2000 in the scientific journal Psychological Science.

But her work was criticized by some, in large part
because it contained a hidden snare: even if Clancy's
''false memory'' recoverers were prone to fictionalizing
memories of abuse, that didn't necessarily mean that
their specific memories of abuse were made up; there was
no way to know whether these people were actually abused.
Clancy had anticipated this cavil while still in the
design stage of the study, and so she rounded up a second
control group -- people who had incontrovertibly been
abused and had always remembered that abuse, in contrast
to the ''recovered memory'' group. When people in this
group took the word-recall test, they tended to
''remember'' words that weren't on the list with no
greater frequency than the average person, and she was
sure she had cracked the nut.

The critics, though, had another objection. What if the
traumas that the recovered-memory group had experienced
were horrific enough not only to repress the memory but
also to cause cognitive impairment that showed up as
memory distortion in the lab?

Meanwhile, hate mail started pouring in, in quantities
Clancy would eventually measure ''by the ton.'' The
reaction was not altogether surprising. The moral
dimension of research on child sexual abuse makes it
uniquely explosive in psychology, and almost from Day 1
Clancy had, beyond the safe zone of her own department,
taken heavy flak for even suggesting that memories of
abuse can be faulty. The simple act of conducting
research into the matter struck some as an enterprise
''designed to cheer on child molesters,'' as one
anonymous letter writer wrote, ''and ridicules the
suffering sustained by children who are abused as well as
therapists who are knowledgeable about the effects of
trauma on children's minds and bodies.'' Clancy was a
''bad person,'' according to another letter writer, to
question such reports. Yet another suggested that she was
probably an abuser herself.

In 2000, when Clancy was invited to give a lecture at
Cambridge Hospital, the chairman of the hospital at the
time told her that several members of its psychiatric
department had protested her appearance. Her colleagues
told her that she had probably ruled herself out of
future academic positions in any psychology department,
Harvard pedigree or no.

Clancy says she thought she could fix the problem by
fixing her word-recall test. She was close, she reckoned,
but she needed to find a different, methodologically
cleaner, subject group than victims of child sexual abuse
-- people whose memories virtually everyone could agree
were false. But whom? She considered options: people who
remembered their own deaths? People who recalled past
lives? No, there was just enough doubt in those instances
to taint the results. She would have to go further
afield.


"Have you been contacted or abducted by space aliens?''
read the ad that ran in a number of Boston-area
newspapers. ''You may be eligible to participate in a
Harvard memory research study.'' Clancy's new plan -- and
it seemed unimpeachable -- was to round up folks who
thought they had been beamed aboard spaceships, or who
actually recalled the experience, and give them the same
memory test she had given the others. If they, too, got
high scores, it would establish that there are indeed
people who are prone to false memories -- which might
eventually help scientists better understand how false
memories are created. Finally, she figured, she had the
makings of a sound study. Out she went into the community
to recruit.

For two years, Clancy advertised in bookstores, visited
Internet chat rooms and haunted U.F.O. conferences,
handing out fliers for her memory study. At one point, in
pursuit of appropriate subjects, she spent three days at
a meeting of a group of supposed alien abductees at an
old seaside Victorian inn in Newport, R.I. She sat in the
hot tub with them as they cheerfully told her their
stories -- an astonishingly consistent set of narratives
involving bright light through bedroom windows,
inexplicable time blackouts, encounters with bobble-
headed small gray people with large black eyes and,
often, invasive sexual medical experimentation. Among
themselves, the experiencers talked business. There was a
consensus about how stupid and misguided scientists were
not to believe their accounts. Someone related a
skeptic's theory that the explosion of U.F.O. sightings
in New Jersey the previous year was caused by migrating
birds, and the crowd exploded into guffaws. Clancy smiled
through gritted teeth.

Finally, she scraped together 11 willing subjects, ran
them and a control group through a battery of tests and
collated the data, which demonstrated, in her view, that
''individuals who are more prone to develop false
memories in the lab are also more likely to develop false
memories of experiences that were only suggested or
imagined.'' She submitted her study to the notoriously
stringent Journal of Abnormal Psychology. It sped through
the review process and, to her great relief, was
published. Her problems looked to be solved.

''I thought, Thank God, man,'' she recalls. ''With alien
abductees, I'm never going to have to deal with the
criticism that it might have actually happened.''

In a mustard-colored suit -- the only suit he owns --
John Mack stands on the stage of the theater inside
Boston's Museum of Fine Arts with a light shining on his
face, like a museum exhibit of the moon. The documentary
film ''Touched,'' by Laurel Chiten, a Boston filmmaker,
has just received its world premiere, and Chiten and
Mack, her main subject, are up there to field questions.
Through interviews, the film conveys what it's like to be
coerced into sexual congress with alien beings -- and, in
at least one case, to become an unwitting participant,
apparently, in a kind of intergalactic hybrid breeding
program.

Mack, a quiet and erudite man, is a veteran of the
Harvard medical faculty whose blue-chip career took
something of a William Jamesian turn toward the mystical
in the 70's. In 1994, he published the book
''Abduction,'' which immediately piqued interest because
Mack seemed to accept the abduction phenomenon as literal
fact. The book was a huge best seller. Mack's Harvard
imprimatur jacked the credibility of abduction accounts
into another orbit. Chris Carter, creator of ''The X-
Files,'' used Mack's work to help sell his show to Fox.

Clancy's study was, of course, a clear rebuke of the
abductee experience -- and it was met with derision at
Mack's nonprofit organization, the Center for Psychology
and Social Change. Clancy had drawn a number of her test
subjects from the institute's ranks, and they may have
felt poleaxed by the disarmingly genial researcher who
seemed to listen so nonjudgmentally to their tales. The
campaign to discredit Clancy began in earnest.

''Obviously there's a mammoth leap of faith involved in
generalizing from a mistake on a word list to the
assumption that whole memories for extended, anomalous
events can be created more or less arbitrarily,'' wrote a
doctoral student named Catherine Reason on an Internet
discussion group. Just who was Susan Clancy, asked
another, to challenge the work of people whose theories
of memory and trauma were cited by the United Nations
when discussing whether recovered memories of torture
were admissible as testimony in an international war-
crimes tribunal? Some simply viewed Clancy's 11
''abductees'' as too small a sample size.

Mack and Clancy seem to have nothing against each other
personally, though the gulf in their worldviews appears
unbridgeable. Clancy describes Mack as ''good-hearted,''
an ''old-school gentleman'' who was insufficiently aware
of the memory-distorting effects of the hypnosis he used
over the years to expand upon abduction memories in many
of his more than 200 patients. Mack is sanguine about the
Clancy study, but blunt. ''I smell a rat,'' he says in
his light-filled Cambridge home a short walk from Harvard
Yard. ''Not that Susan's the rat, but in that a small
word-association test gets to be used, by whomever, to
say, 'This is simply memory distortion.'''

The abductees, in some ways, posed a more bewildering
challenge to Clancy than her previous memory-recoverers.
''Very few of them endorsed the repression hypothesis,''
she says. They don't believe their conscious minds
repressed the memories of abduction trauma out of self-
protection. Rather, she says, ''you'd get
extraterrestrial interpretations.'' The reason they had
no memories of those terrifying events until years or
decades later, the abductees usually say, is that the
aliens, for everybody's protection, erased or otherwise
controlled them.

When I met with her in Cambridge, Clancy still seemed
genuinely surprised, almost awed, at the breadth of
controversy her work has caused. ''Every academic talk I
give,'' she told me as we made our way to lunch near
Harvard Square, ''someone raises their hand and says,
'Who the hell are you to say these stories aren't
true?'''

Not long ago, Clancy appeared as a guest on a nationally
syndicated radio show that takes a broad-minded view of
the paranormal. For nearly 20 minutes, she was called on
that very question. The host pressed: ''Why do you think
that the only life forms are on earth?'' Clancy said she
could feel her blood pressure rising.

''I don't necessarily believe that we're the only life
form out there,'' she said. ''I can entertain the
possibility that there are other life forms out there
without accepting your story that a spaceship picked you
up!''

Many scientists have offered a simple explanation for the
phenomenon: abduction experiences, they maintain, are all
about the mind pumping for meaning after a bout of sleep
paralysis -- a scary but fairly common experience in
which the part of the brain that inhibits motor messages
during REM sleep fails to disengage as the sleeper wakes
up. The sensation is of being pinned to the bed, often
accompanied by hallucinations of some spectral entity at
the bedside.

Some three million Americans believe they have had some
kind of encounter with space aliens. If everyone who
experienced sleep paralysis came to that conclusion, the
number would be a hundred or so times as high. What you
have in an abductee, Clancy suspects, is someone who is
predisposed to believe. ''Here's someone who reads
science fiction. They watch 'The X-Files.' Then one night
they have a sleep-paralysis experience. It's weird and
it's scary, and it becomes one of a multitude of events
that create that wonder.''

As the subject tries to remember what happened,
''source'' errors creep in. ''You think you're recovering
your own memory, when in fact it's something you pulled
out of a movie,'' Clancy said. ''Memory's tendency to be
reconstructive, combined with the desire to believe,
combined with a culturally available script, leads to a
false memory. The content of that memory is dictated by
the society you live in.'' The warnings that experiencers
report receiving from aliens, the Australian sociologist
Robert Bartholomew has pointed out, have changed over
time -- from nuclear destruction during the cold war to,
more recently, ecological doom. These are simply stories,
he says, that give shape to our fears.


Ten years from now, Susan Clancy may remember 2003 as a
year of agreeable spadework in the trenches of academic
inquiry. But if she does, it will be a false memory. The
truth is that Clancy's research, which she hoped might
mend fences -- at least partly vindicating both sides'
positions -- has managed to tick off just about everyone:
sexual-abuse survivors, therapists, experiencers, even a
creationist or two.

Daniel Brown, the trauma therapist, is convinced that
there's a ''political agenda'' to Clancy's abduction
study. As he told one reporter, ''It's all about spin.''
Her own brother -- a corporate lawyer for a top New York
firm -- has ripped into her about the abduction study for
assuming outright that none of the abductions occurred.

On Sun, 3 Aug 2003, Kevin Conde wrote:

> During his interview for the Inside Out show Burroughs said
> words to the effect "I've heard about jokes being played..."
>
> That stuck out like a sore thumb to me, yet I have not heard
> anyone else comment on it.

UFO pranks have been fairly common over the years. The Colorado
project (www.ncas.org), among its 59 case studies, clearly labels
three as pranks -- cases 18, 23, and 45. They also identify a
number of other cases as probable hoaxes, without quite using the
word, and it's clear from the case descriptions that some of
these were pranks that got out of hand.

There's also a Rendlesham-like case, #9, where it appears that
some USAF base security personnel let themselves get "spooked"
in the middle of the night.

More significant is the absence of any response to those
central questions - why did Halt never reveal he knew all
along about Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston's two mile
trek through the Suffolk countryside, before realising
they had mistaken Orfordness lighthouse for a 'UFO' - why

when Burroughs now admits the abortive chase was factual

Magazine' do seem somewhat reluctant to ask any 'awkward'
questions of either Halt or Penniston.

whether Adam and Eve seriously arrived on the scene six
days after 'big bang', or if the animals really did go in
'two by two'.

In our overall context of 'Rendlesham' being regarded and
still defended as founding testimony of not only alien
contact, also an inherent Government cover-up,
comprehensive facts otherwise have been widely publicised
in recent years.

The 'UFO Magazine' rebuttal to same, evades underlying,
problematic, issues and their retort merely emphasises
intrinsic, shoddy, research concerning BBC East's
documentary.

It's an upshot which time has permitted might now be
highlighted in my article for 'The Skeptic', a future
edition of which will be entirely dedicated to the
present-day, factual, credibility of Britain's 'Roswell'.

From: "kevin_conde" <kevin_conde@yahoo.com>
Date: Tue, 12 Aug 2003 14:45:20 -0000
Subject: Re [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary

James:

Just read your last post on the list, about the desk sergeant, very
intriguing. Ask away all you want off-line.

A few thoughts:

Normal flight manning would have been all stirred up if we were on
alert. When we went onto 12 hour shifts the flights became
hopelessly mixed. That meant I was liable to be working with people
I never normally worked with. The point is that you can't use the
fact that my normal flight chief wasn't working during the "incident"
as proof that my joke was not a source of any of the lights. If we
were on alert anyone could have been working with anyone else.

Where LE were posted became mixed during alerts. Security was always
the most important priority. Law Enforcement came in second. When
we went on alert all the various security posts were manned first,
and the law enforcement posts only after all the security posts were
manned. Protecting the warfighting assets was always the first
priority.

What generally happened is that as people reported to work at the
start of the alert, the lowest ranking LE troops got sent to the main
gates at Woodbridge and Bentwaters. This means Airmen (1 stripe) and
A1C's (2 stripes).

The middle ranked LE troops, A1C's, Sgts, got sent to security
posts. The higher end LE troops (SSgt's, TSgt's) went to the LE
patrols. Flight chiefs and desk sergeants went to their normal posts.

The point is that you could have a couple of middle ranked LE troops
working a security patrol, such as an ART (Area Response Team) or a
SRT (Secruity Response Team). The SRT's (Pronounced sart) were not
assigned to a specific area, and a SRT would have responded to East
Gate along with the Woodbridge LE patrol, unless the LE patrol was
tied up.

Although technically the security posts had priority, in reality LE
had more emphasis, as we were dealing with real-world issues.
Accidents, drunk drivers, assaults, family fights, etc. That's why
the LE patrols, desk sergeants and Flight Chiefs always were manned
with the more experienced LE troops even during alerts.

The point is that just because an A1C was LE does not necessarily
mean he was on an LE post if there was an alert on.
As to the East Gate being permanently manned during alerts, that's
true. Once we went on alert the back gates stayed open.

One effect of Burrough's admission of being a jokester is that it
validates what I've said, and slaps down the believer's argument that
I would have been courts martialed. This point of view tries to put
forward the obtuse argument that I would not have done what I said I
did, for fear of being punished. Phooey! We were all jokers! You
don't single out a particular joker in a squadron full of jokers.
Jokes were standard operating procedures.

The "believers" keep recycling the concept that what we did was
stressful and serious, and that we would never behave in such a
facetious manner. Bull! What we did was very, very serious. We
knew that better than anyone. However, when you put a bunch of
intelligent people into a tense and stressful situation humor is a
normal and expected way of dealing with the stress.


Kevin

I've now acquired three archive, filmed, interviews with

All are notable, especially the first feature, which

It's brilliant as the interviewer and narrator have
pronounced 'posh' English accents. At any moment you
expect, "I say Mr Zamora, what a ghastly experience, old
chap".

Zamora retraces his route to the landing site, on camera.
We can see his viewpoint from where the object and two
occupants were briefly glimpsed and also where he stopped
at closest proximity.

Both seem exactly as documented on related maps
published.

Additionally, there's film of the dynamite shack and Box
Canyon beyond, as viewed from Zamora's location, when he
watched the object depart in that direction.

Also interviewed are Opal Grinder and an almost youthful
Dr. Hynek.


The second documentary is American and undated, although
clearly years later. Fascinating historical interviews
are with Zamora, Hynek and Lt. Col. Hector Quintanilla,
former head of the USAF's 'Project Blue Book'.
The third program is an 'Unsolved Mysteries' feature.

Aside from Zamora, there are interviews with Sergeant
Samuel Chavez, patrolman Ted Jordan, Capt. Richard T.
Holder and Jimmy Grinder, son of Opal.

Herein, Zamora makes some significant comments:

"When going up to half-ways, I could see a white object
to my left there. I thought it was a turned-over car.
When I got up on top of the mesa there, I looked down and
I seen this big white object on the ground".

"As this flame come up from underneath it, and I ran back
behind my car, and it went up to twenty-thirty feet up in
the air. It just stayed there for a while and then
finally just took off slowly, to the west".


Regarding Zamora's 'encounter', I have previously
corresponded with Thomas Guengerich, at that time owner
of the 'El Defensor Chieftain' and possibly still is.

Guengerich stated:

"We have contacted Lonnie Zamora ... and he wants nothing
to do with any follow-up stories about his contact. We
think maybe a pint or two may change his mind. Not only
did he suffer ridicule in the community, but he also is
widely known as an uncredible person (unlike the original
USAF account that you quote)".

Dana Bowley, the newspaper's current Editor, did not
realise there had been preceding dialogue, although she
was certainly aware of this by the end of 23 July.

There's now, necessarily, an imminent, published,
challenge to Valerie Kimble's 'Still Unexplained'
article.

All subject to ongoing discussions, with several
interested newsdesks.

I consider it's imperative that Zamora is vindicated as
actually seeing 'something' unprecedented.

As he stated on 'Unsolved Mysteries':

"If I could find out what it actually was, O.K., I'm
satisfied. If you don't want to believe me, do it, if
they don't want to believe me, that's alright too".

One possibility is that someone might actually believe
you, although that may depend on their own beliefs.

From: "kevin_conde" <kevin_conde@yahoo.com>
Date: Sat, 16 Aug 2003 03:48:30 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary

James:

The name Crash McCabe is completely unknown to me. Which is funny as
it is a catchy, therefore memorable name.

I do have a couple of problems with what is in Halt's transcript.

> As I walked into the Desk area, control center, Sergeant
> 'Crash' McCabe was on duty ...

The LE desk was called the LE desk. Security Control was called CSC
(Central Security Control). The person at the LE Desk was referred
to as the Desk Sergeant. The people at CSC were known
as "controllers".

Notice the word "control". We only used the word control in
conjunction with CSC. I have to wonder whether or not the colonel
was referring to CSC or the LE Desk. I knew very few of the CSC
controllers. If you remember, I said I thought the name you sent me
off line was familiar. McCabe is not familiar. That would be
expected if he were a controller versus a Desk Sergeant.

> On that particular night we had two patrol cars, Police 4
> and Police 5, because of a problem with the other vehicle
> both Police 4 and Police 5 were riding in the same
> vehicle.

Two things - it verifies what I said about LE not usually being two
man patrols - which strengthens my belief that my stunt was done
during an alert, and attacks Georgina's contention that I don't know
what I'm talking about because my details don't line up with her view
of what the details should be.. But it makes me curious. My
recollection, and it could be wrong, was that we usually had only one
patrol at Woodbridge, not two.

I think the only time we routinely had two patrols at Woodbridge was
during the day shift. I have very clear memories of Security units
having to come off the flight-line to back me up a Woodbridge because
I was alone. Again, I could be wrong - it was a long time ago.

I also don't remember any devil worshippers. I would not have paid
any attention to them anyway, as I view them as cranks, and a cop's
world is full of cranks. They're like trees in a forest. They're so
many of them you don't pay much attention after awhile.

> Our new ex-Law Enforcement Desk Sergeant contact - I'll
> call him 'John' for the sake of convenience - indicates
> there's perhaps a problem here. John believes you might
> recall McCabe and can verify if the above would be
> consistent with McCabe's normal duties.

One explaination could be that the events happened on the break
between shifts. In other words, the first incident happened on the
last night of on flight's three days of mid-shifts, and the next one
on the following flight's first day of mids. That would explain
unfamiliar names, as you would only tend to remember the folks you
worked with directly.

In explanation, we worked "6 and 3's". Six days on and three days
off. You would work 3 swing shifts - 1700 to 2300, then you would
get a 24 hour break, then you would work 3 mids - 2300 to 0700. Then
you got three days off.

It would be easy for one flight to handle the start of
the "incident's", and the following to handle the next one. Since
you have different people involved you could also have a different
philosophy on the part of the supervisors on whether to pursue or
dismiss "lights" in the forest.

Ask "John" if he would like to comment on the Police 4 and 5 issue,
and if he remembers some of the other names and what they did,
specifically if they were LE or Security. He may have a better
recollection as he was probably unmarried and lived in the dorms, and
knew the other junior ranking folks better than a supervisor like me,
who did not party with A1C's or Sgt's, and lived at home with my wife.

On another subject, ask him if he remembers an incident of an English
suspect kicking his way out of the back end of a patrol car while the
patrol car was driving through the small town just before
Bentwaters. We were transporting the prisoner from Woodbridge to
Bentwaters. I think "John" might have been driving that patrol car.

Kevin

Subject: Re: [UFORL] New Rendlesham Documentary

A question for Kevin.

On 31 July, 1994, Halt was a guest lecturer at the 'UFO
Magazine' [UK] conference in Leeds.

This is a previously unpublished extract, from a rare
transcript I was recently given:

As I walked into the Desk area, control center, Sergeant
'Crash' McCabe was on duty - a very intelligent, very
sharp witted young man. Very enjoyable to deal with. And
he wasn't above playing a joke on some of his
contemporaries.

As I walked in he started to laugh, and I thought I had
walked into another prank. Keep in mind this is holiday
season and a little levity may be in order.

[I'm sure Kevin will note all of this! - James]


And he started laughing, and I thought I'm the brunt of
the joke, or something. And I said, 'What's so funny,
Crash?'. He said, 'Colonel, you're not going to believe
this.' I said, 'Not going to believe what? Try me.' And
he said, 'Well, last night Burroughs and Penniston and
Cabansag were out in the woods chasing a UFO!'. And I
looked at him and said, 'What's the rest of the joke?
What's the punch line?' And be said, 'No, I'm serious'.
'I don't believe it', he said, 'But something happened
last night. And the Lieutenant. . .' (the police officer
on duty on every shift, who is over both the security
side and the law enforcement side) '. . . said, 'Don't
put it in the police blotter.' In other words, don't make
it a matter of record.

And I said to Sgt. McCabe, 'Well, what happened? What do
you know?'. He said, 'Well, somewhere around midnight...'
(he did tell me the exact time, but I don't remember now)
'...around midnight, Burroughs...'...

On that particular night we had two patrol cars, Police 4
and Police 5, because of a problem with the other vehicle
both Police 4 and Police 5 were riding in the same
vehicle. Sgt. Burroughs was driving and Staff Sgt. Bud
Steffens was riding alongside. Steffens, I understand,
was suffering from having been up a long time, and from
having a very good Christmas Day...
[END]


Our new ex-Law Enforcement Desk Sergeant contact - I'll
call him 'John' for the sake of convenience - indicates
there's perhaps a problem here. John believes you might
recall McCabe and can verify if the above would be
consistent with McCabe's normal duties.

Comments duly invited.


It remains John's conviction he was the person on desk
duty that night [this is the first 'UFO' incident - early
hours of 26 December].

As for Devil worshipper's in the forest, he explains:

"I had opportunities because of running late to work to
use the back gate. Even though it was locked I knew how
to get in. There were times that after hours we would use
the back gates between the bases to save time. Several
times I ran into the devil worshippers between the bases.
Scared me to death".

Did you ever come across anything like this!?


James.

Subject: [UFORL] DOUBLE DRICK II

It looks like DOUBLE DRICK all over again.

It's an instant replay of 11/9/1965 in almost exact detail, except for
the localities affected. Even the suspected location of the start of
the outage is the same.

No UFOs this time (yet). We'll see....

Read my page on the REAL CAUSE of the original 1965 blackout at:

http://mypage.iu.edu/~lrobins/howiblak.htm

Wanna bet the same thing happened again?

-----

What's a DOUBLE DRICK?

In 1966, an episode of the TV show "Green Acres" made fun of the printed
sound effects on "Batman". The Douglas farm generator quit working any
they "plugged in an 8", and the caption "DRICK!" appeared on the screen.

Mr. Douglas numbered the appliance cords from 1 to 7 according to how
much load each appliance drew, and told Lisa to never plug in a total of
8. The generator went DRICK again. Lisa responded that 2 plus 7 is 9,
not 8.

Then they tried to get the power company to bring power to the rural
farms of Hooterville. The company installed a duplex outlet up on the
utility pole, right next to where the telephone company put the
telephone. The Douglases ran an extension cord down into the house.
Then Lisa plugged in an 8 again, and the following caption appeared on
the screen:

"On November 9, 1965, an unexplained power blackout occurred over most
of the northeastern United States. Here's what really happened:"

The screen went blank, then read:

"DOUBLE DRICK!"

James:

Very flattering.

The incident he mentioned was with a drunk English civilian. We
called for the Suffolk Constabulary to come to Woodbridge to retrieve
him and were told to transport him to Bentwaters, which we normally
did not do with English civilians.

We were not allowed to handcuff English civilians, so John put him in
the back of his patrol car, unhandcuffed, and started the long way to
Bentwaters - I followed. American cop cars have prisoner cages
between the front and rear seats to keep the prisoners away from the
driver.

The civilian began to be a problem so I radioed John to keep moving,
hoping to get back on base before anything happened. Remember, we
were armed, and I did not want a couple of armed USAF cops fighting a
civilian on an English road.

The guy kicked out the rear window, and while the patrol car was
moving climbed out onto the light bar (the same type I used in my
joke) and then into the front passenger seat with John.

We ended up stopping in the small village just before Bentwaters, I
think its Eike(?), and fighting the idiot.

It was one of the hairyer incidents I've had as a cop, and I've had
more than a few. John was fairly young, but kept his head and did
very well. He did not back down from that fight one bit, and I was
very proud of him.

I'm surprized someone did not report the dude hanging on his light
bar at speed as a UFO. Wonder why not? The no-handcuffing of
Englishmen rule died that day.

Dan Koehler and Dan Combs were friends as well - you could say the
three of us where like peas in a pod.

I can't wait to hear your complete recap.

Thanks

Kevin

What a lot of rubbish! Every claim that Georgina makes can be
reversed and used to argue that I could have been there.

Georgina and Mr. Pope, are not unbiased observers. They have decided
something, who knows what, happened in the forest. To support their
belief they cherry pick words here and there out of volumes of
correspondence and try to use those words to substantiate their
position.

They are the hijackers.

The "normal" people that were actually at Woodbridge during
the "incident" all are consistent that nothing happened. It's all a
misunderstanding complicated by a couple of unstable personalities.
Other unrelated unstable personalities have since made careers out of
trying to convince the gullible that we were visited.

In my opinion anyone who accepts Halt and Penniston as reliable
witnesses, while discounting all the other witnesses who where there
and have said nothing happened, is someone who lacks common sense or
has another agenda.

I'm getting a little tired and more than a little frustrated with the
cranks. Here's a fact: I was stationed at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge
at the time! I was in a key police position. I knew what went on at
RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge, and visits by little green men were not on
the menu!

Want a couple more facts? Georgina and Nick were not stationed at
RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge, and haven't a clue how the base operated.

An example: For some reason Georgina wanted me to confirm that the
fire department was under the SPS Squadron commander. I explained to
Georgina that the fire department is part of the Civil Engineering
Squadron, and was under the command of the 81st CES Commander. The
fire department is not within the chain of command of the 81st SPS
Commander.

Anyone that has spent any time in the USAF can verify that. I'm not
sure why it was important, but Georgina proceeded to tell me that the
fire department was under the command of the 81st SPS, as confirmed
by some unnamed retired general. On another occasion she told me I
must be wrong about my story, as USAF Law Enforcement patrols are
always 2 man units. I explained that was not true, that Security
patrols were two man units, but that most of the time LE were one-man
units. Even when I was stationed on a base in a ghetto in SE
Washington DC we only had one man patrols. Regardless, Georgina
pronounced me wrong according to her, again unnamed, expert. Why the
hell listen to me, I was only an SP for 11 years and in the USAF for
21, what do I know?

Bottom line in this little tirade; if she can't be accurate about the
minor points, why should anyone expect her to be accurate about the
important things?

Kevin

something, who knows what, happened in the forest. To support their
belief they cherry pick words here and there out of volumes of
correspondence and try to use those words to substantiate their
position.

They are the hijackers.

The "normal" people that were actually at Woodbridge during
the "incident" all are consistent that nothing happened. It's all a
misunderstanding complicated by a couple of unstable personalities.
Other unrelated unstable personalities have since made careers out of
trying to convince the gullible that we were visited.

In my opinion anyone who accepts Halt and Penniston as reliable
witnesses, while discounting all the other witnesses who where there
and have said nothing happened, is someone who lacks common sense or
has another agenda.

I'm getting a little tired and more than a little frustrated with the
cranks. Here's a fact: I was stationed at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge
at the time! I was in a key police position. I knew what went on at
RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge, and visits by little green men were not on
the menu!

Want a couple more facts? Georgina and Nick were not stationed at
RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge, and haven't a clue how the base operated.

An example: For some reason Georgina wanted me to confirm that the
fire department was under the SPS Squadron commander. I explained to
Georgina that the fire department is part of the Civil Engineering
Squadron, and was under the command of the 81st CES Commander. The
fire department is not within the chain of command of the 81st SPS
Commander.

Anyone that has spent any time in the USAF can verify that. I'm not
sure why it was important, but Georgina proceeded to tell me that the
fire department was under the command of the 81st SPS, as confirmed
by some unnamed retired general. On another occasion she told me I
must be wrong about my story, as USAF Law Enforcement patrols are
always 2 man units. I explained that was not true, that Security
patrols were two man units, but that most of the time LE were one-man
units. Even when I was stationed on a base in a ghetto in SE
Washington DC we only had one man patrols. Regardless, Georgina
pronounced me wrong according to her, again unnamed, expert. Why the
hell listen to me, I was only an SP for 11 years and in the USAF for
21, what do I know?

Bottom line in this little tirade; if she can't be accurate about the
minor points, why should anyone expect her to be accurate about the
important things?

Kevin

For those who don't subscribe to 'UFO Updates', here's the latest from
"Britain's Fox Mulder", Nick Pope:


List,

Georgina Bruni was the guest last night on James Whale's radio
show on Talk Sport, discussing latest developments in the
Bentwaters UFO case.

Georgina arranged for former USAF airman Kevin Conde to call the
show. Conde has recently come to prominence by claiming that he
inadvertently caused the various UFO sightings by driving a
police car through Rendlesham Forest, with its lights on, in an
attempt to spook a colleague.

Georgina has been in correspondence with Conde for some time,
and his statements on James Whale's show were quite revealing.
While undoubtedly sincere, it was clear that Conde was not
claiming his alleged prank was responsible for the events in
Rendlesham Forest. At best, he thought his hoax might explain
part of the Bentwaters incident (which of course took place over
three nights).

It seemed increasingly clear that Conde's recollections had been
hijacked by a sceptical buff trying to position himself as an
expert on the case. Georgina has spoken to numerous United
States Air Force witnesses to the incident, and other USAF
personnel present at the time. Before the programme ended
listeners were told that the latest information from these USAF
personnel suggested that Conde may not even have been on duty at
the time of the events.

James Whale undertook to try to get Conde back for a future
show, so that he could go into his claims in more depth.


Best wishes,

Nick Pope

special effects guys underneath]

By Nick Webster.

THIS is the "UFO" that got the world asking if aliens were about to
land in Britain.

But those pictured beneath it are hardly the little green men many
had feared were on board.
They are the hoaxers who ran the stunt in a bizarre TV experiment.
The 25ft flying saucer stunned villagers on Saturday as it spun
across the sky 200ft above their heads.
The outlandish sighting made the headlines as far away as Australia.
But the down-to-earth truth behind the "spacecraft" emerged yesterday.
TV firm Chrysalis had it built for a Channel 4 documentary with
workinf title 'How To Build A Spaceship.'
Danny Cohen of Channel 4, said "We were trying to see whether we
could build a convincing looking spaceship and in that regard
undoubtedly we succeeded.
"Dozens of people saw it and couldn't quite understand what they had
seen. So I think it did work.
"It stayed quite high in the sky and looked harmelss, so it
frightened nobody. I think people were more bewildered by what they
were seeing.
"People were left rubbing their heads, wndering what was going on."
It took eight months to research, design and build the £50,000
aircraft.
Model flight specialists Cutting Edge Effects - veterans of four Bond
films - built it using a carbon fibre hoop as the skeleton.
This was set in a reflective plastic balloon filled with helium.
After a US military engine was ditched as too heavy, electric fan
engines from Germany proved the key to making the saucer fly at just
the right speed - 20mph.
It was tested in the aircraft hanger shown above at a secret location.
The out-of-this-world con included using seven pilots to fly the
aircraft by remote control for three miles.
Suspicion for the hoax first fell on UFO buffs holding their annual
Skywatch in the village - Avebury, Wilts.
But producer Mark Raphael said they weren't fooled - despite the
eerie setting of a stone circle.
He siad they spent the rest of the night "looking at nothing, and yet
when the craft flew over they hardly got out of their seats."

[photograph showing craft in air over field in daylight - caption
reads "HOT AIR: The saucer ringed in flight. But it was a hoax using
a balloon.].'

END.

cutting by snail?

Gary Anthony

From: "david CLARKE" <cd292@crazydiamonds.fsnet.co.uk>
Date: Wed, 27 Aug 2003 19:01:42 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Re: New Rendlesham Documentary

Greetings list,

Kevin asked me to re-post this response he sent to me in reply to Nick
Pope's statements on UFO Updates. I've sent an edited version to that list
too:

****
On one hand I am getting tired of it and have seriously considering limiting
my participation in the debate to direct questions from James and others
such as your self.

The problem with withdrawing from the debate is that it allows the believers
to claim that my refusal to participate in the debate is evidence supporting
their contention that my knowledge is flawed.

I don't know what really happened in 1980, and I don't think anyone else
does either. Georgina Bruni and Nick Pope certainly don't. I'm sure a UFO
did not visit RAF Woodbridge.

To a certain extent I think I know what it feels like to be a politician
now. People will parse word by word an entire page or two of
correspondence, and pull a sentence here or there out of context and use
that sentence to jump to a conclusion that they want supported. They then
put words in my mouth and try to say that I said something I did not.

Example from your post from UFO Udates:

"Georgina arranged for former USAF airman Kevin Conde to call the show."

Georgina did not arrange anything with me. The James Whale show called my
office while I was at work and asked to speak to me. My assumption is they
did an on-line search and figured out where I work. The call came out of
the blue. I was not in the office, so my assistant passed the message on to
me. Out of courtesy I returned the call.

Yet Georgina and company would represent that they set this up with me
before hand. Had I known before hand that Georgina was involved I would
have refused to participate. I became aware she was also on air after I was
already on the air.

While on the air Georgina said something to the effect that I had agreed
with her that I was not even on duty the night of the incident. I've never
said any such thing. I believe Georgina has said something similar in print.

My experience with Georgina is that she passionately believes in the
incident. I believe that because of that passion Georgina has a tendency to
ignore and discount anything that might not fit in to her version of events.
I think it's fair to say her passion has led her to misrepresent some of my
comments. The end result is that had I known Georgina was involved in the
broadcast, I would not have returned the call.

If Mr. Whales wants me to answer questions for him and his viewers on the
air, I will do that. I will not participate in an on air debate with
Georgina.

As I surf the Web reading the various positions on the incident I find the
following to be generally true. The skeptics tend to quote me completely
and in context. They usually cite other sources to support or contradict,
and they don't parse my comments.

The believers on the other hand routinely quote out of context, and try to
say that my comments often mean something other than what I intended when
making the comment.

I keep trying to keep things simple.

#1: I was stationed at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge at the time of the
"incident". I was in a senior police position at the time. The flight I
was assigned to would have been working during at least one of the events.
The on duty flight commander during Halt's field trip, Lt. Bruce England was
my flight commander and boss. The fact that I was unaware of the "incident"
until April 2001 is a very strong indicator that no one took the "incident"
seriously at the time. If they did not take the incident seriously at the
time, why should we take it seriously now? As James' research has clearly
shown, the story of the two most prominent personalities has morphed over
the years.

#2. During the time frame of the incident I pulled a practical joke on the
East Gate Guard. That joke involved bright white lights, and flashing red
and blue lights. According to Halt's memo the witnesses reported bright
white lights and flashing red and blue lights. Georgina is correct, I can't
prove exactly when I pulled the stunt, but the similarity between my stunt
and the witness statements is too stark to ignore

#3. Both you and James have talked to several other folks that were either
at the base or involved in the incident in one way or another. They all
say that either that they were unaware of the alleged "incident", or viewed
the incident as not serious or a joke. My own wife, a retired SMSgt, does
not remember anything happening while she was at Bentwaters. Had there been
any kind of serious incident, she would have heard something.

Regardless, Georgina and others elect to dismiss the statements and evidence
of all these people in favor of the more "rational" explanation that RAF
Bentwaters/Woodbridge was visited aliens.

Is this weird or what?
Sincerely

Kevin

Larry, with all respect, I am a little fed up with your fire balloons :-))
Maybe, you has almost convinced me, fire balloons does play a more important
role in the UFO phenomenon than suspected before, but you employ them
everywhere, and this is verging in the ridiculous (Bentwaters, Travis
Walton...).

Let take Travis Walton. I am the first who believe he was NOT abducted by
aliens, but the case is quite puzzling (as commented, among others, by John
Harney in MAGONIA publications).

+The hoax hypothesis. Whatever your idea about this possibility, Travis
Walton should have been one of the hoaxers.
After reading a lot of what has been debating around, I must confess I am
not so sure he was an hoaxer, if only because he has never changed his story
since them, and he denies to have remembered anything else about all those
days missing, despite quite financial rewards if saying otherwise.
Sorry, Larry I do not think Travis was hypnotized before relating all that
he remembered conciously.
The hypnosis was just to confirm the data and "go fishing", curiously
without luck.
Besides, the polygraph debate is a ruse. After the recent findings about the
very low reliability of this technique, neither believers nor sceptics
should mention it again as an evidence in their favour.
Nowadays I believe that the incident took place more or less as described by
the witnesses, but I do not need to believe Travis was abducted, after all,
nobody saw that. They only saw him being hit by a blue ray, run away, and
when returned did not find any corpse. Now I quote Clark's Encyclopedia:

"Rogers drove around in the gathering darkness in search of the spot where
they had seen the UFO. There were a number of clearings and any number of
slash piles in the vicinity, and one looked pretty much like another, so it
was not easy".

What if they DO get confused and looked in the wrong spot?

Travis could have regained conciousness, still dazed, and spent the five
days wandering around in the woods or sleeping exhausted and confused in a
shelter. He may even had fantasized his alien abduction, very peculiar in
itself.

Very unlikely? Yes, but more than an alien abduction?
Then, what about the UFO? It does not bother me too much, they may even be a
real UFO (in the sense of an alien craft) but, of course, I would suggest
something along that other sceptic's favourite: ball lighting.

Yours

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Fri, 29 Aug 2003 11:36:15 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Travis Walton

My opinion of this case is that, because at least one "believer"
hypnotist plied his trade, we will never know what really happened.

Unfortunately, hypnotism is not limited to just reading a person's
experiences. In the wrong hands, it can also edit them. If the hypnotist
asks leading questions the subject does not know the answer to, often
the subject's brain will either create a scenario or adapt fiction the
subject was exposed to, just to provide the answers required.

There is a good possibility that the event was a hoax, designed to win
one of the lucrative tabloid prizes offered at the time.

A fire balloon with fireworks attached could easily explain the
sightings by the other workers.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Fri, 29 Aug 2003 11:20:30 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: FW: More Bentwaters Information - Conde

ALL claims, extraordinary or not, must be backed up with independent
evidence. That's how science works.

In your case, you have a lot more backing than an ET claim has, because:

1. The technology (police cars and flashlights) can be demonstrated to
have existed at the time of the sighting.

2. You can demonstrate that you had access to the technology at the
time.

3. You, possessing the technology, could account for not only the
sighting, but the "intelligent actions" of the object sighted.

4. Occam's Razor states that, among several competing theories, the
simplest theory must be considered to be the theory most likely to be
true, until it is refuted by evidence to the contrary. Your claim is
at the present, the one most likely to be true.

The "extraordinary" part of your claim, if any, is that people don't
normally put colored flashlights on police cars and then drive around
in circles. (Of course, farmers don't normally shoot at stranded
motorists they think are space aliens either, but it happened in 1954
in France.)

What is missing is independent proof that you were actually there with
the equipment at that time, as you claim.

Your claim is still just a theory in the eyes of science. Meanwhile,
the ET theory doesn't even meet the test of Occam's Razor. It requires
the presence of aliens (yet unproven to exist) in an alien spacecraft
(yet unproven to exist) in order to even have any probability greater
than zero.

Right now, I would rank the theories in the following order of
probability:

1. A prank played on base personnel with a police car

2. A fire-balloon prank

3. Accidental sightings of colored lights on the other side of the
forest (remember, it was Christmas)

4. Emergency spy satellite film drop (Iran hostage crisis)
5. Some kind of military drill that was never revealed to the "victims"

6. Other unknown terrestrial cause

7. Extraterrestrial activity

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Fri, 12 Sep 2003 23:42:44 +0100

There is some background case material I've become aware
of in recent months and which might be of interest.

Firstly, during December last year, I wrote:

** BEGIN **
In 'Left at East Gate', Warren discusses the February
1985, CNN documentary and how Chuck DeCaro claimed:

"CNN has also found an officer who says he drove the base
commander to a waiting aircraft to deliver what he was
told was a motion-picture film of one of the UFOs".

Warren adds this was, "followed by the officer's
statement. He had been told the film was on its way to
Germany".

If anyone has an available copy of that documentary,
please let me know.

What I do have, courtesy of Greenwood's files, is a
transcript of the CNN program - whether it was the final
version, I'm not certain.

However, it does accordingly state:

"CNN has also found an officer who says he drove the base
commander to a waiting airplane to deliver what he was
told was a motion picture film of one of the UFO's".

The "ANONYMOUS OFFICER" is then quoted:

"...uh, we drove out and I asked him what was in the
film, and he said we actually have pictures of the UFO
here. And he got off the jeep, went over to the aircraft,
handed the film to the pilot. The canopy closed and the
plane took off, and I asked him where it was headed, and
he said, 'Germany'".

There are various tales of 'unscheduled' aircraft,
usually 'cargo flights', arriving on base after the 'UFO
incidents. As Sergeant Randy Smith told me:

"The following night, I went on duty. At guardmount, Bob
Ball was very serious, he's almost never serious, a very
jovial person. He said, 'I saw something last night, but
I'm not at liberty to discuss it'. And that was the
'end'. I later heard that the morning we got off our
first midnight shift, an A-10 was scrambled and sent to
Ramstein, Germany, by Lt. Col. Halt".

So many rumours...


Who was the, as documented within that transcript,
"ANONYMOUS OFFICER" which CNN cited...

In LaEG, Warren talks about the broadcast and how he
recognised aforementioned, 'blacked out' testimony as
originating from Captain Mike Veranno [Verrano?].

I can say, from the transcript, which seems to be
original CNN material _with notes indicating witness
identities_, that every other 'anonymous' witness is
correctly identified by Warren in LaEG.

Annoyingly, I can't say for sure that it was Veranno who
made that claim - it's the one affidavit which isn't
confirmed in CNN's documentation.

However, there is one other CNN "ANONYMOUS OFFICER"
witness statement which - without going into details why
- does seem to be from Veranno.


Yet, Halt confirms:

HALT: There was no video. There was no film taken that
night to my knowledge. Now, it is possible that one of
the young airman, back at a distance because they weren't
allowed to approach close we're talking about the group
that was back at the light-alls... Somebody may have had
a camera back there, but I don't believe so because they
were on duty and they would have had to go through
guardmount. Somebody could have snuck a small, 35mm or
Instamatic or something in their pocket. It's possible
somebody may have had something, but there was no obvious
overt video filming, etc., done that night. None.

RAYL: There was no official video or film taken.

HALT: None. No, nothing official. No.
[END OF EXTRACT]
[...]

As for the assertion that film of our succeeding
Rendlesham forest spaceship was directly transported to
Germany and presumably Ramstein AFB, headquarters of
'United States Air Forces in Europe' [USAFE]... why would
Veranno, or any other "OFFICER" say this?


Note that it was statedly the "base commander" who
carried purported film - the CNN transcript correctly
identifies Halt as "Deputy Base Commander" and any
"OFFICER" should naturally know the difference.

Was therefore Col. Ted Conrad, the 'Base Commander',
involved outwith Halt's knowledge?

It's so untenable that all we seem to be evidencing is
the sheer unreliability of witness testimony...
** END **


In recent discussions with John Burroughs, he brought up
the subject of that CNN documentary, which he
participated in.

To my surprise, John mentioned an argument between Halt
and Veranno, which occurred during the production.

Just before Veranno was about to be filmed, Halt
reportedly took him aside and told him not to make any
claims about transporting evidence to a waiting aircraft.
So far as John was aware, Veranno had "backed down".

I explained how the claim was actually broadcast and
suggested Halt was simply pointing out to Veranno that
there was no such film and he must be mistaken.

Although this was a long time ago now, John's
recollection doesn't agree with my scenario. Reportedly,
Halt had reminded Veranno he [Veranno] was now at the Air
Force Academy and someone in his position shouldn't be
appearing on TV making such statements.

At present, all we can evidently conclude for certain is
that the anonymous officer who appeared in that CNN
documentary was indeed Veranno.


I wonder if he's referring to a separate event - perhaps
at some later date and amidst the 'UFO' hysteria, someone
had filmed what they perceived to be a 'UFO'.

Interestingly, Burroughs recalls that Veranno said it was
the Wing Commander, not the Base Commander, he drove to a
waiting aircraft and perhaps CNN's commentary is in
error.

The Base Commander, Col. Ted Conrad, had remained behind
at the belated officer's Christmas party and delegated
Halt to investigate what was going on during the night of
27 December.

However, the Wing Commander, Col. Gordon Williams, had
taken a great interest in the 'UFO' stories and it was
Williams who took a copy of Halt's microcassette
recording to an already scheduled staff meeting of the
Third Air Force.


One later east gate 'UFO' sighting involved Steve LaPlume
and he described:

OK just to set the time line up a bit: I was stationed at
RAF Bentwaters between Nov. 4th 1980 and April 10,1981. I
had just turned 18 years old in July.

This incident happened about three weeks after the now
infamous Bentwaters sighting/encounter. It was in the 2nd
week of January 1981. I was booted out of the service
almost three months to the day after this event.

RAF Woodbridge is a sister base to RAF Bentwaters. They
are about five miles apart and the 81st Security Police
Squadron which I was attached to covered the security for
both bases. I had not yet received my Secret Clearance
and therefore was temporarily assigned to the Law
Enforcement flight. I worked on one of the flights that
had rotating shifts. three days on swing, three days on
nights and then three days off.

Since I had no clearance I could not go into the Non
Alert Parking Areas (NAPAS) where the A-10's were nor
could I go into the Weapons Storage Area (WSA) which
housed all the ordinance and some small amount of nukes
though I do not know for sure about the nukes.

With all these restrictions I was relegated to sitting
out on the furthermost reaches of our base in a four foot
square cubical and watch the grass grow. For some reason
I got the East gate a lot. Mostly because I was new and
did not really belong to the Law Enforcement (LE) crew. I
did not mind and for the first few months it was OK.

No one bothered me and I could just hang out, check ID's
until the gate closed at about eight o'clock and then
ride shotgun with the shift sergeant. If I was on nights
I would ride with the SGT. first and then be put on the
East gate just before shift change for the morning
traffic. Most of the night was spent relieving other LE
members while they went and ate or took a leak.

On this particular night an airman named Senior Airman
Palmer was on patrol and I was riding along with him. We
went out to check the gate because some people knew the
combination and were using it after hours. I checked to
make sure it was locked. The car was parked back about
fifty feet to help light up the area. The gate was locked
and I went back to the car.

The night was brisk but not cold and SA Palmer and I hung
out leaning against the patrol car and shot the shit for
a while. I was facing south and talking to Palmer who was
facing north. He said " I guess this is where they saw
that UFO a few weeks back." I said "Oh" and asked him
what exactly happened. He did not know for sure but
pointed out a lighthouse way the heck off in the
distance, toward the north sea., and said that they were
saying that was what they saw. I asked about the rumor
that it had been moving through the trees and he just
shrugged "I don't know."

I faced back south after looking east toward the
lighthouse and something caught my eye. Up at cloud level
, which was very high as the night was pretty clear, I
noticed a light moving across the sky. It was like if you
are outside and see a jet off in the distance and while
you can not make out its image you know it's a jet
because it is a small light moving at a steady pace.

This light was not moving at any "pace" it was darting
across the sky very fast. It was up then it was down, up
then down. It probably changed altitude at a difference
of a few thousand feet in elevation ten times in as many
seconds. I simply turned to Palmer and said "huh, that's
different." He looked and spotted it also. We watched it
for about a half a minute or more and he told me to stay
put, that he was going to go to the control tower and see
what was up.
He came back about five minutes later and said they only
had a C-130 and a helicopter up that night and or in this
area. Well I am not a pilot but we both agreed that this
was neither and asked each other if we should call it in.
We agreed that we should. Palmer got on the radio and
announces "La Plume just saw a UFO outside of the East
gate." I cussed him out, what about him he saw it too.

The phone in the security booth rang almost immediately.
I answered it and it was Lt. Englund my shift supervisor.
He wanted to know what exactly I saw and where. I told
him and he ordered me to stay put and keep an eye on it.
The elapse time thus far is approximately fifteen minutes
from the time I first spotted it.

The night was partly cloudy and the craft went behind
some clouds over the Rendlesham forest. It was still at
least fifteen miles away and at an elevation of about
twenty thousand feet or so. It was not like it was
hanging overhead.

Well holy cow the earth opened up and within twenty
minutes I had more people and brass at my post than I had
ever seen. There was the deputy base commander, his wife
and teenage son. They brought along their cameras. I
remember his wife saying something to the effect of "Oh
boy we get to see one". Lt. Englund showed up and told my
not to be nervous that Colonel Williams was on his way
and that he had had just made General. Who me nervous.

I was told to state that my post was "Safe and Secure" I
opened the gate and everyone piled into a blue Air Force
station wagon and a jeep and took off. Palmer and I were
given a night vision scope and told to let them know if
we spotted it again.

We did not look for it much because we figured it was
long gone. I screwed around looking through the N.V.
scope and waited. about an hour later the vehicles came
back and I was told to man the post the rest of the night
and keep them posted if anything happened. They all then
went back to where they came.
[END]


Perhaps a similar incident explains Veranno's claims,
which, understandably, Halt might caution him about
revealing.
James.

I would ride with the SGT. first and then be put on the
East gate just before shift change for the morning
traffic. Most of the night was spent relieving other LE
members while they went and ate or took a leak.

On this particular night an airman named Senior Airman
Palmer was on patrol and I was riding along with him. We
went out to check the gate because some people knew the
combination and were using it after hours. I checked to
make sure it was locked. The car was parked back about
fifty feet to help light up the area. The gate was locked
and I went back to the car.

The night was brisk but not cold and SA Palmer and I hung
out leaning against the patrol car and shot the shit for
a while. I was facing south and talking to Palmer who was
facing north. He said " I guess this is where they saw
that UFO a few weeks back." I said "Oh" and asked him
what exactly happened. He did not know for sure but
pointed out a lighthouse way the heck off in the
distance, toward the north sea., and said that they were
saying that was what they saw. I asked about the rumor
that it had been moving through the trees and he just
shrugged "I don't know."

I faced back south after looking east toward the
lighthouse and something caught my eye. Up at cloud level
, which was very high as the night was pretty clear, I
noticed a light moving across the sky. It was like if you
are outside and see a jet off in the distance and while
you can not make out its image you know it's a jet
because it is a small light moving at a steady pace.

This light was not moving at any "pace" it was darting
across the sky very fast. It was up then it was down, up
then down. It probably changed altitude at a difference
of a few thousand feet in elevation ten times in as many
seconds. I simply turned to Palmer and said "huh, that's
different." He looked and spotted it also. We watched it
for about a half a minute or more and he told me to stay
put, that he was going to go to the control tower and see
what was up.
He came back about five minutes later and said they only
had a C-130 and a helicopter up that night and or in this
area. Well I am not a pilot but we both agreed that this
was neither and asked each other if we should call it in.
We agreed that we should. Palmer got on the radio and
announces "La Plume just saw a UFO outside of the East
gate." I cussed him out, what about him he saw it too.

The phone in the security booth rang almost immediately.
I answered it and it was Lt. Englund my shift supervisor.
He wanted to know what exactly I saw and where. I told
him and he ordered me to stay put and keep an eye on it.
The elapse time thus far is approximately fifteen minutes
from the time I first spotted it.

The night was partly cloudy and the craft went behind
some clouds over the Rendlesham forest. It was still at
least fifteen miles away and at an elevation of about
twenty thousand feet or so. It was not like it was
hanging overhead.

Well holy cow the earth opened up and within twenty
minutes I had more people and brass at my post than I had
ever seen. There was the deputy base commander, his wife
and teenage son. They brought along their cameras. I
remember his wife saying something to the effect of "Oh
boy we get to see one". Lt. Englund showed up and told my
not to be nervous that Colonel Williams was on his way
and that he had had just made General. Who me nervous.

I was told to state that my post was "Safe and Secure" I
opened the gate and everyone piled into a blue Air Force
station wagon and a jeep and took off. Palmer and I were
given a night vision scope and told to let them know if
we spotted it again.

We did not look for it much because we figured it was
long gone. I screwed around looking through the N.V.
scope and waited. about an hour later the vehicles came
back and I was told to man the post the rest of the night
and keep them posted if anything happened. They all then
went back to where they came.
[END]


Perhaps a similar incident explains Veranno's claims,
which, understandably, Halt might caution him about
revealing.
James.

Robert:

Maj Ed Drury was the operations officer, and Zickler's second in
command. Technically he was the boss of all the working flights.

The individual cops on each LE and security flight worked for either
an NCO under the flight chief or the flight chief himself. The
flight chief reported to the flight commander (Lt. Englund) and the
flight commander reported to the operations officer (Maj Drury), who
reported to Maj Zickler.

Burroughs would only refer to his immediate supervisor or his flight
chief as his "boss". Drury was, in a sense, his boss, but he would
never have referred to him as his boss. The boss, for a normal
flight member, was usually the flight chief. For most of my time I
was a flight chief, and referred to Lt. Englund as my boss.

Just as an aside, it was unusual to have a major and a commander as
both ops officer and commander. As a result Drury and Zickler were
not real popular with each other. Drury wanted to lose Zickler so he
could be the commander, and Zickler did not like Drury always
breathing down his neck waiting for Zickler to screw-up.

The semi-mysterious S. Burns (no relation to Max I hope) wrote:

>All DeAquino did was derive the "general case" for the D/H work
>showing all parameters so an engineering model could be conceived.
>Interesting how this engineering solution correlates closely to UFO
>attributes.

Really. But what exactly *are* "UFO attributes", in any sense
that might involve consistency and coherence? Compare for
instance the passage of an F-15. Or traces that let me know
a fox has passed by the hen house. Also observe we have
neither the Strike Eagle UFO nor the Fuchs McNab UFO in any
concrete sense so that we may be sure some UFOs have four
feet and red fur while others have an unusual steering system
and an instantly recognizable sound signature. We don't even
have furry red UFOs with Pratt & Whitney engines to explain
our confusion. "UFO" is a term like telepathy. Nothing is
known about a UFO, and there is no one "UFO entity" that you
can extract from UFO reports.

I can't help descrying in the way "UFO" is used here that
some assumptions, or conclusions, have been made about what
a UFO is. This is like conspiracy thinking. Any number of
dots can be joined up. The only questions worth asking about a
UFO are "Unknown to whom?" (Hynek) and "What was it"? All
other approaches (and even this one sometimes) lead you only
to observations about [mis]perception and human culture.

>BTW, to date over 500 scientists have reviewed this and
>no one yet has found a mathematical flaw regarding the mg equation.
>Most have personal opinions however. Can you tell us where the math
>flaw is?

No, and I wouldn't dream of trying. Bear in mind it's
perfectly possible to have perfectly adequate maths that
relate to nothing practically useful (or even real). A
positron is an electron travelling backwards in time,
mathematically speaking. So what? We have no way of knowing
whether it *is* actually such a thing. DeAquino can shovel
out maths till kingdom come, but unless they result (thankyou
Larry) in an actual gravity shield they mean nothing, however
elegant the equations. Nothing about DeAquino, most especially
his creationist tendency, threatens my self-assurance --
politically incorrect as that may be deemed. [Please note that
I don't object to the idea of a creator -- only to its
inappropriate intrusion into scientific "discourse".]

Pardon the lapse, however. I should have remembered what
beta particles, and ergo a beta beam, were.

When you then suggest that DeAquino's wheezes -- which some
people seem to think might be given the benefit of some doubt
because some young scientists are weary of peer review: whaaaat?
 -- represent a "plausible" explanation of Travis's Trick, you
are starting at the wrong end of the investigation. No one, with
the very possible exceptions of Mike Rogers and Travis hisself
know what went on that night, and many mundane possibilities
haven't even been explored publicly. Skeptics cannot win this
argument in any case, since it's humanly impossible to
explore every possible alternative scenario to the claim as
made. This doesn't excuse UFO believers from setting up their
own investigations (and assumptions) properly.

And besides, those who have an unshakeable faith in alien
visitation will hang onto that no matter what circumstantial
evidence is brought to bear. Including confessions. Look at
how Michael Glickman & Co deal with crop circle makers.

best wishes
Peter B

Hello Brett
You said re De Aquino:

"Any crackpot who can write something
that looks like a physics paper can get a paper "archived at ... Los Alamos" and they
frequently do ... (which is not to say that arxiv.org is not an invaluable resource for
real physicists.) It is not and was never meant to be a subsitute for peer-review,
simply a way to get access to the latest research results without having to wait for a
year or more when it appears in a real journal."

This is misleading. It isn't true that 'any crackpot' can get any old rubbish archived.
Only crackpots with academic addresses or academic sponsors can get their rubbish
archived. And it's true that web archive wasn't expected to be a substitute for paper
journals but it's the first resort now for most papers and will become the norm. For
many of the younger generation of physicists it already is. Many are disenchanted
with so-called peer-review, and anyway a year's publishing lead-time in today's
environment is completely ridiculous. Maybe many arxiv papers are going to be
overtaken by events before they get a chance to become iconic classics, but that
doesn't mean they aren't important in the cross-fertilisation of ideas. De Aquino might
not have the answers, but at least he's one of those asking the questions.
Martin Shough

One problem with that "fireball" on 10/1/03. It didn't move in 4
minutes.
Fireballs normally progress across the sky.

Either the fireball exploded (and ended its forward progress) at the
instant the first picture was taken, or it was not a fireball. The
second picture (allowing for camera location change - demonstrated
by the two TV antennas) shows the trail in exactly the same place it
was in 4 minutes earlier.

Oddly enough, the first picture reminds me of a gas flare at an oil
production field.

One possibility is that a military jet plane was in trouble, had to dump
excess fuel, and it ignited.
