The answer is a resounding yes!

The Eastern Radar/Heathrow contact lost near RAF
Woodbrige and the Cosmos 749 re-entry are the same event.
The two events were perceived as occurring at the same
time not only by Burroughs and Halt, but also by MOD
and the local constabulary.

In the letter from Suffolk Police to Ian Ridpath dated 23
November 1983, the following asppears:

"The first visit [to the forest, early hours of 26 December]
followed immediately the reported incident and the two
officers who attended the incident made a search of the
area with negative result. A note on the [police] log indicates
that Air Traffic Control at West Drayton were contacted
and that there was no known knowledged of aircraft in
that area to coincide with the time of the sighting. Mention
is also made on the log of reports received of aerial
phenomena over Southern England during the night."

During the night is the night of December 25: ie the Cosmos
re-entry, which occurred at 9.07pm.

In the MOD file is briefing dated 1983 which notes:

"Ops [Ground Environment] has checked the question of
radar traces with NATO who have informally stated that
nothing was seen on any radar recordings although they
did receive a report of a sighting from a civil aircraft."

The sighting from the aircraft is clearly the report of the
satellite re-entry made by the crew of a 737 outbound
from Stanstead referred to by Jenny Randles. They
reported seeing a "bright flash" or explosion in the sky
over Suffolk/Essex.
>
> Is it one coincidence too far, that Cosmos 749 debris
> finally burnt-up on re-entry, reportedly only some 20
> miles from the bases?
>
> Could this now explain the claimed radar tracking which
> 'disappeared' when 'overhead'?
>

The answer has to be 'yes' again:

I have a copy of the article "Re-entry of Cosmos 749 rocket
on 1980, December 25' published in Journal BAA 91, pg
561-66. The relevant section on the rocket track over
Kent and East Anglia reads:

"It crossed the English coast at Beachy Head and went
up the Thames Estuary in the region of the Isle of
Sheppey. The point of crossing the English Coast was
very well defined. Several observers from the area of
Newhaven reported overhead passes but slightly to the
east. Observers from Bexhill, Eastbourne area similarly
reported overhead passes but slightly to the west. This
gave a maximum bandwith of 17 km from these observers
but, when other reports are considered, the most
likely track is thought to be within 2 km of Beachy Head
itself. Because of the extensive cloud over Kent, the loss
of sighting of the fireball did not necessarily coincide with
an extinction point. It is thought that there was no general
extinction point as the many fragments were burning out
or becoming non-luminous over quite a large range of
the track. It is known that at least four fragments were still
luminous as it crossed over the Thames Estuary, but two
of them faded quite quickly. By the time the object was
about 12 km east of Southend only one fragment was
still luminous. The end point of the final fragement could
not be defined accurately, but it is thought to have been
in the region of Clacton. This is supported by the fact that
nothing was recorded on an all-sky camera situated at
Ipswich and which was operating at the time."

I suggest this passage explains the reference to an object
tracked over the Thames Estuary which dropped or
disappeared from radar screens near Rendlesham forest.

The Journal BAA also has a diagram showing the track
of the satellite debris over southeast England. I will
obtain a scan of the article and send to James for
uploading (the original is of poor quality).
Dave Clarke

This is what I know. Penniston got permission on the

Leaving aside whether RAF Bawdsey actually had any
involvement, if John's recollections are correct and both
eastern radar/Heathrow reported a contact which had been
lost near RAF Woodbridge, could that conceivably equate
with the earlier Cosmos 749 space debris re-entry?

Any connection with same is a possibility I've always
kept in mind.

However, at the outset, this would require surviving
debris to have come down near the twin base RAF
Bentwaters/RAF Woodbridge complex.

It's stretching coincidence that Soviet space debris just
happened to land next-door to a base which housed the
67th Aerospace Rescue and Recovery Squadron [ARRS], who
specialised in spacecraft recovery.

Even though it was Christmas...


Yet, although perhaps not generally realised, it is
documented where, approximately, any such wreckage would
seemingly have impacted.

If not 'right on the money', it was effectively, right on
RAF Bentwaters/RAF Woodbridge's doorstep.

Cue the chapter from Ian Ridpath's lengthy case article,
at:

http://users.macunlimited.net/ianrid/ufos/rendlesham6
Ian writes:

"At 21.07 on the evening of 1980 December 25 (i.e. a mere
six hours before the supposed UFO landing in Rendlesham
Forest) the Russian Cosmos 749 rocket re-entered over
north-west Europe and was widely reported as a UFO. A
report on this re-entry can be found in the Journal of
the British Astronomical Association (1981, vol. 91, page
561). It broke up during re-entry, and the last fragment
is thought to have burnt out somewhere east of Clacton".

I attach the permitted saved image from an online map -
inherently noted copyright acknowledged - which
demonstrates the proximity of Clacton [Clacton-on-Sea] to
RAF Bentwaters/RAF Woodbridge (see the nearby town of
Woodbridge, to the north of Ipswich).


Is it one coincidence too far, that Cosmos 749 debris
finally burnt-up on re-entry, reportedly only some 20
miles from the bases?

Could this now explain the claimed radar tracking which
'disappeared' when 'overhead'?

Ian adds:

"As far as I am aware, no fragments from this re-entry
were ever detected on radar, but it is possible that the
radar tapes were examined to see if anything did get
through and this may explain some of the stories about
radar checks that were later attributed to the Rendlesham
Forest UFO".

This might make some sense of the evidence.


Whilst Ian comments, "It broke up during re-entry, and
the last fragment is thought to have burnt out somewhere
east of Clacton... Any surviving fragments would have
fallen into the North Sea, and hence have been
unrecoverable", there's apparently no proof that
fragments had not survived.

If they did, then any fallen wreckage could presumably
have been within a wide radius of Clacton, not
necessarily the North Sea.

Consequently, the chance of this occurring next to RAF
Woodbridge are duly shortened and by default become a
reasonable bet, perhaps at tempting odds.

No such thing as a 'sure bet' though, unless you already
know, for sure, that it is.


Further intrigue is John's remark, "It was within minutes
of the unfamiliar lights".

I would expect he will be able to clarify this.

James, quoting Jim Penniston:

> "I went to the gate shack, phoned in, and spoke with
> Master Sergeant J.D. Chandler, who was the on-duty flight
> chief for both bases. He asked me to stand by while he
> contacted the Control Tower at Bentwaters and also at

> Control Tower, and they, in turn, were in contact with
> Heathrow Airport's Control Tower in London and RAF
> Bawdsey Eastern Radar in East Anglia. I was told they
> reported a bogie about three miles out from Bentwaters
> but had lost contact with it 15 minutes previously. The
> confirmation that triangulated the radar sighting was RAF
> Bawdsey. It had been over Woodbridge, they told me, when
> it dropped from radar imaging".
>

There is no such thing as "RAF Bawdsey Eastern Radar";
Eastern Radar was RAF Watton, near Norwich. Bawdsey
(in Suffolk, near Rendlesham Forest) was not, as far as I'm
aware, an operational air defence radar station in 1980.
It closed in 1987.

The situation in 1980, as far as I understand it, was that RAF
Neatishead was the central Air Defence Radar Control and
Reporting Centre for the whole of Eastern/Southern England.
Data from all satellite stations was fed to its screens.
Coincidentally, I was invited on a guided tour of the
underground operations centre at Neatishead last Sunday.
I was amazed to find the equipment used by the controllers
today was still Cold War vintage (their views on UFOs are
another story...)

RAF Watton was the joint military/civilian ATC centre for the
same area -- its radar picture was fed in real time to screens
at Neatishead - so controllers at Neatishead could "see" the
same picture as Watton, alongside pictures from other ATCs
and CSCs around the UK.

I have already quoted the testimony of Sqdrn Ldr Combe, the
CO at Watton, who received Col Halt's call via Bentwaters
tower in the early hours of 28 December. Halt was in
Rendlesham Forest and was asking for confirmation
of the lights he was seeing. Combe asked his controller to
check and nothing was visible on the radar picture.

Combe could not recall an earlier (ie 26 December) call from
Bentwaters, but he may not have been on duty. We know there
must have been some checks made on the Cosmos re-entry
tracking. If the Cosmos satellite was tracked by the ATC at
Heathrow, it must have been visible to Neatishead and Watton
too -- perhaps there is another MOD file on this matter.

Far more conclusive, however, are the remarks made by
Sqn Ldr Jack Badcock, of RAF (Ops) GE, in the MOD file,
(memo to DS8 dated 28 March 1983):

"Neatishead, which is the Sector Ops Centre responsible for
that area, had nothing unusual to report, and nothing more
substantive has come to light. I have received no evidence
that any radar reported unusual tracks."

Badcock was referring to the whole period 26-30 December
1980 and had access to data from all the operational radar
centres.

Penniston and Halt seem to have jumbled together a lot of
unrelated events and hearsay.

best,

Dave Clarke

the subject. They could not help".

Presuming we can accept SSgt Coffey had been contacted,

"Sgt. Coffey called Bentwaters control tower and he also

Coffey had called _both_ the Bentwaters tower and
Heathrow - Halt had no involvement in this initial
incident and there's no indication he ever interviewed
Coffey.

In going over related evidence, I'm reminded of the
following, from Halt's earliest interview with Salley
Rayl, as published in OMNI Magazine, April 1994:

"Around New Year's Eve, I took statements and interviewed
the men who had taken part in the initial incident. The
reports were nearly identical.

Basically, they reported this: In the early morning hours
of December 26, one of the airmen drove to the back gate
at Woodbridge on a routine security check. He saw lights
in the forest, specifically a red light, and thought
maybe an airplane had crashed. He radioed a report, which
was called into the tower, but the tower reported nobody
was flying.

Eventually, a group headed out to the forest. They
reported strange noises - animals, movement, like we
heard two nights later.

As they approached the clearing, they reported seeing a
large yellowish-white light with a blinking red light on
the upper center portion and a steady blue light
emanating from underneath. The tower again reported
nothing on radar".


How does "nothing on radar", subsequently become the tale
Halt told at the 'UFO Magazine' [UK] conference, only
three months later?

elsewhere.

be alerting Burroughs et al about a radar trace (from
Cosmos [Kosmos] 749), some six hours before.

but had lost contact with it 15 minutes previously. The
confirmation that triangulated the radar sighting was RAF
Bawdsey. It had been over Woodbridge, they told me, when

"15 miles out", or, maybe, "15 minutes previously"...?

Hopefully, this can be further resolved.

perceived as an aircraft crash nearby, then when
Burroughs and Steffans investigated further at the
outset, there should, of course, have been nothing to see
within the forest.

However, from Burroughs' official statement:

"Because I've never seen anything like that coming from
the woods before we decided to drive down and see what it
was. We went down east gate road and took a right at the
stop sign and drove down about 10 to 20 yards to where
there is a road that goes into the forest. At the road I
could see a white light shining onto the trees and could
still see the red and blue lights".

The lights are evidently still visible.

He continues:

"We decided we better go call it in so we went back up
towards east gate. I was watching the lights and the
white light started coming down the road that led into
the forest. We got to the gate and called it in".

Still visible...

"The whole time I could see the lights and the white
light was almost at the edge of the road and the blue and
red lights were still out in the woods. A security unit
was sent down to the gate and when they got there they
could see it too. We asked permission to go and see what
it was and they told us we could. We took the truck down
the road that led into the forest. As we went down the
east gate road and the road that led into the forest the
lights were moving back and they appeared to stop in
amongst a bunch of trees".

And still, those lights have not disappeared.

location".

polite. Even though I was not armed at the time Mr Bennett
took fright, claiming also that Dr David Clarke was about
to push him under a passing No 9 big red London omnibus.
Which ought to have worried him more, had he ever believed it.

But anyway. Being transformed by a formalism remains a
different entity from being able to show beyond a set of
formulae that a particle *is* moving backwards in time,
in yer actual fact. It's a tasty idea. We can't demonstrate
that the maths represents a reality. Why does pointing out
the obvious create such excitement?

telling me the table is "hollow") at certain scales of
consideration. Perhaps "complete" would be the better word.

>"Nothing about DeAquino, most especially his creationist tendency,

This remark would, I surmise, puzzle Moses, the Buddha, Goya,
Mohamed, Beethoven, Dante, Tolstoy, Einstein, Dr Strabismus
of Utrecht and many other famous persons, as well as those less
celebrated such as the headhunters of Equador, and quite possibly
the majority of the world's population even now, including the
Pope, the entire Nobel committee, and some Congolese animists.
This is by nomeans to decry science, of which this field could
tolerate a good deal more, although I would not set the fatuous
kinds of limitation on it that Mr Ego Bennett ignorantly would.

>you might ask yourself 'who here is the one doing

No, but I'm not the one that's lost. Nor am I claiming to
"do" science. A skill not required when calling attention
to science not being done. I can't do competition dressage
either, and wouldn't want to, but I sure do know when
some clown can't tell "collected" from conflicted, or
"impulsion" from speed. Dr Leavis did not write poems.

Okay: despite "unaccredited" not appearing in any previous
post -- or even writing, I think -- of mine, I will concede
that arxiv may be a haven for accredited nuts, fruitloops,
loonies, and persons of dubious plausibility. If you think
academia is free of such characters, take a gander at the
endless list of Ph.Ds (genuine) who are prepared to be named
as "consultants" to MUFON, and the wondrous illogic perpetrated
by almost equal numbers of PhDs in the Journal of the SPR.
Read Polanyi. Admire his guts. Accept peer review.

>I'm interested in why it

Perhaps because I suffer from insomnia and have some time on
my hands after finishing a book against an unkind deadline?
Because I don't have the bald gene? I don't give a toss whether
Steve Burns is right or wrong. That wasn't quite the issue. The
question was whether he was asking the right questions in the
right order (manifestly not), and whether he should put so
much trust in the likes of a DeAquino (a bet one ought to
hedge, I'd say -- I can tolerate ambiguity occasionally).

But let them all be right, despite the intellectual incoherence
that got them there. So what? That nice series on the teevee
has just shown how the London sewer system was built for the
wrong reasons but had the desired effect. It happens. If you
proved the objective existence of UFOs-as-alien-craft, would
you expect human history to turn some unexpected corner? Would
the (scientifically) proven existence of God really answer more
questions than it raises? How could you tell if God hears, let
alone listens to, prayers?

What I am not interested in, because I sense a sterile debate,
is why anyone should be interested in what matters to me.
Arguments stand and fall on their own. Bugger proponents (and
with Nanny Ogg, destiny too).

I don't think I have anything more to add on this...

Scuse me.

>The web *is* the first resort now, backed up in many cases by

Which is fine, of course, in that the medium is faster.
What is less fine is the lack of peer review (one of my
doubts about DeAquino's stuff). The system is not perfect,
for all sorts of reasons, but is probably the best anyone
could devise. Better a high level of caution and conservatism
here than not. For what's worth, Joao Maguiejo sounds *exactly*
like an embittered crank (don't know his age), and he, along
with anyone else interested in why radical but correct ideas
may not get full justice at first pass should read Michael
Polanyi on his own experience of having his scientific
credibility put on the line: see "The Republic of Science".
Polanyi was correct in his conclusions, but his peers
thought otherwise for many years. Nonetheless, he held no
grudge against them. Why, makes instructive reading.

>What I
>reacted to was a knee-jerk dismissal of a whole area of
>legitimate research - not by yourself in the first instance but
>by another (who I see has adopted the tiresome tactic of
>affecting what I assume is supposed to be a lofty disdain by
>responding to my criticism without direct acknowledgement in the
>body of a reply to someone else).

So why are you doing the same here?

>There's a fascinating social
>study to be made of the way people climb over one another to give
>themselves up to a fascistic mob mentality where the words
>'gravity' and 'antigravity' are concerned. Gravity theory sits at
>the sacred centre of the inviolable canon of scientific
>orthodoxy. Peeple [etc]

Indeed. Some peeple might be mildly incensed with the equation
of caution with fascistry, about which I have good reason to
be well informed, and to detest. Calm your tongue. Fascists
have shot people, after a good deal of sadistic foreplay,
for this kind of dozy comment and it doesn't reflect well
on such commentators' imagination or tact to bandy this kind
of extreme about so loosely. It doesn't allow equality of
esteem to the bodies so unkindly clambered over, either,
wherever they may be. (I am looking.)

The problem *actually* with gravity is that it's indetectable
outside the realm of orchards, celestial mechanics, peeple
falling into council workmens' trenches ("Gosh," they say,
through the fine red mist forming around their heads, "I've
had an ongoing gravity situation experience -- Wow! Firkin
great, man! Lookadablud. Whoodja sue?") and mathematics. No
waves, no particles. No damn cat, no damn cradle. Any fruitcake
from Baker Maid to rocket scientist Friedman can float into
this field with some wazzockry of their own. Who is that Ronald
Pearson [?] guy who has "proven" the ether exists, and life
after death along with it? I spy him, and I spy De Aquino
trying to maintain God exists on account of his equations,
and you want me to keep quiet, already?

There is nothing sacred or inviolable about gravity. For all
I know gravity is the new ether. Relativity suggests that
it's a byproduct of something else entirely, rather as the
chemical reactions of hydrogen peroxide will make a sloven
look like a slapper. Does anyone suggest that a bottled
blonde exudes wave-like particles as a result? [This is a
trick question, Martin.] The difficulty with gravity, in
other words, is getting a handle on it. If DeAquino thinks
he has done just that, why doesn't he submit his web-
published papers to "Nature", y'know, just for the hell of
it? What's a year or two's wait when you've proven the
existence of God? Do I smell self-assurance, or at least
the faintest whiff of a hint of a suspicion of crankery?

best wishes
Peter B

Dear Snide of Malaprop

"Bear in mind it's perfectly possible to have perfectly adequate maths that relate to
nothing practically useful (or even real). A positron is an electron travelling
backwards in time, mathematically speaking. So what? We have no way of knowing
whether it *is* actually such a thing."

'So what?' you ask. Well, only that the whole of quantum physics of the last half
century has been transformed by the formalism that contains this insight. I'm sure that
if he were still around that nice Mr. Feynman would love to explain to you why it isn't
just some trivial analogy but a profound physical identity. I doubt you'd listen,
however.

"DeAquino can shovel out maths till kingdom come, but unless they result (thankyou
Larry) in an actual gravity shield they mean nothing, however elegant the equations."

Excuse me but this is pure bull crap. Maybe the huge importance of the Feynman
spacetime representation of QED to generations of theorists and experimenters means
nothing because the Sneak of Maladroit can't buy himself a time machine? Are you
saying that Einstein's general relativity is just meaningless elegant equations because
nobody has developed a warp drive yet? I don't think you are, because your objection
to DeAquino's theorising seems to be that it *so obviously* contradicts what we
*know* about gravity that he just has to be nutty as a fruitcake - and general relativity
is, of course, what we currently *know* in the sense that certain very subtle
predictions can be verified to 14 decimal places. But we also know that it is wrong,
despite this, because it isn't a quantum theory. This is the big issue for a lot of people
other than De Aquino! 'Well then,' you may reply, 'let DeAquino predict some
quantitative effect and let's wait to see some experimental tests then.' I couldn't have
put it better myself.

"Nothing about DeAquino, most especially his creationist tendency, threatens my
self-assurance -- politically incorrect as that may be deemed. [Please note that I don't
object to the idea of a creator -- only to its inappropriate intrusion into scientific
"discourse".]"

It seems to me that it's only insofar as 'the idea of a creator' can be brought into
scientific discourse that it has any status as an 'idea' at all. There is no other
worthwhile kind of discourse. I don't understand the status of a proposition that is
declared to be beyond all scrutiny and criticism. Why should you want to place
barricades around any idea? If it isn't a good idea then it won't survive. As for your
objections to people bringing anti-scientific "creationism" into the discourse - nobody
here mentioned creatonism as far as I know. We were talking about physics. You
brought creationism into your own 'discourse' - twice now.
"Pardon the lapse, however. I should have remembered what beta particles, and ergo a
beta beam, were."

Pardon granted. But don't you think you should revisit your email and reflect on the
gleeful and sneering tone with which you leapt hastily to the offence? Having yourself
committed some errors whilst being unable to demonstrate that De Aquino has
committed even one in his gravitational thesis (despite his elsewhere espousing
creatonist opinions that we both probably disagree with), you might ask yourself 'who
here is the one doing science?' and conclude - a sadder and a wiser man - that it might
not necessarily be you.

"When you then suggest that DeAquino's wheezes -- which some people seem to
think might be given the benefit of some doubt because some young scientists are
weary of peer review: whaaaat? -- represent a "plausible" explanation of Travis's
Trick, you are starting at the wrong end of the investigation."

You're confusing me with Steve Burns in this paragraph. You also traduce the point I
made about arxiv and paper journals to cover the fact that you were wrong to suggest
that arxiv is a haven for any unaccredited nutcase. I'd suggest that DeAquino's
claimed university post is probably genuine if he's submitted to LANL/Arxiv on a
regular basis. You questioned his accreditation. If you have evidence then produce it.
I don't know; I don't especially care. I never mentioned Travis Walton either. I'm not
interested in Travis Walton or De Aquino per se. I'm interested in why it matters *so
much* to you that Steve Burns should turn out to be wrong.

Martin Shough

Hi Brett
I don't think we're really disagreeing re arxiv, or De Aquino.
The web *is* the first resort now, backed up in many cases by
paper publication; but probably *will become* the norm. I'm far
from claiming that De Aquino's work must be correct, and
certainly I'm not saying that web archiving makes it mainstream.
Of course it's highly controversial and quite rightly treated
with great caution. This is not the point - unless anyone is
arguing that new theory must always be non-controversial (there
may well be some on this list who would argue that!). What I
reacted to was a knee-jerk dismissal of a whole area of
legitimate research - not by yourself in the first instance but
by another (who I see has adopted the tiresome tactic of
affecting what I assume is supposed to be a lofty disdain by
responding to my criticism without direct acknowledgement in the
body of a reply to someone else). There's a fascinating social
study to be made of the way people climb over one another to give
themselves up to a fascistic mob mentality where the words
'gravity' and 'antigravity' are concerned. Gravity theory sits at
the sacred centre of the inviolable canon of scientific
orthodoxy. Peeple seem to revel in the permission they feel this
gives them to unload their vitriol and superstitious ignorance
against anyone who questions it!

Re the point about peer-review and paper - take a well-publicised
recent complainant: "The web has changed everything because . .
. journals may be bypassed altogether ... No one reads journals
any more ... they are an anachronism, and they have already
effectively been phased out. ... The refereeing process
associated with current journals provides no real quality control
... Scientific publishing has become fraudulent. Referee reports
are often empty of scientific content and reflect nothing but the
authors' social standing . . . editors can be totally illiterate
. . .." etc. A tad exaggerated? Maybe. But this is Joao Maguiejo
of Cambridge, UC Berkeley, Princeton etc., it isn't some aged
embittered crank - though some mainstream figures treated him,
Albrecht, Moffat and others as cranks for suggesting the speed of
light might vary. They had publishing difficulties -
understandably you might say. Where is VSL theory on the spectrum
from kooky to mainstream today? I'm not quite sure. But Maguiejo
probably speaks for quite a lot of his peers in any case.
According to recent articles I've seen on this topic referees are
often inconsistent, arbitrary and have frequently been caught out
not even reading the papers they report on!
Martin Shough

Hi James, David, List,

I concur with David's assessment. After reading the aforementioned
BAA Journal article by Ian Ridpath, I requested the only element set
available for this particular satellite component from Dr. Nick
Johnson of NASA space debris program and using various orbital
tracking software and also working out the orbital equations by hand
on paper (as Ian Ridpath did) and plotting against an orthographic
map, came up with a similar solution for the Cosmos re-entry over
southern England. As previously noted by Ian, Jenny Randles and
others, this is an event which cannot be entirely ruled out of the
series of allegations made in the Rendlesham Forest UFO/s encounter
and particularly the *The Eastern Radar/Heathrow contact* lost near
RAF Woodbrige.

From: "Robert Mclean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>
Date: Sun, 12 Oct 2003 21:21:34 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham Revelations
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

James

Perhaps the best evidence for the relevance of both the Cosmos 749 booster
re-entry and the 2:50 fireball to the events of 25/26 Dec 1980 comes from
Larry Warren's letter home to his mother, dated 6 January 1981, and
published in Left at East Gate pp 64-65 . I believe this letter is about as
close to the truth as anyone will ever be able to get as regards the Larry
Warren Story:
---------------------------
"Remember I was telling you about the U.F.O. that landed - well I'll tell
you the whole story on it. Over Europe and England a bunch of lights were
seen - Over London one of the lights broke into about twenty smaller
lights - and flew in all directions. At about three in the morning, a guy I
know in D-Flight of Security Police told me he responded to a falling star
outside the Weapons Storage Area...



Anyway he reported it and then everyone started feeling strange - then a guy
on the Backgate at Woodbridge reported a bright light moving through the
pine forest. An officer and two sergeants responded but they could not take
weapons because they were off base.



Over the radio they reported seeing a pie-shaped object - about 7 by 8 ft in
size. But they said every time they would get near it, it would seem further
away all of a sudden. They also said that all the animals in the forest were
going nuts.



Then all of a sudden the light went out - and over the radio they said they
didn't like the situation and wanted to go back to base - but they were told
to keep on investigating.



Then they said the thing appeared behind them - it seemed like it was
playing games. After 3 and a half miles of following the thing through the
countryside and woods - the thing just disappeared in a field. It was only
about 10 ft off the ground. This is what a friend of mine said he heard on
the radio".
At that same time, me and five other guys were walking up a dark path about
2 miles from base . . . cause we couldn't get a ride and we felt like we
were being watched and it was strange cause there were no street lights -
Then we saw a bright light go right over us about 50 feet up and just fly
over a field. It was silent. We first thought it was an A-10 jet. But they
scream. So we ran away, because witchcraft and black magic is a big thing in
this part of Suffolk and we thought that witches were in the woods. That
light just seemed to jump over the trees - Then the next day it turned out
that we were in the same place as the U.F.O. so I think we saw it too. Now
the three people who saw it can't and won't speak about it at all. And
supposedly no animals have gone back into the woods yet - They did find two
landing sights - and supposedly some equipment left behind.



A big C-130 came in and took something in a crate away a few days later and
the guards were flown in from somewhere else - it is strange and now I hear
that strange things have been going on in the forest for the past weeks -
and remember we did get cut off on the phone. . . Say hi to everyone, and I'
ll call soon.



Love, Larry



P.S. The picture is of me in London about a month ago. . . tell Sam to
write.



(P.S. Ma, When I get home I'll tell you the truth about the U.F.O.: I can't
in the mail, they read it!)"

-------------------------

List subscribers can use their own judgement as to whether or not the final
PS was written at the same time as the rest of the letter. Suffice to say
that Warren's official account is that his encounter took place on 28
December, and prior to that he was unaware of any UFO activity. Yet the
obvious reference in this letter to both the re-entry of Cosmos 749 (which
was spectacular, lasting nearly 1 minute and visible over large parts of
southern England) and the 2:50 a.m fireball, clearly identifies the events
he relates in this letter as having taken place the night of 25/26 December.

It is interesting that someone in the Weapons Storage Area spotted and later
correctly identified the fireball. I wonder who that was.
It also seems from this letter that Larry Warren also saw the 2:50 a.m.
fireball, but didn't identify it as such.

Regarding the fireball, some time ago I did manage to get hold of a copy of
the BAA Meteor Section Newsletter No. 4 dated Feb. 1981. What is not widely
known is that including Cosmos 749 there were up to 4 fireballs the night of
25-26/12/1980. In fact, it would have been difficult for a UFO to land at a
time NOT nearly coincident with some other more mundane celestial event, and
no doubt this explains the coincidence of the 2:50 a.m. fireball and the UFO
in Rendlesham Forest. Copied below is the portion of this newsletter
relating the celestial events that night.

----------------------------

Christmas Crackers

Those astronomers observing on Christmas night, 1980, may be forgiven for
thinking they had overdone the Turkey and Christmas Pudding. Roy Panther
discovered his Comet (1980u) in the, constellation of Lyra, early that
evening, and three (possibly, four) fireballs were reported.

The first object occurred at 17.20 UT (plus/minus 2 minutes) and was of
magnitude -5. It was widely seen over Southern England and brightened and
faded smoothly, with no fragmentation or anomalous behaviour. The duration
of this event was only a few seconds, and from Sussex, the object first
appeared near Beta Aurigae and travelled towards the southern horizon,
extinguishing in Eridanus.

Two other fireballs, both of only a few seconds duration, were sighted at
19.20 UT (plus/minus 5 minutes), and at 02.50 UT (plus/minus 5 minutes) on
Boxing Day. The first of these was only reported by 3 witnesses (all
non-astronomers) and the second by 4 witnesses, all of whom estimated its
brightness as comparable to the gibbous Moon and of 3 to 4 seconds duration.
Further observations of all these objects, are required.

Without doubt, the most spectacular and best observed event was of major
interest. It occurred at 21.00 UT, and was a fireball of extremely long
duration and showing considerable fragmentation, followed by eventual total
disintegration. It has been identified as the re-entry of the third stage of
a Cosmos rocket launcher, and observations were made over most of Southern
England, the track passing across the English Channel from near the
Cherbourg peninsula, south of the Isle of Wight and running close to both
Eastbourne and Dover.

Thanks to the energy and efficiency of Assistant Director John Mason, some
300 reports of sightings were collected, following appeals on local radio,
and in the Press, many within the crucial first 24 hours after the event.
There has been close liaison at all times between the Meteor Section and
Howard Miles, Director of the Artificial Satellite Section. At first it was
thought the object had been identified as Cosmos 749 Rocket, but this is now
extremely unlikely, as the object observed had an orbital inclin-ation far
lower than the value of 74 degrees for Cosmos 749 in fact, nearer to 55
degrees inclination.



The investigations are continuing, and the net has now widened to the
Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and Northern France, where an event was also
witnessed on Christmas night. Subsequently, pieces of debris were recovered
on the ground, in particular at Maldegem, near Bruges in Northern Belgium.
However, there is an enigma in that the two sets of data are inconsistent,
and do not appear to relate to the same object. One theory is that there
were two re-entries on the same night but, clearly, much more investigation
needs to be carried out. A full report will be available in due course.
Observations of this re-entry are still needed from observers living in Kent
and East Anglia, so please send any further information to Howard Miles
without delay.


--------------------

What this report does not state is where in the sky the 2:50 a.m. fireball
was visible. I will try to contact John Mason to see if he has this data.

If John Burroughs and Bud Steffens did not see the 2:50 a.m. fireball, then
perhaps they heard chatter on their radio originating from the guard in the
WSA who did spot it.

James, I suggest you copy Burroughs with Larry Warren's letter of 6 January
1981, and ask him some questions about what prompted them to look out in the
woods in the first place.

Best regards,

Robert McLean

>"Remember I was telling you about the U.F.O. that landed

Robert,

Consequently, if Warren did write this letter as claimed,
his mention of a "falling star", circa "three in the
morning", is indeed surely a reference to the 0250
'fireball', evidently also witnessed on base.

Warren's letter continues:

"Anyway he reported it and then everyone started feeling
strange - then a guy on the Backgate at Woodbridge
reported a bright light moving through the pine forest.
An officer and two sergeants responded but they could not
take weapons because they were off base".

Although Staff-Sergeant Jim Penniston was duly
accompanied off base by Airman First Class John Burroughs
and Airman Ed Cabansag, there was another 'Sergeant'
involved - Staff-Sergeant Bud Steffans, who remained back
at east gate.

Checking east gate's security as part of their routine
jeep patrol, Burroughs and Steffans had reported from
that location an observation of unusual lights within
Rendlesham forest, to which Penniston and Cabansag's
patrol responded

Warren then writes:

"Over the radio they reported seeing a pie-shaped object
- about 7 by 8 ft in size. But they said every time they
would get near it, it would seem further away all of a
sudden. They also said that all the animals in the forest
were going nuts.

Then all of a sudden the light went out - and over the
radio they said they didn't like the situation and wanted
to go back to base - but they were told to keep on
investigating.

Then they said the thing appeared behind them - it seemed
like it was playing games. After 3 and a half miles of
following the thing through the countryside and woods -
the thing just disappeared in a field. It was only about
10 ft off the ground. This is what a friend of mine said
he heard on the radio".

Overall, this second-hand account from Warren is in
general agreement with the early January 1981 witness
statements provided by Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston,
at Halt's belated request.


Remarkably, Warren adds:

"At that same time, me and five other guys were walking
up a dark path about 2 miles from base... cause we
couldn't get a ride and we felt like we were being
watched and it was strange cause there were no street
lights - Then we saw a bright light go right over us
about 50 feet up and just fly over a field. It was
silent. We first thought it was an A-10 jet. But they
scream. So we ran away, because witchcraft and black
magic is a big thing in this part of Suffolk and we
thought that witches were in the woods. That light just
seemed to jump over the trees - Then the next day it
turned out that we were in the same place as the U.F.O.
so I think we saw it too".


However, in 'Left at East Gate' [p32], he blatantly
contradicts:

"The day before Christmas, I left for Germany with my
friend Mark. We had met two German girls in London the
previous week at Le Beat Route, a club on Greek Street.

[...].

I think the girls lost interest in Mark and me on the
second night.

[...]

On or about 27 December, we flew back to RAF Mildenhall
to begin our shift the next night.
[END]
Consequently, if Warren was statedly in Germany between
24-27 December, then how to reconcile from that alluded
letter, his corroboration of our founding 'UFO' sighting
at approximately 0300 on 26 December; "Then the next day
it turned out that we were in the same place as the
U.F.O. so I think we saw it too"?

LATEST COUNT
The latest tally of FOTOCAT shows 4,000 entries. Considering an estimate
of 10,000 of the total number of photographic cases world-wide between
1947 and 2003, it shows the big progress accomplished to date.

OUTSTANDING DONATION
An important donation has just taken place. Dr. Roberto Enrique Banchs,
one of the leading, historical figures of UFO research in Argentina, has
generously submitted to the FOTOCAT Project his personal collection of
photographs amounting to some hundreds of prints and slides, which will

documentation files, mainly for Argentina.

CHANGES IN FOTOCAT's STRUCTURE
The FOTOCAT Excel listing is evolving once more. The last version has
included the decision to be in English, because most of potential users
are English-speaking. Also, new columns have been added to include: names
of photographers, media associated to them, special features of
photographs or photography conditions (infrared or other sensibility film
used, stereo o 3D, automatic cameras, gun or satellite cameras, object
invisible to eye, blank photos, spectra or magnetic recording, etc).
Besides, a new column introduced to enter geographical codes for
provinces, States or regions for Spain, United States, Brazil, France,
Belgium, Canada, Australia, Mexico, etc. This improvement will allow the
researchers to tabulate the event listing with larger flexibility, as soon
as it is made freely available through the internet.

RECENT INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
Brad Sparks, a noted US researcher has provided us with a copy of his
“Comprehensive Catalog of 1,500 Blue Book Unknowns: Work in Progress”,
June 18, 2003 version. 24 photographic or film cases are included and
although only 2 reports were new to FOTOCAT, a number of interesting
details and references have been added to the actual documentation.

They were made aware of the article to ensure no
misunderstandings about inherent contents and how it
related to them.

Although my letter of appeal was dated 10 September, no
such newspaper feature has yet been published. Central to
the postponement have been my endeavours to guarantee
responsible reporting and that Zamora must absolutely not
be vilified therein. It wasn't Zamora who championed the
incident as a pivotal 'flying saucer' encounter.

All elements of the newspaper article are now in place
and it will be published within the next week or so.
Presently, I can't elucidate further.


The CIA's still classified hot-air balloon 'Albuquerque
flights' are arguably the main media interest. Should an
evident connection to Zamora's sighting be resultantly
disproven, then fine, especially if someone comes forward
to offer significant new evidence, etc.

Meantime, the following, which seems to have largely gone
unnoticed, might be of interest:

Several thoughts on the questions asked below:

- Upper stages often break into several pieces when they release their
satellites. Often the upper stage either splits in half to reveal the
satellite itself, or it jettisons a nose cone or a set of doors. Thus,
there often is a cluster of related parts in the same decaying orbit.

- Spy satellite technology at the time used film canisters which were
periodically jettisoned. Each one has retro rockets, a heat shield, and
parachutes.

- The hostage situation in Iran was at a critical point during the time
the Rendlesham sightings occurred. Reagan had just been elected
President, and nobody knew whether the terrorists would release the
hostages or kill them, once Carter was out of office (one of their
demands at the time).

What follows is a previously unpublished extract from the
transcript of a recording of Halt's lecture at the Quest
International Conference ('UFO Magazine' [UK]) conference
at Leeds, on 31 July, 1994.

Describing the night of his involvement and its
aftermath, he states:

Now this time frame started around 10:30, 11 o'clock at
night and went on until alter 4 o'clock in the morning.
The object was still in the sky at 4 o'clock in the
morning. We were exhausted, we had been up all day - I
had been up since 9 o'clock in the morning - through a
great deal of emotional stress.

Tired, hungry, we were wet ...[unclear]... we were still
upset about the whole thing that happened that evening.
So we went back up towards where the lightalls were. They
were still playing with the lightalls. I said, 'Pack it
in, and gather them up, let's take everything back to the
base.'.

We went back to the base. That was early Sunday morning.
I caught a few hours sleep, then went over to the office,
to do something, I don't remember why. I had the tape
with me, and I ran into my boss. I ran into Gordon
Williams, we shared a building. He was in the one half
and I was in the other half of the building, a small
building with a foyer in between, a big foyer. And, uh,
he knew something happened, he'd heard part of the
conversation - on the radio. And he said, 'Tell me what
happened.'.

So I told him, basically told him the story, and he heard
the tape. He said, 'May I borrow the tape?', so he
borrowed the tape. I didn't want to give it to him, I
didn't want to be ridiculed. He said, 'I want to take the
tape down to third Air Force, to play it General Bazley'.
General Bazley is the commander of US Air Force
activities in England ...[unclear]... Well, here's
trouble! When I come up for my next assignment, there
goes my potential promotion, and my security clearance is
probably gone. This is the end.
I really worried, until after he came back on Tuesday. He
came back on Tuesday. And I said, 'What happened?'. He
said, 'It was very interesting.' He said, 'I described
the events, as you told me and General Bazley raised his
eyebrows.'. Nobody said anything. He said, uh, 'I
explained about the tape and he said he wanted to hear
the tape.' I played the tape, He said, now based on what
was on it, looked around the room at his staff and said,
'Well, what do we do now?' You could have heard a pin
drop. Nobody said anything, nobody. Then Lieutenant
[unclear] said, 'Wow, this thing's bigger than the
[unclear] affair..'.."
[END]
From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Thu, 23 Oct 2003 00:31:22 +0100

Revisiting early case correspondence, when I had
contacted, via web sites for former base personnel, some
20-30 who had statedly served at RAF Bentwaters/RAF
Woodbridge during December 1980, the following,
previously unpublished, response might be of interest.

As 'nuclear weapons' are mentioned, I will not identify
the source. To be taken 'as read', etc.:

Dear James,

I did serve in the US Air Force during the time the
sightings occurred at RAF Woodbridge. I was a Staff
Sergeant assigned to the 81st Equipment Maintenance
Squadron Missile Shop, located in the weapons storage
area. So here goes my story, I'm not sure if you'll
believe this, but I assure you it's what I heard from
security personnel and a Air Force investigator.

A friend of mine, another Staff Sergeant was taking a
night class on base and a fellow classmate from the
security squadron told him about the incident outside RAF
Woodbridge. This was only 2 or 3 days after the sighting
took place. The next day, David told me what was said and
of course I didn't believe a word he said. We were close
friends and always pulling each others legs so I just
laughed it off, but he assured me it was true. Since
working in the bomb dump and knowing many of the security
guards there, I called a friend in the security squadron
and asked if he knew anything. I felt like a fool for
asking, but by this time I was very curious about all of
this. He transferred my call to his supervisor and he
asked who I was and what squadron I was assigned to.
Since I did work in the munitions storage area and made
the call sound official, he then again transferred me to
the.. as he put it, "UFO investigator".

I'm surprised he was so open about the investigation but
he told me a lot of information and here is what I
remember. There was a landing, as he put it, outside the
base in Rendlesham Forest. Lights were seen by the back
gate security guard one evening and a security alert team
"SAT" was dispatched to the back gate. American personnel
cannot leave the base with loaded weapons so the team
left their M16's and M60 with the gate guard (Later they
were reprimanded for leaving their weapons). After
driving into the forest for just a short distance, they
returned to the base and reported the sighting. At no
time did the control tower personnel see anything by
sight or radar. Knowing them they were asleep!!

I'm not sure when the assistant base commander got
involved but a landing site was found or what appeared to
be a landing sight. An area of a clearing was slightly
burnt, or should be said the ferns that are common in the
forest looked to be wilted by a heat source. Three
triangular marks were found that looked like landing
gear. They were 114 inches apart but I can't remember if
he told me the size of the imprints. Since we did have
nuclear bombs (I didn't say that) located on the base, we
did have Geiger counters. There was a slight reading of
radiation found but nothing that would be harmful.

Another note is that a few days prior to this a British
National was riding her horse somewhere north of the base
and was thrown when a red ball flew over her while
riding.

Soon after all of this, within days of hearing the
British Home Office was notified, the investigators were
gone and everyone involved denied any of the rumors. It
seemed to us not to be a alien craft but a British
experimental of some sort. Why else would the Brits shut
us up so quick?

That's all I know and can remember. Hope I was of some
help...
[END]


Follow-up questions and answers:

Q: I'm interested to hear that you spoke to the official
'UFO investigator'. Was this someone normally stationed
on base?

A: At the time of my phone conversation, I did not know
if the investigator was local or from off base. A few
days later when I inquired the talk was that "the team"
departed the base. I assumed that there was more than one
investigator and they were not assigned to the 81 TFW.

Q: Do you recall which unit/department he worked for?
A: This I have no idea about, all I know is that he was
working out of the base security squadron building.

Q: Were you aware what these investigations involved and
whether personnel were interviewed about the incidents?

A: Not sure on this one. What the investigator told me I
told you. I assume he had to do interviews to gain this
information.

Q: You note that, "At no time did the control tower
personnel see anything by sight or radar". What was your
source?

A: This information was not supplied by the investigator.
Second hand from my friend and his buddy in the security
squadron. It could be just rumor.

Q: You mention, "...a few days prior to this, a British
National was riding her horse somewhere north of the base
and was thrown when a red ball flew over her while
riding".

Can you recall how you learned about this?

A: I believe this was in a local paper but not 100% sure.
I did hear it from a local police constable (he was my
neighbor, the Halesworth Station) but he's living in
Perth, Australia, last I hear.

Q: Re a _British_ experimental craft... A 'top secret'
US aircraft was one conceivable explanation and there
have been rumours of 'stealth' technology.

A: It doesn't make any sense to me that it was an
American craft. Bentwaters or Woodbridge did not have any
buildings that an aircraft could come and go without
being seen. When the SR-71 used to land at Bentwaters,
the plane would do a quick taxi to the Victor alert area
and into a hanger. Since I had a top secret clearance, I
had access to all areas of the base that could hide an
aircraft and I was never turned away from entering any
aircraft shelters. The investigator seemed too open about
giving me information till the British were involved.

As soon as they got their fingers in the pie, everyone
shut up, it just seemed to me the British wanted to keep
this a secret.
[END]
Curious in retrospect: "Soon after all of this, within
days of hearing the British Home Office was notified, the
investigators were gone...".

Was it common knowledge on base that the "British Home
Office", alias [presumably] the Ministry of Defence, had
been notified?

Does this refer to Halt's memo, which wasn't sent until
13 January, 1981? Sounds like tales of the 'team'
departing predated this.

All anecdotal evidence, of course, however, I will ask
John Burroughs for his comments, especially about a
'reprimand' for leaving their weapons behind at east
gate!


James.

Robert McLean had previously also quoted from Warren's
letter home:

>From: "Robert Mclean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>

>"A big C-130 came in and took something in a crate away

This is a claim repeated by Halt, who stated that the
flight brought its own security team to guard the
aircraft.

It's arguably unlikely that Warren's published letter is
a later fabrication, as he should have come up with
something more dramatic than:

"At that same time, me and five other guys were walking
up a dark path about 2 miles from base . . . cause we
couldn't get a ride and we felt like we were being
watched and it was strange cause there were no street
lights - Then we saw a bright light go right over us
about 50 feet up and just fly over a field. It was
silent. We first thought it was an A-10 jet. But they
scream. So we ran away, because witchcraft and black
magic is a big thing in this part of Suffolk and we
thought that witches were in the woods. That light just
seemed to jump over the trees - Then the next day it
turned out that we were in the same place as the U.F.O.
so I think we saw it too. Now the three people who saw it
can't and won't speak about it at all. And supposedly no
animals have gone back into the woods yet - They did find
two landing sights - and supposedly some equipment left
behind".

This is not exactly a substantiation of his subsequent
tales!


In 'Left at East Gate' [p40], Warren describes the night
of 28 December:

"Alabama and I caught the last bus back to Bentwaters at
around 6:00 P.M.

[...]

To our surprise, the bus dropped us and three other
airmen off at the town of Woodbridge. This meant we faced
a four-mile walk back to Bentwaters and it was getting
late

[...]

We noticed a small car parked along the road , a man
maybe thirty years old was standing next to it. He said
he had just seen something strange fly overhead, so he
had pulled the car over to investigate. We saw nothing. I
told him it was most likely an A-10; the man shrugged it
off and drove away.
[END]

This looks like a recollection in later years, compounded
to who knows what extent by intermediate 'hypnotic
regression', of the story in his letter.

As the letter was allegedly written on 6 January, 1981,
it could be that Warren is telling his mother about an
incident which did occur after he returned from Germany
and Warren mistakenly attributes it as being associated
with the 'UFO' sighting he had heard about - i.e.,
Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston's incident at circa
0300 on 26 December.

If so, then Warren's letter reveals the true extent of
his involvement in overall events.
For what it's worth, 'Left at East Gate' evidently
provides proof positive that Warren could not have played
any role during the night of Halt's adventures.

To recap, he writes:

"The day before Christmas, I left for Germany with my
friend Mark. We had met two German girls in London the
previous week at Le Beat Route, a club on Greek Street.

[...].

I think the girls lost interest in Mark and me on the
second night.

[...]

On or about 27 December, we flew back to RAF Mildenhall
to begin our shift the next night".
[END]


Warren then elaborates how on the night of 28 December,
he purportedly became enmeshed in events.

A manifest problem is, of course, that although Halt's
publicised memo reported the date of his personal
participation as the night/early morning of 28/29
December, we know Halt was in error - it was 27/28
December.

After returning from Germany, Warren statedly was not on
duty again until the following night, 28th December, and
if so, that takes him completely out of the picture.


James.

James:

This could be opening a can of worms, but is sounds very much to me
like this person was himself the butt of a practical joke.

His narrative sounds very familiar to a similar prank known as
the "The Keys to the Wing Commander's Aircraft."

In this prank a troop is sent to pick up the "keys" the the Wing
Commander's aircraft (jets don't have keys), which are then lifted
from him. He is then convinced he lost them, and finally is put on
the telephone with an "investigator", who proceeds to tie the subject
of the joke in knots.

This guy's narrative really sounds like he was getting the business.
If anyone seriously thought there were something to investigate, no
one would talk about it as related in this narrative.

You may have been it. I found the term "UFO Officer" in UFO books, so
maybe it wasn't an officer, but just whoever they designated to get
the calls. (Also, some of the UFO book authors seemed to be quite
ignorant on which ranks were officers.) Or maybe they confused UFO
with PIO.

Some UFO book authors seem to be real airheads, making the following
mistakes:

1. Getting the wind direction reported by the weather bureau wrong. The
weather bureau always reports the wind direction as the direction the
wind blows FROM. So in one account, An object moving east "could not
have been a balloon, because the weather bureau reported a west
wind. The UFO was heading directly into the wind." No it wasn't.

2. The witness was interviewed by "high brass from Washington". It was
a colonel and a captain from Wright-Patterson, in Dayton OH.

3. Calling the local airport "confirmed that no planes were in the air."
No, it just confirmed that no planes the local airport knew about were
in the air. Military flights and private flights without flight plans
were not included.

4. Process of elimination. "The airport said no planes were in the air.
It was going the wrong direction for a balloon. It wasn't a star or a
planet because it moved. Therefore, it had to be a flying saucer." But
there are hundreds of possibilities the guy didn't check, and many more
that nobody even thought of.

5. Reporting witness estimates of size, speed, height, or distance as
ironclad truth. In fact, if the object is seen against the sky, is
unidentified, and is more than 30 feet away, NOBODY has the visual
power to determine any of these values without additional information.

Note: If the object is identified (such as an airplane), the witness
knows the true size, and by rough visual trigonometry, he can figure out
the other values.

6. Because they were engaged in covert activities, UFO book authors
assumed that "men in black" were either government spies or were
working for the aliens. We now know that many of them were working for
tabloid newspapers.

Robert:

That would not surprise me. Law Enforcement routinely went off base
for short periods while still armed. We drove between the bases
armed all the time. The only time we took off the gun belt was when
we were driving into town to pick up a GI that had been arrested by
the English police.

LE was a little different; we carried revolvers, which is a story in
itself. That we were armed was not as noticeable as the security
troops, who carried M-16's, often with attached grenade launchers (M-
203's).

We were much more sensitive to security going off base armed, because
M-16's & grenade launchers are much more "militant" weapons.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Tue, 28 Oct 2003 11:23:41 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Passaic 1952
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)
X-Spam-Processed: italianmoda.com, Tue, 28 Oct 2003 23:42:01 +0100

If by "three ball case" you refer to the chicken brooders photographed
by Adamski, Fry, Sheets, O'Bannon, Villa, and others, the Passaic case
is NOT a "three ball" case.

I have the entire set of photos, and some show a bottom view. No balls
are visible on the bottom.

I believe the Passaic case to be a genuine saucer - upside down china,
with a broken cup glued to the top of it. In one photo, you can see
where the handle broke off of the cup.

All of the "three ball" cases are photographs of the same thing: chicken
brooders. My great-grandfather raised chickens on his farm, and he had
one. It's a heat lamp used to keep baby chicks warm when they are not
with the mother. They were made in the 1930s through the 1950s.

The "saucer shape" is the reflector portion of the lamp. The dome on
top is the housing for the special heatproof wiring (usually asbestos
covered). The "portholes" are vents to cool the housing. The three balls
are the dull bulbs which produce the heat. The loop on top is for
hanging the chicken brooder from a chain, since hanging it by the
asbestos covered cord soon frayed the cord and caused a short.

I have a 75 watt dull bulb. It screws into a standard lamp socket, but
gets hot instead of producing light. It glows a very dim red in a
darkened room, but produces a surprising amount of heat. The bulb
itself is an opaque white ceramic. You definitely do NOT want to touch
the bulb when it is on (or for 10 minutes after it has been shut off).
You can easily burn your hand. You must also make sure the bulb doesn't
touch anything flammable.

Modern chicken brooders use R-type infrared bulbs, and are used in
housings similar to photographer's clamp-on parabolic reflector lamps.
Dull bulbs are still sold for both the original brooders and the
reflector housings.

Jim, Jackie, List:

As Tim Printy has pointed out, the photographs did, indeed,
miss the maneuvers. So did nearly all other observers,
incluiding all published 1965 accounts. The guy who claimed
the thing did "figure eights" is also one of the handfull who
claim to have seen the UFO in the woods, armed troops, etc.
In 1992 he admitted to several other men that he told the story
just to get on TV.

A maneuvering UFO (or at least a turn) was first postulated
by UFO writer Ivan Sanderson in an article submitted to the
North American Newspaper Alliance two days after the
incident, and published in many newspapers.

Sanderson believed, erroneously, that the object maneuvered,
and therefore could not be a meteor. He seems to have
spoken to no eyewitnesses, relying on wire service stories
and phone calls to state police spokesmen. His hand-
sketched map was inaccurate and his speeds were grossly in
error, referring to miles/hour when his calculations clearly
referred to miles/minute, thus slowing the speed by 60 times!
Sanderson assumed that the locations of the witnesses of
unverified debris from the object, which was visible for hundreds
of miles, "pinpointed" its path. Witness directions when
observing the fireball were apparently not taken into account,
nor has any test or report ever linked any "debris" to the fireball.

  Sanderson's claims were apparently never checked but just
repeated by Mr. Gordon and others. I drew a line on a real map
("Lake Erie", International Map of the World. Reston Va.:
U.S.G.S., 1974) and compared this to the crude hand-sketches
Sanderson and Stan Gordon used in saucer magazines and on
"Unsolved Mysteries". It shows that a path from Lapeer,
Michigan, to Elyria, Ohio, would be at an azimuth of
52 degrees, and from Elyria to Kecksburg, would be at an
azimuth of 120 degrees, a difference of 32 degrees, not 25 as
Sanderson had claimed. If an object used Sanderson's path
and speed, assuming its reported times in Michigan were
correct, it would have passed no closer than 26 miles to the
south of Kecksburg more than 27 hours later.

Only after I pointed out this slight discrepancy to Gordon more
than 10 years ago did this later maneuvering claim make its
appearance, and only by a couple of the people who claimed
to have seen it all: the maneauver, the armed troops, the actual
recovery and the THING itself.

I prefer the pictures.

Clear skies,
Bob Young

Bob,

For information, during May 1998, I submitted the
following FOIA request to NASA:

....Any records pertaining to a series of incidents which
occurred on 9 December, 1965, in the area of Lake Erie
and other locations to the north and which came to be
known as the 'Kecksburg' case.

This was concerned with the alleged retrieval of an
object which came to earth near Mount Pleasant,
Southwestern Pennsylvania.

For your further information; on 23 November, 1965, a
rocket was launched from a remote area deep inside the
former Soviet Union. The payload was COSMOS 96, a
satellite reportedly based on a modified Soyuz
spacecraft.

Colonel Rodney S. Lusey, Deputy Chief of Staff, US Space
Command, confirmed, "A booster failure caused this
satellite to decay after its launch. ...COSMOS 96 was
launched on 23 November 1965 and decayed on December 9,
1965, at 51.8 north latitude and 85.2 west longitude".

Specifically, I request any documents relating to NASA's
knowledge of, or participation in, recovery of the fallen
COSMOS 96 satellite.
[END]


In relation to 'Rendlesham', I separately requested any
information concerning the Cosmos 749 upper-stage rocket
re-entry.

Patricia M. Riep-Dice, the then FOIA Officer, replied:

All of the information located in the NASA Headquarters
Library and NASA History Office archives on Cosmos 96 and
Cosmos 749 is enclosed. No information was located
linking NASA to the recovery of the remains of either
satellite.
[END]


Said "information located" consisted of two pages from
'NASA News', mentioning Cosmos 749 within its 'Weekly
Satellite Situation Report' and zilch about Cosmos 96.


NASA's 'NSSDC Master Catalog' highlights a conceivable
link between Cosmos 96 and 'The Great Lakes Fireball and
Kecksburg Incident', see:

http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/database/MasterCatalog?sc=1965
-094A

That background revealed; around the same time, I had
written to Dr. David R. Williams, still referenced as
NASA's inherent database contact.

Dr. Williams was statedly unaware of any possible
connection until I queried it and replied he would
accordingly update NASA's entry.


Accepting why our 'UFO' was evidently a meteor, I've
never quite reconciled the following extract, which my
related files record being published as: -

'The Kecksburg UFO Mystery', by Mark Ian Birdsall
UFO Magazine (UK), September/October 1994:

In the late afternoon of 9 December, 1965, many people
witnessed a large, orange coloured light in the sky above
Lake Erie and several other locations to the north.
Small lights were seen breaking away from the larger
object and smoke reported as far away as the bordering
New York State.

The emergency services had been contacted with reports of
an aircraft which was possibly in trouble and a Mrs
Jones, from Mount Pleasant, reported that an object had
crashed into woods near her home.

At around 7:30 p.m. the area was secured by State Police.
Soon the military took command and the local Kecksburg
Fire Department HQ became a temporary base. Military
vehicles, including a flatbed truck and a crane, were
seen heading towards the woods and there was talk that a
high-level team of military and scientific personnel had
arrived on the scene.

Later that night, a large truck was seem leaving the area
at high speed. It carried flashing lights to signal its
importance, but that wasn't all it carried... A large
tarpaulin concealed an unknown cargo.

The military eventually labelled the object a meteor, as
did the Associated Press account published in 'The
Bulletin' the following day.

In 1990, Stan Gordon from the Pennsylvania Association
for the Study of the Unexplained, traced an apparent
first-hand witness. James Romansky recalled seeing the
object on the ground some 25 years previously, when he
was an 18 year old fire-fighter, called on duty following
concerns that an aeroplane had crashed.

He described the object as bronze coloured and shaped
like an acorn.

Some 12 feet long and 25 feet in diameter, it had
slightly raised "blunt" end and strange markings.

"It had writing on it, not like your average writing, but
more like ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics. It had sort of
a bumper on it, like a ribbon about six to 10 inches
wide, and it stood out.

It was elliptical the whole way around and the writing
was on this bumper".

"It's nothing like I've ever seen, and I'm an avid
reader. I read a lot of books on Egypt, the Incas,
Peruvians, Russians and I've never to this day come
across anything that looked like that."
[END]


The 'UFO Magazine' article featured a purported
photograph of our Cosmos 96 satellite, as duly attached.

Yet, despite this being an evident match for Romansky's
"bronze coloured and shaped like an acorn" object, which
had "had writing on it, not like your average writing,
but more like ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics. It had sort
of a bumper on it, like a ribbon about six to 10 inches
wide, and it stood out"... etc., - ultimately an
extraordinary coincidence?


James.

To reiterate, in a 1997 interview with Salley Rayl, Halt

RAYL: Warren also claims that there were on this third

HALT: The Wing Commander at that time was not present. He

I sent a long letter to UFO Magazine in 1994, which I have
included below, which I think summarizes my views. I never
heard from them, nor did they publish anything about the
meteors pictures and decades old research. UFO Magazine
thus because part of the real Kecksbur saucer crash coverup.

"Mr. Graham William Birdsall, Editor          November 1, 1994
UFO Magazine

Dear Mr. Birdsall:
  In Mark Ian Birdsall's article "The Kecksburg UFO Mystery"
(Vol. 13, No. 3, Sept.-Oct. 1994) he says that the biggest
mystery of all is why it took nearly 30 years to conclude this
crashed UFO case.

  The short answer is that it didn't! The meteoric nature of
the December 9, 1965, afternoon fireball was established in
1967 when astronomers Von Del Chamberlain and David J.
Krause published results of their triangulation of two
independent sets of photographs and a recording from the
University of Michigan's seismic station at Ypsilanti. (The
Fireball of December 9, 1965 - Part I, Royal Astronomical
Society of Canada Journal, Vol. 61, No. 4.)

   The seismometer registered the fireball's widely seen
terminal airburst 50 kilometers from Detroit, not a Kecksburg
impact as claimed in the article. An impacting body would have
had to be truly massive to be detected 435 kilometers away!
The photos showed that the fireball was falling steeply
northeastward over extreme Southwest Ontario and was not
moving toward Pennsylvania.

   Although the velocity of the object in the atmosphere is
uncertain, a value of 14.5 km/sec was adopted from the
photographers' estimates, giving an orbit out to between Mars
and Jupiter. This is consistent with an object originating in the
asteroid belt, source of many meteoroids. The fireball was
falling much too steeply to the Earth's surface to be reentering
space debris, something that has been known since 1966, so
Cosmos 96 is out.

   Curiously, leading Kecksburg crash proponents have
known of this work for years but have remained silent about it.
On March 7, 1990, the producers of the NBC "Unsolved
Mysteries" segment mentioned in your article were sent a copy
of the Chamberlain and Krause paper as well as a letter
positively identifying the fireball as a classic meteorite fall after
a telephone interview with one of the paper's authors. This was
unmentioned on the show six months later, which instead had
Stan Gordon sketching a path on a map (like that which
illustrated your article) while reciting an unproven 1965 notion
by the late Ivan Sanderson that the fireball had maneuvered.

   A carbon copy of Sanderson's original manuscript and
correspondence, dated only three days after the event, is in the
files of the National Investigations Committee on Aerial
Phenomena (NICAP), now maintained by the Center for UFO
Studies in Chicago. He seems to have spoken to no
eyewitnesses, but used only wire service reports and calls to
State police spokesmen. One of many mistakes was that he
assumed that if the fireball was seen at a location it must have
been there. The directions the witnesses were facing were
never considered (the object was visible for 550 kilometers
around), and he ignored reports from locations which didn't fit
his maneuvering theory.

   Anyone who checks Sanderson's claims on a real map, as
I have, would see that the object would have had to turn
32 degrees, not 25 degrees, and therefore could have come no
closer than 42 kilometers to the south of Kecksburg! Also,
Sanderson's calculations were off by a factor of 60, referring to
miles per hour when he clearly meant miles per minute. The
speed you cited came from Sanderson's selective use of
widely varying witness times of the sort common for events of
this kind. The most accurate time was from the seismic
record and the many reports from pilots, which place the event
at about 4:43 P.M., plus or minus ten seconds. Key
Kecksburg witness "Mrs. Jones", whom you quoted, gave it as
"4:45", but this has been ignored by crash proponents who
badly need Sanderson's slow speed.

  The long answer is fourfold: 1) Too many writers have not
done their own homework, but have simply repeated what they
have been told by others. For example, Birdsall seemed to
give great credence to the account of a brick-yard lorry driver
who says that he was told the whole Top Secret story,
including about the dead bodies of the crew.

Are you suggesting that Cosmos 96 was a heretofore
unknown 2 X 3.5 metre Soviet two-man mission to Venus?
One can't have it both ways.

   Other parts of this Wright-Patterson Air Force Base tale,
such as the difficulty of entering the craft despite the use of
torches and a diamond-tipped drill, seem to have been lifted
from the grand-daddy of American crashed saucer hoaxes,
the tale in the 1950 best-seller Behind the Flying Saucers
by Frank Scully. This should be required reading for all
"crashed saucer" investigators, but isn't.

   The Lockbourne Air Force Base connection, also
stimulated by someone who called the 1990 NBC TV show's
telephone hotline, bears 15 curious similarities to an oft-
eprinted 1954 hoax from the same city which proved to be
untrue or unsubstantiated. I have found 19 close parallels
between the 1954 crash tale and Behind the Flying Saucers,
including elements which seem to have been lifted verbatim,
confirming 1954 speculation by James W. Moseley who first
investigated this story. ("The Wright Field Story, or Who's
Lying?", Nexus, Sept 1954). Only credulous crash
enthusiasts are still fooled.

  2) Much confusion has been caused by the coincidental
Cosmos 96 reentry on the same day as the Ontario fireball but
more than 12 hours earlier.

   3) The most recent witness descriptions resemble the bell-
haped Cosmos 96 capsule because since the mid 1980's UFO
investigators have been circulating pictures of the spacecraft.
 Early Kecksburg accounts, including James Romansky's,
described an object which was much longer and rocket-like.
 Romansky, by the way, is of Polish extraction and claims that
he knows the Cyrillic alphabet and that what he saw on the
UFO was not Russian writing. Why does Bridsall accept some
of Romansky's claims but not others? (I opt for a folklore origin
of these "hieroglyphics" - Scully's con artist "Dr. Gee" also
described hieroglyphics on his saucer 45 years ago). The
witness "evidence" has been hopelessly contaminated by
enthusiasts.

  4) The last culprits in this story are the new witnesses
coming excitedly out of the Kecksburg woods each time the
case is publicized. Their increasingly more elaborate, bizarre
and divergent accounts fit a classic folklore model for this story.

 The Kecksburg folktale is a dusty, old, solved mystery.
Let's not dress it up in new clothes for the 1990's."

Clear skies,
Bob Young
