I sent a long letter to UFO Magazine in 1994, which I have
included below, which I think summarizes my views. I never
heard from them, nor did they publish anything about the
meteors pictures and decades old research. UFO Magazine
thus because part of the real Kecksbur saucer crash coverup.

"Mr. Graham William Birdsall, Editor          November 1, 1994
UFO Magazine

Dear Mr. Birdsall:
  In Mark Ian Birdsall's article "The Kecksburg UFO Mystery"
(Vol. 13, No. 3, Sept.-Oct. 1994) he says that the biggest
mystery of all is why it took nearly 30 years to conclude this
crashed UFO case.

  The short answer is that it didn't! The meteoric nature of
the December 9, 1965, afternoon fireball was established in
1967 when astronomers Von Del Chamberlain and David J.
Krause published results of their triangulation of two
independent sets of photographs and a recording from the
University of Michigan's seismic station at Ypsilanti. (The
Fireball of December 9, 1965 - Part I, Royal Astronomical
Society of Canada Journal, Vol. 61, No. 4.)

   The seismometer registered the fireball's widely seen
terminal airburst 50 kilometers from Detroit, not a Kecksburg
impact as claimed in the article. An impacting body would have
had to be truly massive to be detected 435 kilometers away!
The photos showed that the fireball was falling steeply
northeastward over extreme Southwest Ontario and was not
moving toward Pennsylvania.

   Although the velocity of the object in the atmosphere is
uncertain, a value of 14.5 km/sec was adopted from the
photographers' estimates, giving an orbit out to between Mars
and Jupiter. This is consistent with an object originating in the
asteroid belt, source of many meteoroids. The fireball was
falling much too steeply to the Earth's surface to be reentering
space debris, something that has been known since 1966, so
Cosmos 96 is out.

   Curiously, leading Kecksburg crash proponents have
known of this work for years but have remained silent about it.
On March 7, 1990, the producers of the NBC "Unsolved
Mysteries" segment mentioned in your article were sent a copy
of the Chamberlain and Krause paper as well as a letter
positively identifying the fireball as a classic meteorite fall after
a telephone interview with one of the paper's authors. This was
unmentioned on the show six months later, which instead had
Stan Gordon sketching a path on a map (like that which
illustrated your article) while reciting an unproven 1965 notion
by the late Ivan Sanderson that the fireball had maneuvered.

   A carbon copy of Sanderson's original manuscript and
correspondence, dated only three days after the event, is in the
files of the National Investigations Committee on Aerial
Phenomena (NICAP), now maintained by the Center for UFO
Studies in Chicago. He seems to have spoken to no
eyewitnesses, but used only wire service reports and calls to
State police spokesmen. One of many mistakes was that he
assumed that if the fireball was seen at a location it must have
been there. The directions the witnesses were facing were
never considered (the object was visible for 550 kilometers
around), and he ignored reports from locations which didn't fit
his maneuvering theory.

   Anyone who checks Sanderson's claims on a real map, as
I have, would see that the object would have had to turn
32 degrees, not 25 degrees, and therefore could have come no
closer than 42 kilometers to the south of Kecksburg! Also,
Sanderson's calculations were off by a factor of 60, referring to
miles per hour when he clearly meant miles per minute. The
speed you cited came from Sanderson's selective use of
widely varying witness times of the sort common for events of
this kind. The most accurate time was from the seismic
record and the many reports from pilots, which place the event
at about 4:43 P.M., plus or minus ten seconds. Key
Kecksburg witness "Mrs. Jones", whom you quoted, gave it as
"4:45", but this has been ignored by crash proponents who
badly need Sanderson's slow speed.

  The long answer is fourfold: 1) Too many writers have not
done their own homework, but have simply repeated what they
have been told by others. For example, Birdsall seemed to
give great credence to the account of a brick-yard lorry driver
who says that he was told the whole Top Secret story,
including about the dead bodies of the crew.

Are you suggesting that Cosmos 96 was a heretofore
unknown 2 X 3.5 metre Soviet two-man mission to Venus?
One can't have it both ways.

   Other parts of this Wright-Patterson Air Force Base tale,
such as the difficulty of entering the craft despite the use of
torches and a diamond-tipped drill, seem to have been lifted
from the grand-daddy of American crashed saucer hoaxes,
the tale in the 1950 best-seller Behind the Flying Saucers
by Frank Scully. This should be required reading for all
"crashed saucer" investigators, but isn't.

   The Lockbourne Air Force Base connection, also
stimulated by someone who called the 1990 NBC TV show's
telephone hotline, bears 15 curious similarities to an oft-
eprinted 1954 hoax from the same city which proved to be
untrue or unsubstantiated. I have found 19 close parallels
between the 1954 crash tale and Behind the Flying Saucers,
including elements which seem to have been lifted verbatim,
confirming 1954 speculation by James W. Moseley who first
investigated this story. ("The Wright Field Story, or Who's
Lying?", Nexus, Sept 1954). Only credulous crash
enthusiasts are still fooled.

  2) Much confusion has been caused by the coincidental
Cosmos 96 reentry on the same day as the Ontario fireball but
more than 12 hours earlier.

   3) The most recent witness descriptions resemble the bell-
haped Cosmos 96 capsule because since the mid 1980's UFO
investigators have been circulating pictures of the spacecraft.
 Early Kecksburg accounts, including James Romansky's,
described an object which was much longer and rocket-like.
 Romansky, by the way, is of Polish extraction and claims that
he knows the Cyrillic alphabet and that what he saw on the
UFO was not Russian writing. Why does Bridsall accept some
of Romansky's claims but not others? (I opt for a folklore origin
of these "hieroglyphics" - Scully's con artist "Dr. Gee" also
described hieroglyphics on his saucer 45 years ago). The
witness "evidence" has been hopelessly contaminated by
enthusiasts.

  4) The last culprits in this story are the new witnesses
coming excitedly out of the Kecksburg woods each time the
case is publicized. Their increasingly more elaborate, bizarre
and divergent accounts fit a classic folklore model for this story.

 The Kecksburg folktale is a dusty, old, solved mystery.
Let's not dress it up in new clothes for the 1990's."

Clear skies,
Bob Young

On Thursday 06 November 2003 22:07, Martin Shough wrote:
| Larry Robinson wrote:
|

| This is true but a fact too often misconstrued in my opinion. Modern SSR

| say, might define a research area from someone else's point of view. Ad
| absurdum, one cannot expect 'flying saucers' to carry transponders! But I

| 'rejected' signal characteristics being of alien origin is not powerful.
| Regards
| Martin Shough

Not sure I follow the 'ad absurdum' part of that. But just to add: the
filtered radar responses aren't just 'noise' - they are also folks like me,
pootling about in our little planes squawking VFR (1200 in US, 7000 most
other places). We clutter up the radar screens so much (especially if we're
*not* squawking Mode C, which means we're not returning any height info) that
some radar operators filter out VFR returns.

Of course, transponders are *required* only in certain classes of airspace. In
many countries (US & Europe) there is no obligation to switch on the
transponder - assuming you even have one - in the Open FIR (or classes E-G).
So that makes for another source of 'noise'.

Steve

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 6 Nov 2003 11:47:34 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)
X-Spam-Processed: italianmoda.com, Thu, 06 Nov 2003 17:59:21 +0100

There isn't any. After 56 years of reports, there is not one piece of
scientifically verifiable evidence that there are intelligent beings
elsewhere in the universe.

What we don't have:

- We don't have any chemical, physical, biological, or recorded
evidence that stands up to scientific scrutiny. Most of it is
either identified as something ordinary, or can't be distinguished
from ordinary items.


What we have:

- Eyewitness reports (most of which have been identified as mundane
objects or events seen under usual circumstances)

Note: The inability of the human visual system to determine size,
distance, speed, or altitude of an unknown object in the air which
is farther away than 30 feet has a lot to do with this.

Note: In my files are at least three cases where police chased the
planet Venus for miles, and one case where they chased Jupiter. In
each of these cases, they tore after the planet with their cars on
several successive nights. Astronomers in the investigating teams
identified the planet involved in each case. The effect described
above contributed to their inability to recognize the planet.

- We especially have a lot of vague reports which are
scientifically useless.

- RADAR trackings of UFOs (most of which have mundane explanations,
when the numerous ways false targets can appear on RADAR are
considered)

Note: Now that transponders are required on most aircraft, the number
of RADAR UFO sightings is very low. This is simply because most of
the false targets were identified as secondary reflections of other
aircraft on the screen. The computer now routinely eliminates these
from the display. Right now, targets without transponders are also not
displayed on most computerized ATC systems, unless the controller
requests them.

- We have advertizing planes with traveling light message boards
hung under the wings. They look like rotating disks with lights on the
rim when seen edge-on.

- We have a lot of hoaxes (false UFO stories) and pranks (fake UFOs
placed for others to see). The motives for doing these things included
childhood pranks, testing public credibility, alibis, excuses for not
performing a job, April Fool jokes, winning tabloid prizes for UFO
reports, explaining discharge of a company handgun, Halloween pranks,
UFO research on what people report, and many others.

NOTE: There are a LOT of cases that turn out to be fire balloons.
These are hot air balloons made of dry-cleaner suit bags, drinking
straws, and candles. Every so often, one of those "home science"
magazines prints a way to make a fire balloon as a cheap weather
balloon for experiments, and there is always a rash of fire balloon
sightings after the article appears. Since fire balloons are known to
have caused at least two structure fires and several fires in farm
fields or brush, I wish those magazines would stop publishing those
articles.

NOTE: Even the police can be fooled by fire balloons. In 1993, a
police helicopter over Louisville KY reported that the UFO it was
sent to investigate was bigger than the helicopter, and that it made
"ramming attacks" on them. But people on the ground reported that
the UFO was much smaller than the helicopter, and that the police
helicopter kept going past it, as if the crew couldn't find it.
The UFO was a fire balloon, and the visual system error mentioned
above caused the crew to misjudge the size of the object, and thus
the distance and speed.

- Physical traces (All of which have nothing extraordinary about them -
anything could have made them. They include the fires mentioned in the
previous item.)

- Found objects:

-- A piece of silicon found at Roswell NM which was said to have a
strange isotope ratios was traced to a miscalibrated mass spectrometer.
-- A strange piece of metal, also found at Roswell, was claimed by a
jewelry maker to be some of his scrap.
-- The Ubatuba magnesium. This was touted as being ultra-pure, but when
analyzed, was found to contain more impurities than most common samples
of objects made of magnesium.

Note: Some of the items analyzed "to see if they were from outer space"
included an aluminum mop handle, bear urine in sand, gunpowder residue
in sand, cow manure, buckwheat pancakes, RADAR chaff, RADAR calibration
drop spheres, slime mold, detergent foam, spider webs, and a copper
shell full of earthly radio parts.
- We have cattle mutilations. Most of them were caused by a group of
satanists with a helicopter performing rituals on stolen animals.
(Whether these people are from "outer space" or not remains to be seen.)

- We have "implants" recovered from people. Most of them appear to be
mundane objects that were introduced to the individual's body through
accidents (Among them being B-Bs, pencil lead, and metal fragments).

- We have a lot of wild stories, all of which conveniently can not be
verified. But we also have a lot of tabloids paying big money for these
wild stories.

- Hypnosis does not always recover memories. It often edits them in a
way that the subject feels will please the hypnotist.

- Finally there are a lot of strange objects or events which people
simply do not know about, including the following which have been
reported as UFO events:

-- A large inflatable car got away from a car dealer and flew upside
down over the city.
-- A farmer was burning the chaff off of his fields, and tended the
fire on a motor scooter.
-- A motorcycle rider rode around and around while waiting for his
date. leaving a worn circle on the ground.
-- A teenager used Round-Up to make a "target for planes" in his
girlfriend's back yard (I investigated this one).
-- A fire in a junkyard caused an explosion that hurled a water heater
into the air.
-- A 6-foot length of 4-inch sewer pipe made into a rocket by "rocket
scientists" buried itself in the back yard of a real-estate agent.
-- A new employee put the wrong detergent in a restaurant dishwasher.

idea of using the stove's exhaust fan to get rid of the foam. Big
blobs of it were blown over the city by a brisk wind.

-- Edmund Scientific made a model hot air balloon in the shape of a
flying saucer. It had the letters "U" "F" "O" on the side.
-- A building fell down, creating a huge dust cloud and illuminating
it with sparks from the electrical lines it also knocked down (I saw
this one myself).
-- A large oil-filled transformer supplying a shopping center shorted
internally and blew up, sending a huge orange ball of fire into the
sky (I saw this one too).

- LAST, but not least, we have a lot of BAD SCIENCE going on. This is
where people do not follow scientific methods, make unwarranted
conclusions, or even doctor their data to obtain the conclusions wanted

On Friday 07 November 2003 18:41, Robinson, Larry wrote:
| That's not what happens. They don't just reject on a noise threshold.
| In fact, modern RADAR systems usually operate at much lower power now.
| The lower power emissions are not powerful enough to produce skin
| reflections. Instead, they now rely entirely on the power of the plane's
| transponder to produce the RADAR return itself.
|
| Air Traffic Control RADAR now ignores all returns that do not have
| transponder signatures. They also know how to reject second trip echoes
| and multiple reflections of planes with transponders (because the false
| echo must always be received after the real one, and because the return
| doesn't match the GPS coordinates the transponder sent).
|
| If the controller wants to see objects without transponders, he must
| turn that function on. This increases the power of the transmitter so
| skin reflections are produced, and enables the receiver to display
| them. Many ATC installations no longer have this capability, though
| all military RADARs and cockpit anticollision RADARs must have it.
|
| If an aircraft without a transponder gets into the airways, it is
| usually
| first detected on an anticollision radar. Then the pilot tells the ATC
| controller about it, and the controller switches on the skin reflection
| function (if he has it).

I think you're getting a little confused there Larry. It may be possible that
some radar systems - for example, those used by en-route controllers - do
something similar to what you suggest. But the fact is that most radar are
perfectly capable of detecting non-transponder-equipped aircraft. The reason
for this is that there are still lots of (predominantly) light aircraft
without transponders. And that's why, when I'm flying and receiving a radar
information or advisory service, I'll so often get the message from ATC to
the effect of "unknown traffic at two o'clock".

Oh, and transponders do not return GPS co-ordinates. Standard transponders
(Mode A) simply return (via a radio signal) a four-digit code where each
digit is in the range 0-7. Mode C transponders also return the aircraft
altitude (taken from a suitably approved altimeter and therefore accurate to
within +/- 50ft). The new Mode S transponders (which are still quite rare,
especially in general aviation) have a datalink capability. The transponder
is programmed with information - eg, aircraft type, registration etc - which
ATC can receive. ATC can also upload data to the aircraft, and in the future
this might include weather & airport info etc. There are moves to make Mode S
obligatory in Class A airspace, but general aviation has shown great
resistence to it because of the cost of installation. Nevertheless, there are
now more than 120 Mode S radar installations in the US (each with a range of
about 50 miles) and this will double soon. But it's mostly the big iron that
is adopting it.

Mode S is most useful for Traffic Collision Avoidance Systems (TCAS), and this
is another area where I think you've got a little confused. TCAS is *not* an
'anticollision radar' as such. The way it works is that the TCAS unit
installed in each aircraft (and again, we're talking about airliners here,
not Piper Cubs) keeps a watch for the transponder returns sent out by other
aircraft (a transponder sends out its signal each time it is 'painted' by
radar). Certain systems (so-called 'active' systems) have the ability to
interrogate the transponders of other aircraft. But this is all done by
transponder radio signals - the only radar involved is the ground-based radar
that causes the transponders to send their signals.


+a
Steve

Chad;

I am a little critical of the question. What would constitute
"scientifically verifiable evidence" that we are not alone in the universe?
There is nothing by way of existing technology or chemistry that we have for
testable, comparative analysis..

If a flying saucer lands at the most famous "White House Lawn" and a gray
colored, child-sized, big eyed occupant comes out and professes to be from
the Zackonian Star Cluster, how do we know he is not lying? How can science
demonstrate that this hypothetical creature is from outer space and not from
some secretive underground laboratory, a foreign country or, for that
matter, a time traveler from the future?

And also, for further discussion, does your question take into consideration
that an advanced ET culture might wish to and be capable of subverting or
manipulating our present method of observation and testing for concealment
purposes?

I wish I could recall the specifics of a 1973 (or early 70s) paper that
dealt with S.E.T.I. and similar issues involving the criteria for
determining evidence for ET visitation and how the data cannot be truly
satisfied due to the unknowable circumstances, and that the quest for some
'uncommon material or chemistry' may be a bogus presumption. If anyone has
any idea of this article or paper, I would appreciate the input.

Thanks and take care,
Kenny Young
Florence, KY

@ Larry Robinson wrote:
@
@ > "Now that transponders are required on most aircraft, the number

not
@ > displayed on most computerized ATC systems, unless the controller

@
@ This is true but a fact too often misconstrued in my opinion. Modern
@ SSR radars are certainly designed to eliminate noise, but one has to
@ remember that signal criteria chosen as defining noise for air traffic
@ purposes, say, might define a research area from someone else's point
@ of view. Ad absurdum, one cannot expect 'flying saucers' to carry
@ transponders! But I don't disagree with your general remarks, that the
@ evidence for such 'rejected' signal characteristics being of alien
@ origin is not powerful.
@ Regards
@ Martin Shough

That's not what happens. They don't just reject on a noise threshold.
In fact, modern RADAR systems usually operate at much lower power now.
The lower power emissions are not powerful enough to produce skin
reflections. Instead, they now rely entirely on the power of the plane's
transponder to produce the RADAR return itself.

Air Traffic Control RADAR now ignores all returns that do not have
transponder signatures. They also know how to reject second trip echoes
and multiple reflections of planes with transponders (because the false
echo must always be received after the real one, and because the return
doesn't match the GPS coordinates the transponder sent).

If the controller wants to see objects without transponders, he must
turn that function on. This increases the power of the transmitter so
skin reflections are produced, and enables the receiver to display
them. Many ATC installations no longer have this capability, though
all military RADARs and cockpit anticollision RADARs must have it.

If an aircraft without a transponder gets into the airways, it is
usually
first detected on an anticollision radar. Then the pilot tells the ATC
controller about it, and the controller switches on the skin reflection
function (if he has it).

When transponders first came into use, the "UFOs" displayed transponder
codes too. It was obvious that they were secondary reflections or second
trip echoes, because they displayed the same transponder codes that some
of the real planes displayed. It also became a simple test to ask the
pilot to switch off the transponder. When he did, the "UFO" shut up too.
That showed that the "UFO" was a secondary reflection of the beam that
hit the plane.

I remember a few of the possible criteria from that SETI paper:

1. An information-laden radio signal from outer space: This one
would be hard to fake, because a local signal would not show up at a
verification site. It would also be hard to decode.

2. A material shown to have an isotope ratio different from the
isotope ratios found on earth: I disproved this one in 1996 when I
demonstrated that anyone can order purified isotopes of almost any
element from chemical supply houses (Our lab has the catalogs).
Anyone could cook up a batch of isotope-enriched aluminum (for
example), make an artifact, and offer it as "evidence" of an ET
visit.

3. Life organized in a way different than what we know (different
cell types, lack of cells, different kinds of genetic material, etc.)

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Mon, 10 Nov 2003 11:06:18 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

I now have more information on this, from a friend who programs ATC
computers for the FAA:

The small local ATC control centers have at their sites only the kind
of RADAR set that displays just the targets that have transponders. One
controller in local ATC center has a screen that contains data from the
larger RADAR located at the regional control centers. Those larger
RADAR sets can display both skin returns and transponder returns. In
addition, airliners carry anticollision RADAR, which displays both
kinds of returns. UFO returns could appear on only the last two kinds
of displays.

In the event a plane loses its transponder, control of that plane is
transferred to the ATC controller with the special display. That
controller is also in charge of keeping planes away from other planes
which do not have transponders. And he is the only one who could report
a UFO.

Most general aviation aircraft have transponders which send the same
ID number (1200), so the computer has a harder time eliminating
secondary echoes of those, but they are all marked as being general
aviation aircraft whether the return is real or not. None of them
could be confused with a UFO. Note that most general aviation aircraft
are restricted to flying below airway altitudes, and must keep out of
the approach and landing zones of major airports. Thus, they are
rarely a problem for air traffic controllers unless a pilot gets lost,
or a secondary echo appears in an approach or landing zone.

The local centers send out more of an inquiry sync signal than a beam
designed to reflect from the skin of a plane. The transponder then
returns the requested information. Through a series of inquiries, the
RADAR can learn the plane's ID, GPS position, and altitude. The FAA
computer also has simple software to weed out false returns. It uses
the following logic:

1. If the return arrives after another return of the same ID and
inquiry (unless the ID is 1200), don't display it. It's a secondary
echo.

2. If the transponder answers the previous inquiry instead of the
current one, don't display the return. It is a second trip echo of a
plane far beyond the horizon.

3. If the transponder answers any inquiry other than the previous or
current one, don't display the return. The transponder is answering
a different RADAR set, and has been picked up through atmospheric
skip.

4. If the transponder always answers the same inquiry, no matter
which inquiry the RADAR makes, display the return. It's probably a
busted transponder.

Why were these changes made? The more powerful RADAR sets caused
interference to radio, TV, police radio, emergency services radio,
and military radio receivers located within a few miles of the RADAR
set. They also interfered with each other, causing UFO reports. In
addition, the EPA was concerned about exposure to RADAR signals by
airport workers. Under the new system, regional ATC centers are in
rural areas, far from those receivers and workers and from each
other. Thus they cause very little interference and no EM
exposure. The local transmitters are dinky by comparison, needing
no more power than aircraft communications radio, and do not cause
the indicated troubles.

You seem to be under the impression that GA transponders only send 1200 and
that's that. Wrong. All transponders are capable of sending the full set of
codes. Pilots set 1200 (in the US, 7000 elsewhere) when they are flying VFR
(ie, it's not to do with them being GA, but the flight regime). When a pilot
- any pilot - contacts certain types of ATC, they are assigned a squawk code
which they set in the transponder. Therefore ATC are capable of identifying
*any* aircraft with whom they are in radio contact. Many radar sets can be
switched to filtering out all VFR returns, which is often done because these
returns often don't return altitude information (ie, they are Mode A) and are
likely coming from traffic below the airspace the ATC is monitoring.

| There are some mode S units that can send GPS.

Yes, but not in widespread use - very rare beasts at present.

| The anticollision RADAR I am talking about is also used to
| prevent collision with the ground (such as mountain peaks). As
| we know, the ground has no transponder.

Not 'also used' - the phrase you want is 'solely used'. What you're talking
about here is the Ground Proximity Warning System which is linked to a radar
altimeter (used to get an accurate height reading in low-altitude flight
modes such as approach to landing). Of course, the significant thing about
radar altimeters is that they are angled *downwards* - that being where the
ground is usually found.

Subject: Re: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?

Larry, see my other comments in my reply to your reply, plus:

| Note that most general aviation aircraft
| are restricted to flying below airway altitudes, and must keep out of
| the approach and landing zones of major airports. Thus, they are
| rarely a problem for air traffic controllers unless a pilot gets lost,
| or a secondary echo appears in an approach or landing zone.

This is inaccurate. You seem to be confused between 'general aviation' and
VFR. If flying VFR, it is true that aircraft must generally remain outside
Class A airspace. In Europe, VFR is permitted in all other classes (and I
assume the new US classifications are similar). To fly in Class A airspace,
the aircraft and pilot must both be instrument-rated, must have filed an IFR
flight plan (though this can be done in the air, by radio), and must be in
contact with (and under positive control of) ATC. So all flying in Class A is
IFR with one exception (see below).

*However*... many GA aircraft are suitably IFR-equipped, and many private
pilots have IFR ratings. Of course, GA also includes a great deal of
commercial flying, too. So you will often - indeed, usually - find a
significant number of GA aircraft in precisely the types of airspace you
mentioned. However, they will all be in contact with ATC and so will have
been positively identified and assigned squawk codes.

Plus: there is a thing called 'Special VFR' which, under certain
circumstances, allows a non-IFR aircraft & pilot to transition Class A
airspace. I've been on a Gazelle helicopter that flew SVFR through Heathrow's
airspace, parallel to one of the main runways, so close that I watched
aircraft taking off and I swear I could see the pilot's face :-). This SVFR
clearance was given via radio shortly before we entered Heathrow's airspace,
and this is typical for SVFR. Under SVFR, you are also under positive control
and will be assigned a squawk. So your assertion becomes true if you replace
'general aviation' with 'VFR' - but I think it's important to get our
terminology straight.

Note also that the number of airports within Class A is actually quite small.
Here in France I think there are two, maybe three (counting all the Paris
airports as one, as they're all inside one big Class A zone). There are many
significant airports with scheduled commercial jet traffic which are also
open to VFR traffic. During my flight training I did a lot of flights into
Melbourne Regional in Florida where I'd share the circuit with DC-9s and
737s. Same goes here in France at places like Rennes (Class D) & Dinard
(Class E - which means I could go in there non-radio as clearance is not
required to enter Class E!). Even airports like Strasbourg and Toulouse are
only Class D. Now, when entering Class D one has to obtain clearance and,
normally, you'll be assigned a squawk. But I've gone into Class D airports
still squawking VFR (7000) while being told to hurry up because there's an
Air France jet behind me. It's amazing how much speed you can get out of an
old Piper Archer under those circumstances :-)


--
+a
Steve

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Tue, 11 Nov 2003 11:27:32 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?

Not just anyone, but anyone with the equipment to melt metal could make
any isotope mix he wants of that metal, and then cast it into artifacts.
It's a case of producing a homogenous mixture of the purchased isotope
and metal stock. My brother has a small foundry in his basement, and I
have done some alloying with it. Alloying is basically the same thing,
except that I used two different metals, rather than two isotope mixes
of the same metal.

It would be somewhat harder to produce compounds with altered isotope
ratios, but you can buy isotope labeled compounds too. In the labs where
I work, we have some rat food labeled with isotopes, and as a result we
also have some lab rats with altered isotope ratios. This is used to
study which parts of foods go to which molecules in the muscles during
protein synthesis.

Of course, if you find some silicon dioxide with altered silicon isotope
ratios, but UNaltered oxygen isotope ratios, you had better start
looking
for the "isodope" who faked it.

My point was that altered isotope ratios are not proof of ET, because
they can be made right here on earth.

Altered isotope ratios have been found in rocks near the atomic bomb
test sites in New Mexico and Nevada.

The idea of creating a list of "best cases" goes back to Hynek/McDonald.&nbsp; Roy
Craig states that Condon wanted to take this on but Craig convinced him it would be
fruitless because:<BR>
<BR>
"...such sparring would be endless.&nbsp; If one proved six of ten arguments wrong,
the opposition would merely drop those arguments and substitute six new ones,
leaving us with where we started.&nbsp; The situation was similar to pursuing Dr.
James McDonald's "Twenty best UFO case," which he told various groups of people
were worthy of detailed scientific investigation.&nbsp; As soon as te investigator
showed several of the twenty to have no merit, those were simply dropped from the
list and replaced with different cases. Since Condon seemed to love a good fight,
many of which he had experienced in his past activities, he must have found it
difficult to yield to such arguments, and merely let erroneous testimony fall of its own
weight..." (Craig p. 212).<BR>

From: Malcolm Stroud <malcolm@ttauv.freeserve.co.uk>
Date: Wed, 12 Nov 2003 22:01:07 +0000
Subject: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)
X-Spam-Processed: italianmoda.com, Wed, 12 Nov 2003 23:11:23 +0100

In 1996 a document was published to world leaders attempting to bring
the UFO subject into the open once and for all. It was written by Don
Berliner and funded by Laurence Rockerfeller, listing 19 cases. I have
not been able to trace a full copy on the Internet quickly, but
reproduce a summary below by Dave Vetterick (http://www.v-j-enterprises.
com/rockrept.html), adapted with my own comments, plus some of my
favourites. I admit that I know little or nothing about some of them. It
is interesting to see how many have been 'discredited'. Possibly, 95
percent of every residue can be eliminated ad infinitum.


1944-45: Foo Fighters Over Europe and Asia
- "Foo fighters" sighted by WWII fliers during 1944-45, notably on
August 10, 1944 over the Indian Ocean, and December 22, 1944 over
Hagenau, Germany

1946: Ghost Rockets Over Scandinavia

1947: First American Sighting Wave
- Kenneth Arnold's sighting on June 24, 1947 (possible birds)

1952: Second American Sighting Wave
- Presumably the Washington wave (interesting, but has been attributed
to radar effects)

1956: Radar/Visual Jet chase Over England
- Presumably the Bentwaters/Lakenheath radar/visual case (interesting)

1958: Third American Sighting Wave

1958: Brazilian Navy Photographic Case
- photos of a Saturn-shaped UFO over Trindade Island in the South
Atlantic, February 21, 1958 (convincingly argued to be a mirage of
Jupiter by Steuert Campbell)

1967: Burn Injury in Canada
- May 20, 1967, near Falcon Lake, Manitoba, Canada. Amateur prospector
Steven Michalak: with personal injury (I have always assumed this to be
a hoax because of the neat burn mark in the photos)

1967: Landing Case At Socorro, New Mexico
-Lonnie Zamora near Socorro, New Mexico, on April 24, 1964. Zamora said
he witnessed an egg-shaped craft on four thin legs, along with two small
beings in white coverall-type outfits (I just have a bad feeling about
this case)

1975: Strategic Air command Bases UFO Alert
- bold incursions of unidentified craft over several Strategic Air
Command bases during late October and November, 1975, including Loring
AFB in Maine, Wurtsmith AFB in Michigan, Malmstrom AFB in Montana; Minot
AFB in North Dakota and Falconbridge in Ontario, Canada

1976: Multiple Witness Case - Canary Islands

1976: UFO Dog Fight Over Tehran
- a "dogfight" between a UFO and two F-4 jets over Tehran, Iran in 1976
(seems solid)

1980: UFO Incidents At Rendlesham Forest, Eng
- the strange sightings in the Rendlesham Forest between Bentwaters and
Woodbridge RAF bases in England in late December, 1980 (in doubt)

1981: Physical Trace Case Trans-en-Province, Fr (as I recall, a single
witness sighting where traces might not have been caused by the
'object', but still interesting)

1986: Japan Airlines 747 Case Over Alaska
- visual and radar sighting of an aerial object "two times bigger than
an aircraft carrier" by the flight crew of a Japan Airlines 747
freighter over Alaska on November 17, 1986

1986: Jet Chase Over Brazil

1989: Multiple Witness Case USSR Missile Base
- July 28, 1989, a UFO was clearly observed for a period of two hours
over a Russian army missile base at Kapustin Yar, Astrakhan region.

1989-90: UFO Sighting Wave In Belgium
- Belgium in 1989 and 1990. Numerous drawings and photos by witnesses
show a huge triangular shaped craft with bright lights at each corner
(presumably military FTs, plus hoaxes)

1991-94: Recent Cases



To this list I will add some of my own favourites:

1926: Mongolia
- A crystal clear contemporary account of a big, shiny object flying in
the sky above Mongolia by American artist/traveller (and spiritualist?)
Nicholas Roerich.

1949: Rogue River, USA
- An interesting recurring object. This was a distinctive hamburger-
shaped aircraft with a single tail fin but no wings or obvious
propulsion. A Blue Book case, it was classified until 1976. A very
similar aircraft with some identical details was reportedly seen in
Bedfordshire, UK in 1957 and sketched by a witness some time before
1978. Jenny Randles made the link between these two cases. A similar
object was reportedly at Ft Riley, USA in 1964 and may have been
published soon after (presumably a military aircraft, but an amazing
kind).

1950: McMinnville, Oregon
- The famous photographic disc case, supplemented by the Rouen (France)
1954 photograph. More information is needed on the Rouen photograph (but
with its tail fin, presumably military - but amazing).

1952: Puerto Maldonado, Peru
- A photographic case showing an odd finless rocket flying low and
emitting what seems to be thick, white vapour. Interesting, but not much
information (presumably a secret rocket test).

1955: Namur, France
- The Postman's photographic case. A repeated saucer type, one of the
three photos would be difficult to fake, with its vapour trail.

1973: Mansfield, USA
- Helicopter crew and independent witness sight strange flying object -
long with cupola and spotlight (another helicopter?).

1990: Montreal, Canada
- Photographic case, multiple witness; an enormous disc with
circumference lights hovers for long period in the fog (presumably a
military blimp).

1997: Boomerang, Carefree Highway, Arizona
- One of a series of similar boomerang shaped flying wings seen in the
US since 1991, probably going back much earlier. Can travel slowly or
hover (presumably military - but amazing).

Some of these are further referenced at http://www.ttauv.freeserve.co.uk

@ -----Original Message-----
@ From: Malcolm Stroud [mailto:malcolm@ttauv.freeserve.co.uk]
@ Sent: Wednesday, November 12, 2003 5:01 PM
@ To: UFORL@yahoogroups.com
@ Subject: [UFORL] One scientifically verifiable sighting?
@
@
@ In 1996 a document was published to world leaders attempting to bring
@ the UFO subject into the open once and for all. It was written by Don
@ Berliner and funded by Laurence Rockerfeller, listing 19 cases. I have
@ not been able to trace a full copy on the Internet quickly, but
@ reproduce a summary below by Dave Vetterick
@ (http://www.v-j-enterprises.
@ com/rockrept.html), adapted with my own comments, plus some of my
@ favourites. I admit that I know little or nothing about some
@ of them. It
@ is interesting to see how many have been 'discredited'. Possibly, 95
@ percent of every residue can be eliminated ad infinitum.
@
@
@ 1944-45: Foo Fighters Over Europe and Asia
@ - "Foo fighters" sighted by WWII fliers during 1944-45, notably on
@ August 10, 1944 over the Indian Ocean, and December 22, 1944 over
@ Hagenau, Germany

Many of these were probably attempts by the Resistance to make the
Germans waste ammunition. It is known that they made fire balloons out
of tissue paper, and disguised them as party lanterns if they were
found in a house. The Japanese were also using fire balloons as both
long-distance bombs (some reached the west coast of the US) and as
barrage balloons.
@ 1947: First American Sighting Wave
@ - Kenneth Arnold's sighting on June 24, 1947 (possible birds)

Whatever it was, Arnold demonstrated the inability of the human eye to
resolve distance, speed, and size. His distance, speed, and size
estimates could not all be true simultaneously.

@ 1952: Second American Sighting Wave
@ - Presumably the Washington wave (interesting, but has been attributed
@ to radar effects)

This has now been attributed to RADAR operators using old techniques
(which no longer worked) with the new Moving Target Indicator (MTI)
RADAR sets. In both this case and the next one, the new sets had just
been installed when the case happened (and again at the Kinchloe AFB
case in 1967). An operator using old operation methods was bound to
get lots of UFOs on the screen, because he unwittingly decalibrated the
new equipment.

There were also atmospheric bending effects from a temperature inversion

affecting the RADAR in the Washington case. One pilot said he tried to
intercept the same UFO 3 times, and each time he found himself flying at
a steamboat on the Potomac.

@ 1956: Radar/Visual Jet chase Over England
@ - Presumably the Bentwaters/Lakenheath radar/visual case (interesting)

This has also been mostly attributed to RADAR operators using old
techniques (which no longer worked) on (MTI) RADAR sets, combined with
weather and meteor effects.

@ 1958: Third American Sighting Wave

Should that be 1957?

@ 1958: Brazilian Navy Photographic Case
@ - photos of a Saturn-shaped UFO over Trindade Island in the South
@ Atlantic, February 21, 1958 (convincingly argued to be a mirage of
@ Jupiter by Steuert Campbell)

This has now been shown to have been a hoax perpetrated by the
photographer. Investigation of the photos shows a rectangle of halftone
around each UFO image. The images were probably taken from a comic book
I used to have.

@ 1967: Burn Injury in Canada
@ - May 20, 1967, near Falcon Lake, Manitoba, Canada. Amateur prospector
@ Steven Michalak: with personal injury (I have always assumed
@ this to be
@ a hoax because of the neat burn mark in the photos)

The burns remind me of the grille on a certain type of picnic fireplace
which used to be provided in the picnic areas in state parks.

@ 1967: Landing Case At Socorro, New Mexico
@ -Lonnie Zamora near Socorro, New Mexico, on April 24, 1964.
@ Zamora said
@ he witnessed an egg-shaped craft on four thin legs, along
@ with two small
@ beings in white coverall-type outfits (I just have a bad feeling about
@ this case)

I am convinced that the object was a hot air balloon, and that Zamora
got the visual size and distance wrong. And the case was in 1964, not
1967 (as you have right on the next line).

@ 1975: Strategic Air command Bases UFO Alert
@ - bold incursions of unidentified craft over several Strategic Air
@ Command bases during late October and November, 1975, including Loring
@ AFB in Maine, Wurtsmith AFB in Michigan, Malmstrom AFB in
@ Montana; Minot
@ AFB in North Dakota and Falconbridge in Ontario, Canada

This has been conclusively shown to have been a test of both stealth
technology and military readiness. The UFO reports were indications that
the flights had been detected. But the bases were not told what was
going
on at the time. The info was released at the time the Stealth Fighter
was revealed.

@ 1976: Multiple Witness Case - Canary Islands

This is a known Polaris missile test launch.

@ 1976: UFO Dog Fight Over Tehran
@ - a "dogfight" between a UFO and two F-4 jets over Tehran,
@ Iran in 1976
@ (seems solid)

The problem is that it behaved TOO much like a fighter plane - even
launching anti-heat-seeking-missile "stars". Russian spy mission?

@ 1980: UFO Incidents At Rendlesham Forest, Eng
@ - the strange sightings in the Rendlesham Forest between
@ Bentwaters and
@ Woodbridge RAF bases in England in late December, 1980 (in doubt)

There are so many conflicting stories that I don't know if they will
ever figure this one out. My vote is a spy satellite drop for info on
the hostages in Tehran, and a UFO story used to cover-up that secret.

@ 1981: Physical Trace Case Trans-en-Province, Fr (as I recall, a single
@ witness sighting where traces might not have been caused by the
@ 'object', but still interesting)

If this is the one I am thinking of, it was later confessed as a hoax
after the police became involved.

@ 1986: Japan Airlines 747 Case Over Alaska
@ - visual and radar sighting of an aerial object "two times bigger than
@ an aircraft carrier" by the flight crew of a Japan Airlines 747
@ freighter over Alaska on November 17, 1986

What I want to know is how they found out the size. RADAR can't do that,
and the human eye is limited to an accuracy range of 30 feet, unless the
object is a known object.

I am constantly flabbergasted that UFOlogists take the sizes and
distances reported by witnesses as ironclad truth, when the human visual
system is totally incapable of making those kinds of measurements.

We don't even know if the visual object and the RADAR object were in
fact
the same thing.

@ 1989: Multiple Witness Case USSR Missile Base
@ - July 28, 1989, a UFO was clearly observed for a period of two hours
@ over a Russian army missile base at Kapustin Yar, Astrakhan region.

Could it possibly have been something secret launched from the base?

@ To this list I will add some of my own favourites:
@
@ 1926: Mongolia
@ - A crystal clear contemporary account of a big, shiny object
@ flying in
@ the sky above Mongolia by American artist/traveller (and
@ spiritualist?)
@ Nicholas Roerich.

Could it have possibly been a kite?

@ 1949: Rogue River, USA
@ - An interesting recurring object. This was a distinctive hamburger-
@ shaped aircraft with a single tail fin but no wings or obvious
@ propulsion. A Blue Book case, it was classified until 1976. A very
@ similar aircraft with some identical details was reportedly seen in
@ Bedfordshire, UK in 1957 and sketched by a witness some time before
@ 1978. Jenny Randles made the link between these two cases. A similar
@ object was reportedly at Ft Riley, USA in 1964 and may have been
@ published soon after (presumably a military aircraft, but an amazing
@ kind).

Oh, come on! I have had copies of the Rogue River case since 1967. It
was in the original Project Sign report, and in a book full of Air
Force case files published in 1964 (of which I have a copy). Most
likely the UFO was an airplane seen nearly edge-on.

@ 1950: McMinnville, Oregon
@ - The famous photographic disc case, supplemented by the
@ Rouen (France)
@ 1954 photograph. More information is needed on the Rouen
@ photograph (but
@ with its tail fin, presumably military - but amazing).

Recent investigation shows that it was probably the side mirror off of
the truck in the background. I also found that the Dual 1000 record
changer had a record balancing disc that looks remarkably like the
object.

@ 1952: Puerto Maldonado, Peru
@ - A photographic case showing an odd finless rocket flying low and
@ emitting what seems to be thick, white vapour. Interesting,
@ but not much
@ information (presumably a secret rocket test).

This has been shown to be a hoax. The object was a child's sausage
balloon (the knot is visible at the leading end in blowups). The
balloon and some cotton "exhaust" were superimposed on a large print
of the scene, and then rephotographed.

@ 1955: Namur, France
@ - The Postman's photographic case. A repeated saucer type, one of the
@ three photos would be difficult to fake, with its vapour trail.

The photos were of an overturned toy sailboat in surf.

@ 1973: Mansfield, USA
@ - Helicopter crew and independent witness sight strange
@ flying object -
@ long with cupola and spotlight (another helicopter?).

There are several theories on this, ranging from a fire balloon
misperceived by the pilot (reference the similar case in 1993 by police
in Louisville KY) to a re-entry.

@ 1990: Montreal, Canada
@ - Photographic case, multiple witness; an enormous disc with
@ circumference lights hovers for long period in the fog (presumably a
@ military blimp).

This sounds like a cluster of fire balloons from the description in the
link. Too bad the photo is gone from the page. Anybody got a link to a
photo?

@ 1997: Boomerang, Carefree Highway, Arizona
@ - One of a series of similar boomerang shaped flying wings seen in the
@ US since 1991, probably going back much earlier. Can travel slowly or
@ hover (presumably military - but amazing).

I worked on this case. This series of sightings has been conclusively
identified as two separate series of objects in the sky:

1. A drop of rescue flares from a plane by the Air National Guard of
Maryland, on a training mission over the Gila Bend test range.
Triangulation from the 4 videos of the 3/13/97 flight prove this. This
was the second case that night (around 10 pm).

2. A series of fire balloons launched by pranksters.

@ From: Martin Shough [mailto:mshough@parcellular.fsnet.co.uk]

@ Larry,
@ re your comments below: I should like to point out that the
@ Washington National radar echoes on both dates in 1952 were
@ very nicely explained qualitatively and quantitatively by
@ Borden & Vickers without recourse to any anomalies connected
@ to MTI or 'techiniques which no longer worked'. Nobody was
@ familiar with the theory behind wind-driven partially
@ reflecting domains in 1952, and they were honest-to-goodness
@ radar UFOs in terms of the state of the art.

Here is how the MTI of the 1950s worked:

- Every target the antenna is aimed at produces an echo of the
emitted RADAR pulse.

- Every echo received is fed to both a gating circuit and a delay
line.

- The delay line delays the echo by exactly the time between
emitted RADAR pulses.

- The delayed echo operates the gate. This closes the gate exactly
one pulse interval after the echo was received.

- Meanwhile, the signal going to the gate directly from the
receiver is passed through to the display, unless the gate is
closed.

- If the target has not moved, the gate closes at exactly the same
time the new echo from the same target is received. This will
completely obliterate the display of the echo. Note that this does
NOT keep the second echo from entering the delay line, it just
keeps it from being displayed.

- If the target has moved between RADAR pulses, then the gate
is closed either too early or too late. Now, part of the echo gets
through the gate and is displayed on the screen. Notice that in
most cases, the gate still chops off part of the signal, but it
lets enough through to be displayed.

It was the partially reflecting domain in conjunction with the
MTI errors that made the 1952 sighting so believable to the
RADAR men. There were two quirks about the new MTI RADAR that
caused the confusion:

1. When the existing RADAR set was converted to MTI, one control
on the old part of the set still existed, but its function
changed. That control adjusted the gain of the receiver. On the
old setup, this control adjusted the strength of the display, and
was constantly adjusted by the operator. On the new setup, that
function was moved to a new control, and the old control became a
calibration control, which also affected what was sent to the
delay line. But the operators, by force of habit, kept grabbing
the old knob and decalibrating the MTI. When the MTI was
decalibrated, it either could no longer reject stationary targets,
or it rejected real targets.

2. Partially reflecting domains had the nasty habit of tricking
the MTI display into not only displaying them, but making them
appear stronger than real aircraft echoes. The tricky part is that
the partially reflecting domain is not always strong enough to
close the gate. The gate closes on some pulses, but not on others.
When the gate does not close, the displayed echo is brighter than
the echo of a moving target normally is, since there is no closed
gate removing part of the signal.

One way I have learned to recognize this effect is that the
operator often says something like "Never have I before seen such
a strong clear target."

@ As for Lakenheath 1956 your attribution to 'old techniques',
@ MTI problems and meteors is just hand-waving guesswork in my
@ opinion. It isn't at all easy to attribute this case to
@ propagation, ionisation trails or electronic anomalies. Maybe
@ you've already thoroughly studied and dismissed the rather
@ detailed analyses presented here:
@ http://www.parcellular.fsnet.co.uk/Lakenheath.htm If so, or
@ if not, then I'd welcome your comments (or
@ anybody's comments).
@ Regards
@ Martin Shough

I am not dismissing the analyses, but amplifying them. The items
listed in them were there. The MTI errors made them stand out in
a way that the old standard RADAR would not have done. Again, the
equipment had just been installed shortly before the sighting. To
wit:

- Stationary targets were observed in MTI mode in the case. This
was specifically commented on by the operators at the time. Both
errors 1 and 2 (above) can make stationary targets show up on the
MTI.

- MTI would also magnify any weather targets, due to the
intermittent gating.

- Meteors would be strengthened because the gate would close
nowhere near the time of the next echo of the target. This is
because the meteor is going very fast.

An 'open reply' to a letter in the latest edition of
'Fortean Times' [FT], received today - manifestly still
the most thought-provoking magazine around.

Acknowledging FT have published lead articles with fairly
less content than my 'letter'... 'sorted' in due course.

Meanwhile... to FT:

Steve Mansfield [FT178:72], observes that the 28
December, 1980, photograph published in 'Left at East
Gate' [LaEG], co-authored by Larry Warren and Peter
Robbins and which depicts a notice at the entrance to RAF
Bentwaters declaring an 'ALERT CONDITION', does not
display the current condition.

Although Warren did additionally explain in LaEG that the
base was indeed on an 'alert status', hence his nocturnal
assignment to "Bentwaters Perimeter Post 18", which was
"manned only during alerts", said photograph ceased to
have any significance since my published research
developments some 18 months ago.

On 17 April, 2002, I began compiling and assimilating
evidence why RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge, a joint
base complex, were on a higher alert status during the
precise period when Kevin Conde's dramatic 'UFO' hoax
reportedly took place.

I was also, during this period, now in regular contact
with John Burroughs, one of the three central
participants in our inaugural 'UFO' incident, circa 0300
on 26 December.

Amongst John's many ensuing revelations, is a claim he
first made to myself on 28 May, 2002: "Yes, there were
people brought in and they were out in the forest for
days. I was even posted on the east gate for 3 days from
1500-2300 while helicopters and personnel were out in the
area".

"Also, the gate always closed at 1800 hrs on week days
and was closed on weekends".
John confirmed that his abnormal late-night posting was
due to an existing 'alert status'.

A more detailed summary of the related background was
also published on 31 August, 2003 in direct response to a
question raised on the 'UFO Research List' [UFORL], by
Dr. David Clarke, who enquired:

"Re-posted below are Nick Pope's latest comments on UFO
Updates. I was particularly interested to read his
convoluted argument about why the 'Alert Condition' was
not really an alert condition. Have you any comments on
this explanation?"


I duly replied [edited for brevity]:

Dave,

Thanks for noting those queries.

This is the raw evidence for Kevin Conde's first
realisation of his possible involvement with the late
December, 1980 infamous 'Rendlesham forest UFO' incidents
and contact with myself:

Dear Mr. Easton,

I'm a retired USAF SMSgt. Last night I had some time on
my hands, and was surfing the net looking for Web sites
on airbases that I had served on during my USAF career.
One of those bases was RAF Bentwaters. I was amazed to
find a couple of Web sites describing a UFO incident at
Bentwaters during my tour. Shocked actually, when you
consider what I know about these so-called incidents! One
of the web sites had an article by you.

I was a Security Policeman at RAF Bentwaters/Woodbridge
from mid 1978 to mid 1981. I arrived at Bentwaters as a
SSgt, and departed as a TSgt. I was a law enforcement
specialist. While there I worked as a patrolman, desk
sergeant, assistant flight chief, flight chief, training
NCO, and QA evaluator.

During the time that of incident I will recount occurred,
1st Lt. Bruce Englund was my Flight Commander. He figures
into one of the accounts you investigated. I also
remember a Lt Col who was a bit of a cop buff, and used
to ride along with the law enforcement patrols on a
regular basis. As I remember he was either the Vice Wing
Commander, or worked for the Wing Commander. He must be
the Lt Col Halt mentioned.

I can provide copies of my APR's (Airman's Performance
Reports) if asked, to validate the dates and positions in
which I served at RAF Bentwaters.

[...]

There were two incidents that I was personally involved
in.

Both occurred on the back gate of Woodbridge. This gate
was open during the day, and for brief periods during the
night for shift change. Woodbridge was mostly housing,
and we would open the gate during shift change so folks
could come and go between home and job during shift
change.

The gate sits out at the end of the runway at Woodbridge.
It is isolated, dark, surrounded by woods, and a little
lonely.

[...]

Cops have a tendency towards practical jokes. Practical
jokes are a tradition in the Security Police that at
times approaches the status of high art.

It was during an exercise, so I was not alone, as was
normal for the Woodbridge Law Enforcement patrol. As I
remember there were three of us.

Like I said, the back gate at Woodbridge is out all by
itself at the end of the runway. Just before you got to
the gate there were a couple of revetments surrounded by
high dirt berms. These berms would hide anything in them
from the gate guard's view.

It was dark, and a little foggy. I shut off my headlights
and drove my patrol car into one of those revetments. We
stuck several military issue flashlights out of the
windows, pointing upwards. We simply pointed the
flashlights upwards and rolled up the windows to hold
them in position. These military flashlights come with
several different color lenses in a screw on compartment
on the end of the light. These lenses come in red, amber,
blue, green and a white opaque color. Most of us carried
spare flashlights with us, so we could stick several
flashlights out the windows with different colored
lenses.

Leaving my headlights off I turned on the overheads
lights, which on American cop cars are red and blue. We
then proceeded to drive the car in slow circles while
making weird noises over the PA system. Remember, there
was a light fog, which was the key to the joke's success,
as each light appeared in the fog as a moving beam of
light.

[...]

This happened more than 20 years a go. I don't remember
the specific date, but it would have been right about
then.

I went back to Flight duty about 6 months before I left
Bentwaters. I left sometime in the summer of 1981. My
Shift Commander was Lt Englund, and the Security Flight
Chief at the time was MSgt Bobbie Ball (Bobbie was known
for how shiny his boots were, even in the mud and rain).
If I left QA six months before I left Bentwaters in the
summer of 1981, and my Shift Commander was Lt Englund,
and the Security Flight Chief was MSgt Ball, then my
incident is right in the ball park.

The Time. I had someone with me on patrol - that was
unusual on Woodbridge - not exactly a hotbed of crime.
The only time we had multiple folks in an LE patrol was
during alerts - exercises.

The joke would have had to have happened late - after all
the initial patrol duties like relieving the main gate
for chow, and getting the first round of building checks
done, and before things began to pick up again, and we
got bored and started looking for a way to cause trouble.

I can not say for sure, but I would guess between 1:00
and 4:00 AM.

Were there other UFO hoaxes? I don't know of any, but it
is entirely possible. It was a good stunt. Someone else
could have repeated it. In fact, most good cop practical
jokes did get repeated. We had some classics - sending
someone out for 100 feet of flight line to rope off an
area. Sending someone out for a gallon of prop wash to
clean patrol car windows with, sending someone to the
emergency room for a box of fallopian tubes for the
breathalyzer, etc.
We used at least three flashlights pointing upwards
rolled up in the windows of the patrol car. These lights
were red, blue, green, and possibly amber. The patrol car
itself had the American style square red and blue
emergency rack on top with revolving high intensity red
and blue lights. It also had bright white alley lights -
these are lights that point to the side in order to light
up buildings as you drive past them at night. It also had
a bright white spotlight that I pointed as close to
straight up as I could. I had everything except my
headlights on.

The flashlights, which were green, and maybe amber, where
nowhere as bright as the red, blue and white emergency
lights, which really lit up the night.

I don't know if I'm helping clear this up or just adding
to the stew, but I'll do all I can to help.

The only UFO incidents that occurred during my tour were
ones I participated in. The only alien that landed was
Mrs. Conde's little boy, Kevin.

This is the truth, the details are the best I can
remember after more than 20 years, and I'll take a
polygraph on that.
[END OF KEVIN'S COMMENTS]

This issue has been discussed extensively on the UFO Updates list and
I have acknowledged that Steve is, of course, correct about the "Alert
Condition" sign. I established this myself within days of writing the FT
column during a visit to the RAF Neatishead open day when I examined
one of the very same "Alert Condition" signs at the entrance to the
Operations Block. They are permanent signs with a little slot for a placard
underneath where the alert status is displayed. Unfortunately on the
photograph taken by Larry Warren this placard is obscured.

So it is certainly true that the Alert Condition sign in itself is
meaningless,
but that does not mean the bases were not on alert status at the time.
What we need to know is the "actual" alert status of RAF Woodbridge-
Bentwaters for the period 26-30 December 1980. I've discussed this
matter with Nick Pope and as a result I have written to USAF 3rd Air
Force at Mildenhall with an FOIA request for confirmation of the
alert status in force at the relevant time. I will copy this to MOD as an
additional inquiry.

we will be able to clear this matter up once and for all.

best,

Dave Clarke

In a message dated 11/19/2003 11:21:25 AM Eastern Standard Time,
Stuart.Miller4@btinternet.com writes:


> What I saw were dim lights travelling at great altitude in a >very disorganised
formation. In all there were probably about >20 of them and they took something like
15 minutes to pass >out of sight from when first spotted, so we're not talking >about
great speeds.

Well, speed is relative. What you are addressing is that they were slow ANGULAR
speed. An object traveling 50mph at 1000feet has the same angular speed as an object
traveling 500mph at 10000feet. This is why the shuttle/space station travel relatively
slow across the sky despite traveling at speeds around 17,000mph! So, your sighting
was moving at a slow angular speed but the actual speed could have been very high
especially if they were at high altitudes (as you suggested).

> Altrincham is near Manchester airport so there was a fair >bit of ordinary
commercial activity but that was much lower >and very obvious. They weren't
satellites as they travel >noticeably quicker and in fact one satellite did pass over
>while I was stood there but was going in the same direction >as the wind.
>

Satellites usually travel west to east simply because that is how their orbits are (if I
recall correctly, send the object in orbit in this direction requires significantly less
thrust because of the earth's rotation). Some travel north to south and vice versa but it
is rare that a satellite travels in a westerly direction.

I am not sure what to make of your lights but I am inclined to think they were high
flying military aircraft. That is my two cents (or is it pence?) anyway.

Tim Printy

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Thu, 20 Nov 2003 12:18:16 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Pretty lights in the sky
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)
X-Spam-Processed: italianmoda.com, Thu, 20 Nov 2003 23:33:30 +0100

Over here in the US, wind (and cloud) direction is defined as the
direction the wind comes FROM. So an easterly wind blows FROM the
east, and a westerly wind blows FROM the west. Your description
seems to indicate an opposite meaning was used.

I have seen people get this turned around constantly in UFO cases,
because they do not understand the weather bureau definitions of
wind direction being the direction of the ORIGIN of the wind (the
direction most important to farmers and sailors). APRO used to
constantly confuse wind direction in this manner. So clouds moving
in an easterly direction would be moving toward the west, according
to our definitions of wind direction.

Also, winds at different altitudes often tend to move in different
directions. This is especially true near a seashore, where winds very
near to the ground are influenced more by the sea breeze and land
breeze effects than they are by general weather.

The time of your sighting would be favorable for a land breeze to
form at low altitudes, moving the air away from the land and out to
sea. Assuming you meant that a westerly wind was moving the clouds
toward the east, this land breeze would move objects floating in
the air (but close to the ground) out to sea, rather than following
the much higher clouds. Thus, they could move in an opposite
direction to that of the clouds from your location.

How did you determine the altitude of these lights? The human eye is
unable to measure the distance of an unknown light in the sky beyond
a range of 30 feet. So you could have been looking at tiny lights as
close as 50 feet away, or huge lights in space.

You also did not give any color for these lights. That would be
extremely helpful.

spotted, so we're not talking about great speeds. They were traveling in
the completely opposite direction to the wind I.e. in a westerly
direction.

whatsoever, or at least none that could be seen.

ordinary

weren't

From: Phil Rotsky <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Fri, 21 Nov 2003 10:32:33 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Pretty lights in the sky
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

-------------------
On Thursday 20 November 2003 18:18, Robinson, Larry wrote:
| Over here in the US, wind (and cloud) direction is defined as the
| direction the wind comes FROM. So an easterly wind blows FROM the
| east, and a westerly wind blows FROM the west. Your description
| seems to indicate an opposite meaning was used.

Larry's absolutely right. The same principle is used in the UK and worldwide,
as far as I know, but not everyone's aware of it I guess.

| Also, winds at different altitudes often tend to move in different
| directions. This is especially true near a seashore, where winds very
| near to the ground are influenced more by the sea breeze and land
| breeze effects than they are by general weather.

In fact, the wind direction (and speed) is nearly always different at ground
level everywhere, due to ground friction which reduces the coriolis effect.
Typically, the wind at 2,000ft will be different by about 15-20 degrees from
the wind at ground level. But direction can continue to change in various
directions as you go up through the air. I once had a balloon ride in Reno
and was hugely impressed by the way the pilot could choose his direction of
flight by changing altitude. (He kept dropping pieces of paper to assess the
wind direction at various altitudes). So, it is impossible to accurately
judge the wind affecting clouds by the wind direction at ground level. This
is why met reports for aviation usually report wind directions at 2000, 5000
and 10000ft (and they can be very different).

--
+a
Steve

One of my points (which I have stressed repeatedly in this forum)
is that NOBODY has the power to visually determine the height of
an unidentified object which seen against the sky from farther
than 30 feet away. The human visual system does not have the basic
equipment to be able to do that.

You can estimate the distance, altitude, and speed of an airplane,
but that is because YOU KNOW IT IS AN AIRPLANE. Thus, you already
know what the actual size is. But if you see a plain white
cylinder against the sky that you can't identify, you can't tell
if it is a mailing tube up close, a water heater farther away, or
a city water tower miles away. You must have other information to
find the size, distance, altitude, and speed. You can't get that
information visually unless special circumstances reveal it.

> Although the sighter mentions at one point seeing a satellite he starts out by saying
there was a 'medium density' cloud base. Military aircraft taking 15 minutes to go out
of sight seems unlikely, 'high flying' or not, especially as an intervening cloud layer
would restrict visibility increasingly
> towards low elevations.

Agreed, assuming that the time duration is accurate and we are only talking about a
sighting that encompassed a small section of sky overhead. 15 minutes seems a long
time but my experience has been you can follow aircraft for a long time if given a
clear sky and a clear enough horizon (which may not be the case here). It depends on
how low an angle one first identifies the lights. One can see an aircraft that is lit from
a great distance at a low angle. Of course, they do tend to travel at much lower
angular speeds than when directly overhead when observed from this situation. When
taking astrophotos of low objects like comets, I experience this problem quite often. It
can often take an airplane up to 2-3 minutes to transit my field of view when it is
distant.

In a message dated 11/21/2003 7:51:43 AM Eastern Standard Time,
Stuart.Miller4@btinternet.com writes:

> In other words, if I looked from west to east, was I looking at a width of distance of
say, 50 miles?

The distance can vary depending on where you are looking. Anything in the sky can
be seen from over a hundred miles away if it is bright enough. I have seen aircraft
and their contrails reflecting sunlight from great distances away. They move VERY
slowly but I know they are moving hundreds of miles per hour. The distance to them
makes it appear that way. Of course, anything astronomical (i.e planets, stars and
such are much further away). You can't confuse the situation with making a fixed
distance across an angular distance.

>while certainly not claiming to be an aviation expert by any means, because I do live
quite close to a major airport I am used to watching aircraft. Looking at these things, I
did get the impression of airplane speed as opposed to
> something quicker.

As stated before, you can't confuse airplane speeds around an airport with airplane
speeds at a great distance. The two are not the same when discussing angular speed
(the apparent speed you saw). Do you watch a satellite and assume it is moving at
speeds just above that of an aircraft because this is the apparent speed most aircraft
appear to travel? This is a common misconception. It is just not possible to
accurately determine a moving light's speed based on what you think it is moving at
unless you know the distance to the light or the actual size of the light (therefore being
able to approximate a distance).

Tim Printy

flying objects?

<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Tim</FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Agreed you might see an aircraft at great distance
down to low elevations for several minutes. My point remains not only that 15
minutes is unbelievably long in the best of circumstances, but that Stuart
reports a *fairly dense cloud base". As I'm certain you realise, visibility
through&nbsp;a broken cloud base to objects at higher altitude might be
intermittently good&nbsp;near the zenith but will rapidly become near zero at
lower elevations just because of simple geometry. I don't know what you mean
about 'assuming we're talking about a small section of sky overhead'. The point
is that aircraft can't stay in a small area overhead for many minutes. Not much
that's flying can. If the cloud deck was low one has to assume that if the
objects were seen *above* the clouds for anything like 15 minutes then they were
being watched at fairly high elevation and didn't move far so are still less
likely to have been aircraft. Conversely if they did move far and&nbsp;were
watched for 15 minutes then they were probably below the cloud deck and cannot
have been moving very fast. Hence my 'birds' suggestion.</FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Regards</FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2>Martin</FONT></DIV>
<DIV><FONT face=Arial size=2></FONT>&nbsp;</DIV>

flying' or not, especially as an intervening cloud layer would restrict
visibility increasingly <BR>&gt; towards low elevations. <BR><BR>Agreed,
assuming that the time duration is accurate and we are only talking about a
sighting that encompassed a small section of sky overhead.&nbsp; 15 minutes
seems a long time but my experience has been you can follow aircraft for a long
time if given a clear sky and a clear enough horizon (which may not be the case
here). It depends on how low an angle one first identifies the lights. One can
see an aircraft that is lit from a great distance at a low angle.&nbsp; Of
course, they do tend to travel at much lower angular speeds than when directly
overhead when observed from this situation. When taking astrophotos of low
objects like comets, I experience this problem quite often. It can often take an
airplane up to 2-3 minutes to transit my field of view when it is
distant.<BR><BR>Tim Printy<BR><BR><BR></TT><BR></DIV>

First "they" would have to figure out:

1. That we use radio for communication (if they developed some form of
light communication first, they would not bother with the reduced
bandwidth of radio).
2. What frequency to listen on (remember that our channel widths are
determined by our senses of sight and hearing, and that they might miss
us because their channels are too wide or too narrow).
3. what the transponders are for.

But a "better" idea would be for them to NOT respond like a transponder.
Then they could hide as a VFR flight, and expect to not be given ATC
instructions.

Of course, it's much more likely that RADAR signal propagation anomalies
(like the one that cleared out the White House last week) would be
responsible for any extra transponder signals detected.

Too many people think of RADAR as being like a "television picture of
what's in the sky." It's not nearly that clear a picture. Think of a
fun house mirror that keeps changing and you get the idea.

On Monday 24 November 2003 17:39, Robinson, Larry wrote:
| @ You did *not* get your wind direction wrong, either

| @ perfectly precise.
|
| In American English, he did. This may be a difference between

|
| In American English, "westerly" always means "from the west",
| never "to the west." Use "westward" for "to the west."
|
| American weather ALWAYS reports the direction the wind blows
| from. A west wind or a westerly wind blows FROM the west.

No difference, Larry. It is an international standard to describe winds in
terms of the direction *from* which they are blowing, and this applies to the
UK as much as to the US. The OP's description may have been plain English and
prefectly precise, it's just that (in technical terms) it was precisely
wrong. I don't mean to criticise the OP here - there are many cases where
colloquial usage may differ from the correct technical usage (eg, the way
people say 'velocity' when they mean 'speed' and the whole weight/mass
thing). It's just that, in a subject like this where we want to deal with
accurate data, getting the terminology correct is important. I think the OP
has already said as much.

Steve

Subject: [UFORL] Chasing phantoms
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

Given the recent dicussions about radar etc, I thought people might find this
interesting. It's from the e-newsletter AVflash, published by AvWeb. To put
it in context, it was recently reported that there were more than 600
incursions into the restricted zone over Washington since Feb 10. This zone
is what's known as an Air Defence Interception Zone (ADIZ). Normally, ADIZ
airspace is used just on the US international borders. You must contact ATC
and have a flight plan to enter an ADIZ. Failure to do so means you will be
intercepted (usually by F-16s or Blackhawks) and may be shot down. Post-911,
restricted airspace has sprung up all over the US, some of it temporary (eg,
restricted zones wherever the president happens to be), some of it - like the
Washington ADIZ - effectively permanent. 'Incursions' are defined as aircraft
that enter the zone without permission, the vast majority of which are also
*unidentified*. By all accounts, USAF has been kept very busy chasing
unidentified aircraft all over the country.

Anyway, here's the AvWeb piece:

...NORAD CHASING PHANTOMS
In the eye of the security storm around Washington, FAA officials brace
for a rash of airspace violations whenever good VFR weather happens on
the weekend. And if it's not enough that F-16s and Blackhawks are sent
in pursuit of the numerous real targets that blunder into the Washington

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
