But that makes no sense at all to me. Those are exactly backwards to
American usage.

In American usage, "Easterly" means "coming from the east" in almost
all contexts. "Easterly" is not used in the context you used of a car
"proceeding in an easterly direction." One of the following words is
used instead to indicate that context.

In American usage, "Eastward" and "Eastbound" mean "going toward the
east" in all contexts. So here, cars proceed in eastward or eastbound
directions when they want to go east.

An American east wind is an easterly wind, and is coming from the
east and blowing westward, making all the leaves pile up against the
east wall of the house.

An easterly American train comes from the east. But the east train is
the eastbound train, going toward the east, or in an eastward
direction. And the east coast train runs either north or south.

There is only one American case of driving easterly to go eastbound,
and that is on a cloverleaf interchange, where you have to turn right
to end up going to the left.

But you blokes have that turned around too, by turning left to go right
on a cloverleaf motorway junction. Right? :D

And I know that nearside and offside get in there too somehow, but in
America, offside is when a football player crosses the line of
scrimmage too soon.

taught to be precise. A case of inept inaccuracy I am writing a letter

Phil/Steve & Larry
Sorry to have to hammer this small point ad nauseam but since you
both insist on the virtue of exactness let me repeat that 'the
OP' did not - *did not* - use the term easterly to give a wind
direction. He was describing the *direction of motion of the
clouds*. His statement was that "the clouds were moving rapidly
in an easterly direction" whilst the lights were "travelling in a
westerly direction". This is quite different, and conformable to
the very ordinary English usage "the suspect's vehicle was
observed proceeding in a westerly direction". Had he said "the
clouds were rapidly moving east" you might as well have objected,
with equal irrelevance, that the word "east" should be reserved
only for use in the phrase "east wind" to avoid confusion. The
confusion I'm afraid is yours!
MartinS

conjunction with 'Raven Industries', of Sioux Falls,
South Dakota".

You replied:

"The CIA can neither confirm nor deny the nonexistence of
records responsive to your request. Such information -
unless it has been officially acknowledged - would be
classified for reasons of national security under
Executive Order 12958. The fact of the existence or non-
existence of such records would also relate directly to
information concerning intelligence sources and records.

[...]

Therefore, your request is denied under FOIA
exemptions...".

"I would like to modify my request to something which may
be more amenable. On 29 April, I wrote:

'I am particularly interested in a project which took
place during 1963 and 1964, known as 'The Albuquerque
Flights'. These involved some of the earliest hot-air
balloon flights made and the balloons were launched north
of Albuquerque, close to the Rio Grande.

Ed Yost, still alive and in his eighties, has confirmed
he participated'.

project.

allied feature is scheduled for publication by the

those 'Albuquerque flights' was responsible for Zamora's
close encounter and ideally, if other flights tie-in with
the Rio Grande 'UFO' sightings

about and as the USAF discovered regarding 'Area 51' in
Nevada, pretending that something in clear sight isn't
really there, is a guaranteed means of attracting more
attention. However, I do appreciate the CIA's concerns
about possibly compromising sensitive data, even almost
forty years later.

[...]

significantly helpful and you now realise that I don't

related to CIA test-flight/training, etc. operations.

have no need to know.

I'm trying to give the CIA an easy 'out' here, rather
than a repeat of, 'The CIA can neither confirm nor deny
the existence or nonexistence of records responsive to
your request...'."


On 20 August, you consequently wrote:
"In addition [to the 'Albuquerque flights' - James], you
also ask if there is 'any documentary evidence which
either confirms or disproves that on 24 April, 1964, the
apparent hot-air balloon which landed near Socorro was
related to CIA test-flight/training, etc. operations.'

Please be advised that our 1 July, 2003 response to you
also applies to this subject and timeframe".


On 10 September, I appealed your decision.

I look forward to hearing from you in that respect and in
the meantime, enclose an entirely separate and new FOIA
request, which has no implied association with any
classified CIA projects.
[END OF 28 OCTOBER LETTER]


My secondary, 28 October request read, simply:

"On 24 April, 1964, local Socorro, New Mexico, police
officer Lonnie Zamora encountered a puzzling white, oval-
shaped, aerial vehicle.

The source of this enigmatic craft remained unsolved and
the incident became a celebrated 'UFO' case.

Under the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. subsection
552, I am requesting any information or records
pertaining to those events".


My reasoning was that the CIA could not adopt their
previous response concerning still classified hot-air
balloon test flights, i.e., "The CIA can neither confirm
nor deny the nonexistence of records responsive to your
request..." etc.

This was a stately separate, brief and straightforward
FOIA request, which should normally elicit a confirmation
that relevant documents had been located, or otherwise.
If affirmative, it would be telling, irrespective of any
decision about their availability.

In short, an unconnected and typical 'UFO' FOIA request -
do you have anything on record about this...?


Yet, despite affirming "no implied association with any
classified CIA projects", the CIA evidently take a
different view, now declaring:

This acknowledges receipt of your 28 October 2003 letter
requesting records under the provisions of the Freedom of
Information Act (FOIA). Specifically, your request is for
information or records pertaining to "those events" which
you describe in the first and second paragraphs of your
letter. You write about Lonnie Zamora, a police officer
in Socorro, New Mexico, who on 24 April 1964 allegedly
"encountered a puzzling white, oval-shaped, aerial
vehicle".

We note that on 10 September 2003 you appealed the
response to your 29 April 2003 FOIA request, reference
number [deleted]. Please be advised that the subject of
your appeal encompasses the subject of this 28 October
2003 request; therefore, we are cancelling this request.
[END]


Their letter is dated Monday, 19 November.

Presumably before writing, someone within the CIA was
actually aware that previously unrevealed CIA 'cold war'
exercises had just been publicly disclosed in the 'El
Defensor Chieftain', two days beforehand.

As the article did reference ongoing FOIA dialogue, was
its publication duly highlighted internally and noted
within the CIA's corresponding FOIA case file.

Once again, the CIA decline an opportunity to make known
they hold no related documents, instead officially
closing down that afforded avenue.

Surely it has been understood why the additional FOIA
request was to be regarded as independent - I couldn't
have made the point much more emphatically!


It will be interesting to see how the CIA now contend
with seemingly paradoxical responses to an appeal against
their 'no comment' disposition, whilst a more wide-
ranging FOIA 'UFO' enquiry is upheld as 'encompassed'
therein.


James.

The main idea was that the "UFO" could be an invading aircraft, either
in disguise, or seen under unusual conditions. The entire concentration
was on Soviet invasion, not space aliens. You have to remember that
civilian spotters were hired in many areas to watch for invading
aircraft during the period of the Robertson report. Note that only a
few reports were from spotters (the Fargo ND and Rapid City SD cases
stand out here) and most of them were moving lights.

There was a difference between debunking the UFO reports of the space
alien type, and responding to the UFO reports of the invading aircraft
type. Remember that Adamski, Fry, Menger, and others were plying their
trades to collect (as Ruppelt put it) "Disc shaped dollars" at that
time, and collecting hordes of "believers" in the process. THESE were
what military debunkers were up against at the time.

My uncle was in the Air Force and stationed at Wright Patterson at that
time. When I asked him about UFOs long after he had been discharged, he
also told me that the main reason for collecting UFO reports was to
detect Soviet invasion, not to solve what people saw in the sky. Once
the report was immediately determined to not be invading aircraft, it
was turned over to Blue Book for analysis of not only what the UFO was,
but of how conventional objects are misperceived.

This interpretation of the JANAP 146/CIRVIS regime is arguable, but not
wholly convincing because it conflicts with the clear priority of the
Robertson recommendations to *reduce the number of UFO reports* by the
armed services and *reduce the emphasis on UFOs* in the military and the
public mind - as you rightly point out. Specifically encouraging reports
of "unidentified flying objects" in the instructions for electronic
flash-reporting of "vital intelligence sightings" that went out to the
military in 1954 under CIRVIS (and later to civilian operators too)
would have been directly counterproductive from the Panel's point of
view. I think it's plausible from historical evidence that the
'official' response to UFO reports at this time was more complicated,
more ambiguous than you suggest. (**there was a helpful little drawing
of a 'flying saucer' and a buck-rogers-type rocket on one 1950's US
Navy MERINT radiotelegraph instructions poster I've seen, but I don't
know the exact date)

Subject: [UFORL] History Channel Fiasco
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

I watched the History Channel UFO shows: "UFO HOT SPOTS" and "WHEN UFOS
ARRIVE". As usual, there was some truth scattered among the hokum.

Among the truth presented:

- "Once someone notices a UFO, then everyone starts looking for one."

- Most UFO hot spots have a single individual who is the focus of the
activity.

- The FEMA 1993 Firefighters Guide has a section on what to do if UFOs
arrive (but most of the material is based on ETH being true).

Among the hokum presented:

- Trying to link the reason for ET arrivals to favorite liberal
causes, such as nuclear testing, global warming, and rainforest
destruction.

- Sacred spots around the world attract UFOs (even the ones that have
been shown to be hoaxes).

- James Gilliland's "Power portals" and his Mt. Adams "UFO Sanctuary",
where people drum drums, shake shakers, play flutes, meditate, and
look for UFOs. Very scientific!

- The 1975 test of stealth technology and air base readiness is
represented as an alien test of our defenses.

- A UFO video was obviously a streetlight on a pole behind a tree which
was swaying in the wind. Another was obviously a car approaching in
desert heat with sun reflecting into the camera from its windshield.
And a third was a cluster of toy helium balloons released from some
public or promotional event.

- The idea that JANAP 146 and CIRVIS were written with extraterrestrial
invaders in mind: (The entire purpose of the regulation was to make
sure that all information on possible attacks (by Soviets and other
earthbound enemies) gets sent to the right place.

- The idea that the Robertson Panel wanted UFO reports suppressed to
hide the presence of extraterrestrials. The purpose of the debunking
was to suppress the cult activity surrounding UFOs, because the
sensationalizing of UFO reports was clogging security channels. The
possibility of an enemy starting a UFO flap to hide an invasion was
very real in 1953.

- The Brookings Institute report on what the public would do if aliens
landed was based largely on the 1938 "War of the Worlds" broadcast.
But part of the panic was caused by the time compression of events in
the broadcast (to fit the time allotted), and part by the newsflash
format of the fictional account. Their conclusion was largely proven
false by the events of 9/11/01, when real threats which were much worse
materialized, and 8/14/03, when hardly anyone was talking aliens.

- The idea that the mention of UFOs in the SALT-1 treaty refers to
alien spacecraft, instead of anything unidentified that might start a
nuclear war by seeming to be a missile (like the time our antimissile
RADAR first got an echo back from the moon).

size="2"><span class="postbody"><a
href="http://www.newsday.com/news/local/wire/ny-bc-nj--
jerseydevilhunts1129nov29,0,4910933.story?coll=ny-ap-regional-wire"
target="_blank">http://www.newsday.com/news/local/wire/ny-bc-nj--
jerseydevilhunts1129nov29,0,4910933.story?coll=ny-ap-regional-wire</a>
                           <br>
                           <br>
                              <span ><span ><span>Jersey Devil
Legend Continues To Fascinate in Pine Barrens</span></span></span> <br>
                              <br>
By KRISTA LARSON <br>
Associated Press Writer <br>
                              <br>
November 29, 2003, 8:38 AM EST <br>
                              <br>
                              <br>
PEMBERTON, N.J. -- As Russ Juelg guides groups through the Pine Barrens
by the light of the moon, he always instructs them to keep their eyes
up in the trees. They're watchful for a strange form crouching from a
tree limb or a pair of glowing eyes emerging from the shadows. <br>
                              <br>
The search for the legendary Jersey Devil may include plenty of
skeptics, but Juelg says curiosity still draws dozens of thrill-seekers
to southern New Jersey each month to go on "hunts." <br>
                              <br>
"Being out in the wilderness at night and hearing and seeing strange
things that you can't account for is kind of a thrill, and it kind of
puts you in touch with the mysterious side of nature," said Juelg, who
leads the outings for the Pinelands Preservation Alliance. <br>
                              <br>
The tale of the cloven-hoofed creature with the wings of a bat remains
one of the best known examples of a New Jersey legend, according to
Angus Kress Gillespie, a professor of American studies at Rutgers
University and director of the New Jersey Folk Festival. It's also
become a popular culture figure, even lending its name to the state's
professional hockey team. <br>
                              <br>
There are multiple versions of the tale familiar to most New Jersey
schoolchildren, but a popular version describes the creature as being
born to a woman named Mother Leeds, who already had 12 children and
cursed the baby. <br>
                              <br>
"It's a powerful story so it has a grip on our imagination," Gillespie
said. "It's been in oral circulation ever since 1735 so that's a pretty
hardy story." <br>
                              <br>
It's also a tale that's seen a resurgence in part because of two books
about it that were written by James F. McCloy and Ray Miller Jr. That
heightened interest in the Jersey Devil has drawn curious visitors and
hard-core investigative types alike into the woods. <br>
                              <br>
McCloy attributes some of its current popularity to New Jersey's
distinction as the most densely populated state in the country. <br>
                              <br>
"I think the legend's going to keep on going," he said. "It's been
around since 1735 and we're getting sightings all the way into the
present day. I think people want it to be there." <br>
                             <br>
The tale's roots in southern New Jersey culture also set it apart from
fearsome creatures in movies and popular culture, said Abbie Mylod, who
opened the Jersey Devil Cafe in Medford last year. <br>
                             <br>
"It's local townspeople who pass it around," she said. "Many people
have claimed to have seen the Jersey Devil out in the woods. It's
almost a pastime to search for the Jersey Devil. There's a lot of
things that people have said the Jersey Devil is responsible for and we
haven't been able to prove it otherwise." <br>
                             <br>
Still, Mylod comes across plenty of skeptics at her cafe, which serves
up Jersey Jabberwocky salads and Leeds BLT sandwiches, along with
Jersey Devil T-shirts and books. <br>
                             <br>
"People come in and say it's like our own little Loch Ness monster. I
guess it's hard unless you live here and you're with your peers as far
as people who believe." <br>
                             <br>
Some have truly turned the search for proof into a full-time interest. <br>
                             <br>
The Devil Hunters, started almost five years ago by Laura Leuter, now
has more than a dozen members who go out on weekends to locations of
reported sightings and do research _ complete with a night vision
camera and boom mike in tow. <br>
                             <br>
Leuter, 25, of Old Bridge, says she and her colleagues approach their
interest in a scientific way and are willing to accept that the legend
may be nothing more than a tale passed down through the generations. <br>
                             <br>
"We get people every once in a while who e-mail us and tell us, 'You
need to get a life, you need a job' and we're like whatever," concedes
Leuter, who works for a major financial institution. "What are you
doing on my Web site? If I'm the one who needs a life, why are you
looking up things you don't believe in?" <br>
                             <br>
The legend likely began by playing a rule in childrearing or by
discouraging outsiders, Gillespie said. <br>
                             <br>
"It's not too terribly helpful to get too hung up on whether or not the
Jersey Devil exists," he said. "

From: Martin Shough [mailto:mshough@parcellular.fsnet.co.uk]
Sent: Tuesday, December 02, 2003 4:23 PMSubject: Re: [UFORL] History Channel
Fiasco

I don't believe the emphasis here is correct. Whatever else one can say
about Robertson, the concern about overloading of the military detection
and reporting system was given a high priority. Of course defence
against the Soviets was the immediate issue. But it's precisely because
of the need to be able to instantly identify and respond to signs of
foreign aggression that such emphasis was laid on minimising the amount
of system noise from electronic and psychological phantoms, as I already
pointed out. The panel absolutely *did not* recommend increasing this
noise level by encouraging observers to report anything and everything
unidentified. They recommended educating personnel so as *not to
report*, and they recommended desensitizing the whole military
establishment to this issue for exactly the reasons you indicate. Their
concern was not just the mass of civilian reports but the mass of
military reports, which had become huge during 1952. Reports from Korea
were interfering with routine military channels. The radar phantom
problem was creating real front-line ambiguity with real costs in Air
Force man-hours and materiel. The panel wanted this *military*
excitability damped down. They would not have seen the act of including
"UFOs" under the flash-reporting CIRVIS regime as at all consistent with
that aim.

There's nothing very amazing about this when you consider the COMSEC and
COMINT concerns of the NSA being incubated at this time - especially
considering that Robertson himself was the first head of the NSA science
advisory committee, along with Alvarez and Berkner (and Menzel of
course). But it doesn't remove the inconsistency of the CIRVIS reporting
system . . . Unless, that is, one re-evaluates the presupposition that
Robertson should be taken at face value. And here I think you are
mistaken in assuming that the 'entire' issue was Soviet aircraft. The
documentary evidence is very strong that a lot of influential military
and intelligence people *were* concerned about UFOs per se at this time,
and it's certainly true that corralling the electronic reporting chain
under NSA authority as JANAP 146 effectively did would fit both its
intelligence collection and communications security remits quite nicely.


CIA scientists were convinced that there was something else going on,
they instigated their own external science review panel, then pressed
in-house for a National Intelligence Estimate and forcefully urged a
major intelligence and research programmes on the government via Bedell
Smith and the 'cardinals', who dragged the issue through the IAC to
within an inch of the national security council. The CIA had discussed
some aspects of implementation with other bodies, including ADC. They
had a draft NSC memorandum of authority ready to go. At this point
Robertson enters the frame, in effect tells the CIA and the Air Force
not to be so silly and silence reigns. Did anyone ever wonder why the
CIA's *internal memos* from Feb 1953 contain not one whisper (that I
know of) of demurral or even faint embarrassment about this fiasco? Top
CIA scientists don't urge expensive 'community wide' intelligence and
R&D programmes on government whimsically. No, there were clearly some
convinced and quite worried people before January 1953. I find it very
interesting that not one secret in-house memo from the time mentions
regrets, dissensions, justifications, sackings - not even a mild ragging
about any of it.

Werner,

I'm not aware of Geller having photographed a 'UFO',
although he does - no surprise - have an interest in the
subject.

There was an article published by 'The Idler' magazine in
its summer 2000 issue. Entitled, 'Uri Geller Solves
History's Greatest Mysteries', he expounds on the true

caused spooked drivers to bump their cars.</font></p>

    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">Several
people reported seeing a huge silver object in the area as they drove
past at around 8.45am last Wednesday.</font></p>

    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">Drivers
were so distracted by the bizarre sighting that at least two minor
bumps were reported, as the attention of motorists wandered from the
more mundane forms of transport before them on the road.</font></p>
    <font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2"> </font>
    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">A
local woman, who did not wish to be named, contacted the News to
describe the experience of a friend who was driving towards the retail
park at that time.</font></p>
    <font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2"> </font>
    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">She
said: "My friend saw something hovering, which was silver in appearance
and looked like the dishes you see on the side of television
transmitters.</font></p>
    <font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2"> </font>
    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">"It
was huge, and it was pulsating - he wasn't the only one who saw it, as
you couldn't have missed it.</font></p>

    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">"He
saw it and just thought: 'Good God', and was really quite shaken by the
whole thing.</font></p>

    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">"Then
the object just suddenly disappeared - it was so strange.</font></p>
    <font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2"> </font>
    <p class="headtypea"><font face="Arial,sans-serif" size="2">"My
friend thinks the accidents at Kingsgate were a result of other people

it disappeared in the intense blue sky. We even had time to take our
field glasses and saw quite distinctly an oval form with shiny surface,

"Enrico Fermi's famous question, now central to debates
about the prevalence of extraterrestrial civilizations,

of 1950. Fermi's companions on that day have provided
accounts of the incident".

saucers might be due to extraterrestrial people (here I

An interesting early snapshot, albeit as remembered many

The number of UFORL subscribers has risen steadily in
recent months.

A number of submissions from new subscribers have been
outwith the list remit and consequently not posted.
Unfortunately, I no longer have time to address each of

was unsuited to UFORL.

The list is statedly, "open to subscription from those
who advocate and adopt a consistent, scientific appraisal
of purported 'UFO' related evidence".

It is not an apt forum for zealous 'believers'.

Contributions from self-proclaimed 'contactees',
'abductees', or anyone reasonably taking issue with
content from a previous posting and then bemoaning that
the list has many subscribers who adopt a more skeptical
approach, will simply not be authorised.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@jeaston.com>
Date: Sat, 6 Dec 2003 21:54:00 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Socorro
X-Spam-Checker-Version: SpamAssassin 2.55 (1.174.2.19-2003-05-19-exp)

I haven't mentioned the following previously and it might be of
interest.

Some time ago, I wrote to Dr. Frank Etscorn:

[BEGIN LETTER]
I wonder if you might please assist with some research and
clarify the following, which originates from 'Kestrel's Nest -- A
weblog by Eric Wagoner' - see:

http://www.ericwagoner.com/weblog/archives/2000_08_20_archive.htm
l

[this URL will 'wrap around']

Monday, August 21, 2000

New dad Mike Gunderloy at Larkfarm pointed to UFO netzine Saucer
Smear. Lo and behold, the current feature story is new
developments in the famed Socorro, New Mexico UFO landing.

Physics professor emeritus Charles Moore, the man behind the
Project Mogul balloon flights that almost certainly led to the
Roswell hulabaloo, suggests that the Socorro sighting may have
been a lunar lander flight test that went off course from the
White Sands Missile Range, south of Socorro.

Regular readers of Kestrel's Nest know that I went to school in
Socorro, and ended up staying in town for eight years. I've met
Lonnie Zamora and have seen the area where the sighting occurred.

For much of the time I was in school, psychology professor Dr.
Frank Etscorn, inventor of the nicotine patch and all around
really smart guy, was dean of the school. He was fond of telling
the story behind the sighting. I don't recall all the details,
but his story involved a couple of students (Tech students are
notorious pranksters), back projection, and making "eep eep"
noises while wearing strange coveralls. He giggled when telling
how these students managed to fool not just Officer Zamora but
also a horde of UFO experts.
[END]


Can you perhaps help to solve the mystery of this 'UFO hoax'
story.
[END OF LETTER]


Dr. Etscorn kindly replied:

The stories I told were pretty much the stock stories that had
been going around campus for years regarding Tech student
involvement in the incident. I bet most NMTech "old timers" would
agree that the whole thing had an air of "Tech Prank" -- the
students were as you mentioned notorious (and, I would hope,
still are!). I did have a student in my Paranormal Borderlands of
Science class do some research regarding the story depicted in
"The Socorro Saucer in a Pentagon Pantry" book. Can't remember
her name. As I recall, she tracked down some Techies of that era
and talked to them and also found out that a rear projection
device had been removed/borrowed/checked-out etc. from some place
on campus.

Possibly another stock story. Funny how the story changes: I
don't ever recall relaying to students that the "people" were
wearing "strange coveralls" and making "eep eep" sounds. Maybe
that was just me -- I do originate from Kentucky.

I always thought, if the incident had been a student prank, that
they would have salted the ground where the purported saucer
landed with ground-up trinitite (available from White Sands -- as
well as school geology dept) and then mixed in with the sand on
the ground.

Do I think something from outer space landed there? Not in a
million years!

Do I think officer Zamora could have misperceived something more
mundane? -- yes -- he's human just like the rest of us. Test
aircraft from White Sands - greater than zero probability. Tech
student prank -- that really, really worked well -- same
probability, maybe more.

Take care
Frank Etscorn
[END OF REPLY]


Inventor of the Nicotine patch?

Evidently so and a somewhat Fortean tale. From:

http://www.wku.edu/news/releases/october/etscorn.html
"Dr. Frank Etscorn, the inventor of the nicotine patch and member
of Western Kentucky University's Hall of Distinguished Alumni,
will deliver the 21st L.Y. Lancaster Memorial Lecture Nov. 10.

[...]

Etscorn developed the concept of the nicotine patch after
accidentally spilling liquid nicotine on his arm. Although he was
a nonsmoker, Etscorn felt as if he had chain-smoked several
cigarettes. This prompted the idea that putting nicotine on the
skin could be an effective way to get the chemical into the
bloodstream and suppress smoking.

When the patch was perfected, he patented it and sold it to Ciba-
Geigy Pharmaceuticals. The patch earned Etscorn numerous honors
and was named one of the best products of 1992.

Etscorn received a bachelor's degree in psychology from Western
in 1971 and a master's in experimental psychology in 1973. He
earned his doctorate in experimental psychology from George
Peabody College in Nashville.

After graduating from Peabody, he went to New Mexico Tech where
he was a professor of psychology and dean of students. He
received the school's distinguished teaching award in 1990.

Etscorn, who was inducted in Western's Hall of Distinguished
Alumni in 1993, retired from New Mexico Tech in 1993. He lives in
Wyoming with his wife, Sheri.
[END]


Incidentally, although a professor of psychology, Dr. Etscorn
does have an association with space science; from:

http://www.nmt.edu/~astro/eco.html

"The Frank T. Etscorn Campus Observatory, dedicated 25 April
1993, is on the campus of New Mexico Tech in Socorro, NM".

Dr. Etscorn is a noted amateur astronomer and was for many years
a stated "advisor" to the 'New Mexico Tech Astronomy Club'.

[BEGIN]
6 December, 2003

"REPORTS THAT say something hasn't happened are
interesting to me, because as we know, there are known

Professional Skeptics Group Proves UFOs Real!

Organization expected to retract defamatory claims,
facilitate $1,000,000 award to Swiss man

by Michael Horn

LOS ANGELES - It was only a matter of time before a
breakthrough in authenticating the existence of non-
terrestrial UFOs would take place but, surely, nobody
thought it would come about this way. Despite mounting
evidence over the past half-century the arbiters and
manipulators of public opinion in media, governmental and
scientific circles, along with professional skeptics and
debunkers, have marginalized serious discussion of UFOs
and dismissed all evidence as inconclusive and flawed.


Defamatory Claims?

A special target, at the top of the hit list for skeptics
and debunkers for more than 25 years, are the claimed
contacts of a Swiss man, Billy Meier. Meier, who claimed
that his contacts with extraterrestrial human began in
1942, when he was five years old, also says that they
continue to this day, more than 60 years later. But the
skeptics, in labelling Meier and his evidence as
fraudulent, claim that he hoaxed his 35mm photos and 8mm
film segments of the UFOs during the mid-1970s using
models or some unidentified form of special effects
wizardry to accomplish the alleged deception.
Professional skeptics, such as the international
organization CFI, magician/skeptic The "Amazing" Randi
and science writer/skeptic Michael Shermer, have long
been in the forefront of those accusing Meier of hoaxing
his physical evidence, which also includes video and
sound recordings, as well as metal alloy samples.

Meier's supporters state that these claims run counter to
the results of scientific examination of Meier's evidence
by experts from JPL, IBM, USGS and Nippon TV, as well as
special effects expert Wally Gentleman, known for his
work on Stanley Kubrick's "2001", among many films. They
also claim that all of Meier's physical evidence remains
irreproducible even with today's technology.


The Challenge

In order to definitively resolve the matter, in early
February 2001, a number of Meier's more than 1200 photos
and eight film segments were presented for examination to
case investigator Vaughn Rees of CFI West, the Los
Angeles branch of CFI. Mr. Rees concluded that, in his
expert opinion, they were all "easily duplicated hoaxes"
and that the two lights seen flashing alternately from
two different parts of the UFO in the film (Hasenbol,
March 18, 1976 at:

www.figu.org/us/ufology/videos.htm

were accomplished simply by Meier's scratching the film
with a pin.

Mr. Rees agreed to back up his claims by duplicating one
of Meier's UFO photos along with the film segment, which
should be the easiest to duplicate because it was the
only one of Meier's that had no other objects in it to
compare to the UFO. Mr. Rees stated that he already had a
35mm photo camera and knew where to acquire an 8mm movie
camera. His work wasn't required to be exact to the last
detail, just convincingly comparable in quality to
Meier's.

Over the next two months Mr. Rees failed to submit
anything to back up his claims and, in May of 2001, it
was suggested that he could try using any high-tech
equipment available to him, i.e. computers, special
effects, Photo Shop, etc., to fulfil his commitment. It
was also suggested that, if he wished to be sporting
about it, he should use only one hand since Meier is a
one-armed man.


The Results

Two years later, at a UFO conference in February of 2003,
Mr. Rees was confronted about his failure to meet the
challenge. He responded that he still didn't have access
to a photo-processing lab, which Meier himself never had
access to, having sent all of his films off to a local
shop for developing. Mr. Rees was reminded that he could,
and perhaps had already tried to, use any high-tech means
at his disposal instead. In a comparable two-year period
Mr. Meier had, with one hand, produced hundreds of
photos, while the able-bodied, technology-savvy Mr. Rees
had produced none.

Now, about three-years have passed and Mr. Rees has still
failed to provide even one photo or film to back up his
claims. In a three-year period of time Meier had taken
nearly 1,000 photographs and, in about one year's time,
he took at least one- half dozen of his 8mm films, and he
did all of this using only one hand! A comparable number
and quality of such types of films for an individual
special effects person during the mid-1970s (and maybe
any other time period) would be quite respectable, though
an Internet search will reveal that no such cinematic
accomplishments, professional or otherwise, exist.

This may be the first, and most important, time in
history that skeptics have set out to disprove a presumed
hoax and ended up proving its authenticity. And, in this
case, what they proved is undoubtedly the factuality of
the most important event in human history, the existence
of, and contact with, extraterrestrials.


What Integrity Demands

The professional skeptics of the Meier case have
concocted all sorts of fanciful notions and theories as
to how he hoaxed the evidence. But when challenged to
prove their claims they repeatedly replied that it was
not their job to attempt to duplicate the evidence,
although conducting themselves according to the
scientific method would require it. Their time for
freely, and irresponsibly, attacking Meier ran out when
Mr. Rees and CFI West utterly and completely failed to
meet the challenge they had finally accepted. In so
doing, they effectively proved Meier's UFOs real and
their own claims unsubstantiated and defamatory.


Unequivocal public retractions and apologies are now due
Meier from CFI West, Vaughn Rees, Randi, Michael Shermer,
etc. They have indulged in character assassination,
slander and libel, and the sloppiest, least scientific
thinking imaginable. It is now absolutely incumbent upon
any and all of the skeptics who have offered money for
proof of "paranormal" phenomenon, to offer it to Meier
and his non-profit organization in Switzerland, FIGU.

Specifically, the offer by Randi of $1,000,000 for proof
of a paranormal ability has been more than satisfied and
must be paid.

Integrity demands that they now live up to their word.
There can be absolutely no argument, dispute or doubt
now, especially considering the abysmal, failed attempts
by the skeptical accusers themselves, with any tools at
their disposal, to debunk, let alone duplicate, Meier's
stunning proof. Now it's time to recognize that the most
important event in human history has occurred and to
discover what meaning it holds for us.


Addendum

While the skeptics have offered an unexpected
contribution to authenticating what have come to be known
as the Meier Contacts, it's really only the tip of a very
deep and solid iceberg of irrefutable proof far beyond a
reasonable doubt.


Noted Astronomer Corroborates Additional Evidence

In April of 2003, Dr. Joseph Veverka, Chairman of the
Astronomy Department at Cornell University, was presented
with documentation of specific information on Jupiter,
its rings and its moons, published by Meier in October,
1978, five months before the Voyager probe photographed
and relayed the information back to Earth. When shown the
evidence that Meier described the moon Io as being the
most volcanically active body in the solar system, prior
to the first official knowledge of it in March of 1979,
Dr. Veverka was direct and candid, "If he said that 3-5
months before, then all that I can say is that he's
right."
Meier also documented the fact that Jupiter had rings;
described the chemical composition of the planet's
surface, the coloration of it's moons, Io's smooth
surface and Europa being encrusted in ice. But far more
amazingly, Meier accurately described both the
composition and the source of Jupiter's rings 20 years
before scientists from Cornell announced their findings,
in 1998!


Prophetically Accurate Information

In February of 1995, Meier published a lengthy document
of enormous complexity in which he foretold the
likelihood of certain specific future events. In
September 2001, portions of that information were
included in the book "And Yet They Fly!" written by Guido
Moosbrugger, an Austrian former schoolteacher and
principle acquainted with Meier for about 25 years.

The following seven items, foretold on pages 347 and 348
of "And Yet They Fly!" have recently occurred and
virtually in the sequence Meier foretold:

1. The strike or attack by the US and its president
(Iraq). Meier even used the word "stun" when he said the
strike would "...stun the entire world..." "Stun" is a
synonym for the term "shock" used by the US as in "shock
and awe".

2. Meier correctly predicted the following upsurge in
unrest and violence from Islamic fundamentalists.

3. Meier foretold the spread of AIDS, which has indeed
become very widespread.

4. Mad Cow Disease has since spread to other animals and
humans as Meier also predicted.

5. Meier said that a new disease and epidemic would then
appear and SARS did just that.

6. His warning regarding a renewed threat of chemical
warfare is more in the news than ever.

7. Meier specifically warned of the possibility of an
accident, one that he said could be avoided, however, at
the nuclear power plant near Lyon, France. The emergency
scenario, and the timely shut down of that exact plant,
occurred on August 12, 2003.

Now, in case the astronomically high odds against any
kind of coincidences or lucky guesses aren't apparent,
consider that Meier identified the following eight years
in advance:

1. The exact country and leader (out of hundreds) that
would launch a stunning attack and a synonym for the term
actually used by that country's leader (impossible to
calculate).

2. The exact religious group (out of thousands) that
would respond with their own attacks.

3. The exact disease (out of thousands) that would spread
widely among humans.

4. The exact animal disease (out of thousands) that would
spread to other animals and humans.

5. The sudden appearance of a new disease and epidemic.

6. The exact kind of weapons and warfare that would cause
renewed threats.

7. The exact location (out of 436) and type of facility
(out of several) that would have a near-accident.

If this doesn't qualify as a genuine demonstration of
psychic or paranormal abilities nothing does.

And it far exceeds any reasonable requirements to garner
the financial award promised for such a demonstration,
though that never has been the purpose of Meier's
mission. It is only fitting, however, that those who have
long accused him of being a hoaxer out for non-existent,
and unproven, financial gain, should now have the
opportunity to reward him, not only for his abilities,
but also for suffering the fools and their defamation for
so long.

For those who may be unaware, in addition to character
assassination, Meier has survived 19 (documented) actual
assassination attempts.


The Sound Recordings

Finally, the skeptics (and others who've actually tried)
have also been unable to reproduce the sound recordings
Meier made of a UFO, using only a cassette tape recorder,
in an open field in front of 15 witnesses. There are 32
simultaneous frequencies occurring, 24 in the audible and
eight in the inaudible range. To date, they remain
irreproducible even with state-of-the-art synthesizers,
let alone with cassette machines outdoors.

You can hear, and download, a three-minute sample of the
sounds at: and experiment with them yourself. You will
also find more documentation on the Meier Contacts at
this website.


The Most Important Event In Human History

Now that the authenticity of the Meier Contacts have been
firmly established, we can begin to examine the
information, and the real purpose, behind the most
important event in human history.

Hint: It has to do with our future survival.


Michael Horn is the American Media Representative for The
Meier Contacts and has researched the case for 25 years.
He can be contacted at: michael@andyettheyfly.com
[END]
